en: We pay homage to that Bhavānī, who is skilled in removing the afflictions of worldly existence,
who is Śāradā, and whose lion-throne is as white as the autumnal clouds.
Independent of the words of a teacher, it correctly shatters all knots; it reveals the supreme secret; may its own power of discernment be victorious! Now begins the sequence of salutations.
Salutation to the peaceful radiance, whose form is infinite pure consciousness alone, unconditioned by space, time, and the like, and for whom self-experience is the sole means of knowledge.
O Lord of the Earth, in the performance of the acts of creation and dissolution for the sake of the world’s welfare,
you exert yourself with effort, awakening and full of grace.
Salutations to that Supreme Lord, for whose single eyelashes the worlds are like a mere fraction.
Salutations to Viṣṇu, the showerer of light, the cause of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of the three worlds,
and the bridge for crossing over the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra.
Homage to the Lord of the three worlds, to Hari in the form of a lion, whose feet are sprinkled with the radiance of the crest-jewels of gods and asuras.
Salutations to that Varāha, the bearer of the earth, who effortlessly lifted up the world; for him,
Mount Meru, situated between his hooves, appeared as small as a mere hoof-print.
Homage to the Blessed One, who is kissed by the moon upon his lofty head,
whose movement is like a fly-whisk, and who is the foundational pillar for the construction of the city of the three worlds.
Salutations to that Lord of the Gaṇas, who is worshipped even by the gods for the sake of accomplishing the intended goals of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Bāṇa,
and who cuts through all obstacles.
Homage to that God of Love, for whom women— with hips as graceful as elephants and full, elevated breasts— serve as the temple.
Homage to the one whose conduct is transcendent, who is named Ananta, the fashioner of all forms, who is expressed by all mantras, and the sole lord of the universe.
Oṃ. Salutation to the Supreme Being, whose singular form is the ultimate reality;
to the Source (Saṃbhava), who, by his own will, appears as the manifold diversity of unreal phenomena.
Homage to him who presides over the lotus-throne with its infinite stalks, which has the mountain ranges as its petals and the golden mountain Meru as its pericarp.
Salutations to that Supreme Greatness, which, like gold in its ornaments such as earrings, and like water in its various forms such as waves, remains both differentiated and non-differentiated.
Homage to the Supreme Lord, whose greatness transcends both speech and mind,
who is embodied as the three qualities, the eight qualities, the infinite qualities, and the quality-less.
Salutations to Śiva,
who is tranquil through the cessation of all afflictions, and who severs the bond of worldly existence that is difficult to break due to the knots of the three *guṇas*.

Salutations to that certain divine being, however he may have come into existence, for whom the very conjunction of all auspicious marks is the defining characteristic— [these verses belong to Paṇḍita Jagaddhara].

Homage to the one who has arisen as the very form of *saṃsāra*, yet who is free from *saṃsāra*— the sole cause of *saṃsāra* and the sole adversary of *saṃsāra*. He who is worthy of worship in whatever way, and he who is honored wherever he may be.
Whether it be he or even another, whoever that deity may be—to you, him, let there be homage!
Homage to the wondrous Sambhava, who transcends that dualistic state of existence consisting of being and non-being,
and abides in the third [state].
Salutation to some [deity] named Keśava, who possesses sovereignty sealed by the independent power of consciousness,
whose form is both unmanifest and manifest, and who exists as the embodiment of mantra.
Homage to the wondrous Sambhava, who is both near and very far, hidden and manifest to himself,
easy to attain yet exceedingly difficult to reach.
Homage to the Self, whose nature is the radiance of the entire expanse of the moving and unmoving world,
and whose secret is difficult to comprehend even for those endowed with yogic power.
Whether it be Viṣṇu, the destroyer of Tripura, or Brahmā, the lord of the gods; or the Sun, marked with the discus; or the Blessed Buddha; or a Siddha;
or one who is free from the arrows of passion, hatred, and delusion, and is intent upon compassion for sentient beings— [may he protect us].
Homage always to him who is endowed with all the multitudes of virtuous qualities.
This verse, composed according to the rules of poetics by the one named Kavi, was written by Svāmidatta for the sake of remembering him; it bears the title *Cakrapāṇijaya*.
Homage to him— whether he be Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, or the Jina— in whom the passions such as attachment, which are like clouds raining upon the sprouts of the seed of existence, have come to an end.
Hemacārya [composed this] for Śrīkṛṣṇa, who bears a musk-paste tilaka upon the surface of his forehead, the Kaustubha gem upon the region of his chest,
a fresh pearl at the tip of his nose, a flute in the palm of his hand, and a bracelet upon his wrist.
Wearing pure yellow sandalwood paste on all his limbs and a string of pearls around his neck,
the crown jewel of cowherds shines forth, surrounded by women.

May the body of the Self-born (Brahmā), whose bodily hair quivers with the joy of composing charming works, protect you— his voice appearing as if mingled with the thick filaments emerging from contact with the lotuses of the uninterrupted quarters.
May the tree-like arms of Ānandavardhana protect you— arms radiant with the beautiful vine-patterns reflected on his cheeks, providing dense shade for the sun and yielding great fruit.

May the goddess Earth, who assumes the form of an image, who steals the luster of the crescent moon, and who is the lamp in the subterranean abode of the Great Boar, protect you. May she, the daughter of Hari, protect you.
May that Kṛṣṇa,
who is preeminent in valor, having descended to the Yamunā— a river whose waters tame the pride of the serpent Madaya—
bring me joy; he who is devoted to surpassing even the immortals in his splendor.
May He who bestowed the nectar of the *Bhāgavata* protect you—
He at the sight of whose remaining eyes, though colored by collyrium of the same hue as those [slain] and endowed with loveliness,
the demons themselves tremble, even before His own lovely lotus-like eyes.
May the body of Viṣṇu, who as a cowherd boy took the form of Cāṇūra, protect you— his body adorned with the severed fragments of the staff-like arms of Cāṇūra.

May the smile of Hari protect you— He whose mind was humbled by hearing the praises of all the cowherds at the lifting of Govardhana, and who, remembering that feat, displayed tusks as bright as the crescent moon while lifting the earth in his boar-incarnation form.

May the words of Madhuripu— words uttered with repeated intensity to cease his activity of summoning gods and asuras— protect the world; words whose syllables are tender like the sprouts of smiles shining from within a flood of fresh nectar churned by the power of his majesty, and whose skin is thrilled with joy and longing.

May the breaths of the Blessed One, whose form is that of the Boar, protect you— those breaths which, by following the rhythmic movement of the moments of his refinement, cause the ocean’s coming and going to proceed tirelessly as if it were the ebb and flow of the tides, and which even today do not cease their labor.
These breaths are like the moonlight from the peak of Mount Mandara when it was being whirled by the churning rod of the Lord’s curved tusks, causing the ocean to remain ever awake.
As he drinks from one breast while his eyes are slightly narrowed,
and wipes the other breast with his hand as fresh drops of milk flow from it,
the smile upon his face as his chin is caressed by a single finger of his mother— [this is enough].
May the luster of his teeth protect you, falling like a row of pearls from a golden vessel.
O Hari, while these two of yours play with their maces upon the sands of the Yamunā’s bed, drink the water from Karburikā’s mouth; thus shall your crest-lock grow.
May Hari protect you— he who, having heard the words of Yaśodā, was delighted as he touched his own crest while drinking milk out of childishness and intent on deception.

Ānanda, [the earth] was long made joyful by Yaśodā and the cowherd women; it was filled with apprehension by the enemy of Bala (Indra); it was strewn with flowers by the Siddhas; it was agitated by the inhabitants of the earth;
it was full of envy by the cowherd boys; it was full of compassion by the citizens; and it was full of smiles by the gods.
May that Madhupati, who was seen lifting up Govardhana, purify you once again.
"Mother, Kṛṣṇa has gone to play; he ate the clay by his own will.
"Kṛṣṇa, who said that? The wielder of the pestle [Yamunā] says it is true. "Mother, look! It is false.
"In 'Open your mouth,' when the mother had opened her mouth, the entire world—"
May that Keśava protect you—he at whose sight the world fell under the sway of wonder.
"What indeed is right for you to do now— to cast aside even me, your devoted one who dwells upon the region of your chest with undivided mind, and instead create thousands of other beloveds?
Having spoken thus, she regarded her own body as if it were the very hood of the serpent from which it had emerged.
May the smile of Lakṣmī, which interrupts the sleep of Hari, protect you.

O Hari, since you were awakened by the sidelong glances cast from the corners of the eyes of the Queen of Life— who was being entreated with a vision she herself had prepared— and who were moved to tears, why indeed is this reversal of the proper order? For it is you who ought to be consoled by me.
May the deer-marked one protect you with that cry of "O you who dwell in the forest! which was uttered by him out of shame.
Bowing low with devotion, her gaze full of longing, rivaling the blue lotus,
she was made an object of meditation by those devoted to samādhi for the sake of attaining their welfare;
she manifested the beauty of Lakṣmī and the grace of the two breasts, acting as a great treasury of loveliness.
Therefore, perform for yourselves either the eyes or the body of Hari, which remove the suffering of worldly existence.
By him, who had destroyed the Mind-born (Kāma), the body of Bali was formerly made to wear a woman;
he who cast off the coils of the serpent-king from his arms and held up the Gaṅgā;
and whose praiseworthy name the immortals call "Hara, the one with the moon on his head."
May Mādhava, who himself causes the destruction of the blinding darkness of sin, protect you at all times.

May the two eyes of Viṣṇu, which consist of the cool-rayed moon, protect you— eyes that, as they are slightly opened like the sky when clouds have ceased to sleep, surpass with their own luster the mass of jewel-lamps upon the heads of the lords of serpents.
O Lakṣmī, half of the lotus remains standing, while the other half succumbs to sleep.

To the Mallas [he said]: "He who is like the king of mountains (Sailendra), who is praised by gods and all people, who is the source of flowers and water for the courtesans, whose nature is primordial, who bears a thunderbolt in heaven, whose body is the universe, who is immeasurable,
who is enraged by Kaṃsa like Time itself, and who is the form meditated upon by yogis with eyes trembling in fear— [he has come]."
May Hari, who brings joy to the gods upon entering the arena, protect you.

May that [river] purify you— she whose millions of waves are made resonant by the wind of the sighs of the god of love as he shatters the hearts of women, and who has transferred her seven streams into the hollow of his stomach.
Then the conch shell quickly sounded with a roar even more terrible than the clashing of thunderbolts.
May that conch of Hari— white as a kumuda lily, a jasmine flower,
or a stalk of lotus, filling the sky of his palm like the full moon— [protect you],
by whose sound the playful wives of the enemies of the gods [are terrified].
Some have flabby hips.
He whose form, when beheld upon the battlefield by Hari,
caused a great surge of sorrow to spread on all sides,
[is that form] which contains within it the reflection of the sun situated in his eye.
May that speech shine forth, dispelling the wheel of the spokes of Māra.

May the noble discus of Hari accomplish our desired aims— that discus which is a torrent of thick blood and marrow gushing from the severed throat-pavement of the leader of the Daitya host as he was being uprooted.
It bore the splendor of a sky filled with the intense fire of a conflagration at the end of an eon.

Having contemplated that discus— which acts as a hatchet for felling the dense forest of the trees of rising evil, which possesses a stream of sharp, thick, and abundant iron shards, and which has emerged [from his hand]— he conceived a desire to devour the fleshly, well-flowing rays of the sun, the maker of day.
Even now Rāhu is deluded; may he, like the slayer of the Daityas, swiftly burn away all misdeeds.
The mountain peaks, which have become thick with mud from the streams of blood flowing through the crevices torn open in their skeletons of Daityas,
are adorned with the crescent moons upon their summits and possess the brilliance of the beaks of peacocks.
May the claws of the lion-bodied one protect you, like the thunderbolt of Indra.
Are these suns that have assumed their positions in the sky out of fear of the dissolution [of the world],
or are they masses of fire raised up to burn the three worlds? Thus did the hosts of immortals cry out in terror to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, as he bore the body of the Man-Lion.
O Subhūti, may my nails, reddened by the blood flowing from the mountain-like chests of the arrogant asuras that I have torn open, be victorious!
By him the earth-lotus was uprooted from the waters— its stem being the body of the Lord Śeṣa, hanging down from its base, with Mount Meru as its filaments and the vast horizons as its petals.
May that Boar protect you, like the tip of a lotus stalk.
How could the earth not be crushed by the trampling of the hooves of the steeds?
How could this mountain of gold not melt away from the flames of fire issuing from their mouths? And how could the seven oceans not be dried up by their breaths?
"May the Boar protect me"—thus he was surrounded by vast waves of anxiety.
O Madhava, the omnipresent Lord of the three worlds, why do you resort to begging?
Or rather, what has not already been created by you, the Creator of the universe; from where could anything else be given to you?

"O you who are the most excellent among the noble, incomparable to our kinsmen for the sake of liberation; having been entreated by the powerful one with unsurpassed eloquence, may Hari, who has been humbled, protect you! Subhūti 0056–4.
When the space in the region of the ear has vanished, when the light in the eyes has gone somewhere else,

when the wind has been consumed by a single breath, and when the ocean has been drunk up even to half its depth through the anus— then the arrow of Śārṅgapāṇi is sought within the cavity between a single hair at the edge of the nose.
May the majesty of the syllable *kra*, which has the earth as its unconstructed object, purify you.
Where are those proud lords of the quarters, intoxicated by the thick fragrance of their own pride?
O Meru, Mandara, Indra, Malaya, and Himavat, well done, you have truly fulfilled the duty of being mountains!
O Śeṣa, you are praiseworthy with your many heads, broad and capable of bearing the heavy burden of the world.
May the Boar, who upholds the earth and whose roar causes the stream of saṃsāra to tremble, protect you!
O Vāmana, may you be free from ailment; for the three worlds, reflected in your Kaustubha gem, have become as if gazing with curiosity at you from within your belly.
While you remain as the sole essence of life, we behold the quintessence of the entire world.
O Śyāma, the eye of one who possesses little merit does not rest upon this form of yours;
for whom else, other than you, could there be such exceedingly vast delight? Indeed, your very sight is nectar.
While being thus addressed by the Daityas and even by the sages, Hari assumed the form of a woman.
With his back struck by the torrents falling from great revolving mountains,
he slept a deep sleep, finding the pleasure of scratching his itchy skin;
with a long, rattling, and terrible roar, he slumbered on.
May that Kamaṭha protect you—he who made the ocean his own by overwhelming it.
May he, whose matted locks are adorned with the crescent moon, arise for the victory of living beings—
he upon whom even today the Gaṅgā creates the illusion of a single grey hair.
May he protect you, upon whose mass of matted hair sits Śaśāṅka, white as a radiant pearl necklace,
like a stalk amidst a cluster of blue lotuses.
While falling asleep, he was like a swan in autumn.
May he who is adorned with cool rays [the moon] bring you auspiciousness—
he whose head is like a lotus stalk, upon which the pure crescent moon shines like a swan with wings of shimmering waves.
A stream of blood, resembling the celestial river, fell down.

May he whose crest-jewel is the most excellent river of the gods (Gaṅgā), white as a pale cloud, shining brightly— [and] by whom [the world] is being dissolved by the heat of the blazing upward-glance— grant you prosperity.
Like a river of nectar flowing forth from the moon during the season of autumn.
Having slowly joined together the crescent moon fallen from her head and the bracelet broken during a moment of passion,
the Daughter of the Mountain, with a smiling face, said: "May that Śiva and she, the Mountain-born, protect you— whomsoever you behold."
And that Kriḍācandra had his body filled with rays of light from his teeth.
O Hara, who is this fair-limbed woman? Which one among them stands upon your head? What are the matted locks?
Why does the swan resort to the matted locks? It is not the moon; the moon resorts to the water.
This is a deluded ghost—where is there water here? The ghost is merely tossing about like a wave.
In this way, he who conceals the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā) would surely be a Śaṃkara.
Due to our preoccupation with the smiles exchanged during the pleasure of kissing the bimba-like lips of the lower lip,
this mutual gazing of faces has become difficult to obtain even from afar; thus,
our efforts to bring our single body together have been rendered futile.
May the Lord of the Snowy Mountains, whose smile is his wealth, protect you from this deception of affection!
“Mother, what is this that my father hides in his cupped hands?
My child, it yields sweet fruit; why does he not go to our home himself?
Thus addressed by her mother, he went home and, drawing her toward him, broke her evening salutation.
May the outburst of laughter of the Sambhu, which possesses the intense force of upholding the broken samādhi, protect you!
One half of his eye-lid throbbed from the recitation of prayers, while the other half trembled from anger;
one hand was placed upon his head to bow, while the other was raised to strike; one eye was closed in meditation, while the other was unable to look at the unbearable [sight].
May that beautiful form of his, which remains lovely even when equal to the end of twilight, protect you all.
May the curved lotus-stalks of the house— whose pair of breasts is occupied by the two sons of the Ocean King, and which are weary from the drinking of milk— remove your impurities.
May that unprecedented web of rays from the sun,
which bestows the desired objects, grant liberation from the bonds of existence to those who bow down and serve it.

May those rays of yours, which partake in the redness of their rising and bring about auspiciousness, bestow blessings upon you— those rays which act during the great festivals of the birth of the day in the first vault of the sky.
The cities of the quarters were like women whose faces were smeared with vermilion.
Whose foremost warriors— possessing the brilliance of the tips of raised sword-blades, with their chests and arms armored, adorned with garlands,
scarred, crushers of the hearts of enemies, and fierce—
cast aside their garments and revealed the full weight of their forms.
The deer-skin does not possess the beauty of the breasts of a beautiful woman.
Is he perhaps the Sun, yet not the Sun, for he possesses feet that drip with the essence of eternal nectar?
Or is he the Moon of the Night, yet not the Moon, for nowhere is his mark a spot?
Is he the Wish-Fulfilling Gem itself, yet his vast fruits are manifold? Whence could such exquisite delicacy possibly come?
May that form of the Sage, first beheld by those of deluded intellect out of doubt, protect us.
May the draws of the bow, which produce a twang mingled with the roar of the bowstring and which have long been the very essence of his affection for the enemy, protect you from foes.
In the lake of the head of the great Asura of the eastern quarter, he sported with his row of nails as lotus-stalks entwined with golden threads;
while the anklets on his feet, shimmering and moving with fierce grace,
tinkled melodiously.
Carrying the syllable *jhaṃ*, [he] bears the two lotus-feet.
She is gentle with a face full of compassion, wearing an elephant hide as her garment; she is terrified by the serpent yet filled with wonder at the moon dripping with nectar;
she is distressed in her longing to behold the son of Jahnu, while resting within the hollow of a skull.
May the glance of Pārvatī, affectionate at their first union, be for your welfare, O Śiva!
As she rose at the end of their dalliance, supporting the weight of the lord of serpents with one hand and holding her garment with the other,
her loosened tresses falling over her shoulders,
she was carried by Viṣṇu, whose love for amorous pleasure had been doubled by her beauty at that moment.
May that form, led by Śayyāmālā as she embraced him with her languidly shimmering arms, purify you through its splendor.

May he whose face is like that of the lordly elephant, and who, with his great trunk raised into the sky like a white lotus-stalk sprout rooted at its base, protects these three worlds— be victorious!
The lotus-like orb of the sun does not appear as blue.
When the serpent-king, his body contracting out of fear of the peacock of Kumāra— who was summoned by the sound of the drum struck with joy-filled hands by Ānanda—
entered the opening of his nostrils,
the world-systems were filled with the roar of the rows of Gaṇḍodīna bees as the wielder of the trident entered.
May the long, rhythmic shaking of the faces of Vaināyaka’s followers, accompanied by the sound of *siṭkāra*, protect you for a long time.

The bowstring is the garland of his quiver; the swarm of bees is the target, the frail woman; the mind is the object to be pierced; and these five senses, beginning with sound, are the arrows—he who possesses such power to conquer the three worlds, though he is bodiless.
May that Kāma, who dwells in the side-long glances of his beloved, grant you your desires.
Brahmā, Dakṣa, Kubera, Yama, Varuṇa, the Maruts, Vahni, Candra, Indra, Rudra;
the mountains, rivers, oceans, the hosts of planets, humans, Daityas, Gandharvas, and Nāgas;
the continents, the lunar mansions, the stars, the sun, the sages, the sky, the earth, and the two moons.
May that Blessed One of universal form, in whose body all [beings] are merged, protect you.

O charming girl, abandon your despondency here; the one who has conquered strength (Viṣṇu) trembles at the thought of being rejected by you. O lotus-eyed one, cultivate true affection and do not honor pride.
[This is] through the verbal artifice of Dhanvantari, who himself awakened Lakṣmī during the rite of her self-choice marriage (*svayaṃvara*).
May Hari protect you—he who, while negating anything else, prescribes [the reality] within the Self.
May Nṛhari, the sole hero of the world, grant happiness;
for when he was intent on crushing the sons of Diti in battle,
none were able even to look upon his face, which was agitated with wrath.
O Knower, you do not bow even before your own nails.
"Welcome! Hail to you, O worthy one! Speak, O Lord: what shall be given? The earth? "What measure [of land] do I require?
"Three paces. "It has been given; it has been accepted by me.
"Do not give it! said Uśanas. "Why? This is Hari. What recipient could be greater than him?"
May that Vāmana, who was indeed honored by Bali here at the commencement of the sacrifice, protect you.
O Discus, speak! O Lord, go forth! O Conch, command Hari! Victory!
O Nandaka, live on, O enemy of serpents! O Lord, has he been pierced by me?
Which demon is this? Who is Hiraṇyakaśipu? Speak the truth to you all.
May he who, when asked "By what weapon? replied "By my claws," protect you—Viṣṇu with his face turned toward the poison.
Alas! O you who possess the wheel of thought, the wheel of fear, the hunchbacked seat, and the lotus seat;

O you who hold the sharp-rayed jewel that would be lost were there even a slight suspicion; O you whose mind is wavering yet wise, who are pure, and who have brought an end to the Lord of Death (Kṛtānta).
May he, who caused distress to the assembly of the Kālakūṭaka and the Kavalikāra, protect you!
The eternal human condition, which has its sole authority in personal experience,
the abode of bliss, the unique seed and sprout of the world,
[is that] which [grasps] all directions, places, times, and measurements with its hands.
May the great light of the Great One grant us protection that is difficult to overcome.
In whom this world arises and dissolves, like a mass of clouds in the sky, like a multitude of ripples in a lake, or like nectar from the moon in its thousandfold radiance.
May that power of Śambhu lead to the increase of your prosperity.

He who performs the play of the arising, dissolution, and maintenance of the three worlds; he who, through his own action, assumes the state of being an enemy to Hari, Hara, and Druhiṇa; that God, the protector of all people, [is beyond] the reach of the mind.
May Śakti, the auspicious one, whose essence is the sound of bliss, grant us prosperity.
Indeed, this entire world,
which is dependent on the human body and its causes, attains skill in the arrangement of the manifold universe through his grace.
He is the protector of the three worlds, the sole great lord of the three realms.
The immeasurable Lord, whose majesty is unsurpassed, plays with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods as if with balls— He who is the consort of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain.
He is beloved, the destroyer of Kṛtānta, and he lightens the burden of the earth.
Liberation indeed is the supreme goal of man; those who possess inner knowledge encounter it as their sole objective. What more need be said? Let that very [liberation] be the moonlight of nectar.
His arms were adorned with the grace of the decorative ornaments upon the crests of his locks of hair.
The nakṣatras of Śrīkaṇṭha are Kṛttikā, Ārdrā,
Bharaṇī, Rohiṇī, Jyeṣṭhā, Bhadrapadā, Punarvasu, Citrā, Viśākhā, Aśleṣā,
Dhiṣṇyā (Śatabhiṣaj), Aditi (Pūrvabhādrapadā), Hasta, Mūla, Āṣāḍhā, and Maghā.
"It is indeed better to be endowed with outflows than to be like the Blessed One's Nakṣatrapālī."

The Lord is the protector of those who have become terrified, the master of both the sentient and the insentient, the destroyer of the suffering of the virtuous and the source of happiness for the wicked;
he is the benefactor of the devoted, the impartial toward both doers and non-doers,
and the divine ground upon which the three worlds— Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ— are fashioned for the enjoyment and liberation of his servants.
May Mṛdaṅka protect you—he who manifests the acts of emanation, maintenance, and reabsorption.
May Māra— who was led away by him so that the minds of self-restrained ascetics might not become enamored with Māra— protect you; he whose feet are honored by kings,
whose crown serves as a crest-jewel for the serpent king Ananta, and who adorns his body, white with ashes,
with the half-moon born of the ocean.
May he who possesses three eyes protect you—he who, like seven suns rising at once, shines with rays resembling molten gold.
From the palace of Candraāvalī, Rādhā went to the temple of Rādhāmohana.
Having heard her beloved’s words, “Rādhā, may there be well-being,” Candraāvalī said: “Well-being for whom?
From whom? My dear, your beloved Kaṃsa is enraged; where have you seen Kaṃsa?”
"Subhūti! Where?"—may that smile arising from the two of them, whose minds were filled with joy, protect you.
When the bow was drawn in battle, he placed his right hand [upon it].
"O, O right hand! While you were performing such tasks as eating and giving alms, it is improper for you to go [to the battlefield] afterwards.
To this, he replied once more: "I am not fleeing."
O Subhūti, quickly praise Rāghava; why do you not split apart the multitude of Rāvaṇa’s heads?
Has that Keśava been seen anywhere? He has gone off taking some woman from Vraja.
Indeed, we have all been deceived; he must be sought out by us!
Having cried out, "Go two by two," he suddenly seized Rādhā by the hand.
May Hari, who shares his dwelling with Gopī and has reached the bower-houses, protect you.
Mother: "I am not going to the banks of the Yamunā for the protection of the calves.
Why so, my child? Because the cowherd women are crushing [the butter] with their pair of full breasts. [The boy:
"Even though I was turned away many times by the knitting of her eyebrows, I spoke thus before her face."
May that Keśava protect you, his face sealed by the lotus-like hands of the cowherd girls.
At midday, you prostrate before the world and, with palms joined, you beg;
yet at night, shameless one, you carry a river upon your head—how shall I endure that? If Śrī emerged from the churning of the nectar, why did Hari swallow poison?
May Hara protect you—he who was told by Gaurī, "Do not touch me; do not desire women."

Now begins the section on *vakrokti* (indirect speech). "My dear, who are you? "I am Śūlinī. "Then seek out a physician. "My dear, I am Nīlakaṇṭha. "Then utter a single cry. "I am not Paśupati; I cannot be seen by the weapon. "Then [seek] poison. [She says: "I am not Viṣāṇinī. [He says: "Then seek out a mirror. [She says: "I am not a woman. [He says: "Then seek out a man. [She says: "I am not a man. [He says: "Then seek out a eunuch. [She says: "I am not a eunuch. [He says: "Then seek out a woman. [She says: "I am not a woman. [He says: "Then seek out a man. [She says: "I am not a man. [He says: "Then seek out a eunuch. [She says: "I am not a eunuch. [He says: "Then seek out a physician. [She says: "I am not a physician. [He says: "Then seek out a patient. [She says: "I am not a patient. [He says: "Then seek out a nurse. [She says: "I am not a nurse. [He says: "Then seek out a king. [She says: "I am not a king. [He says: "Then seek out a minister. [She says: "I am not a minister. [He says: "Then seek out a servant. [She says: "I am not a servant. [He says: "Then seek out a master. [She says: "I am not a master. [He says: "Then seek out a slave. [She says: "I am not a slave. [He says: "Then seek out a lord. [She says: "I am not a lord. [He says: "Then seek out a king. [She says: "I am not a king. [He says: "Then seek out a minister. [She says: "I am not a minister. [He says: "Then seek out a servant. [She says: "I am not a servant. [He says: "Then seek out a master. [She says: "I am not a master. [He says: "Then seek out a slave. [She says: "I am not a slave. [He says: "Then seek out a lord. [She says: "I am not a lord. [He says: "Then seek out a king. [She says: "I am not a king. [He says: "Then seek out a minister. [She says: "I am not a minister. [He says: "Then seek out a servant. [She says: "I am not a servant. [He says: "Then seek out a master. [She says: "I am not a master. [He says: "Then seek out a slave. [She says: "I am not a slave. [He says: "Then seek out a lord. [She says: "I am not a lord. [He says: "Then seek out a king. [She says: "I am not a king. [He says: "Then seek out a minister. [She says: "I am not a minister. [He says: "Then seek out a servant. [She says: "I am not a servant. [He says: "Then seek out a master. [She says: "I am not a master. [He says: "Then seek out a slave. [She says: "I am not a slave. [He says: "Then seek out a lord. [She says: "I am not a lord. [He says: "Then seek out a king. [She says: "I am not a king. [He says: "Then seek out a minister. [She says: "I am not a minister. [He says: "Then seek out a servant. [She says: "I am not a servant. [He says: "Then seek out a master. [She says: "I am not a master. [He says: "Then seek out a slave. [She says: "I am not a slave. [He says: "Then seek out a lord. [She says: "I am not a lord. [He says: "Then seek out a king. [She says: "I am not a king. [He says: "Then seek out a minister.

"I am not a minister. [He says: "Then seek out a
"O deluded one, how can that Lord of Life move about as a stationary pillar? May the Moon-crested Lord, who spoke these words to Śivā when she said, "I must go," protect you.
"Who is this at the door? Hari has arrived at the grove. "What is it here, O Sakhāmṛga?
"I am Kṛṣṇa, my dear; I am very much afraid of a black monkey.
"O innocent one, I am Madhusūdana. Drink that very creeper, my friend! "Then [I shall drink] that very [creeper], my friend!"
May Hari, who was thus rendered speechless by his beloved and carried off, protect you.
O shameless Hari, why do you wander about perpetually overcome by intoxication? O charming one, what is so surprising in this—that intoxication arises from contact with you?
Subhūti said: "I declare that your affection for women is excessive. Why do you prattle such nonsense? For whom is there love for enemies?"
Why do you thus delude me? I speak of attachment to you;
how could there be no attachment toward one's elder brother, Rāma?
Why do you thus delude me? "I grieve for your calamity alone.
Tell me, when you are angry without cause, what small calamity could there possibly be?
May that son of Sūri protect you— he who, having surpassed the cowherd’s wife with these crooked words,
embraced her whose heavy breasts were bunched together.
O Pārvatī, be gracious! Even Śiva has prostrated at your feet. How can you call him "Śiva" (the Auspicious One) when he is covered with the bloody hide of an elephant?
"If you say 'Śiva' and I become twice as red, I shall become a pillar;
if this is true in your mind, then you are indeed a pillar, for there is nothing at all in your heart."
O proud woman, abandon your anger and recognize me as the Lord worshipped by the three worlds.
O Three-Eyed One, if you are the Lord, why are you naked and covered in dust?
"Now, what will you say to this? O Pāṇḍurakapola, I am a paśupati.
Since you do not take account of what is proper or improper, you are indeed a paśupati yourself."
O deluded one, why do you wander thus? Know me to be this very Truth.
You are indeed that Truth, O rogue, by which you possess such exceedingly diverse forms.
O wise one, if you say that Tryambaka is known here in this world, then you do not even speak of his mother; how much less, then, could there be three?
Know this: I am indeed Anangadāhana (the burner of the bodiless one), and here I have a great dispute with you; for by such deeds as these, every limb of mine has been consumed by you.
May he who, having conquered the faults of twilight, intoxication, and pride, is impetuously embraced by Pārvatī with her breast, take away all misfortune.
"O Bhavānī, let there be no affection for me from you as you have declared;
O Goddess, from where has this desire for affectionlessness arisen in you?"
Enough with these foul-smelling corpses! Why do you stand over the river?
What is this garland of hell-guardians on my head? Take them away!
Like one who is infatuated with a person, you cause distress by acting falsely;
the rows of hell-wardens will surely stand over you.
"Why are you angry? Abandon your resentment and cease this dispute with me;
for a conflict with you will never bring us any ruin."
May that Śiva bring you auspiciousness— he who, having humored Gaurī with words of consolation during her quarrel with the Gaṅgā, silenced her with unsurpassed speech and then led her away.
"In victory, I am skilled at dice, but I am not able to play with this three-eyed one. I am skilled at victory, but this pair of eyes does not exist on his hand."
What is the use of this gamble for me? If Gaṇapati is not pleasing to you, who would feel aversion toward him? Do you not know that he is beloved by women?
Why are you not ashamed to play with one who is devoid of wealth?
Why do you look upon those before you as if they were gods and demons deprived of their riches?
"Without the eclipse of the moon, I find no pleasure; why do you act thus?
If this is pleasing to the Queen, Nandin, summon Rāhu!"
O Rāhu, who would feel pleasure in the presence of the white-toothed one (the Moon) appearing in a terrifying form?
If you do not desire it, then abandon this necklace right now.
O fool, why do you falsely claim that I am not aware of your body?
Having remained for a divine thousand years, it is appropriate to speak thus.
May Bhavānī protect you— she whose sidelong glances are playful with the curved expressions of her eyes,
which tremble with the lashes of her laughter.
O innocent one, is this Madhava [Kṛṣṇa] striking the temple with his finger? Is it Spring?
No, he does not have a discus; is he a potter? No, he is not the bearer of the earth; is he the king of beasts? No, he has two tongues.
O charming girl, is he the terrible winter? No, he is not the lord of birds; is he the king of monkeys? No, he is Hari.
Thus, by Lakṣmī, he has been rendered one whose words are thwarted; we are those whose splendor has been struck down.
“O beloved, why this exhaustion? Do you not know that the solar disc is renowned throughout the world?
You must not be angry; we have never seen a water-dweller above [the surface].”
Anger is fit to be abandoned by one in whom thirst does not arise; O proud woman, abandon your pride—what is the use of this pride toward me now?
Of what use indeed is that poetry for one who,
being crushed by it, does not experience a succession of aesthetic flavors (rasa), just as the ocean [does not overflow] with streams of nectar?
Of what use is the poetry of that poet, or the bow of that archer,
if it does not cause the head of the enemy, fixed upon his heart, to whirl?
Some poets, like children, have many words but lack confident expression; their compositions are causes for aversion toward their mothers.
What poetry is there now that, drenched by its cascades of aesthetic flavor,
would not cause even the dull-witted to sprout within?

A novel theme, a birth not of common origin, smoothness, lack of harshness, clarity, and aesthetic flavor; as well as a composition with a striking arrangement of syllables—all these difficult elements combined in one place [constitute excellence].
A person who is heartless can produce poetry merely with his mouth,
just as Rāhu casts a dark shadow upon the moon, the lord of the stars.
Buddhas are seized by envy, those of power are scorched by pride, and others are struck down by ignorance; thus, O old man, my well-spoken words have gone to waste.
Indeed, the wicked lack the ability to compose even two lines;
nevertheless, they remain unperturbed by the difficult verses of others.
Reflecting in his mind, "Where can I find fault here?
the wicked man proceeds to listen to the works of the virtuous.
The expressions of those with true insight are not withered by repeated births, nor are they distressed by instructions;
their essence is to be experienced through self-awareness.
In the speech of some they are like cuckoos, yet in the hearts of others they are like the mute; for some, however, beautiful well-spoken words leap gracefully from the heart to the mouth.
Many human heads, hairy and large,
were fastened to their necks, reaching up to their ears.
Like a virtuous Bharata woman, she shines, observing the vows of well-spoken verses;
though she touches upon the objects of common worldly matters, she remains external to them for the sake of the great poet.
They are to be honored, they are great-souled ones, and their fame is firm in the world— those by whom poems have been composed, or those who are celebrated in poems.
Through the merits of someone, there arise in their mouth words that are pleasing, captivating in their luster, and skilled in various forms of eloquence; likewise, in their home, there are women.
When the ears of the wicked are pierced by the well-spoken verses of great poets, which indicate profound and hidden meanings,
how could they not experience pain?
It shall pass into the hands of the virtuous, it shall delight them, and it shall remain faultless;
even when merely brought forth, the poem brings joy, like a daughter.
Everything that has reached its proper time attains auspicious whiteness, even if it is poorly prepared;
even a meal of coarse food becomes exceedingly sweet for one who eats at the right time.
The gold of poetry attains purity when heated in the fire of wicked people;
therefore, one should show it with effort to those whose minds are free from envy.
Those who, out of a desire for mere aesthetic flavor, do not consider the rules of prosody, the breaking of meter, or the loss of meaning,
are like pimps and bad poets.
The fool feels distress not toward his own ignorance, but toward poetry that requires a vast capacity of heart;
generally, like a woman with withered breasts, he merely reviles his own cloak.
A good man brings his reputation to him, while a skilled poet composes a poem for him alone;
the sun nourishes the lotus with water, but it is the sun that endows it with beauty.
Some are skilled only in explaining the treatise, while others are capable of putting it into practice;
the hand brings the food to the mouth, but the tongue alone knows its flavor.
For the venerable Vāgīśa, these two well-spoken verses were like his very life reaching his throat;
they remained a source of painful distress for the poet until the arrival of a conscious being who caused the opening of his eyes.
Furthermore,
there exists in the works of great poets another very real entity,
which is distinct from its well-known constituent parts.
It shines like the beauty [of youth] in women.
The poet’s intention, which lies beyond the scope of words and manifests solely within these tender verses, is being expressed by our limbs through the transformation of their hair standing on end.
But this salutation with joined palms is for the people who are now silent.
Those few among them who possess hearts attuned to the compositions of poets are not unrestrained,
like birds alighting upon creepers full of aesthetic flavor.
The essence of the heart is the juice; it is not the touch of the mouth.
It is well known that kings have attained fame by providing patronage to poets,
and poets have attained renown by relying on kings;
there is no one who is a greater benefactor to a poet than a king.
For the king, there is no companion equal to a wise man.
This poem, which generates faith in the hearts of the supreme wise ones,
is delightful and imbued with all aesthetic flavors;
yet it finds no place in the heart of the wicked man.
It was like the drinking of blood by Rāhu as it turns toward his mouth.

Just as thieves who have been bound by the power of the King of Wealth (Kubera) after being first subdued would suddenly cease their talk of riches, so too do the exceedingly harsh [critics] of great poets.
Furthermore, words convey other meanings as well through implication (*arthāntara*).

Therefore, why should one not compose poetry that, like honey from a vast flower, causes the hair on the body to stand on end even at the mere mention of its aesthetic flavor (rasa) for those whose minds are clouded by envy— hair that stands on end,
trembling of the head, horripilation on both cheeks, and eyes blurred with tears?
Speech is the support for the hand, being intent upon the description of things that have been superimposed.
Those whose intellects are embellished by their own virtues regard the entire world as a forest;
those who have become envious do not wish for the virtues of others even in a dream;
while the minds of others, though attached to them, are somewhere else, being indifferent and cold.
May the groves of asceticism now consider themselves surpassed by the well-spoken words of the great ones.
That vision which does not loudly proclaim the praise of the virtuous— though they are like the virtuous themselves— and which keeps the wise and good silent out of envy, is not real;
whereas that which has suddenly come within the range of hearing, with throats overflowing with the joy of its splendor...
Even animals do not release their mouthfuls of grass until they have finished chewing; why then should the words of poets be otherwise?
Fortunes, brought forth by clouds of luck as fragile as one’s own whims, cannot be restrained;
the drumbeat of the constant departure of life-breaths finds no rest.
Therefore, those who provide protection here through the nectar of their poetry for this body composed of fame— [they alone are the true refuge].
Therefore, O lords of the earth, show honor to the words of the Sugata; let wise poets compose them without pride.
O King, do not abandon your bond of affection for good poets;
for by your grace, pure fame surely shines forth. Therefore, let the noble life of the Lord of the Raghus be composed in an elaborate style by those who are contented.
Led by the Rākṣasas, the conqueror of the three worlds, the Ten-faced One, became an object of ridicule.
Homage, repeated homage, to that essence of poetry, by whose poured-out nectar even the face of a common person attains the golden luster of a noble man.
And it becomes difficult to deal with for an evil person.
Those who harbor pride regarding the path of poetry, without having studied the mantras of Garuḍa, do not understand the seal of the secret of wisdom.
They begin to taste the Hālāhala poison.
How could he, who for a long time did not suckle at the breasts of the goddess Sarasvatī—
the breasts that are thick with the milk of poetic skill and learning—
ever attain the full maturity of all his limbs?
Day by day, he attains a distinguished maturity.
Victorious are those discerning poets who, like royal swans dwelling on the Sarasvatī situated in the heart, are skilled in distinguishing between milk and water.
The nectar of poetry, led away by the sun-like wicked, would not be attainable even for those born of noble lineage,
were it not for the excellence of its singular, unblemished brilliance, shining with the wheel of truth.
Apart from the connoisseur of literary composition (*sāhityavid*), the merit of poets does not manifest in any way elsewhere;
at that very moment, it sinks away as if into water.
Elsewhere, there is no spreading of a drop of oil.
What is the use of that which is excessively crooked and meaningless,
which reveals [the self] as empty of all other qualities,
being itself untouchable and uncorrupted?
With words as empty as the wagging of one's own tail.
May his ears, which have become extremely black from constantly listening to base things,
be nourished by the people who uphold the true Dharma;
for otherwise, how could that [Dharma] ever be born?
Through the *Kṣoda* [mantra], there is the grace of the Sarasvatī-mantra.
If there is meaning, there is no purity of words; if there is purity of words, that [meaning] does not exist.
If there is a meter, where would its composition come from?
And if that too exists, then there is no ninefold crookedness—this is [the case].
Oh, without flavor, profound poetry is utterly useless!
The winding course of that beloved friend of the clouds— the creeper-like bow of the speech of the best of poets— is indeed praiseworthy,
provided these virtues reach as far as the ears.
The minds of those possessed by stinginess snap instantly asunder.
Those few poets of old who, having repeatedly squeezed out the essence of aesthetic flavor (*rasasāra*), produced the true taste of reality (*tattvasparśa*) through their words; today,
however, those poets produce it in that work according to their respective capacities.
Those who [compose] collections of *anuprāsa*, *thoracitra*, *yamaka*, *śleṣa*, and so forth;
Surely there are many poets here who, by practicing even a few verses of others day after day, might compose four lines;
for they are friends to the surging waves of the ocean that rise up incessantly.
Indeed, the words of certain people are said to convey clarity through their very sweetness.
Where now are those hundreds of loads of gold belonging to Paṃmaṅkhaka, or those herds of rutting elephants, which Śrīharṣa bestowed upon the virtuous Bāṇa?
Those glories of his, which have been raised by the multitude of his well-spoken verses,
I do not think will suffer even the slightest fading, even at the dissolution of the aeon.

Fortunate are those who, having gathered the well-spoken flowers from the creepers of speech that have emerged from the garden of their own mouths— flowers that are pure, fragrant, and endowed with excellent qualities— remain in the solitude of the virtuous.
The various colors [of the flowers] act as earrings upon the sandy banks of their ears.

Victorious are the great poets, who, like Sāṃkhyas, have seen the truth through the fire of their own experience; for I recognize [the truth] by means of the tiny cloves of the blossoms of their poetic utterances.
Being peaceful and constant, they perfume the faces of others with their fragrance.
There exists one who is the kinsman of the multitude of virtues that are the ground of the three worlds;
he is the sole poet, the second creator. The gods honor his immeasurable greatness with their heads.
Even for the lords of the earth, he performed the ritual salutation by grasping their feet.
Even those who do not understand even the mere meaning of the words,
like deer drinking from [trickling] streams,
become such that the movement of all their faculties is completely obstructed.
Like figures fixed in a painting, we pay homage to the words of the sovereign poets.
When applied out of place, the Goddess of Speech leads those of impaired intellect to derision,
defeat, great suffering, or even sin;
but when employed in its proper place, she brings about the renown and prosperity of the virtuous.
For the sake of the mind's liberation, for the sake of benefiting others, and for the sake of attaining ultimate peace.
King Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, was indeed described by Vyāsa; King Vikrama, marked with the title *Śrī*, by the poet Kālidāsa;
and King Bhoja, as well as Karṇa—the lord of learning—by Citrabhānu, Bilhaṇa, and others.
They become renowned among the best of poets, not by the loud sounds of drums, but by being free from faults.
Having resorted to the shade of the forest of their arms, those of great majesty whose seat was the ocean,
this earth became free from fear from any quarter;
yet those kings do not even come to mind without your favor.
We pay homage to that Great One of primordial nature, the creator of the works of poets.
Those whose feet resembled golden jars, those who attained prosperity,
and even those in whose houses young women dwelt like the moonlight of day— this world regards them as if they were never born, even in a dream, O ornament of the world.
O brother, what is the use of hundreds of praises by good poets to this blind world without you?
What is the use of this [nose] with its pervasive abundance of fragrance? Even that essence which is the source of its destruction is indeed worthless;
though it possesses a beautiful form, it does not cultivate true mental well-being.
If the goddess who bestows the flow of honey should stream forth.
It bestows wonder upon the mind in the art of composition;
when recited in assemblies, it leads to the attainment of unequalled and virtuous renown;
and having reached its first stage, it spreads exceedingly noble fame.
Like a jewel that is the essence of poetic thought, he does not fail to fulfill any desire.
He who spreads the clear honey of poetry, as if standing upon six legs, within the lotus of his own mouth for the sake of another—
[that person] is like a swarm of ants produced by the fault of an improper location.
The dark line of his hair shines like a row of written letters.

If there should be one who is devoted solely to the definition of the object [to be defined], who is not stained by contact with logic (*tarka*), whose intellect is not charmed by the investigation of ornaments, and who has abandoned the training of knowing poetry— if from such a person a poem rich in aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) should arise, it would be exclusively beautiful.
Then, due to the crow's blackness, the white palace of the lord of the earth would become black.
Like a certain key of one’s own wisdom,
some lord among poets [has opened] a certain treasury of word-meanings that possesses the graceful turns of Sarasvatī’s eloquence.
Having removed the universal ornament, he makes it into a mallet.
Some divine words bring fulfillment to those who have achieved their purpose, yet they only cause distress to the deluded; for such drops [of truth] fall from the mouths of the eloquent.
Those alone are liberated, but not among the Cātakas.
Even those who are eloquent bear the vow of silence only among people who understand their exertion; there are those who observe the restraint of speech even without living together.
The male cuckoos [sing] even more melodiously than the fifth note.
Just as the serpent Vyaḷa and Rāhu, having attained the favor of nectar,
became fierce in their grasping of tongues and heads,
so too do the malicious become terrified.
They are averse to all things except for the aesthetic flavor of poetry.

A wise person speaking of reality— which is free from conceptual construction and is the sole domain of one’s own self-awareness— will surely incur ridicule from those whose intellects are deluded by ignorance. Indeed, it is not fitting for a learned man to behave like a fool.
What is this futile effort regarding the arrangement of colors and forms for one who is blind from birth?
Now begins the *Sujanavarnanapaddhati*.
Victorious are those who have conquered envy, who are exerted for the sake of the welfare of others,
who are firmly established in the prosperity of others, and who are agitated by sorrow at the misfortunes of others.
The virtuous ones, whose curiosity has been aroused by hearing the discourse concerning the Great Being,
are like suns that manifest the destruction of the ship of all misfortunes.
O Venerable One,
he who is mute when censuring others, blind from birth even when looking at the wives of others,
and lame when taking the wealth of others— he is the Great Being who triumphs in this world. (Aśvaghoṣa)
The mind of some great person becomes as delicate as a blue lotus in times of prosperity,
yet as hard as a mass of rocks from a great mountain in times of adversity.
The conduct of a wise man is twofold, like that of a cluster of flowers on a tree:
either he stands at the head of all the world, or he withers away in the forest.

The wise, who have been shown compassion by Ravigupta, do not grieve nor do they endure [suffering]; even in times of calamity, they are difficult to distress, for they are eternally free from sorrow.
Trees grow through the sprinkling of water, not from a mere accumulation of atoms;
for that which is capable attains substantiality upon encountering the appropriate action.
For those at the lowest level, there is the fear of rebirth; for those in the middle, the fear of death;
but for the highest of beings, the supreme fear is that of being held in contempt.
This association with the virtuous, which destroys the suffering of Vyāsa Muni, bestows happiness, grants life, and produces radiant fame— this very gateway to immortality is difficult to attain.
The moonlight of association with the virtuous is like an elixir; it bestows supreme bliss—what person indeed does it not delight?
Those great-souled ones who protect the auspicious flower of discernment, born from the tree of association with the virtuous,
are the vessels for the glory of its fruit.
"Emptiness, when unmixed with other things, makes even death seem like a festival;
it appears as prosperity does in the midst of a gathering of learned men."
Victorious in this world is the singular meeting of the virtuous with the virtuous; it is like a cool breeze that removes the frost from a lotus pond and acts as a necklace of enchantment.
Know that association with the virtuous is the supreme nourishment for the intellect, the eradication of the tree of ignorance, and the complete removal of mental afflictions.
For one who has bathed with the cool, white water of association with the virtuous,
what need is there for gifts, what need for sacred fords, what need for austerities, or what need for sacrifices?
It is my conviction that these hearts of the venerable sage Vālmīki are indeed as hard as stone;
for they are not pierced in the slightest by the sharp arrows of the wicked's speech.
"Why is this mind of the Lord of Tathāgatas, the Lion, so difficult for the wise to fathom, like the ocean?"—
as if angry at this thought, he filled it with the sufferings of others, which are hard to pierce.
Those for whom glass is glass and the emerald is glass are indeed other embodied beings; those wise ones for whom glass is glass and the emerald is an emerald are truly enlightened.
A speaker is unable to turn faults into virtues or virtues into faults; faults remain faults and virtues remain virtues. That which is not so is not reality.
If virtuous people feel reverence for one whose interior is filled with the fullness of the great ornaments of the jewels of excellent qualities, what is so wonderful about that?
May such a quality of the virtuous dissolve into its very own self—
that which, even when manifested by itself, does not consider itself as "mine."
Even a very small amount of respect arises from contact with those who possess virtues;
because of its attachment to a garland of flowers, even a blade of grass is carried upon the head.
To whom could the fall of a virtuous person— well-conducted, uniform, firm, elevated, and pleasing to others— not bring satisfaction, like that of a pair of breasts?
The sun rises red and sets red;
likewise, for the great, there is a single uniformity in both prosperity and adversity.
The noble one, even when falling, springs up like a ball struck by a foot;
the ignoble one, however, falls just like a clod of earth.
Even when fallen, a ball rises up again by the strokes of the hand;
for generally, the misfortunes of those who follow the right path are not enduring.
Even one who has fallen away rises up again if they possess wisdom, but not one of dull intellect;
a ball rises after falling, but not so the pair of breasts of a beloved.
Without regard for affection, nor for a worthy recipient, nor even for their own livelihood, these supreme ones are always engaged in the welfare of the world, like lamps of jewels.
Virtuous people show compassion even toward beings who are devoid of merit;
for the moon does not withhold its moonlight from the house of a caṇḍāla.
Light is not created for the sun, nor is the earth supported by its reflection; for among the virtuous, there is no expectation of a return for their services.
Even while doing harm, one generally attains great merit from the great;
for even the ocean satisfies the submarine fire that consumes it.
The noble, the upright, the pure, and those who cultivate virtues are fruitful; having seen them, the visible is truly seen, and having heard them, it is heard again.
In truth, no redundancy is perceived in the conduct of one who acts virtuously.
The virtuous are upright, pure, fruitful, and devoted to excellence;
though their virtues are equal, the noble are diverse—gentle yet firm, and firm yet gentle.
Those who seek gain are base, yet they desire honor;
the wise man, however, is like a crane seeking fish in a lake, for whom the clarity of the water is the desired state.
A person who is naturally straightforward, upon perceiving the suffering of others,
experiences pain in their heart because they are unable to provide assistance.
They are to be venerated; they are successful; indeed, their birth and origin are praiseworthy—those who, having abandoned their own interests, accomplish the welfare of their friends.
If Fortune does not take refuge in a man who is free from deceit, steady, straightforward, generous,
affectionate, and possessed of discernment, then Fortune herself is indeed deceived in that case.
Health, wisdom, friendship with the virtuous, birth in a noble family,
and self-reliance— these constitute great sovereignty for men, even without material wealth.
Even a very small amount of wealth, when possessed by the virtuous, is enjoyed as a great abundance; yet even the entire earth, when the glory of a wicked man, is never enjoyed.
Water that is full of essence alone is drawn from a well, but never from the ocean.
It does not happen, or if it happens, it does not happen for long; yet if it happens after a long time, it fails to bear fruit.
The indignation of the virtuous is equal to the affection of the base.

A great virtue of the virtuous becomes a fault for the wicked; likewise, the good deeds of the wicked become a fault for the virtuous—just as grass serves for milk to cows, yet milk serves as poison to serpents.
Even when they have attained complete prosperity, the wise do not seek the stream of insults that comes with wealth;
these are like the *cātaka* birds, who do not drink the muddy water of the earth because it is full of dust.
The virtuous attain their goal in the human world through mere fitness, even without destruction [of past karma];
indeed, parrots with clear speech remain confined within the cage.
Having seen a person even once, the wise weigh their worthiness or worthlessness; for even with the hand as a scale, those who are skilled understand the measurement of weight.
A virtuous person, devoted to the welfare of others, does not harbor enmity even when faced with untimely harm;
even when being cut down, a sandalwood tree perfumes the edge of the axe.
The virtuous generally do not abandon one who is devoted to them, even if that person lacks merit;
the moon, though possessing a spot, bears it forever, sharing in its growth and decline.
Even in his final state, the wise man does not abandon his own virtue because of the purity of his birth;
nor does a conch shell relinquish its white nature even when released after being swallowed by a peacock.
Even those who delight in virtues are not weary of seeing a person possessed of virtues;
for out of affection, the world perceives even a blemish as a mark of beauty on the moon.
Friendship extends for seven steps even among those of naturally pure minds;
how much more so between those whose hearts are bound by the confidence born from recounting each other's virtues?
To whom would those noble-minded ones not be desirable— those of pure intention whose heart, speech, and conduct are all three alike? (Haribhaṭṭa)

One who dwells in the proximity of the virtuous is worthy of worship by the world, even if they themselves are devoid of virtue; just as an eye afflicted with cataracts attains the power of sight through the application of stainless collyrium.

This is accomplished spontaneously by the great: lack of attachment to wealth and fame, compassion toward virtues, timidity regarding the suffering of others, and great fortitude in the face of one's own suffering.
Even those who are extremely angry become gentle through the application of skillful means, but the base do not;
there is a way to melt even hard gold, but none for straw.
Virtuous people do not even count an injury when it is accompanied by a thousand acts of kindness;
for the flames of a lamp produce light by consuming their own fuel.
The redness of lotuses, the altruism of virtuous persons,
and the cruelty of the wicked— this triad in these three things is established by their very nature.
Some recognize those who are capable of helping, who are patient with the ungracious, who give what has not been asked for when they have little,
and who intend to honor others with their virtues.
One who possesses virtues delights in a virtuous person, not in one of wicked character; the virtuous person finds satisfaction in the virtuous.
A bee goes from the forest to the lotus, but the frog does not go even to its own dwelling place.
In the beginning they are very faint; in the middle they are of equal flavor;
and at the end, being conjoined with the wise, they are drawn toward affection.
This is some kind of extraordinary hardness of heart belonging to those great beings who possess the dignity of high-mindedness;
for after having rendered assistance, they keep themselves at a distance out of fear of receiving a return favor.

If there were even a single hair-tip of compassion toward a benefactor who is free from envy, why would there not be a hundred thousandfold [compassion] for one who has suddenly committed an injury against you?
He whose mind is compassionate toward the Sangha is a leader among the virtuous.
Kindness exists toward virtuous people from beginning to middle to end,
but not toward other people;
[it is characterized] by cutting, giving, pouring out, and heating.
Gold does not undergo any change into something else.
Lamps illuminate objects that are present;
however, some become lamps for their lineage,
illuminating even those ancestors who have long since passed away.
They illuminate [the world] through the excellence of their own virtues.

Those who are lofty in nature are even loftier when they are capable of destroying the afflictions of the mind, but those who are base are not; only those who bear rain-clouds are truly the "bearers of the earth."
Rivers do not remove the heat of the summer's forest fire.
Virtues become virtues when they encounter those who possess virtue;
having encountered one devoid of virtue, they become faults. For rivers that originate from sweet water remain sweet.
Having reached the ocean, they become undrinkable.
The wind does not uproot the grasses,
which are soft and bowed down in every way;
it strikes only the trees that stand tall.
The great indeed undergoes transformation only among the great.
A self-possessed man, whose mind has long been purified by association with the virtuous, does not fall into the company of the wicked,
even when wandering through the range of captivating and excellent sensory objects.
A bee never settles upon a rotten tree.
Even when deprived of wealth or fallen from his own position,
a man of noble soul does not seek service under base people; even when afflicted by hunger, a lion does not feed upon mere grass.
He generally drinks the blood and marrow of elephants.
Generosity toward wealth, patience in adversity, absence of dejection in suffering, and freedom from hypocrisy in virtuous conduct— this is the innate nature of the great-souled ones.
Indeed, when deprived of even a tiny fragment of happiness, a wicked man wallows in vice; he stumbles and clings to even slight afflictions, like a needle of despair.
The minds of the virtuous become neither unrestrained by pride nor filled with dejection.
It is difficult to overcome because it is profound, even amidst pleasures and the absence of pleasure.
Kindness toward one's own kin,

affection for virtue, lack of arrogance in joy, secrecy regarding counsel, wisdom in sacred learning, generosity upon the rise of wealth, devotion with respect for the virtuous, aversion toward the wicked, and extreme fear of sin.
Enduring suffering and afflictions, they long for the great ones who possess a virtuous nature.
Fortitude in adversity, equanimity in prosperity, eloquence in the assembly, valor in battle, delight in fame, and devotion to sacred learning— these are the marks of a noble man.
For this is indeed established by nature for the great-souled ones.
For the wise declare this to be the sign of the greatness of the great:
that their minds remain equanimous when pleasure or pain arises.
He does not fall under the power of the god of love or the planet Saturn.

Delight in what is virtuous and well-spoken, lack of pride; through prosperity, an activity characterized by a readiness to accomplish the welfare of others; and an insatiable longing for virtues, as well as respect for those who possess them.
This conduct of the great-souled ones is free from guile.
The virtues of the virtuous are true; however, due to the reversal of the cosmic order, even those acquired through effort become fruitless in the Kali age.
Yet, this very [practice] of theirs possesses an exceedingly great fruitfulness.
Yet it pierces the hearts of the wicked once again.
When a wicked person, whose mind is intent on deception and who is full of guile, speaks with feigned purpose while facing a task,
the virtuous do not fail to recognize it; indeed, they know it well.
They are not able to fulfill his request for a favor.

The base person, devoid of compassion, practices evil; the one of middling intellect, however, remains compassionate even when encountering calamity; but the virtuous person does not abandon their noble conduct even at the cost of their life.
He is capable of leaping over the boundary, just as the ocean [leaps over its shore] at the time of the ebb.
"He alone is pure, he alone is of noble birth,
and he alone is wise, who does not abandon his own nature even in times of calamity—
just as the heated [earth] is by the network of rays of the sun."
One may even abandon the body, but not its coolness.
Having experienced that state which is like the suffering of death,
what indeed can be gained by giving even in great abundance? For here, the virtuous ones seem to mock even the wish-fulfilling trees.
That which one gives away, having been excessively distressed by what was previously intended [for oneself].
Those virtuous ones have become the crowns upon the mandala of the world,
they who demonstrate goodness even toward those who have done them no service;
they have disciplined their weary bodies for the sake of their own spiritual purpose.
For even a cruel person feels compassion toward those who have previously been benefactors.
A virtuous person does not harbor even the slightest ill will within their mind; though unprovoked, they do not perceive evil in the slanderous words of others,
for even the rays of the sun that fall upon the face are considered excellent.
The rays of the moon, the lord of the stars, indeed scatter nectar.
One born of noble family does not speak what is unspeakable even when provoked; one who is free from malice utters only sweet words even amidst afflictions;
and a base person, though served with hundreds of virtues, [remains as such].
In jests, he says what ought to be said in quarrels.
Let those skilled in logic either revile me or praise me;
let Fortune fall away or go wherever she pleases;
let death come this very day or at the end of an eon.
The wise do not waver from the path of what is right.

Good people, though they may encounter some slight obstacle, do not hesitate; being naturally noble, they most clearly undertake what must be done. Why, having risen, would they not go to the Lord of the Ocean, even from a distance?
The Blessed One Agastya drank even the mud at the bottom of the ocean.
A conduct that is dear and righteous is difficult to maintain even when one's life is at stake;
for the wicked are not to be petitioned, nor should a friend who has lost his wealth be entreated.
In times of misfortune, one should stand firm in a high position and follow the example of the great.
By whom was this uneven vow of the razor’s edge prescribed for the virtuous?

Generosity; a hospitable reception with due ceremony when a guest arrives at the well-sheltered home; freedom from pride even in the face of prosperity; refraining from speaking ill of others; maintaining silence after having done a kindness; and speaking only when it is beneficial in an assembly.
"Learning indicates that one is born of a noble lineage and possesses complete devotion."
Whose command causes the seven-horsed sun to dispel the darkness of living beings?
By whom is the salutation joined on the path for those scorched by the heat, as a refuge from the shadows? And by whom are the clouds that shed drops of water entreated for the sake of rain?
By their very nature, these virtuous ones are bound by their resolve to accomplish the welfare of others.

The accumulation of its own fruits causes the breaking of the branches of the tree; even the plumage makes the peacock slow in its movement. A horse that is noble by birth is made to carry like an ox.
In a person possessing [these] ninety qualities, these faults generally do not exist at all.
Where qualities do not manifest, how can there be respect for the possessor of those qualities? What can even a man of great learning do for one who has become like a stone?
[He cannot produce] the sound of a throat turned back by the intoxication of pride in a playful woman mounted on passion.
For what benefit can even a heart-stealing whistling sound produce for one who is deaf?
There are thousands of Śūdras intent solely on the task of supporting themselves;
yet that man whose own interest is indeed the interest of others is the singular leader among the virtuous. A forest fire drinks up the ocean merely to fill its own insatiable belly.
But Jimūta, for the sake of dispelling the heat that torments the world during the summer season.
By their humility they appear exalted; by praising the virtues of others they cause their own limbs to seem diminished;
they nourish their own welfare while constantly exerting effort for the sake of others;
and by means of patience alone, they consume those with harsh faces whose mouths are noisy with insults and abuse.
Whom would those peaceful ones, whose conduct inspires awe and who are highly esteemed in the world, not attract?
Only virtuous people proclaim the abundance of the virtues of the good;
generally, it is the winds that spread the fragrance of flowers in all directions.
Only the virtuous person should be one who partakes of the nectar of true qualities;
it is said that the cuckoo alone is skilled in tasting the fresh mango sprouts.
Generally, those who possess intelligence are worthy of instruction, not those who are dull-witted;
sesame seeds may sometimes capture the fragrance of flowers, but barley never can.
The heart of a wise person maintains its clarity through very little harshness;
indeed, a mirror generally attains its state of brightness through ash.
The supreme person is capable of enduring the affliction of defilements, but no other is;
just as a jewel can withstand the friction of a great grindstone, but not a piece of clay.
When the sun rises, virtuous people generally bear suffering,
just as white lotuses, upon the rising of the sun, bear the anxiety of closing.
Generally, only one who knows [the subject] understands the distinction between qualities;
the eye does not perceive the fragrance of the jasmine flower, but the sense of smell does.
The virtuous do not abandon their own nature even through contact with the wicked;
cuckoos do not lose their sweet song because of association with crows.
The mind is tender in times of prosperity, yet hard in the face of severe adversity;
the leaf of a tree is delicate in spring, but becomes rigid in the heat of summer.
A virtuous person does not abandon their innate nature even when fallen into adversity;
camphor, even when scorched by fire, retains its fragrance all the more.
Even the time of adversity for a virtuous person becomes worthy of praise;
even the period of the moon's affliction by Rāhu is beautiful.
Having witnessed the wickedness of the evil, people take delight in the virtuous;
like a traveler who has ascended a mountain, he attains complete peace.
The noble do not delight in enjoyments that are fraught with danger and perish in an instant;
having abandoned the filaments of the lotus, swans feed upon the moss.
The onset of suffering afflicts the lower parts more intensely, but not the upper;
the touch of cold quickly pains the hands and feet, but not the eyes.
Even by fate, one who possesses virtues and is long-enduring cannot be tolerated;
for the glorious moon, with its full orb, remains for only a single night.
In every place where its excellence is praised, it shines forth most brilliantly;
whether on the head, the neck, the arm, or even upon the footstool, it is beautiful.
Supreme and enduring prosperity is never truly overcome by calamities, just as the moon’s momentary loss of luster caused by the eclipse of Rāhu does not prevail over its long-term excellence.
One becomes most excellent through praise, while one becomes base through great wealth;
the gods are propitiated by recitations, and the spirits and demons by offerings.
The mind of the virtuous never extends toward evil deeds;
even though it flows swiftly through the waters, it does not enter the hollows of the mouth of a jar.
In this world, it is said that some people are indeed worthy of refinement;
though they are born into the same lineage, possess the same age, and even the same intellect,
this distinction arises here from the practice of clear familiarity through repeated cultivation.
"A parrot is able to recite verses, but a crow is never able to do so."
Even wealth given by another becomes a source of suffering for those who lack the sense of propriety,
yet that very same thing brings joy to the hearts of others; a drop of sandalwood paste causes pain to the eye, yet it soothes it when applied externally.
And that very same [eruption] produces a pleasant sensation in another part of the body.

Even if a flaw should arise by fate in a virtuous person— one who is born of a noble lineage, who dispels all affliction, who is well-conducted, pure in soul, and an ornament to the entire world— [it is not to be condemned].
It will certainly lead to virtue, like one who is liberated from a debt.
The home has been destroyed by wretched kinsmen, the preceptor’s residence by arrogant students,
the hermitages by those intent on performing sacrifices,
the forest by lions and other beasts, the royal assembly by the wicked, and even the far reaches of the earth by thieves.
Having observed these impure things, where can the virtuous one, who is truthful and straightforward, find rest?

Those who are elevated by virtue do not speak words that are accompanied by pride, impossible, devoid of propriety, or unpleasant; nor do they utter words that cause suffering, humiliation, or dejection.
The good person who has extensively proclaimed the virtues of others attains an exceeding state of good fortune;
the radiance of the moon, causing the night-lotuses to bloom, bears a twofold splendor.
Even for those possessed of virtues, the realization of their own true nature occurs only through another;
for the perception of one's own majesty arises only from the tip of the eye of a blind man.
What is a burden of ten million to the capable? What is distant for those who are persevering? What is a foreign land to the learned? Who is a stranger to those who speak kindly?
