A horse, a weapon, a treatise, a lute, speech, a man, and a woman—
these become either fit or unfit depending on the particular excellence attained by the person.
One who is endowed with enthusiasm, not prolix, knowledgeable in the methods of action, unattached to calamities,
brave, grateful, and firm in friendship.
Lakṣmī herself desires him for the sake of a dwelling.
Even when suppressed, the quality of creation cannot be extinguished in one of great intellect;
even when turned downward, the fire remains.
"O Lord, the crests [of the flames] move only occasionally."
Justice has indeed been abandoned by the wicked, and the Dharma has wavered; the Kali age alone has now set in with its impurity. For the most part, the people are wicked and full of power.
It is better to be without a retinue and simply a target for contempt.
He suppressed dispute regarding his vows, doubt regarding solitude, suspicion regarding truth, agitation regarding discipline, contempt for virtues, and obstruction regarding wholesome qualities.
The virtuous person does not create opposition toward the Dharma.
He is worthy of veneration by men and celebrated by the gods,
because through his acts of increasing compassion and virtuous conduct,
he has reached the very essence of cyclic existence.
"The body is a vessel for benefiting others."
One may worship [the Buddha] without distinction, whether he is staying within the interior of a night-lotus (*kumuda*) or has departed from a rival lotus (*ambhoja*) toward a honeybee;
for there is no one who is incapable of training himself and others.
This is the continuous tradition of the virtuous, sweet because it is free from selfish motives.

Those intentions which, when spoken aloud before people, cause one to become agitated; those which, even when not being voiced, produce some internal pain; and those which, throbbing within the heart, remain somehow stuck in the throat—[these are the intentions of the wicked].
Those who possess merit obtain here a friend whose virtues may be recounted.
The earth is bounded by the ocean, yet that treasure of waters extends for a hundred *yojanas*;
the sky is always a traveler, yet it speaks of the measure of the heavens as being vast as a man.
Thus, for the most part, all things are sealed with the bud of a shimmering limit.
Furthermore, this awakening of wisdom of the virtuous shines forth as boundless.
They do not become angry even when insulted, and they benefit others out of compassion;
they do not desire awakening for themselves alone, for they are capable of uplifting the entire world.
It purifies the vessel but does not cling to its qualities; it does not withhold moisture, nor does it produce impurity;
it possesses no attachment to the beautiful creepers that end in faults.
Association with the virtuous is a certain lamp within the abode of meritorious deeds.
Even a tiny jewel is equal to a life-saving gem for those who have consumed poison;
even a lion cub, out of fury, challenges elephants;
and even a small spark arising from the trunk of a tree consumes a forest.
In the species born from primordial matter and the great principle, light does not depend upon a physical form.
Salutations to the wicked; for who indeed would not pay homage to them here, if they desire to live— those who,
like the great sages, [bestow their favor] even without a fault [on their part]?
They lead [beings] to the subterranean realm (rasātala) by means of a serpent.
Wise men do not speak falsely when they say that a wicked person is even more extremely similar to a snake,
because this one is always a slanderer who hates mongooses and hates snakes.
The intellect of the wicked is exceedingly clever when it comes to performing what is extremely defiled;
for the vision of those born blind perceives forms in the darkness.
The wickedness of the base becomes exceedingly foul when they have destroyed the virtues of others; even water-bearing clouds appear more soiled when they have obscured the light of the moon.
Just as a villain, like a hand soiled by mud, scratches a virtuous person, the more he does so,
the more that person becomes stainless and radiant, like a mirror polished by rubbing.
Bowed down while being seized alive, yet rising up again—what are these wicked people like the buckets of a water-wheel? Are they the younger ones or the elder ones?
Homage to the mortar, which is always fit for crushing and possesses a hollow interior; homage to the mortar, which contains many seeds and is a vessel for the wicked.
With a tongue as long as a sharp blade, greedy for morsels of food and fierce in quarrels, the slanderer always carries a mouth that is like a vessel of impurity.
Alas! By virtue of his own merits, even a fool becomes a scholar who has not studied; he becomes a master of speech in censuring others, intent on proclaiming his own virtues.
In this world, which is empty of virtuous people, the wicked man looks about in all directions with his head held high; having ears everywhere, he stands encompassing everything.
When a fool hears words of praise from the virtuous,
his tongue— afflicted by the disease of envy— is not moved at all, even when pulled by the hook of a fisherman.
By its very nature, the world is composed of illusion and is agitated by passion, hatred, and delusion;
like a wicked person, it causes even the great to fall into confusion, just as the cycle of existence does.
Even a magician creates a painting effortlessly;
because he does so with ease even among the great, he is known as a "kha-lu" (an adept).
Alas, O subjects! Where will you go, now that you are ruled by one who is a mere grain-thresher, intoxicated by wealth, base, powerful, treacherous, and established in his position?

A hundred good deeds performed for those who are wicked are lost; a hundred well-spoken words addressed to the ignorant are lost; a hundred instructions given to one who does not act upon them are lost; and a hundred insights offered to the insentient are lost.

A gift given to an unworthy recipient is lost; a beneficial act is lost when disregarded due to a lack of recognition for its fruit; virtue is lost when one fails to recognize virtue; and courtesy is lost when one fails to acknowledge kindness received.
With his hand raised from afar and his eyes fixed in longing, he leaves half his seat and is intent on a firm embrace;
when asked about pleasant news, he is intent on giving an answer; with his mind hidden within while his exterior is full of sweetness, he is exceedingly full of illusion.
What indeed is this unprecedented method, never seen before, that has been learned by wicked people?
Those who seek to destroy the long-accumulated merit of the great—those crooked-souled ones are to be pitied;
they are like wicked people posing as the virtuous.
Oh, how difficult it is to grasp the minds of the wicked, whose intellects are so crooked!
One thing is in their speech, another at their throat, and something else entirely resides in the corner of their lips.
While there are honest men in the markets, we have gone out to acquire virtues; this is that deceptive act of buying jewels in a village of thieves.
Both of these increase as if in rivalry through their abundant wealth and their hundreds of branches:
the sprout that has emerged from a refuse heap, and the man who has arisen from a noble family.
Being burned by that most intense and supreme fire, the lowly ones were unable to reach that state; consequently, they began to utter reproaches.
That very thing by the mere recollection of which the virtuous bring an end to the continuity of their distress,
the wicked indeed bring about with effortless ease, even while laughing.

How can a person who does not know the scriptures concerning virtues, faults, and the self distinguish [between them]? Does a blind man have the capacity to perceive the various distinctions of forms?
Generally, that which is impure becomes radiant by the obstruction of the virtuous;
for had the lion not devoured the son of Siṃhikā, who would have known the sun?
A wicked person is constantly intent on causing suffering to others;
because their actions are performed out of necessity, they do not look for a reason [to act].
With a slight [weight] it rises up; with a slight [weight] it goes down.
Oh, how similar is the behavior of a scale-beam and that of a wicked person!
Oh, how natural is the similarity between phlegm and a wicked person!
Phlegm increases through sweet things and subsides through bitter ones; so too does a wicked person.
Just as a lordly elephant, exhausted and seeking shade, resorts to a tree, yet having rested there, destroys that very tree; so too does a base person destroy his own support.
A wicked person should be avoided even if they are adorned with learning;
can a snake wearing a jewel necklace ever cease to be terrifying?
Beauty is for the sake of another's wife; wealth is for the torment of the world;
and lordship is for the destruction of the virtuous—such are the even more wicked qualities found in the wicked.
For those who subsist by obtaining mere knowledge through the injury of others,
the gathering of virtues is like a net for rogues, as if for slaves.
Even the sweet words spoken by a wicked person produce in me a sense of terror, like untimely blossoms.
The wicked man feels no shame at all for his crooked behavior, like that of a serpent— a conduct which is to be shunned even by the virtuous.
Indeed, a wicked person considers even cleverness to be a practice that leads to false pride and delusion.
Kṣemendra highly prizes his own commentary in his heart; with words of compassion,
he clearly censures his own limited intellect while offering praise for its fitness.
He does not speak of resorting to censurable means, even when describing a stable calamity;
for upon hearing of suffering that is sharp and piercing, an ordinary person spreads forth intense pain.
If it is not for the sake of his own pleasure, then he would not have eaten it even before; how much less so now?
If it is for his own benefit, why does he not share it with the wretched who are his own kin?
If he fears that I might see his weakness, then why would he, being greedy, abandon it?
Thus ends the section on the lowest of men, who for the most part acknowledge their obligations only after they have been rendered a service.
This is the marvelous martial prowess of Kahlaṇa in battle, which was unimpeded and shattered the circle of the quarters; by his gift of a golden vessel,
the Lord of Lakṣmī (Viṣṇu) was made to rest upon his back.
The sovereignty consisting of the seven worlds obtained by his own hand, and the fame that had reached the further shore of the ocean—
all this was suddenly and clearly destroyed for Bāli through association with wicked men.
"He who pacifies the afflictions leads one to a miserable and inauspicious state; he produces agitation and exhaustion for people and brings about derision;
he causes the intellect to wander, destroys pride, and diminishes life."
Association with the wicked scatters the entire multitude of virtues.
For those born of indiscipline and ignorance, even though they possess learning, its practice leads only to the increase of wickedness due to their innate crookedness;
yet may that same learning be the complete destroyer of the darkness for those who are filled with the fear of snakes.
The light from the jewel on the crest of the head of Śubha disperses all darkness, yet it causes fear to increase greatly.
Even while being honored, he who is intent on the world's ruin causes terror at every sight, like a wicked person within one's own home.
A person who has fallen away from truth and righteousness is like a cruel butcher provoked to anger;
for even an atheist trembles before such a one, let alone a believer.
Those for whom the slaughter of living beings is a sport, whose words cut to the quick, and whose duty is to torment others— they are the death of even Death itself.
Alas! What a great misery is this reversal of the world, wherein the virtuous man feels shame, yet the wicked man finds satisfaction!
Evil-minded people do not wish to know the virtues of others as much as they desire to know their faults.
A wise person should avoid both friendship and enmity with the wicked;
for even one who is charming or one who is harsh will cause harm to oneself.
Therefore, nothing else in this world is found to be more laughable than when a wicked person calls a virtuous person "wicked."
A virtuous person may find contentment even when suffering harm at the hands of the wicked;
yet that is no gain for the serpent which is not devoured while being coiled around by its own coils.
Having obtained [power], he will become arrogant, crooked, foolish, and a ruler who is exclusively cruel; that wicked man, having caused many virtuous people to die, shall himself die.
What rivalry can there be between a wicked person and a virtuous man who possesses self-respect?
For such a man, speaking the truth is his speech, and censuring the wicked is his ornament.
Thorns pierce with a single point the foot of one person;
but the wicked, with a thousand faces from afar, are the snatchers of all living beings.
Having created a wicked tip of a tongue that would take the lives of all people,
why did Prajāpati in vain produce weapons, poisons, and fire?
Just as a virtuous person is ever vigilant in acts of benefiting others,
so too is a wicked person constantly vigilant in acts of harming others.
One who is always modest and possesses a sense of shame fears slander; however, one whose heart is deluded does not fear the censure resulting from his own actions.
For a wicked person whose fire of anger blazes in vain and who speaks with harsh words, there is no medicine whatsoever other than the Unsurpassed One.
There are only two ways to deal with wicked people and thorns:
either by wearing shoes or breaking their faces, or else by avoiding them from afar.
Even while living, a good person is not able to do for others that which a wicked person, though dead, might perform as a supreme benefit for others.
Whatever is most desired, that indeed should be given to one who possesses virtue;
for this very reason, the wicked man bestows his faults upon the virtuous.
Disease, old age, the sprout of rebirth, fire, poison, serpents, woodworms, and parasites,
as well as men who destroy their own nature— these all perish without destroying their own substratum.
A wicked person does not find pleasure without disparaging others;
for even after tasting all flavors, one is not satisfied without filth.
A virtuous person is indeed better when easy to associate with, even if they are utterly fruitless,
than a wicked person who is like a sharp sword that takes one's life, even if it bears fruit every year.
Sharpened by his very nature, even though he has taken sides with a faction,
who would not be divided by a wicked man who is devoid of all virtues?
A wicked person cannot be made into a good person even with great effort;
who, by means of refinement, can make garlic fragrant?
Just as a snake, having emerged from its hole and reached the shelter of another, finds delight in a fissure; this is the illustration here of the state of being a thief.
In the speech of others he has ten faces; in observing the faults of others he has a thousand eyes;
in seizing the conduct of the virtuous he is the thousand-armed Arjuna; and he is base.
For men whose minds have been corrupted by wicked people, there is no trust even in a virtuous person;
a fool, scorched by hot milk, blows upon it before consuming even curd.

If there is even the slightest thing well-established in the speech of one who associates with the wicked, it causes shame at the beginning, brings contempt in the middle, and leaves one empty in the end.

Who indeed will ever relax their suspicion toward these wicked men, who by their very birth are accustomed to concealing their enmity, and who are devoted to deceit? They have pierced the vital organs of others with divine arrows.

One who lacks knowledge is easy to please, whereas one with specialized knowledge is more difficult to please; even a Brahmin does not delight a man who is overly clever and arrogant due to his learning.
One who is dogmatically attached to what is impossible is generally a fool, not a wise man;
for who other than a child would desire to smell the reflection of the moon shimmering in water?
For even a wicked person who has attained prosperity first brings distress upon his own kin;
like a rising forest fire, he consumes the very wood of his birthplace.
Generally, one who has heard but a tiny fragment [of the scriptures] displays a great abundance of eloquence;
for it is everywhere the case that only a villain excels at mimicking a drama.
Only the deceitful, having seized the lead, exert themselves at the forefront of those possessed of virtue;
for it is only straw and wood that float upon the ocean, not jewels.
That which is placed upon the heads of the great, that very same thing the lowly consider as their own; the wise bow to the mark [of honor], while the crows merely turn their beaks toward it.
Even for those who dwell together, there may be a lack of intimacy between the good and the wicked, like that of the lotus and the water;
yet even for those dwelling afar, there is affection between the virtuous, like that of the night-lily and the moon.
Even when relying on a perfectly pure livelihood, a wicked person causes suffering to others;
even serpents that feed only on air do not relinquish their tormenting of others.
Whatever purpose the ignorant person accomplishes is, for him, like the "clapping of hands" (accidental);
even a crow, by chance, may somehow scatter grains into its own nest.
Generally, those of base nature do not become fit for benefit unless they have been thoroughly utilized;
Aśoka flourished even more through the assault of the courtesan’s foot.
The skill of a wicked person in piercing the vital organs of others is not for a virtuous purpose; the potency of poison in causing destruction is not for the sake of benefit.
Even when treated with extreme honor, a rogue never abandons his innate nature;
indeed, was not the sword held crooked even when supported by the head with a great cry?
Like the wind, the common person generally assumes the form of another through contact;
but the virtuous, like the rays of the sun, remain unmixed even when in conjunction with both the good and the bad.
The Supreme Noble One urges: "Even a single pauper, when intent on harming the world, sharpens the edge of his sword;
yet a stone, though itself incapable, cannot cut."

A person is swift to perceive the transgression of another even when it is far away, yet not so quick regarding their own, even when it is close at hand; one does not see one's own wound, but scrutinizes the spot on the moon.
It is better indeed for those whose heat of passion has been extinguished to reveal their own true way of life;
hunters kill deer, but they do not seize the lion.
Noble people reproach even those who are changeless, as if they were ignoble;
what has the lotus done here to the frost, that it always burns it?

The wise are not able to speak of the faults of others, even when they exist, just as they do not speak of their own virtues; whereas the wicked proclaim the faults of others, even when they do not exist, just as they do of their own virtues.
Even when reproached by others, a virtuous person feels shame for having committed a fault; yet a base person, without even doing it himself, proclaims it aloud—fie on such meanness!
A wicked person does not count the suffering caused by another's misfortune as equal to his own destruction;
indeed, at the front of a battle where thousands perish, the headless torso dances.
In the wicked, even a virtue acts as a fault because of their innate depravity; it confounds the minds of people just as the fragrance of poisonous flowers, though sweet, bewilders the senses.
Having attained a high position, one who is lowly is the first to bring ruin upon his master;
for dust on the road first settles upon those who have just arrived.
Garlic, though perfumed with the scents of musk, camphor, agallochum,
and sandalwood, does not abandon its foul-smelling nature, just as a base person does not abandon their innate character.
Thinking, "He has done me a kindness," one should have no expectation of well-being from a wicked person;
like a fire that has been stirred up by the *hotrī* priest, it will surely burn its own dwelling.
Indeed, doing a favor for the wicked becomes the cause of their most grievous fault; for diseases become exceedingly aggravated by treatment that is agreeable.
For nothing else bears fruit like the threshing floor, which brings about only misfortune;
yet it instantly destroys the poison residing in the body, dispelling fatigue.
For the virtuous, the harming of others regardless of their own interest is indeed a calamity;
a serpent does not cease from its venomous fangs simply because it lacks food or water.
When water and milk have attained a state of union,
the swans and the wicked alike possess the power to effect their separation.
Even a spear, though it strikes the teeth and is smeared with deadly *hālāhala* poison, can be endured;
but the harsh words of a wicked person, provoked by a single misdeed, cannot be endured even by the wise.
In this world, deer, birds, and virtuous people— who subsist on grass, water,
and contentment— are the enemies who extract no profit from hunters, fowlers, and dogs.
The affection of the wicked is terrifying, like the horn of a buffalo: vast at its beginning, yet causing division and defilement at its end, and as crooked as the horns of a buffalo.
Like the flame of a lamp, the friendship of a wicked person turns a vessel into a non-vessel, burns away virtues,
quickly destroys affection, and brings impurity to the stainless.
Whose faults have not been surrendered by that wicked man, nor whose virtues forcibly taken away? Even so, he is not freed from those very faults.
The world is not variegated by virtue of a single quality alone.
That one who is being propitiated in many ways is not indeed propitiated— what is surprising about this? But this is an unprecedented excellence of intuition.
That which, when cultivated, leads to the state of being an enemy.
Having encountered censure, the wise man turns away from his faults and is filled with remorse,
thinking, "I have been found out in every way."
An evil person commits an even more evil deed.
In this very way, one cannot live with a wicked person;
what then can be said of one who is a favorite of the king?
For Nala was already difficult to endure from the outset.
How much more so, then, when it is driven by a powerful wind?
Neither was the nectar drunk by the immortals from the ocean,
nor was the virulent Hālāhala poison swallowed by Hari;
rather, it was deposited by Fate within the speech of the wicked.
These two are external; one is internal and the other is different.
For he who becomes angry upon perceiving a particular sign will certainly become placated when that sign disappears;
for his mind indeed harbors hatred toward the cause.
How will he satisfy others?
That which is otherwise is called "outward-facing," but that which vibrates within the heart is indeed other than that;
this conduct is the domain of the courageous victors.
Like a reflection in the water on the yoke, it belongs to those who are non-existent.
Wherever the progress of a slanderer is obstructed,
he perceives even that which has been seen and heard as extremely difficult to endure,
his vision being undifferentiated.
Furthermore, this [is established] by means of scriptural authorities and by the eyes of direct vision.
Let fools depart by hundreds of elephants and horses; let the wise go on foot, devoid of wealth.
Even a flight of crows perched upon a mountain peak does not equal the royal swans on the riverbank.
One who puts you to shame with pleasant words while displaying respect, and who belittles you through flattery— such a friend of fools is to be avoided in every way.
This assembly of the virtuous does not conceal an evident fault out of greed for even a mere atom of merit;
yet they are exceedingly harsh toward those who are without faults.
For those who speak slander and are full of anger, time passes away.
When he rejects [the teaching], his reputation is destroyed;
yet when he practices loving-kindness, his virtues are defiled.
Thus the examiner, having observed the situation in both ways, [acts accordingly].
It renders the ordinary person (pṛthagjana) afflicted by contempt.
Whether cherished by hundreds of good deeds,
or guarded against hundreds of calamities,
a wicked person never produces goodness through their own ill-nature.
He sleeps with confidence in the midst of his arms, like a serpent coiled within its coils.
She cries out and becomes enraged without cause;
she defiles [him] through touch and prevents entry;
she bites in a shameful manner and is never satisfied.
And what indeed is the difference between a dog and a wretch?
A snake, it is said, kills only that which has been struck by a foot or crushed by a firm staff; yet now, another person entirely, acting as a slanderer, behaves like a serpent.
One person merely touches upon [the truth], while another destroys it at its very root.
Some, relying upon that wisdom by which they claim to restrain the spreading darkness of pride in this world— wherein [the mind] has indeed attained a continuous flow— [are thus engaged].
Alas, they expand a pride that is like the blindness of a tree with a hundred branches!
O Kālakūṭa, by whom was this foundation of your abode taught— this succession of ever more distinguished steps—
upon the heart of the ancient Vṛṣalakṣmaṇa?
Now you dwell in the throat, yet again in the speech of the wicked.
Generally, a rogue who is naturally defiled stands near great men and inflicts injury upon those seeking their welfare;
even though he brings happiness to the entire world, he is tormented by cold.
While smoke persists, fire cannot be enjoyed with ease.
Smoke, having somehow reached the state of a cloud, quenches the brilliance of the fire with its showers of rain; likewise,
one of impure nature, having by chance attained greatness, [extinguishes the heat of others].
For the most part, one disregards even one's own kinsmen.
Of this man who hates virtue, who by fate has obtained power, who has gladdened all the wicked, who is free from restraints, and who has forgotten his own base conduct and past deeds.
By whom is happiness experienced when they have entered the range of the Noble Ones?
It is no wonder now that,
through the stroke of ill fate, this base man of no great character remains in such a high position;
for even a street crowded with hundreds of lepers and outcasts can be filled with filth.
In that case, there is merely rubbish, but no treasure.
One might forcibly extract a jewel from between the fangs of a makara’s mouth;
one might even cross the ocean, which is agitated by rows of surging waves;
one might even place an enraged serpent upon one's head like a flower.
But one should not seek to please the minds of foolish people who are stubbornly attached [to their views].
One might obtain oil from sand by pressing it with effort;
one afflicted by thirst might drink water from the mirages of a desert; but one would never find a seat made of the fangs of a venomous serpent.
But one should not seek to please the minds of foolish people who are stubbornly attached [to their views].
I wept in the forest; my entire body was rubbed with ashes;
I planted lotuses on dry land and rained down for a long time upon the desert; I lowered my own tail and made the ears of the deaf ring.
The ignorant person, whose face has been adorned with blindfolded eyes, has been sprinkled [with the water of instruction].

A cow, though long burdened by the weight of her udders, was milked in vain; a eunuch was embraced for a long time as a young woman endowed with loveliness; and a piece of glass was fashioned into a beryl vessel amidst rays of light.
By me, a fool, bowing down to you—who are pitiable and ignorant of virtue—[this has been done].

Even when placed upon the path of the heart, an arrow from a bow meets with the severing of its own side, or the loss of its well-aimed fruit, or the breaking of its own form, or a fall into the fire, or destruction.
Indeed, when straightness becomes crooked through attachment, it is clearly manifest as impurity.

The attachment to virtues leads to calamity; therefore, it is fitting that the Creator, seeing that the virtuous are afflicted by misfortune, has not allowed me to be joined with them. Thus, having observed the misfortunes of the virtuous, I remain devoid of virtue.
In his own home, he will certainly perform a festival of abundant and constant prosperity.
Having observed his own self to be devoid of merit, he likewise desires others to be so;
yet this does not bear fruit unless he laments, for there are no truly virtuous people here.
Therefore, he exerts himself to wipe away, to lick up, or to insult [others].
Oh, how wonderful! This delightful victory over the virtuous has been ordained by fate.
If you do not acknowledge the virtues of others, strive to acquire them yourself; for the envy of others cannot be wiped away by the pretext of disparaging them,
unless you cease from the mental habit of being addicted to desire and hatred.
With parasols formed by the rays of the sun, you shall dispel fatigue.
In their natural association, born of their very birth,
the jewel does not incur the faults of the serpent, nor does the serpent partake of the virtues of the jewel;
indeed, a person becomes either wicked or virtuous by nature alone.
There is neither malice nor wickedness, nor is there goodness in anyone at all.
It is not possible, even with hundreds of efforts, to make that which is unequal equal;

the *nimba* tree does not abandon its innate bitterness, even when situated in a lake of milk. Likewise, a wicked person does not speak words refined by virtue, even if they have become familiar with them.
Even after a long time, iron remains only iron; how could it ever take the form of gold?
It is better to have one's hands placed in the mouth of a wrathful beast;
it is better to drink poison and fall asleep in the presence of Death;
and it is better for one's own body to be shattered into a hundred pieces when hurled from the peak of a great mountain.
But one does not achieve one's own welfare by means of goals attained through base people.

One who dwells in the forest does not calculate the relative weight of things, nor does he harbor any suspicion; he does not examine forms at all, nor does he inquire about a man’s conduct—how could there be such talk?
He does not fear hardship, nor does he fear great calamities or even vulgar speech.
Death, a foolish poet, a wicked man, a bad king, and a thief—these all perform the same action.

A lion took away the life-breaths dear to Pāṇini, the author of the grammatical treatise; an elephant violently crushed the sage Jaimini, the author of Mīmāṃsā; and a crocodile killed Piṅgala, a treasury of knowledge in prosody, at the edge of the shore.
What is the point of virtues for those who are struck down by ignorance, whose minds are afflicted by passion, and who are like animals?
He reviles those worthy of worship, mocks the suffering, and afflicts his kinsmen; he hates the brave, despises those fallen from wealth, and issues commands to his dependents;
he makes secret matters public and, with great effort, fosters a disposition of enmity.
He said: "Swiftly abandon what should not be spoken; one who is worthy of virtues does not accept the shackles of faults."
In the midst of the intense suffering of others, he laughs and sports;
out of delusion, he stumbles and falls upon the dregs of his own impurities;
moreover, being base, he shouts and speaks what is censurable before those who are proud.
"Having heard the harsh words of the enemy, he comes to kill me."
If you will be devoted to the company of the virtuous, you will flourish; but if you fall into the company of the wicked, you will perish.
In that kingdom, they proclaim with the sounds of drums whatever has been proclaimed;
they speak with compassion through the bowing of their bodies, so that one may become free from shame;
they praise that which is exalted, even if it is not fierce, for it does not strike at the vital organs.
Indeed, those who are repositories of both beauty and simplicity are the ones who delight the people of the earth.
The rat clearly attains cleverness in the house of a mountain-like king through its greed for morsels of food,
while the peacock, though possessing a beautiful crest, remains in the pits of the earth within the courtyards, the alleys, the four streets,
and the marketplaces.
They go elsewhere to various [realms], comparable to tortoises dragged from a lake.
Today, hypocrisy is counted as modesty in one who delights in vows; deceit in one who is pure; cruelty in one who is brave;
hostility in one who is upright; wretchedness in one who speaks sweetly; arrogance in one who is spirited; garrulity in one who is eloquent; and incapacity in one who is steadfast.
What indeed could be the merit of those possessed of merit that has not been marred by wicked people?
A mouse, longing for the flesh of a hawk perched on its hand, weighs itself against Mount Kailāsa;
a restless mongoose, wishing to kill a snake, shakes the base of a bamboo tree;
and a frog, desiring to reach the other side of a great abyss, even climbs upon a serpent coiled in the water.
For the most part, one who is not near death remembers their appropriate task, but not a trivial one.
Two types of virtuous people, though possessing merit, meet with misfortune here by fate when they fall into the mouths of the wicked:
one spreads like oil upon water, while the other becomes solid like ghee.
"What refuge have they resorted to that they are being devoured by the enemy?
Why are these riches neither abandoned nor enjoyed by this wretched man?"
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a donor equal to Kṛpaṇa,
who bestows his riches upon others even without being asked.
The misfortune that occurs when wealth is lost is not new, for it is like the loss of a serpent's skin;
yet that very same wretchedness has already been reached by the one who lacks wisdom.
If those who possess wealth are wealthy merely through wealth that is empty of both giving and enjoyment,
then why are we not wealthy by means of that very same wealth?
If one delights in wealth buried deep within the house,
why does that person not delight in Mount Meru by following that same logic?
What can a hungry man do with a mango tree, even if it is laden with fruit?
What can dependents do for a wealthy man who does not give?
If that fortune which is barren of both giving and enjoyment, and which is not enjoyed by friends, belongs to men,
then what indeed would be misfortune?
The wealth accumulated by one person serves as a cause for another;
it is gathered with effort by some, yet the honey is consumed by others.
Whatever you give to the distinguished and whatever you eat day after day—that, I consider, is your wealth; the rest you merely guard for someone else.
In a man who is a slave to the whims of others, fortune is merely a deception; what desire-laden woman here would take pleasure in fashioning bracelets upon his wrists?
He who, having rendered a service, desires a return favor from that person, is wretched;
because he is not master of his own thirst, he even spits upon the one who has helped him.
Wealth has three destinies: giving, enjoyment, or destruction.
For one who neither gives nor enjoys it, the third destiny—destruction—is certain.
If the wealthy possess nothing but the mere attachment to wealth, lacking both generosity and enjoyment, why do we not likewise become wealthy? For Meru is not made of gold.
Even the wealthy are counted among the great poor if they lack the practice of giving;
for since it does not quench thirst, even the ocean is like a desert.
Those who are devoted to the virtuous and who, day after day, have become thoroughly disenchanted with what has passed and what is yet to come,
sleep as it were when they encounter the company of pitiable people, even though they are seekers of the goal.
For those men who are anxious about their enjoyments and intent on the accumulation of wealth,
riches remain in the house like a jewel of a maiden, for the sake of another.
Those in this world who possess wealth yet lack the virtue of renunciation are the most foolish;
they experience only the sufferings of protecting their possessions and being separated from them.
Even among those who are highly skilled in the arts of compassion and supernatural powers, some are destined for destruction;
like a vessel filled with water, they perish in the submarine fire of the world's dissolution.
Even when they have attained them, the wretched do not obtain enjoyments to consume due to their own past actions;
for it is said that the crows suffer from a disease of the mouth when the grapes are ripe.
Wealth does not emerge from the hand of a miser, just as oil does not come from sand;
it may sometimes, by fate, belong only to the one who employs it.
They desire to go forth together with the impurities.
That wealth which is accumulated but not employed in sacrifices, nor given to the virtuous when requested, is the wealth guarded by a miser.
And he goes among thieves, kings, and robbers.
Better these trees, whose dwellings are the forest, their glory of fruit plundered by flocks of birds; but not those wretched, hooded serpents, who are worthy recipients of wealth yet remain miserly.
Their movements were like those of cobras with jewels placed upon their hoods.
With your life well-restrained and guarded as if it were your own body, and with your senses held in check,
you shall follow my path through the cycle of existence.
The fivefold path was not fulfilled by wealth acquired through deceit.
Oh, how great is the cleverness of riches! Though they dwell in the house of a miserable man who is cold and suffering, they neither go toward being abandoned nor toward being enjoyed.
And they cause others as well to attain some degree of liberation.

The body is not refreshed by the contact with water, salt, or rain; it possesses but a faint luster due to long-term consumption of tasteless and coarse food; and it suffers from lack of sleep and weak digestion due to the fear of kings, water, thieves, and fire.
For the miserly, misery is clearly even more severe than the misery of poverty itself.

Each one of them possesses a hundred million [treasures], they are unique masters of the knowledge that perceives the virtues of others, and these wealthy men are teachers of all the arts and the conduct of their preceptors;
yet, alas, even they tremble at the mere hearing of the words of Sumanas for fear of his praise!
O ascetic, let earrings arise upon your head from the scratching of the itch.

He does not manifest joy toward a friend for fear of the expenditure of wealth; he does not allow himself to be drawn in by service out of fear of having to return a favor; he speaks falsely out of fear of losing his path to riches, and even through praise, he is not made to feel affection.
How can one who is afflicted by thirst and terrified by the loss and exhaustion of worldly existence continue to breathe?
If, by the turn of fate, you had placed this essence of virtues upon your head,
would not the entire waning orb have been brought to fullness in an instant?
Thus, for the sake of worldly devotion, you loudly proclaim your own straightforwardness toward the virtuous as being entirely false.
Those whose minds are terrified by the expenditure of wealth make their honor empty of its true purpose through material riches.
What greed can there be for a wise person regarding a mere fragment of the cosmic egg?
The ocean is never agitated by the leaping of small fish.
Those of unrestrained mind do not set foot even upon the path that leads to liberation,
for their desires remain bounded even when they have attained the entire world.
For men whose minds are haughty, these two bring happiness:
either the cessation of all attachments or extensive sovereign power.
Whether this person is a kinsman or a stranger is a calculation for those of small minds;
for men of noble heart, the entire earth itself is their family.
Old age, death, misfortune, and disease already afflict those who exist;
why then does birth itself not repeatedly cause shame to the wise man?
In this ever-turning cycle of existence, who is there that dies and is not born again?
He is truly born by whose birth his lineage attains greatness.
Perhaps that man of excessive pride might be seen on earth by whom the wealthy, with their faces swollen with arrogance, were never looked upon.
O King, the earth and its virtues are held in high esteem by those who possess discernment;
why then do even those of exalted intellect fall into states of humiliation caused by others?
It is fitting for a blind man, whose face has been struck by the unseen, to beg; alas, what a great misery it is that even one who possesses sight must beg!
The torment of the fire of poverty is stilled by the waters of contentment; who indeed would look upon the internal burning caused by the frustration of those who beg?
He alone possesses the majesty of effortless mastery over all perfected qualities; for even toward the wealth desired by the three worlds, he has no longing.
For those who are intoxicated by their learning alone and yet remain miserly despite possessing wealth,
fire has arisen from the water for those cursed by fate.
What is the use of that fortune which is like a bride who remains alone;
it is not common property to be enjoyed even by travelers, like a prostitute?
For those who possess wealth, generosity is their virtue; for those who possess generosity, it is their wealth.
When wealth and generosity are separated from one another, they are merely a pretense.
Like a cluster of blossoms, the conduct of the wise man is twofold:
either he stands at the head of the entire world, or he withers away in the forest alone.
Among men, he alone is fit for the foremost rank who,
with the hand of renunciation, wipes away the dust of supplication from the faces of those who seek his favor.
Blessed are those who do not hear the piteous words of suppliants, their desires already fulfilled by the mere sound of the syllable "A."
That intellect which is devoid of the quality of being (sattva) is considered mere womanhood; and that being which is not endowed with wisdom is considered mere beasthood, not manhood.
The wise renounce even their dear desires and their very lives,
but they do not seek great honor from their enemies.
I consider this nature of the high-minded one to be most wonderful:
that even when being assisted, he feels affection rather than dissolving [in resentment].
The mind feels ashamed even toward one who has previously returned a favor; yet a favor bestowed upon one who has already rendered a service is greater than death itself.
Even one who returns a great favor does not become equal to the original benefactor; another merely imitates what was done, while yet another acts as if it were without reward.

For he who sustains his kinsmen, his dependents, and his friends, the glory of his household is truly fruitful; fie upon the accumulation of wealth that serves only as a means of subsistence for others!
Even a cloud, though consisting of water, becomes beloved to all the world;
yet the sun, though its rays are constantly extended, causes those without eyes to become blind.
It is not attained by anyone, for even their desires turn back from it;
yet even if that is not obtained, what is the fruit of pride for other wise men?
The formation or the destruction of effects occurs through the application of destiny;
yet, regarding appropriate or inappropriate actions, my own engagement and withdrawal depend upon me.
Life lasting for an eon is not attained, nor is that which is desired;
yet the world still performs what ought not to be done—aiming at what indeed?
Abundance of wealth is not the cause for anyone to be naturally open-handed;
what is the excellence of the clouds in the rainy season compared to that of the ocean?
If she was produced by herself, then she is one's own daughter; if she was produced by her father, then she is indeed one's sister, O Śrī;
and if she has union with another, then she is the wife of another.
The wise, whose minds are bound to the renunciation of that [worldly existence], become truly enlightened.
The toil of acquiring wealth is fruitless for this person,
even when it bears fruit;
the acquisition of wealth is merely for one's own gratification.
To attract others to the supreme acquisition of virtues.
The man of deluded intellect who, out of greed for a mere fragment of wealth, praises another man before the boon-granting goddesses while they are present—
I consider him to be the foremost among men.
"Just as it is said that the body, when deprived of life,
appears like a piece of wood,
even so do I perceive my own life."
It is empty because it is pervaded by that which transcends the world.
Even though they are peaceful, where could they scatter their splendor?
Where could they not blaze? Where indeed could they not spread forth? Surely the Creator himself has obstructed them.
In the upper reaches of the cosmic egg, they are like lamps within jars.
For even when one whose conduct is steadfast is treated with contempt,
their quality of being a true being cannot be destroyed;
just as fire, even when turned downward, cannot be extinguished.
"Noble sir, the crests [of the flames] move only at certain times."
It is illogical to say that those who have been born will not perish;
for arising itself is necessarily the cause of perishing,
and it is indeed equal when one is afflicted by the calamity of death.
Death is better for one whose mind is intent on the welfare of others.
Even in this boundlessly vast expanse of time, only two or three such virtues as these pass into the count; alas, the worldly person is vulgar, for he finds no supreme satisfaction in them.
Stiffened with pride, he regards even this entire world as a mere blade of grass.

These wise ones do not experience distress within themselves merely by reflecting on their own minds; for as long as there is no suffering caused by that [external world], they remain untroubled. Yet those who here, day and night, follow the will of others— ||| Subhv_0531-3 aharniśamihaiva ye paramanuvṛttyā punar- ||| [they are truly afflicted]. ||| Subhv_0531-4 kṣaṇamapi hi viśramya na śaktāḥ kleśavṛttibhiḥ / ||| Subhv_0531-5 parārthamudyamaṃ kartuṃ kāruṇyaparivarjitāḥ // ||| For, deprived of compassion, they are unable to exert themselves for the sake of others even for a moment, being overcome by the activities of the afflictions. ||| Subhv_0531-6 tasmādye svahitābhyāsavyāvṛttāḥ sarvabhūtaye / ||| Subhv_0531-7 teṣāmabhyudayo dṛṣṭo bhūtānāṃ bhūtabhāvanaḥ // ||| Therefore, the prosperity of those who have turned away from practicing their own self-interest for the welfare of all beings is seen to be the true cultivation of the elements for living creatures. ||| Subhv_0531-8 ye tu svārthaparāsteṣāṃ dṛṣṭā svārthasya hānayaḥ / ||| Subhv_0531-9 parārthabhāvanāyuktāḥ svārthaṃ prāptā mahātmabhiḥ // ||| But for those intent on their own self-interest, the loss of their own welfare is observed; whereas the Great-Souled Ones, engaged in the cultivation of the welfare of others, have attained their own true purpose. ||| Subhv_0531-10 tasmātsvārthaṃ parityajya parahitārthamudyatāḥ / ||| Subhv_0531-11 bhavantyabhimataprāptāḥ svārthatyāgānmahātmabhiḥ // ||| Therefore, having abandoned their own self-interest and striving for the sake of the welfare of others, the Great-Souled Ones attain their desired goal through the renunciation of self-interest. ||| Subhv_0531-12 tasmātsvārthaparo loko nāstyevetyupadhāryatām / ||| Subhv_0531-13 parārthabhāvanāyāṃ hi svārthasiddhirvidhīyate // ||| Consequently, it should be understood that there is no such thing as a person solely intent on their own interest; for the accomplishment of one's own welfare is established precisely through the cultivation of the welfare of others. ||| Subhv_0531-14 tasmātparārthasampattau yatnaḥ kāryo mahātmabhiḥ / ||| Subhv_0531-15 svārthasiddhiḥ parārthena vidhīyate mahātmabhiḥ // ||| Therefore, the Great-Souled Ones should exert effort toward the fulfillment of the welfare of others; for the Great-Souled Ones accomplish their own welfare by means of the welfare of others. ||| Subhv_0531-16 tasmādyathā svahitābhyāse svārthāśā na vidhīyate / ||| Subhv_0531-17 tathā paropakāre 'pi svārthasiddhirvidhīyate // ||| Therefore, just as no hope for one's own interest is entertained while practicing for one's own benefit, so too the accomplishment of one's own interest is established through helping others. ||| Subhv_0531-18 tasmādyathā hitābhyāsātsvārthāśā na vidhīyate / ||| Subhv_0531-19 tathā paropakāre 'pi svārthasiddhirvidhīyate // ||| Therefore, just as no hope for one's own interest is entertained while
They carry away one who has been conquered; what need is there for even a slight object of compassion?
In the past, some with vast hearts brought forth the world;
others maintained it, and still others gave it away as if it were a blade of grass.
Indeed, here in this world, other steadfast ones enjoy fourteen worlds.
What is this fever of pride among men who are merely the lords of a few towns?
For that earth upon which not even a single moment has passed without being enjoyed by hundreds of kings— what kind of high regard could there be for its acquisition on the part of rulers?
For they become masters over but a fraction of it, or even over a mere remnant of a portion of that fraction.
When it is time for departure, fools instead feel joy.
O heart, why do you immerse yourself daily in the manifold impurities of affliction, when you could instead lead others' minds toward serene faith?
For when you yourself are gracious, you are like a wish-fulfilling jewel that spontaneously grants its desires.
Secluded from conceptual thought, what desired object do you not attain?

Even without wealth, the wise man attains a state of high honor and exaltation; whereas the wretched man, though embraced by wealth, falls into a state of humiliation. [The wise] naturally experience that vast [joy] arising from the attainment of a multitude of virtues.
Even one who wears a golden garland does not obtain such splendor as this.
He whose wealth is enjoyed by supplicants with happiness as if they were staying in his own home,
and he whose intellect is intent on the destruction of darkness— these two alone are truly living.
But he who is concerned only with himself, even though possessed of great power, is wretched if he lacks true learning.
Like a form held by one who cannot draw, its existence is indeed neither existent nor non-existent.
To this group of benefactors— who provide support, offer shelter and space, grant the vision of the sky,
and possess various other qualities that establish the majesty of their own radiant selves—
it is always most difficult to part.
O Great-minded One, how can the mind of those who possess great intelligence abandon the ornament of the shame of wretchedness?

That which is enjoyed perpetually by teachers, parents, kinsmen, and good friends, and not according to one's own whim; which enemies, though greedy, do not covet when it is acquired through valor; and for which there is no possibility of occurrence through the loss of virtuous ones or the destruction of friends—[that wealth is truly secure].
That joy of the virtuous toward one who is not endowed with excellence is like that [joy] toward a two-legged being; how great indeed is that [joy]?
For those virtuous ones who do not abandon the path of righteousness, misfortunes may arise by fate;
let such things befall them as befell Bali when he himself surrendered the sovereignty of the three worlds to the Primal Person (Viṣṇu),
or as befell Indra through his many loathsome and censurable deeds.
May even my sovereignty over the gods not be a cause for shame.
A bed of grass, a seat upon a verdant lawn, a pure stone for a dwelling, and the forest floor for a chamber;

cool water from mountain cascades for drink, roots for food, and deer for companions—when all such desired luxuries are obtainable in the forest, this alone is its sole defect: [The presence of wild beasts.]
For those who seek their own welfare yet remain idle, though they are never fruitless in accomplishing the welfare of others.
For the wise do not give up even a very small portion of their native land out of negligence;
jewels that have been removed from their place still retain their value.
The crow-faced frogs became the heads of kings.
"Brave men who have mastered the sciences and women endowed with beauty—
wherever they may go, there they shall find their dwellings prepared."
Rudra has fled to Mount Kailāsa, Hari to the ocean, and the gods to the heavens;
even the powerful lords of serpents have first retreated to the depths of Pātāla.
I believe the lotus-dwelling deities have hidden within the lotus forest out of fear for the caravan of supplicants.
In the Kali age, virtuous persons are solely intent upon uplifting those who are fallen.
The base do not indeed begin [an undertaking] out of fear of obstacles; the mediocre, having begun, desist when struck by obstacles;
but even when being struck by obstacles multiplied a thousandfold, the superior do not cease.
Those of supreme virtue do not abandon what has already been undertaken.
How can there ever be fullness for that perpetrator of faults, whose good qualities do not blossom even as his hands stretch out?
The moon, though waxing and waning, reaches proximity and fullness, yet never departs from its distance; likewise, it is fitting that the friend and others are always somewhat obscured.
How was that storehouse of splendors, the creator of such a being, not ashamed,
having reached a mere fragment of the cosmic egg and stretching out his feet?
The rising of the sun alone is praiseworthy; what other rising could be so esteemed? For when it has risen, there is neither darkness nor light.
Was her loveliness not sufficient by itself, she who was adorned with beauty-marks, that even the lotus, though scorched by the heat, sought refuge in her?
By extending his arm that hung down from his right side like the sun,
he not only diminished himself, but also shortened the day itself.
The zodiac sign through which the sun moves for two months and two years does not pass through for the moon in even three days.

"Even though the moon is borne upon his head by Śambhu, it is still consumed by Rāhu; alas, dependence on another is indeed a hardship. Let the water of the Pañcāpaka fall, let it go to another direction!"

How can he who is devoid of teeth be called the "Sun" (Sūrya) by the wise—when, having already consumed the multitude of Pisces, he is now prepared to devour Aries? Or how can he enter the fire or go to the earth?
[He is so called because] he has indeed devoured the multitude of Pisces and is intent on devouring Aries.
Let him fall into water, let him go to another region,
let him enter fire, or let him go to the earth;
what concern is there for the virtues of one who has been swallowed by the rays of the sun?
There is a longing for the wonders that delight the entire world.
At that very moment, the great earth trembled as soon as the moon began to shimmer,
before the orb of the sharp-rayed sun had even appeared;
and when that treasury of all light had fully risen—
And what is the difference between a cloudless sky and a portion of white clouds?
Behold how those of virtuous conduct, who discern between what is real and unreal, describe him;
for the thieves, the false ascetics, and others speak of him in such a manner.
If that were perceived as something produced, then it would be [perceived] by the sun.
There is indeed one certain [portion] of the essence of nectar, most beautiful and priceless—
a certain digit (*kalā*) of Śaśadhara—
by which he was installed as the Supreme Lord by the Knower of Qualities.
In the Cūḍāmaṇi [Tantra], it is said that for him there is no stain or fault.
Although many great and mighty fires rise up,
and even the moon is sufficient to adorn the circle of the world,
it neither rises nor sets apart from the sun.
By its rising, day is produced; by its setting, night.

He who does not cease from worldly joy, even while being tormented by suffering, would surely find that the dawn of his own life was never truly new; for fate, in some inexplicable way, has made him carry only himself.
O friend, look at this moon as well; it passes its time distractedly.
The waning moon enters the circle of the stars month after month;
having regained some portion, it follows ever more and more distantly.
If, by some chance, it should become full, it rises in rivalry with the sun.
He did not cease from wickedness due to pride, nor did he desist from wretchedness due to dejection.
Having placed his foot upon the summit of Sumeru, the king of mountains,
he who has traversed the middle realm of Viṣṇu where darkness is destroyed—
that very moon now falls from the sky with only a few rays remaining.
It is difficult to ascend even for the great when one stands at the very top; yet, the fall of a water-jar is auspicious and does not lead to great distress, because:
Who has not gone to their end in the course of time? Others have gone, and others will go—where is that splendor of yours, possessing such blazing majesty, compared to the destruction of dogs?
Where is this supreme splendor of the moon, whose head is severed by the sharp-edged Rāhu?
This [beauty] is appropriate for the Creator’s design; yet it causes pain, O friend, because it moves through the sky devoid of shame.
The death of a child does not lead to great suffering because: "Who has not passed away in due time? Others have gone, and others will go;
only this causes distress—that one is overtaken by the darkness that lies outside the light."
Having obtained space within that very same primordial great void.
That very earth, which was awakened and nourished by hundreds of flavors day after day from the beginning of creation, was at the time of the end of the eon consumed by its own rays; thus,
having performed some action of its own, it is subject to the destruction of both past and future.
That sun as well, its rays withdrawn at the end of the day, has gone to the setting mountain.

Since this entire world has been rendered truly possessed of sight by Your Majesty, the one of fierce luster, who has utterly uprooted the thick masses of darkness rivaling dense clouds; now that the Sun has set, how cruel indeed is the wicked person!
Just as one who is full of apprehension provides support for all the world, or like a lamp in the darkness.
First, the Lord of Mountains (Himavat) is to be pitied for his sovereignty,
since he bears upon his head both the stainless skull of a human being— complete with its aperture— and the moon, which is likewise touched by the Gaṅgā;
yet the moon is even more pitiable than he, for despite such an insult, he remains as he is.
With a body as white as the moonlight, laughter, and lotuses, he cultivates the foremost joy.
The ocean, acting as a father, embraces the waxing moon with joy at its own increase, yet abandons it from afar when it is waning; for, having become the reservoir of waters,
he gradually brings about the rise of that very moon by means of its diminished substance.
And since he remains even further away from fullness—oh, homage to that friend!
By whom has the rising of the moon— the lord of planets— strung together with darkness, standing afar off,
not been desired as bringing joy to the circle of the virtuous?
Yet now, by this very same [moon] having risen, such a painful deed has been performed!
One does not perceive this world as it truly is, thinking, "This is the maker of the world."
Even the hundreds of *piśācas* who daily flee in terror from the darkness seized by the thousand hands [of the Lord], find it strange when that very darkness is destroyed by the moon,
which has its rays severed by Hari.
The sun alone seizes that splendor, even while accompanied by a mass of clouds.
The sun is ever-striving to protect the entire world seized by darkness;
yet not even one person in this world is capable of protecting that [sun] when it is seized by darkness.
That the lotus of the Ocean of Virtues blooms at night while the lily of the Ocean of Fools does not, and that Fortune has reached the former— this is surely the majesty of the King.
A night devoid of the moon never shines;
the moon, too, when deprived of the night, is indeed shorn of its splendor. What is the reason that, of these two, one [is absent] every month?
The embrace [of the consort] is practiced for the sake of transcending birth.
Having left the night, the moon departs for the bright fortnight while remaining reclined upon his celestial bed in the sky;
but during the dark fortnight,
it is night [for him], as he withdraws from that bed where he was asleep.
If that is so, what of it? Does that much constitute the status of husband and wife?
He who, having destroyed the cataracts [of ignorance], illuminates the world; who bestows the vision of awakening; who is adorned with manifold virtues;
and for whom there is no weariness in acts of altruism—[to him I bow].
The wise person pays homage to the one who is praised, not to the one who is miserable.
Whether this deliberation be true or false,
what matters is that for one who has crossed over the scales, whose greatness is celebrated and whose darkness is destroyed, there arises a loud clamor of people from his lofty station.
For the splendor of the sun does not become diminished by having entered a maiden.
Even the moon, the leader of the stars, though possessed of nectar-like form and endowed with splendor,
becomes devoid of its orb’s radiance upon reaching the sun.
Who, when seated in the assembly of others, does not incur insignificance?
O dull-witted one, arrogant with pride, do not harbor rivalry toward this Sun, my own progenitor, who is high and yields excellent fruit; for by his very majesty,
all your misfortunes have been destroyed from afar on their own.
This friend of the virtuous, a treasury of splendor, does not desire to conceal his transgression from anyone.
"O King, do not harbor the rivalry 'his state of happiness is equal to mine' even toward your own father, the cause of your birth; for he,
O Prince, is the one who [sustains] all the world."
His soul was purified by the rays of the sun, which is like a hand to the mountain that destroys darkness.
Having recognized his own fitness for the smoke-bannered fire (the sacrifice), the Lord of Day, intent on laughter and tranquility, abandoned his grip out of parsimony and bestowed the poison;
yet he who does not know fate is called a "peacock"— let him be born from that very source.
By whose power even the lamps become like the fierce-rayed sun for the world.
Those lotuses that are devoted to me suffer when struck by the wind;
even those days that have me as their sole refuge reach a state of extreme emaciation.
Thus departing toward a distant quarter, as if out of love for the people he has relied upon—
In the winter, the Blessed One, the Lord of Day, has departed from the world; let him be served.
Neither anointing nor consecration is performed for the lion in the forest;
for one who has acquired his strength through valor, the sovereignty over the king of beasts comes of its own accord.
"I am alone, without companion; I am solitary, without retinue.
Even in a dream, such a thought never arises in the lion, king of beasts.
The lion, who shatters the temples of intoxicated elephants with his thunderbolt-like claws,
incurs only contempt by the mere mention of his name as the "enemy of deer."

The claws of the lord of beasts, though sharp as they spring forth, do not at all fall upon the temples of elephants that are eager to crush them; nor do the harsh talons of the lion descend upon the bounding deer.
What can we do, and who is to be blamed, for this inconsistency?
Even a single hair is not the price of a lion, yet ten million is the price for an elephant.
How could deer, even while sleeping, fearlessly tread upon the paws of a lion whose frontal globes have been crushed by his play?
How can this wretched lion, with hands smeared with the blood from splitting the temples of rutting elephants,
dare to vie with the Lord Hari?
The elephant, sluggish with the weight of rut, roars in the forest only so long as the lion, with his mane clinging to his head, does not approach.
Having torn out the teeth of a lion that is adorned with the tusks of its own kind—teeth swollen with the pride and strength of its solar brilliance—do men dwell in happiness? No.
What need is there for an extensive description of Hari’s battle with the lion, in which intoxicated elephants fell, struck by the blows of his single palm?
For as long as the lion’s paws remained clung to the bones,
the inhabitants of that forest continued to sustain the life of the herd for that moment.
His stride is a fierce and terrifying prowess that shatters the temples of roaring elephants; he is the conqueror of the endless, wearying battle with the deer.
How can Hari accept the consequence?
Even a lion falls upon elephants whose temple-walls are stained with rut;
this is simply the nature of the courageous, for age is certainly not the cause of their majesty.
To the solitary forest-dweller, who is a jewel among women and skilled in the science of political ethics,
the title "King" is applied to that lord of beasts who stands preeminent among living beings.
The lion displays his prowess against an elephant whose trunk is marked with scars from the tips of its tusks,
but not against a mongoose that dwells within the hollows of mountains scratched by the points of its own claws.
Who would venture to place the palm of their hand upon the mouth of a lion whose mane is smeared with the rut from temples dripping with ichor?
While hundreds of young elephants, devoid of restraint, were leaping about out of delusion and rushing forward in their childishness,
his mental disposition was such that it was accustomed to splitting the temples of rutting bulls.
For a lion, it is only appropriate to close one's eyes.
Having seen before him the lion, the enemy of deer, who was like Death itself, with his mane and shoulders bristling and darkened by rage,
and being approached by flocks of birds eager for his flesh and blood—
It is like being deluded upon the heads of a herd of elephants blinded by rut.
He who is the lion, by whom the enemy of existence— like an elephant— is torn apart by the fierce claws that are like saws,
and who has cast aside the darkness with a fresh mass of blood arising from the shattered frontal globes of that foe;
he is the one who has destroyed the Tīrthikas.
He was once eternal; fie upon him today, that seeker of wealth who is surpassed by a blade of grass!
A body that is putrid, an intellect intent on the slaughter of others,
and a discernment of right and wrong that exists only in name— thus, there is nothing at all virtuous about the king of beasts.
But its radiance flashes forth as that which makes the world appear like a jewel.
May the Lord of the Simhas, the enemy of the charioteer of the deer, be my refuge;
yet I consider even that to be merely duality.
For him, by the blow of the vajra at the tip of his quivering hand—
The foot of the elephant, which is like the trunk of a rutting elephant, has been cast down by the blow.

In the cave of Hari, where the hosts of choice serpents were made famous by the scratching of their nails, claws, and the tips of their hoods as they swayed, Kṛṣṇa was drawn out by the gaze of the son of Saramā,
who was struck with fear.
"Those who were established in the dhāraṇīs have now been seen here today in such a wretched state."
Where is the lion in this world, who— his trunk agitated by the desire to split the temples of intoxicated elephants, his tusks like thunderbolts with tips of lightning—
would be satisfied by a mere trifle of pride?
Even when his life is at stake, he maintains the sustenance of his own body.
May he protect me— from this cloud that roars loudly in its station with the intent of supporting the entire world, whose mind is intoxicated by the rut-fluid of the elephant,
who is fond of licking the lion’s mane, and who, having shattered the earth with thunderbolts, rains down hailstones.
The inconceivable breaking of his own limbs occurred through the falling of the state of being and non-being upon the state of being and non-being.
Does the ground of the battlefield, adorned with pearl-like drops trickling from the temples of towering elephants pierced by the sharp claws of lions,
not steal away the enmity of Hari toward his lion-like foes?
Even when combined, it is entirely not a single, uniform effect throughout.

Hari effortlessly shatters the fierce, clawed hands of the enemy of Ugra, who is adorned by mountain-like testicles that follow his movements, and who is accompanied by the dense, humming sound of swarms of bees circling those testicles.
In the three worlds, majesty alone is the teacher, not a distorted form.
O Lord of Heroes, let not the lion— the king of beasts, whose prowess is naturally formidable and who dwells in mountain peaks, thickets,
and caves clothed in his own skin— be provoked by us, for he is constantly occupied with drinking the rut-fluid flowing from the temples of elephants.
Whatever has been obtained by your own mind, which is agitated by calamity, let that be reflected upon.
To King Mīraśāha,
who desired the *kāśmīrāṅgatuṅga* [sandalwood], the lord of the earth Śāhabuddīna dispatched a messenger with this message:
Why do you wish to wander here with steps as restless as a peacock’s tail-feathers, thus unafraid? Desist! This forest is not empty;
it stands here, filled with the blood spurting from the crushing of the lord of elephant-herds.
The lion, adorned with a magnificent mane, shone brilliantly upon the surface of the earth.
The lion, whose magnificent mane is stained with blood trickling from the frontal globes of elephants struck by his thick claws,
[is heard] through the utterances of those who are extremely distressed and terrified by his deep roar.
Like Patañjali, he feels shame upon reaching the level of the battlefield.
O bulls, roam at will through the thickets of the forest, O fearless ones;
O lords of the earth, drink again the clear water from the beds of lotuses;
O elephants, once more bear the beauty of rut upon your cheeks.
Through his inability to endure [the challenge], the lion was driven far away.
O lion, that you sprang forth from afar upon seeing the cloud thundering in the sky— though it was merely a mass of water—
has already distressed the minds of the great; for now,
out of fear of the unsubstantial, you take on the appearance of a hero before our eyes.
Upon seeing that very thing, we were overcome with shame; what more need be said? We fled to the depths of Pātāla.

He who was once the rival of dense clouds rumbling with the weight of water— those clouds whose sole amusement was the sport of shattering the jars and pots of the city of the many blinded by pride— is now [that very same one].
The lion, his body crouched as he leaps from his cage, assumes the ten postures of a sage.
Even when his life-force was exhausted, even when he was afflicted by old age, even when his vital breaths were failing,
even when he had reached a state of suffering, and even when his intellect and fortitude had collapsed as his life was departing—
he remained like a thunderbolt with the tips of its claws lashing out to split the temples of the lordly elephants puffed up with pride.
Does the lion, the foremost of those great in pride, eat withered grass?
His body is not too tall, his teeth are not too prominent, and his trunk is not overly long;
truly, O Varāṇa, this lordly lion does not rival the clouds with its mane.
For the seed of irresistible splendor was placed within his heart by the Creator in the beginning.
Because of its similarity to that [meat], one easily considers even the vegetable food to be animal flesh.
Intoxicated by the pervasive and lingering scent of the thick ichor from the frontal globes of rutting elephants, his mane bristling with the brilliance of fully released pearls,
he was a destroyer of disease and widowhood, whose majestic splendor was seized by the pride of the strength of his own arms.
Who has ever seen a lion that is constantly unable to endure the caravan of deer, terrified by the sound of a thunderbolt?
Who, who, where would this boar not grunt with a roar as terrible as thunder?
Who, who is not prepared to make every lotus pond stainless? And which forest groves would not be uprooted by the army of the God of Love?
The five-faced lion dwells there, bound by his attachment to the playful sport with the lioness.

How could the hand of that man— who, even as a child, delighted in the pearls and coral-like blood flowing from the frontal globes of intoxicated elephants split open by his nails— ever stretch forth before others, even in the midst of the most dire calamities?
When Hari seizes the breath of one who is being turned over in a pit or a whirlpool, he takes away their life.
Seeing the lion’s teeth, which resembled the tips of claws smeared with blood-stained meat,
the herds of deer fled even from the direction of the thicket;
such was the miserable condition of that aged lion.
There is no means of subsistence even with the limbs of jackals and dogs.
Roaring at the rain-clouds, the representatives of the Vindhya mountains, driven by the wind,
rushed impetuously like surging oceans; having slain elephants in battle, they moved from tree to tree with their bodies slightly wounded, [resting] upon the branches of the *Sākāmaṛga*.
Even you, having become angry, alas, have fallen into the fifth state of wretchedness!
The herds of elephants, intoxicated with rut, having brought low the splendor of the peaks of Mount Kailāsa with their trumpeting that skillfully mimicked thunder, and the lion,
by his roar, have filled the ten directions with harsh cries as they exert themselves in their combined state.
Even among cows and jackals, why would one who possesses the profound wisdom known throughout the entire world exert himself?
Then the elephant said: "O young elephant, abandon your fickleness;
O long-faced one, practice the vow of discipline."
Fragile as the tips of a lion’s claws,
that heavy goad of yours cannot endure even a slight touch.
O Bāṇabhaṭṭa, engage in play; enjoy the lotuses; plunge into the waters of the mountain cascades.
O elephant, whose limbs are cherished by a herd of females devoted to him,
release your longing for the navel of the king of deer.
By this elephant,
rendered frantic by unrestrained and independent intoxication,
this [world] has been thrown into confusion.
Having placed his foot upon the head of the elephant trainer's son, he said: "How was this dull-witted one forcibly brought under my control?"
The trunk of the elephant,
served by its herd, was honored by the heaps of pollen falling from the flowers on the trees of the Vindhya mountains, which were showering light like rain.
He who was once the lord of men and a master of the earth has now become a bull; how is this so, and for what purpose, or is it simply the power of time?
O bull among elephants,
whose limbs were scorched by the intense heat of the fire of separation arising from within, you who have mastered what was heard— abandon your grief!
Who is capable of wiping away the marks written by the Creator’s own hand upon the forehead?
"O, O lord of elephants! For how many days now have you been passing through this desert?
Somewhere, with the waters of the Revā river applied by your own trunk to your own trunk—"
Furthermore, you shall cause [them] to attain equanimity during the summer heat.
"In this world, who indeed possesses such great authority that he would not become a vessel for sin?"—
thinking thus, she struck down even him who had approached her.
Why is he called "Mātaṅga" (the Outcaste) even beyond this?

In the water filled with the filaments of fresh lotuses, she does not take up even a morsel; she finds no pleasure in the mud, though it be half a piece of a lotus stalk; and she cannot endure a woman who dangles about her, even if she be moist with affection, should she prove unfaithful.
The lord of elephants remembered his beloved wife, who had fallen from the sky.
The elephant,
though bearing a trunk as long as a creeper, does not take the cool water from its tip; nor does he approach the lovely lotuses where bees cluster, for he has become separated from his mate.
Even while stretching out his final breaths, alas, he finds no rest at the end of life.

Having uprooted rivers like trees from their banks and having struck down rut-maddened elephants with his hands, feet, and tusks as if they were rival elephants, he reached old age— an ignoble state that engenders hatred in young people.
This very same elephant endures the insults of young elephants.

O leader of the elephant herd, it would be better for this foot of yours— marked by the goad and adorned with the webbed toes— not to fall upon my head out of a desire to discipline me; it would not be better to suffer the blow of the tips of the thunderbolt-like claws of the Lord of Lions at the end of time.
Of the sharp lion of the forest that has arisen with violence.
Having abandoned those who are self-reliant in the remote forests of Śailaka and Takṣa,
your mind has fallen— devoid of true devotion— into the company of city-dwellers;
this [state] consists of the exhaustion resulting from the labor of binding it with firm ropes.
O intoxicated elephant, the fruit that has ripened through your actions corresponds to your passion.
Where is that mountain-like form, and where is this movement with such speed and playfulness?
Where are those glances, so effortlessly closing the eyes like buds, and where indeed is that majesty?
Where is the delight in striking with the body, and where is that hand? Alas, how it has come to this!
Having mounted you, he causes you—who are under the control of another—to move about at his command, O "Si"su.foot.
The earth trembled at the stamping of his feet; the birds were terrified;
the lakes were marked with mud; and the trees had their branches stripped by hundreds of elephants whose ichor was flowing.
Having reached this forest, which was empty of tigers due to the power of fate, he was accompanied by young elephant calves.
That very thing is called "the made" (kṛtam), which cannot be spoken of due to its state of being utterly beyond conceptualization.
Even while eating lotus roots, consuming meat, rice,
and other foods at every season, carrying various kinds of burdens, wearing garlands of bones, and holding a chowrie-tassel in his ear— the elephant nevertheless remembers [his mate].
Now, he dwells forever in misery amidst the dense forests of *sallakī* trees in the Indhyā mountains.
