Having seen that elephant— whose growth was nourished by handfuls of the finest sprouts of young shoots, who drank from the lotus-leaf cups the milk remaining after the oblation, and whose trunk was encircled by a swarm of bees sluggish with intoxication; [He saw] that very calf, who had drunk the milk left over from the fire-sacrifice from the hollow of a lotus leaf.
Standing at a distance, the ascetic looked back again and again with longing and fear.
Placing your trunk between your tusks, with your head hanging down and both eyes closed—O elephant, why do you suffer because of a courtesan? Who indeed has not been deceived?
Take your food with a peaceful mind; let this constant sorrow now be abandoned.
Those who are intoxicated, lacking discernment, and of unsteady intellect, fall into calamity.
The sustenance provided by the morsels of food remaining from her husband’s mouth,
and the water drunk from the remainder of what was left after the hand had stirred it— having first abandoned her very life for these, this is the fruit obtained by the virtuous wife.
The face of the elephant, distressed by the infliction of its bonds, was never seen to suffer in such a way.
O young elephant calf, abandon your bond of affection for the female elephant as you take up morsels of food;
now provide a coating of mud as a welcome balm for the wounds caused by the knots of the tethering rope.
These women, charming with the playful allure of the wives of the best of Śabaras, have been left far behind.
The foothills of the Vindhya mountains are grey with the pollen of flowers from the trees in the groves of the Revā river.

The noble elephant, however, performs the shaking of its trunk, the moving of its limbs, the lowering of its head, falling to the ground, and the exposing of its face and belly for the giver of its own food.
The wise one gazes [upon it] and enjoys it with four hundred [attendants].
That which is the Vindhya mountain, that which is Mount Śikhari, that Pippala tree beloved by Piṅgala within it,
the peacock that rushes toward the clouds with longing due to their sudden arrival, and the elephant—
why does the crow remember even one of these out of goodness? For fate indeed scrapes away everything.
Yet even more difficult to endure than death itself is this: that I, so dull-witted, have been placed at the yoke.

In the midst of the Vindhya mountains, he who had grown great through the jasmine buds and young shoots tossed by the gusts of wind from the river Narmadā— now, by the power of fate, that very same elephant,
separated from his mate, makes a mournful sound.
Alas, what a miserable state is this, where one is rendered helpless by the rope of vajra that sinks into the depths! What can be done?
O elephant among perfumes, O great mountain-elephant,
even now do not remember [the past] with eyes closed by intoxication;
abandon your pride and resort to the present.
The crookedness of fate, the command above, and the goad.

O lady with eyes like those of an elephant in rut, do not cast away the rivers of clear and sweet water to quench your unbearable thirst; for even when all the water in the autumn-dug ponds has been drunk,
your thirst finds no peace in that water.
Since this village has but a single path, there will certainly be doubt regarding his life.
Blessed indeed are those deer in the forest who feed on durvā grass and young shoots,
for they do not behold the faces of those whose minds are intoxicated by worldly power.
Deprived of her mate, breathless, with her heart’s wound still raw,
she stands motionless as if bound, like a doe beside a deer caught in a snare.
The quarters are stretched out with ropes, the waters with snares,
the earth with nooses, and the forest edges are ablaze with fire;
hunters, holding their arrows, follow his footprints.
To what region does the leader of the herd of deer resort?
Go from here more quickly, O deer; you are being parted from your life-breaths.
Why do you stand with your neck turned, looking back again and again? Those wretched hunters do not feel even the slightest bit of compassion for you.
When the Kaṭhina ceremony has been concluded, these are the delusions of the eyes.
A thirsty deer, following the tracks of deer that have been burnt by the heat upon the dry land,
does not cease even though its mind is exhausted;
for one who lacks knowledge of reality does not seek anything other than a lake.
On the great stage, there is no expectation, nor does it bear fruit, and it creates an obstacle.
O deer, you sustain your life by means of grass, antelopes, water, and even plants;
or if you should subsist on the wind, even that is your refined sustenance. For by this [wind], you possess a beautiful luster like a carpet of blooming blue lotuses.
The gaze of a fool, puffed up with the pride of learning, does not rest upon his own face.

O beautiful deer, having abandoned these delightful forest lands where one falls with even the slightest stumble and where rising up is achieved only with great difficulty, and where the process of entry through the door is arduous due to the dense thicket of entwined cane creepers— having abandoned them, O seeker of excellence!
O King, why have you uselessly restrained your hooves, being so intent on the calamity of remaining stationary?
These are not the grounds of the Malaya forests where clear, flowing waterfalls exist, by the mere sight of which the thirst of embodied beings is quenched;
rather,
this is the desert, filled with harsh sounds and dust, where delusions expand.
O lion, these are but the mirage of a deer-thirst; this is not water, so do not go there.

The forest of birth was abandoned like a patch of young grass; the ground was left behind as if it were a mother; the trees, which provide a refuge for resting, were not counted as kinsmen; and that doe, distressed by the grief of separation from her young offspring, was no longer looked upon.
Even though they have searched for a path and a way out, these pitiless hunters still do not release them.
Having broken his bonds, cast off the snare, and forcibly shattered the trap, the deer emerged from the forest far away— his matted locks like a mass of flickering flames—
and having leaped with speed even beyond the range of the hunters' arrows, he fled.
When one has fallen into the depths of a well, what can human effort achieve against adverse fate?

O Lord, you wander about at will; you desire the doors of others' houses and do not exert yourself [to visit] yours. You do not look upon a face that is now distorted by causeless anger and harsh speech;
nor do you release even for a single moment your beloved wife, in whom affection is manifest.
O Sāraṅga, by whom was this exceedingly beautiful vow of yours taught?
That fresh cluster of blossoms from the *śāla* tree, which was encountered by chance while Hari was wandering at will—
its profusion of milk-drops trickling from its breaking [branches]—
proclaims its internal agony like tender grass scorched by the smoke of his sighs.
Meditating upon that very [truth] day after day like a sage in the forest, one will find bliss.
He whose limbs are withered does not delight in the creepers of the mountain slopes, nor on the dusty ground;
he finds no pleasure even in the cool, verdant shades at the edge of the forests.
Day after day, he meditates incessantly upon that very beloved one with her long eyes.
His mind went to the interior of the belly of the mountain-king Sailendra; he remained within the core of the Śṛṅgāri mountain.
The young female deer, wandering slowly and at her own will, avoids the dwelling of the herd-leader out of fear; she suffers for the sake of attaining familiarity with the body of the stag,
yet she is instantly marked by the glances of that doe-like woman as they fall upon her.
With his limbs trembling from suffering, he entered another herd, having been separated from his own by the power of adverse fate.
"O hunter, having taken all my flesh except for my breasts, do not release me; go, have mercy! Even now, I am unaccustomed to swallowing mouthfuls of fodder."
This son of mine is intent upon purifying the path of my doctrine.
In front is the river Revā, its far bank possessing mountain peaks exceedingly difficult to climb;
on the left is a lake, and on the right is the distress of a forest fire;
behind him, with bow in hand, a hunter runs very swiftly, striking with arrows.
Neither to go nor to stay does Hari, the Lord of the Asuras, have the power.
Where does he play? Where does he roam? Where does he find his livelihood?
Where indeed does he drink water? Where indeed does he sleep? Thus, [he dwells] without harming this innocent deer.
Taking up his bow for the sake of slaughter, he runs after the sick man.
The moon, the son of Atri, the lord of the twice-born and the nectar for the gods—out of merit, he was obtained by me as a refuge. O foolish one, worship him; do not abandon this sinner.
Then the young elephant,
having suddenly seized the fish that had already been enjoyed by the crocodile, [dragged it away].
O young elephant, if by some chance through the turn of fate you should ever be led by a swarm of bees to the honey,
desist, desist from it; there are other forests that are free of thorns.
In the first taste of eloquence, they indeed become silent afterwards.
Just as a young elephant, having left behind the forest floor dark with emerald-green grass and adorned with lakes of blooming white water-lilies and full-blown lotuses,
longs for the trees of the desert sands; so too does he remember [the Buddha].
That delight in cultivation is difficult to restrain; it is not an enemy to virtues.
O beloved Karabhaka, why do you lament so anxiously because you have not obtained that honey, so difficult to find even once, which you tasted while in the forest?
Maintain your fortitude with the familiar *piṇḍa* leaves in this desert region.
In this entire world, who has attained uninterrupted happiness?
O beloved Karabhaka, that *piṇḍī* tree which you, greedy for its honey,
once abandoned without respect because it lacked the shade of wealth— now,
even that tree has sprouted firm new shoots like trembling *kiśalaya* leaves.
It is enjoyed happily by others, such as Karabhadra, his beloveds, and their retinues.
"O camel, why do you sigh so deeply? Why do you wither your body? Cease this delusion! O friend, for whom has ultimate happiness arrived?
Wander among the young shoots; being at ease, abandon the longing for the filth of honey."
Furthermore, you will once again become a vessel for the virtuous.
O camel, alas! You desire to bite with impetuosity; indeed, you suffer from the fever of hearing.
Or rather, your own long neck is straight and serves as a refuge; weary from moving through the wide openings of the nostrils, your tongue will emerge from your mouth.
When it is given at such a time, who knows what will happen to whom?
Likewise, having become content with *saṃjñāla*,
*vrīhi*, *śyāmāka*, *bilva*, and *badara* fruits, the young elephant calf wanders happily in the vast forest, free from sorrow, his heart inclined toward the taste of honey by the power of fate.
Just as he does not eat anything else, nor drink, nor sleep, nor take delight.
He who was once satisfied even with a mouthful of unripe *vilva* leaves or jujube fruits,
whose path could not be followed even by his own herd-mates on the long journey—
now that very same young camel, his vigor exhausted, goes toward death.
I think that this wretched creature, cursed by fate, has surely never tasted the nectar of the bee.
O camel, having chewed the fruit of the *piṇḍīru* tree— free from bitterness—

in the desert, you ate the tips of its branches with such affection as they were offered by the mouth of a beautiful young she-camel; yet, remembering that, you now cry out long and piteously, overcome with distress.
That very sound suddenly became like the music of departure for all living beings.
The camel, fond of soft things, despises the camel who is greedy for thorns;
yet both find equal pleasure when they are together in the desert.
One should maintain impartiality and not mock either side.
There is but one bird that considers itself wise and dwells in the forest: the sparrow;
it either dies of thirst or begs from the palace.

O startled and innocent sparrow, why do you run fruitlessly with neck outstretched across the desert? In this summer heat, the sky is filled with the smoke of forest fires; there is no lightning here.
Even one who is thirsty awaits water with longing, as Śikhāṇḍin awaited her who was as dear to him as his own life and whom he drank in; surely his gaze was bound by affection for his beloved.
One sees only a very small amount of water in rivers.
Afflicted by the calamity of excessive height, the cloud shakes its head and extends its affection toward the *cātaka* bird,
saying,
"I am yours"; for it does not desire this while the quarters of the sky are wide open.
Where indeed have we not encountered kings who were pure, cool, and sweet?
The peacock, whose beauty is like a decorative mark upon the forest floor and who possesses the majesty of a beautiful plumage,
is indeed difficult to distinguish from crows and other birds in the sky.
Even in his dreams, he did not experience a state of movement comparable to that of a cat.

Just as a peacock drinks the drops of water from a rain-cloud, even while setting aside the clear masses of water that possess a flavor superior to nectar and are drawn from the pollen of heaps of blue lotuses;
I think that, out of excessive fear, he was arrogant regarding his head.

O Cātaka bird, whom could this restriction of drinking divine water delude? Even that fault becomes a virtue for those who possess the power of concealment (*saṃvṛti*), if they wish to drink the water standing on the ground; yet you would only reveal the soreness of your throat and your own unworthiness.
Who could be deluded by your rule of drinking divine water? Even that fault becomes a virtue for those who possess the power of concealment (*saṃvṛti*).
Are there no reservoirs of water, encircled by rows of swans that resemble the crowns of the newly risen gods? Alas,
what a heavy burden this fate has become for the *caṭaka* bird!
It pours down a stream of rain upon the city-dwellers, just as they desire.
Are the clouds far away? Do others not rain above? Have we heard of the blame of the sinful ones? Have the wings gone to their own bellies? What indeed is the destruction?
Is there no beautiful wandering in the sky? But what of the row of fierce crows?
Out of fear of the slowness of understanding through various methods, the peacock remains established on the ground.

Neither by the cascade of nectar from your eyes, nor by the warbling of your voice which is an elixir for the ears, nor even by your plumage, O peacock, which is as radiant as a beautiful rainbow— your beauty cannot be fully described.
The arrow will not pass through without reaching the crest of the flame.
O father Cātaka, how great a peerless misfortune have you brought upon yourself,
since not even a drop of water falls from the fresh rain-cloud into your beak?
Deprived of the gift of water from clouds, with its white peaks clearly revealed, O Cātaka bird, why do you cry out in vain? This is but an autumnal cloud.
There are wells of shimmering form all around, and beautiful rivers;
yet even so, for the single chataka bird, the rising of the cloud alone brings fruit.
O Cātaka bird, you half-heartedly consume grains of rice that have been parched by the sun, yet you dance with shimmering plumage for the sake of delight; thus you strive toward the cloud.
You obtain not even a drop of water, and yet you feel no shame.
Having made the son of Iṣvara (Śiva) a carrier for his own peacock,
he has now grown weary even of his own tail-feathers;
why was that Supreme Person not propitiated by you?
He who would pacify that thirst with showers of clouds of hair.
Then, as the swans and cranes dwell with exceeding affection in the waters of the pond, abiding in a manner befitting Lake Mānasa,
the very nature of being a swan is attributed to the swan alone.
The bees, grey with pollen, drink the honey from the lotuses; the swans eat the *śaivalā* moss. Fie upon this inconsistent fate!
Even if, by some stroke of fate, the lotus-less world should ever produce a mass of dust for both of them,
would they scatter it like a crane over a flock of swans?
Where the speech of the venerable Vāsudeva is harsh and his words are sharp,
there the swan finds no refuge other than retreat or silence.
Although there is water adorned with lotuses everywhere,
the mind of the swan does not delight unless it is at Lake Mānasa.
Even one who is well-nourished abandons the pollen-covered filament within the heart of a lotus; for the swan,
though it has taken refuge with the virtuous, holds the lotus stalk in high esteem.
O female swan, sporting in the fragrant lotus-stalks of the lake where the *samāna* wind blows, why do you agitate my gaze with such longing?
Descend into the pond; you shall return again to the thicket of lotuses.
The water in which the pollen from the rows of lotuses—
charming with the songs of female bees and swans— is scattered; in this [water],
may the venerable Bāṇa’s [work] be victorious.
O swan, having abandoned the delightful river of the Snowy Mountain, tell me, O wretched soul, to which direction you are now longing?
O swan, where has your intellect gone now that you are unable to distinguish the water mixed with milk? For when a digit of the moon falls into the waters of a lake...
O deer, you desire to give [your life] out of a longing for the sprouts of lotuses.

Having wandered for a long time through the waters of the celestial river— waters that are beautiful, purifying the world, and possess the merit residing in the hair-tufts upon the head of Śikhin— the gods, by fate...
You wish to abandon what you have obtained here; you are no swan.
Having stood for a long time in the sky with motionless stars, and having gazed upon the lotus pond turbid from contact with elephants,
he let out a roar deep with the sound of rising fury.
With tears, he turned back his gaze; it did not remain fixed on what had gone.

O Creator who has struck me down, it is by your own doing that this bird has destroyed that beautiful lotus stalk— white as frost or a conch shell— which was once brought to me by the mouth of my companion.
It creates a mass of lotus stalks and lavalampas.

O wretched bird, why do you cry out so loudly at night in competition with my voice, you whose mouth is stained with excrement and blood, while the waters are beautified by the reflection of your outstretched white wings?
A crane does not possess the splendor of a swan that frequents the lotus groves.
A traveler on the road, wishing to dispel his fatigue at the end of the day,
entered a grove of *kāraṇḍava*, *kāka*, and *baka* cranes;
they mocked him, saying, "This one is mute," and plucked at his wings.
For a lowly station is indeed a ground for the contempt of the great.
Where is the hard *kaṭhina* robe of the Pilu tree, and where the soft lotus sprouts?
Where is the bitter, salty water of the well, and where the nectar of the red lotus? Where is the heart-pleasing pollen of flowers, and where the coarse, irritating dust?
Where is the cemetery, that field of jackals? And where are you, O swan, the lord of the world?
"O royal swan, why have you come here?
That crane who was here has been mistaken for a swan.
Therefore, let us depart from there with all haste at dawn."
As far as they speak, this is a crane; it is not a foolish person.
O mind, do not be distressed by the contraction of your own dwelling here in this body; look instead at the birds flying through the sky.
These are the deer who uphold vows honored throughout the world.
For those who are free from grasping, even the oceans become like blades of grass.
When the two banks have risen high and your body is covered by leaves somewhere, pass through this uneven rainy season with its falling torrents;
for when it has ended, the lake will be filled with blossoming lotuses.
You are that very same swan; here again are your playful pastimes.
That depth has vanished; even the water is covered with hundreds of webs.
O friend, crane, rise up first from this burnt lake, before its body becomes further muddied by the silt and water as it wails aloud upon the earth.
A crow does not place its pair of feet upon the head while uttering a cry.
The ruddy goose does not nibble at the lotus stalks, nor does he drink water that has been broken by his own excessive passion; he does not go to the mass of moss to sleep,
nor does the *sārasa* bird engage in the playful sport of breaking the buds of the lotuses.
Where is your compassion? [He is] seized by grief, distressed by separation from his beloved.
At night, the swan, seeking the shade of the many-leaved lotus thicket and searching for the water-lilies,
does not bite the white water-lily even during the day, suspecting it to be a star.
The world, wary of deception, looks toward even the lower realms despite their reality.
O swan marked by a row of other swans, here indeed exist, in every region of this level land, waters with the luster of pearls, lotus-stalk knots shimmering like milk,
and sands expanded by the nectar of full-blown red lotuses,
all suitable for the sport of wandering.
In this old lake, where clusters of lotus stalks have withered, what is this obsession with dwelling?
“May this reservoir of water be filled once more with waters shimmering with schools of leaping fish and surging waves, and may we behold its lotuses blooming again”—
thus, night and day, the wretched-minded one keeps his heart bound by the threads of hope.
On the shore of a lake, free from heat and cold, there was an old crane.
He was radiant with the glow of the pollen from trembling lotuses falling upon his body,
and he felt a surge of joyful excitement hearing the sweet warbling of bees;
yet he remained indifferent even when his beloved offered him a bite of a lotus stalk from her own small mouth.
Now this very same swan, having gone to the desert, longs for bitter grass.
Those who, having remembered her, suddenly abandoned Lake Mānasa in their quest for excellence, and who, with longing hearts, saw that very same lotus pond inhabited by cranes,
sink back down into it once more, their pride and vanity having vanished.
Those who are not swans are not white like swans; they are generally nothing but cranes.
Embracing the *yāma* [night], the crane cries out bitterly, its throat parched by long-drawn sighs;
here these fish leap about in water struck by the touch of raw flesh.
This night is frequented even by cranes whose very nature is impure.
If that lotus is abandoned by the wise swan, it is [only] because of its own merit.
Their form is captivating and heart-stealing; their companion is the lotus for drinking; their sport is in the waters;
their dwelling is among the lotuses; their ornament is pollen;
their livelihood is the lotus stalk approved by the virtuous; and their friends are the bees with sweet voices.
Free from servitude, wretchedness, and humiliation, the swan lives happily.
Even fish know how to distinguish milk from water;
however, the renown well-established for royal swans is attained only through meritorious deeds.
Even when their own nests are falling apart due to the claws of angry owls,
certain other birds— those whose bodies are nourished by excrement— do not abandon them.

But those royal swans who have been nurtured by the touch of the lotus stalks on the waves of the celestial river of heaven—even they would abandon the turbid waters of the Gaṅgā; how much less so others?
Then the cuckoos [spoke]:
"O male cuckoo, why do you utter such exceedingly tender words in this abyss,
which is terrifying with the heavy roar of a thunderbolt?"
The sweet notes of a cuckoo, though raised among crows, remain as they are; how could there be cruelty in one whose nature is inherently auspicious, even when in the company of the wicked?
O sweet-voiced cuckoo, who here does not hear your song— a festival for the ears, a messenger sent by the union of Rati and her husband?
In forest regions where the thickets of dense trees had been consumed by forest fires, the sound of peacocks crying out emerged from the clearing.
O cuckoo, becoming silent for a moment, wait for that very friend of spring, who brings a breeze favorable to the fragrance of the *mālatī* flowers swaying in playful sport.
But those summer days, which are filled with the rising dust of your feet and bring about intense heat, attain fruitfulness only where these well-spoken words of yours prevail.
Enough, enough with the warbling of cuckoos, for its virtues do not even merit comparison;
it is merely a hollow tree trunk covered here and there by a mass of withered leaves, frequented by flocks of crows and herons crying out harshly from the groves of garden trees.
"Friend, this is the time of winter; it is not the festival of spring now."
In one place the sound of crickets, in another the incomparable clamor of crows; in one place the cry of herons, and in another the tumultuous chatter of monkeys;
in some places the dreadful howling of jackals—alas, what a concatenation of fate!
How can the startled young cuckoo utter its sweet, high-pitched cry?

... [The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a self, nor a being, nor a soul, nor a person; he does not perceive form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor formations, nor consciousness; he does not perceive the eye, nor the ear, nor the nose, nor the tongue, nor the body, nor the mind; he does not perceive forms, nor sounds, nor odors, nor tastes, nor tangibles, nor mental objects; he does not perceive the element of earth, nor the element of water, nor the element of fire, nor the element of wind, nor the element of space, nor the element of consciousness; he does not perceive the realm of desire, nor the realm of form, nor the formless realm; he does not perceive ignorance, nor volitional formations, nor consciousness, nor name-and-form, nor the six sense bases, nor contact, nor feeling, nor craving, nor grasping, nor becoming, nor birth, nor old age and death; he does not perceive suffering, nor its origin, nor its cessation, nor the path; he does not perceive the fruit of a Stream-enterer, nor the fruit of a Once-returner, nor the fruit of a Non-returner, nor Arhatship, nor Pratyekabuddhahood, nor even Buddhahood. Subhūti, because he does not perceive anything at all, he is called a 'Bodhisattva'. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive a self, nor a being, nor a soul, nor a person, up to and including Buddhahood, how then does he train in the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom by way of non-apprehension. He trains in the perfection of giving by way of non-apprehension; he trains in the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom by way of non-apprehension. He trains in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path by way of non-apprehension. He trains in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion by way of non-apprehension. Subhūti, it is in this manner that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all these dharmas are empty, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, training in the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, although all these dharmas are empty, yet a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, through skillful means, enters into the emptiness of form, the emptiness of feeling, the emptiness of perception, the emptiness of formations, and the emptiness of consciousness; he enters into the emptiness of the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind; he enters into the emptiness of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects; he enters into the emptiness of the elements and the realms; he enters into the emptiness of the links of dependent origination; he enters into the emptiness of the fruits of the holy life and even the emptiness of Buddhahood. Subhūti, it is because he enters into the emptiness of all these dharmas through skillful means that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, training in the perfection of wisdom, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty, what is the distinction between a Śrāvaka, a Pratyekabuddha, and a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, although all dharmas are empty, yet the Śrāvaka, relying on the teachings of the Buddhas, realizes the emptiness of the self and the dharmas, and thereby attains the fruit of a Stream-enterer, up to and including Arhatship. The Pratyekabuddha, relying on the teachings of the Buddhas, realizes the emptiness of the self and
Even while being devoured by bees, the *ketakī* flower continues to serve them; what indeed can faults do to one whose mind has been captivated by virtues?
Even after drinking from the lake, O young bee, you still long for the *bakula* bud right before the lotus;
O dark honey-drinker, how can there be truth in you?
Having observed that the intoxication of kinsmen's lives is fruitless and subject to impermanence,
this bee has now approached its teacher and become intent on the repetition of mantras.
O bee, wandering through the various quarters of the world,
have you ever anywhere seen or heard of such a thing? Tell me the truth, setting aside your partiality.
If the flower resembles the *jātī* flower;
The lotus is the dwelling place; passion is the dust; drinking honey is the sweet chatter of beloveds;
and the soft filaments are the pillow for the bed.
What royal sport is there for a bee in the water?
Falling and rising, standing still and motionless,
crying out with compassion, going and returning—
the lotus, soiled and struck by the frost.
For there is nothing that, having been beheld by him, was not brought to completion.
The lotus plant, though once cherished by him, cannot endure being frequented by him now that he has placed the spring within his heart.
She remembers the essence of delight day and night.
One who approaches another out of a desire for the taste of pleasure would not seek intoxication, just as a lion, if it were to obtain the tip of an elephant's ear, would not pursue the elephant.
Such a person indeed becomes a dwelling place for rebirth in other states of existence.
O honey-bee, you have rejected many flowering creepers with their well-blossomed tips, which were like grass; now experience the fruit [of your choice], though it is covered with thorns.
This, O shameless one, is from the ketakī creepers.
Behold today, at the end of autumn, the fate of that bee who once sported within the bellies of lotuses in full bloom and among the blossoms dwelling in the heart of buds.
The days pass with great difficulty through the openings of the reeds.
Having drunk the fragrant honey-scented pollen from the flowers,
the bee, once seated upon the lotus and anointed with the red dye of its filaments,
now cries out piteously as it is bound by the rays of the moon.
What misfortunes do not befall those who are full of hatred in this world?
O bee, for now divert your restless mind toward other flowering creepers that can endure being crushed;
do not seek the bud of the fresh-faced goddess at an improper time.
O fool, why do you torment the *navamālikā*?
His body was embraced by the celestial nymphs who were clinging to him as he fell from the peak of Mount Airāvata,
which was drenched in the spray of the rut-fluid of the elephants;
his wings were shattered and their joints torn apart by the fierce winds.
The wise one lies here on the ground like a bee that has settled upon the earth.
Why do you wander about in distress, your composure having fallen away, O bee, crying out piteously in your longing for the nectar of flowers? Restrain yourself among other plants and creepers.
For that blossoming mango creeper has indeed been broken.
When the lotus bud— filling the quarters of space with its own fragrance, red in color, possessing a charming face and a delicate form—
becomes fit for service;
Then, by fate, the honeybee was led away to another region.
Upon two lotuses, radiant with their natural splendor and possessing sweet,
tender stalks, two bees have entered simultaneously; of these two, one has its body completely filled and overwhelmed by a great abundance of honey.
In which [state] is he not even joined with a trace of passion? There is no second [state].
The swarm of bees, having abandoned the *madhuka* grove, went to the new jasmine;
then it went again to the red *aśoka*, and from there to the *kadamba* tree.
Having stayed there for a very long time as well, it departed from them and proceeds to the lotus.
The world, having become accustomed to its own virtues and vices, seeks ever-new things.

What indeed was not done there by a bee, wandering with a longing for honey, his soul intensely enamored by the beauty of the painted lotus? Having attained its nectar, that dull-witted creature did not even depart from it for a moment.
But it has been placed at the forefront by discerning people for those who are blind with craving.

The bee wanders through the *bakula* and the gentle *kunda*, yet finds no rest; though it is attached to the naturally fragrant *aśoka*, it does not attain freedom from sorrow, for its mind is drawn by the longing for the scent of fragrant flowers in the forest.
The bee, remembering its former garland, hums most softly upon her limb.
She desires to kiss him slowly with her limbs,
she performs pressing embraces, and she even strives to break the seal by falling at his feet;
unable to endure the delay due to the longing of her heart, she waits for the moment appropriate for the ritual union.
Through merits, a young bee obtained a fresh *navamālikā* flower.
Having seen the lotus plant withered by the frost, its stalk destroyed, the bees—formerly devoted to the temples of elephants—have suddenly retreated;
alas, what a pity! Such is this nature of living beings, which causes no confidence.
No one at all reckons even the scent of the first quality as being of any value.
O bee, why do you wander for so long in the delusion that this is a grove of *āmoda* flowers?
Indeed, O bee, you do not know the truth: it is the scorching summer season.
Behold the forest, standing empty of flowers and clearly revealed as parched by the heat.
The splendor of the month of Caitra has departed; though naturally beautiful, it was once rich with fragrance.
By whom has its magnificent fragrance been smelled? By whom have its filaments been kissed? By whom has its nectar been drunk, or by whom has it been stirred up by its pollen?
O, O simple honey-bee, go quickly to other blossoming trees!
In this world, what little fruit can possibly be obtained from a mere leafless pipal tree?
Just as one who is eager to drink the sweet juice of fresh sugarcane,
yet whose heart is deceived by the agitation of thirst and lacks the realization of its true nature,
does not cease his fruitless labor even when despondent, so too one does not desist from the lotus-bed of painting.
Though he is of evil intellect and addicted to vice, the honey-drinker still wanders about, driven by the hope of finding sweetness.
Having disregarded the ponds filled with blooming blue lotuses out of a longing for union with her,
and having attained supreme bliss by embracing her with an eager mind— yet now,
seeing that sandalwood creeper broken, it is the bee that lives on.
Let that be called fortitude; it was not, however, performed in accordance with affection.
By him who, of his own accord, drank the honey from the opening bud of the *kesara* flower;
by him who spent the nights, white as the moon, within the heart of the autumnal lotus;
and by him who wandered upon the temples of elephants, stained by flowing ichor—
How can this young bee find satisfaction while bound within the thickets of the *karīra* tree?
May it not be that our death occurs through this very [enemy] by some stroke of fate;
for if, with life destroyed by thirst, we were to die then, what would the world be without its flowers?
For he by whom that beloved Padmākara was mercilessly uprooted—[he is the same as this one].
The bee of his fame, followed by the swarms of his gifts, waters, and virtues, is ever restless for that very elephant.

O bee, you have previously experienced the distortion of the sense of taste and its causes, as well as fickleness; you have seen that state where one forgets the distinction between self and other due to intoxication.
What more need be said? O bee, you have already ascertained all this, since even now you are still attempting to enter [the lotus].
"O brother, who is this obsession that causes you to neglect the one who makes [the world] empty?"
O bee, you whose body is exhausted by the distress of being tossed by the wind from the ears of the rut-blind elephant as it moves about—
why do you endure this suffering in vain?
For the beauty of your interior is not at all obscured by the circle of bees buzzing with intoxication.
In every step, there are indeed lotus-pools, fragrant and with clearly visible blossoms.
The bee, having abandoned the fragrant *navamālikā* flower, went to the *yūthikā*;
having abandoned that as well, he went to the sandalwood tree; from there he went to the lotus.
There, bound by the moon for a long time, this dull-witted one now cries out in distress.
Without contentment, a greedy person does not attain even a hundredth part of the excellence of others.
"The night will pass; a beautiful dawn will arise; the sun will emerge;
and the lotus pond will bloom.
Thus does the bee dwelling within the calyx reflect.
Alas, alas! The elephant has trampled the lotus pond.
Wandering at the edge of the forest among the forest creepers,
he did not smell the fragrance of the *gandhaphalī* fruit; was that [the place] not delightful, and was he not one who delights?
The will of the Lord alone is more powerful.
The fish, its body grown large and embraced on all sides by the daughter of Śrī, remains motionless at night as it is being thoroughly drunk by bees that have arrived,
their mouths wide open in intense joy from the embrace of Śrī.
Even from afar, with eyes closed and vacant, he gazes upward at the lotus.
The crane, like a sage, is seen swallowing living fish; yet the vulture does not even swallow the dead. Shame on the title of "Lord of Sages" given to such a one!
Standing on one leg alone with its neck tucked in,
the old heron creates the illusion of a white water-lily for the young fish.
That crane suddenly perished. "Alas! Where indeed has his life gone?
O Fate, you have acted well; is there anyone at all like you?"
No one at all is able to deceive him.
O crane, even though you wish to abandon your own family’s customary conduct and fly away like the swans, your vow remains exactly as it was.
This very thing bears fruit for those people who strive accordingly.
Their voices were not like the harsh cries of common birds;
their gaits were not like those of wild asses;
nor did they possess variegated plumage like that of peacocks.
Likewise, even in one who possesses such qualities, there is the "crane-vow" (hypocrisy) in a crane.
To discern the true nature of the water and milk that have been mixed together, you must employ that skillfulness;
and that is a graceful sport consisting of the tender placement of words.
O eloquent one, if you know it thus, then loosen your grasp slightly for a moment.
O friend, since you have come here to dwell with me, how could you not be my swan?
Who are you, O red-eyed one, wandering here? I am a swan from Lake Mānasa.
What is there? There are groves of golden lotuses and water resembling nectar.
Are there pearl-oyster shells, heaps of conch shells, or beds of lapis lazuli anywhere there?
The cranes, having observed whether there were indeed water-lilies or not, uttered cries of "hīhī."
Clad in plumage of equal color, black and mingled with cuckoos—
by what means is a crow recognized if he does not speak for himself?
Even while crying out in rivalry with the peacocks, do these wretched crows know how to produce the "kekā" cry? They merely mimic it from their own nature.
Let the male cuckoo bear its black body and kiss the excellent fruits;
let it wander through the lovely interiors of the mango groves and indeed perform the behaviors of a male cuckoo.
Indeed, in the matter of making sound, it is surely only the crow that is the crow.
Having attained a lovely splendor through flocks of cuckoos, and having been forcibly brought into close proximity by their sweet notes, alas,
what can this wretched [cuckoo] do when fate has rendered him destitute?
A crow may imitate them, yet it did not attain their likeness.

This village has been completely overrun on all sides by Bhillas who delight in improper undertakings and who behave like venomous serpents; therefore, O Kirāta, spend your time upon the trunk of this tree.
Speech is not auspicious; here, silence alone is the refuge.
With the tips of his feet, he scrapes away the dung remaining from what was eaten by the mouths of the deities;
and with his pride destroyed, he walks along, fearing that he might step upon the heads of the virtuous.
What indeed will a wretched crow not do once it has reached the sky?

Misfortune, the dullness of speech and body, and the wretchedness of restless activity—these are known to arise from that very [state of mind]; its conduct is indeed beyond description. Thus, like the swollen fruit of a tree nurtured by rain, even so [is the state] of the afflicted one.
The crow, with a luster like the hue of the cuckoo's plumage, faints repeatedly in distress.
The peacocks, singing charmingly and reciting melodiously, look upon him with pleasure; indeed,
they are not driven away by anger here, nor are they even forbidden,
because of this [man] who has attained his lineage through the talk of obtaining the beloved woman of the traveler.
Now this [wealth] is being consumed without restraint by a deceitful crow.

O crow, let your harsh words be disregarded; your greed is not even worth mentioning here. This behavior of yours is merely your own ornament, for all this is ordained by your very nature, just as heat belongs to fire.
However, that even a single neck of yours, being devoid of virtue, is not tolerated [by us].
The crow, having raised up the cuckoo, causes him to taste the fruit of the mango tree; the osprey, intent on sport, drives away the royal parrot;
and the owl, his friend, sleeps happily upon the crest of this mountain peak.
Alas! Today, while the hawk has gone out of sight, that which was born in the forest has been overturned.
Is his body adorned with a crest like a peacock? Is he a reciter of the Vedas like Brihaspati?
Is he sweet-voiced like a male cuckoo? Does he possess a noble gait like a swan? Is he one who provides the pleasure of play, like the young of an ordinary bird?
By what quality was the crow placed in a cage made of gold?

The birth of the Lord of the Maruts on the day of the Yuga, the proclamation of it as a festival for all the world, the great renown during the recitations of "Auspicious Day," the fullness of human life,
the conflict with enemies equal to that of Rāma, and such-like skill in astrology— [all these belong to you].
Because of that quality, the crow was placed by him in a cage made of gold.
This was the initial moment of the onset of the Kali age,
when the multitude of aquatic creatures and birds had been driven away; on that very day,
at the conclusion of his austerities, he was addressed with devotion.
O twice-born one, who indeed would accept a gift where the recipient himself is worthy of worship?
Whatever contact with an object occurs in the moon other than through the sun is produced by that [moon];
yet it is called "firefly" by someone who is satisfied with that [name].
O Goddess whose teeth are like a thunderbolt amidst a mass of thick darkness, that which shines at night is one thing;
but by day, it is another—a beautiful white ray intercepted by a multitude of stars.

The firefly, independent of itself, shines as if proclaiming its own state of being a mere insect, while failing to reveal its true nature as something that merely destroys the pride of those who possess withered, old, and broken horns.

The glow-worms, whose intense and heavy radiance was once manifest, now shine with a feeble light in the sky; their brilliance, once vast as the darkness of night, is now bound to their own tiny bodies.
The seven-horsed sun does not arise until then.
That night, in which even worms as wretched as we appeared like kings,
has now departed; today,
this day has arrived, illuminating all directions with the lamps of the sun’s rays.
Even the moon does not shine here in this mass of darkness; how much less you?
The moon will depart,
the splendor of the stars will perish, and the lamps of jewels,
shrouded in the darkness of night, will remain; O jewel among men, the entire world will become blind.
"That you will attain equanimity toward suffering—this is far-fetched."
May there be well-being for that mere fragment of light, which deludes the timid; it is either a flickering at the end of existence, or a trifling superimposition of merit and the like—
this [fragment] which, shimmering with a crimson glow from the reflection of its shadow, is studded with those named "fireflies."
Therefore, even though it is harmful, we are deceived by the illusion that it is a moving jewel.
Adorned with fresh clusters of blossoms upon its very trees, does it abandon those same [trees] when they have grown old? What is so surprising about one of low birth?
O Mother, where have those mango trees gone— the trees that were adorned with young sprouts,
possessed the excellence of flowers and fruits, and were lofty with the abundance of their fruit?
It is indeed right that the Creator was pained by such a state for him;
for what is the use of sandalwood fruit that does not correspond to its own nature?
Desiring jujube fruit and being ignorant of trees, I sat beside a khadira tree in the forest because of its thorny appearance.
Either it becomes a great tree with its roots intact, or it perishes;
the sprout of a *nyagrodha* seedling does not undergo the process of becoming a sprout [if it lacks the necessary conditions].
Blessed are those trees whose shade, flowers, fruits, roots, bark,
and wood do not turn away from those who come seeking them.
Whether one falls into a bed of glowing coals or is swept away by the wind of universal destruction,
the palm tree that has begun its ascent with rigidity perishes along with that very rigidity.
The great trees by the wayside provide shade, protect from wild beasts, offer good fruit for those who ride upon them, and exist solely for the benefit of others.
For those who have no recourse, suffering does not arise from being struck;
for the most part, those who are free from sorrow are like sprouts that grow even when trampled by feet.
Even if a sandalwood tree is fashioned according to rule but deprived of its fruit and flowers,
it nevertheless dispels the distress of others by its very form alone.
When the month of spring has arrived, the entire king of forests attains growth;
that the tree does not produce a leaf—what fault is that of spring?
When the sun’s brilliance is shattered by the dense, dark foliage of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) laden with fruit,
what person— even a beast— would seek shade, let alone one who is fond of old shrubs?

When a traveler stands near a tree on the road whose trunk is obscured by a mass of rays from the sun, brightened by its fruits, flowers, and tender shoots, who would experience exhaustion? None at all.
Those trees on earth that have exerted themselves for the sake of quelling the heat of people, whose tiny bits of wealth have been carried far away— we know not how they have become so helpless.
The abode of Prajāpati is here.
We can endure the thorns within the sandalwood;
why then is this beautiful object left unprotected? Tell me, what is your own well-being worth to you?
You have gathered together the thorns of the *khadira* tree.
This great elephant, bound by deceptive fetters and mounted by those who carry off its wealth,
has been approached by sandalwood trees adorned with blossoms.
For this very reason, it is not joined with a fruit.
Whatever is unaccustomed yet connected with what is appropriate—has not sandalwood ever produced flowers or fruit? We are deeply ashamed; let this improper course simply pass away.
From him he received a large, spread-out rug.
O young campaka tree, with your beautiful blossoms accustomed to the pleasure of kissing the loveliness of a maiden’s cheek—
why do you bloom? Abandon this laugh of full-blown flowers!
The land of Maru is like a desert devoid of water and jewels.
Where is the thought of blossoming for a campaka tree whose roots are being scorched by the sands of a parched desert? Generally,
such a hope belongs to those who dwell in an unsuitable place.
"It is better to merely sustain one's own life."
The Creator has made his own wickedness manifest toward others by granting fruitlessness to the *bhūrja* tree;
for what is the use of hundreds of sharp weapons cut from its bark?
That [wealth] does not satisfy the succession of supplicants.
O friend, what is the use of one who delights only in thorns and hates the fruit; what is the use of one whose curiosity is fixed on the boundary of bitterness;
and what is the use of one who turns his back on the play of shade? For such a person, what indeed is there among the virtuous?
Then, indeed, this khadira tree was created by the wicked student.

Would that which has been obtained after a long time be for death like nectar? Or would it grant long life like an elixir? This is the fruit: that this traveler, scorched by misfortune, [finds relief].
A palm tree that has become rigid bears fruit only after a hundred years.
O tree, O Sobhita, renowned throughout the world for producing coolness and tranquility through the beauty of your great burden of fruit—
how is it that this [fruit] has somehow fallen down from you?
One fruit, bitten by a bird, was obtained in small measure.
O you whose nature is auspicious due to your extreme coolness,
there is truly no tree whatsoever that is equal to you;
for even those seeking shade, [you are not like] those with forked tongues.
Through attachment, he is no different from a sandalwood tree.
How is it that in this forest there is not even a single such noble tree,
tall and rich with flowering creepers and fruit,
by the command of the one who inflicts suffering upon the world and whose constituent elements are consumed?
The Dhava, Khadira, and Palāśa trees enjoy only growth.
O traveler, behold indeed the course of destiny for that very tree which, having obtained the expanse of the sky where the continuity of branches was utterly ceased,
provided you with its shade— a refuge from the many calamities of the heat—
only when you had already become old. Why do you waste your time?
Today, on the surface of the earth, one who has committed evil is burned intensely, as if by hot sand and glowing coals.

O traveler, that very tree on the road— whose broad branches, joined together like three painted wings, once provided shade, rest, sleep, food, and shelter with its abundant fruit upon your shoulder— is now being torn up by a wicked doer.
The skin of a cowherd boy, which is free from dust and hair, is suitable for the *kaṣāya*.
Is it incapacity, or perhaps a lack of faith in that [flower]?
Or is this the very beauty of the forest’s abiding nature? Or is it simply malice?
Alas, by cruel fate, the splendor of the flowers has become so disproportionate and yet so fruitless!
Why have you not even made a connection with sandalwood, despite its suitability?
Having considered this— that one who has climbed the palm tree must rely on a man who possesses six roots, whose fame is widespread,
whose shadow is dense and radiant, who stands upon the path of the virtuous, and who is worthy of being served by the good—
it remains to be seen whether such a man’s devotion will bear fruit today, tomorrow, or perhaps later.
The Creator is the master over whether [an event] occurs at a certain time, or in a certain place, or perhaps never at all.
Since you stand at the crossroads, why are you thick with deep shade?
If you are endowed with shade, why are you laden with fruit? If you are full of fruit, why are you bowed down?
O noble tree, my friend, endure now the pulling of your branches and the tugging of your tips.
People destroy their own beautiful bodies by their own wicked deeds.
O slender one, now that your entire body has been pervaded by the quality of the fragrance of your excellent hair, and you have felt the touch of the beautiful breasts of the cowherd girl,
this certain fault caused by contact with a serpent has suddenly flared up.
By which way the travelers pass you by and go far away from the sandalwood tree.

The sandalwood tree, its beautiful roots severed, has fled; we, who were accustomed to the pleasures of worldly enjoyments, have forgotten it there every day. If we do not repay that striker with the firebrands of ten million venomous fangs— ||| Subhūti 0815-1 to 0815-3 ||| ...then what is the point? ||| Subhūti 0815-4 ||| What is the use of this body, which is like a vessel filled with filth, a heap of excrement, urine, phlegm, and mucus? ||| Subhūti 0815-5 ||| It is a source of suffering, a vessel for disease, and a dwelling place for worms; it is a mere tool for the sake of others. ||| Subhūti 0815-6 ||| What is the use of this body, which is like a house on fire, a vessel of many pains, and a prison for the senses? ||| Subhūti 0815-7 ||| It is a vessel for old age, death, and sorrow; it is a mere tool for the sake of others. ||| Subhūti 0815-8 ||| What is the use of this body, which is like a boat on the ocean, a vessel of many dangers, and a prison for the mind? ||| Subhūti 0815-9 ||| It is a vessel for birth, decay, and dissolution; it is a mere tool for the sake of others. ||| Subhūti 0815-10 ||| What is the use of this body, which is like a dream, a vessel of delusion, and a prison for ignorance? ||| Subhūti 0815-11 ||| It is a vessel for attachment, aversion, and confusion; it is a mere tool for the sake of others. ||| Subhūti 0815-12 ||| What is the use of this body, which is like a mirage, a vessel of vanity, and a prison for pride? ||| Subhūti 0815-13 ||| It is a vessel for arrogance, conceit, and self-importance; it is a mere tool for the sake of others. ||| Subhūti 0815-14 ||| What is the use of this body, which is like a bubble, a vessel of emptiness, and a prison for vanity? ||| Subhūti 0815-15 ||| It is a vessel for insubstantiality, unreality, and non-existence; it is a mere tool for the sake of others. ||| Subhūti 0815-16 ||| What is the use of this body, which is like a shadow, a vessel of transience, and a prison for impermanence? ||| Subhūti 0815-17 ||| It is a vessel for change, decay, and disappearance; it is a mere tool for the sake of others. ||| Subhūti 0815-18 ||| What is the use of this body, which is like a reflection, a vessel of illusion, and a prison for appearance? ||| Subhūti 0815-19 ||| It is a vessel for deception, falsehood, and unreality; it is a mere tool for the sake of others. ||| Subhūti 0815-20 ||| What is the use of this body, which is like a cloud, a vessel of instability, and a prison for flux? ||| Subhūti 0815-21 ||| It is a vessel for arising and passing away; it is a mere tool for the sake of others. ||| Subhūti 0815-22 ||| What is the use of this body, which is like a mountain stream, a vessel of turbulence, and a prison for agitation? ||| Subhūti 0815-23 ||| It is a vessel for restlessness, distraction, and unrest; it is a mere tool for the sake of others. ||| Subhūti 0815-24 ||| What is the use of this body, which is like a wheel of fire, a vessel of suffering, and a prison for torment? ||| Subhūti 0815-25 ||| It is a vessel for pain, affliction, and distress; it is a mere tool for the sake of others. ||| Subhūti 0815-26 ||| What is the use of
O serpents, why did you not go to your destruction together with him yourself? Why do you remain here?

At the root of your life, this human existence has reached its end; even for a mere moment, O Kṣaudrīyāṃśa, there is no power to live beyond the view of others. Therefore, may you be well; attain great prosperity now—for what haste is there for us?
Are you flourishing with auspicious results among your sons, grandsons, or great-grandsons?
The dense, fragrant shadow of this very tree dispels the scorching heat;
the recognition of its virtues is itself its quality—why then speak further of the sandalwood?
Yet, from its very roots, it is tormented by serpents that have made their dwellings there.
Know this: run toward that which is excellent, whether it be *khadira* wood or even something else; do not run toward this.

There are no sweet fruits, nor is there a shade formed by tender leaves; nor is there even that beautiful flower, nor are there birds pouring forth the nectar of their song— for this is but a decayed, impure body, filled with the excrement of a flock of crows.
Alas! How is it that you were created by the wicked Ordainer at the foot of a tree that is devoid of stability?

It has no sweet fruit, nor beautiful flowers, nor glossy-leaved creepers; it offers no shade to relieve fatigue, nor do its birds warble melodiously. Is this indeed a khadira tree, or has it been mistaken for such by you, O traveler?
O traveler, why have you come here seeking shelter for your limbs from those with throats as harsh as thorns?
Glossy and leafy, dispelling the fierce heat with their abundant shade,
bending low with sweet fruit, and removing the distress of those who take refuge in them—
may those trees on these very paths be reduced to ashes for you, O traveler!
The paths have become thorny, filled with holes where snakes dwell, and trees have grown up once more.
The shadow that belongs to no one else is not the self; how could it be grasped by another?
During the heat of summer, why is there coolness on the ground from the wind’s movement?
When a hundred years have passed, the talk of what fruit will come is indeed mere talk.
How long indeed have we, alas, been deceived by this length! We are but fools.
“Who are you, sir? Tell me. “Know me to be one cursed by fate, a wretched fellow.
“You speak as if out of dispassion (*vairāgya*). “It is well known; why is this being asked?
“Here, the travelers on the road are serving the mango tree with their whole soul, even though it stands to the left.”
Nor does even his shadow exist for the sake of benefiting others, even though he stands upon the path.
The gods have rested by you with your fragrance, the deer with your sprouts, the ascetics with your hanging bark,
the forest-dwellers with your flowers, the birds— afflicted by the heat— with your fruits,
and the scent-elephants with your branches; thus, you are ever distributed for the relief of all.
O Druma, you have attained the path of the Bodhisattvas; truly, others are deluded.
In whose shade, fragrant with the flowing honey from blossoms bent low under the weight of swarming bees, throngs of travelers rest as if in their own homes; and who,
their thirst quenched by the constant waters of mountain torrents, find delight in the fruits.
May those trees flourish, bear fruit, and attain the highest excellence.
O you who have adorned the path, O you who are the life-breath of those wandering on the path, O equanimous one!
Even today, those eternal quarters of space are still covered by your heat; they kiss the sky with their flames, for you did not merely roll about at the foot [of the tree] as if seeking rest.
Those suffering from the heat were liberated, and they were satisfied by hundreds of fruits until they were satiated.
That tree, whose growth had been long entreated by hundreds of desires, has now been born from the lake; it yields fruit even to those dwelling afar and serves as a refuge for all who depend upon it.
It is not occupied by other birds from various lands who have arrived there unobserved.
Even though he had obtained that opportunity, the old bird remained at a distance and watched.
Even though they have encountered the suffering of being scorched by forest fires, the affliction of harsh winds and water, and the heat of the sun;
even though they have met with calamities as grave as being dragged away by elephants; the *vajra* tree still yields its wood, shade, fruit, bark, flowers, clusters of blossoms, and sprouts.
Oh, how excellent is the conduct of these trees, for they ward off those seeking their fruit day after day!
The crows [rest] upon the beds of lotus groves;

the vultures upon the beds of flesh; the travelers upon the beds of sweet fruits; and the bees upon the beds of fragrant scents—[all these] on the lofty streets devoid of essence, where clusters of red flowers bloom far and wide.
O silk-cotton tree, who has not been deceived by you every single day?
O traveler, do not resort to this sandalwood tree for rest, thinking it is like a brother who has mastered the task of dispelling the fatigue of wandering through the desert;
for those dwelling near it are being consumed by rows of thick, spreading flames.
How many travelers are there who, having been led away by those resembling the thieves of mindfulness regarding the horse of the self, have gone astray?

That summer, which was resorted to by hundreds of travelers to dispel their fatigue from the heat, was loudly celebrated with songs set to composed melodies by swarms of female bees whose minds were greedy for honey,
and by flocks of birds arrived from distant lands.
This very tree, once providing cool shade, has now been crushed by a rutting elephant.
Sweet fruits were eaten, a bed was made with the tips of branches and young shoots, water cooled by the shade of your bark was drunk, and fatigue was subdued;
having rested there for a very long time, a supreme peace of mind was attained.
You are the tree on the noble path, and we are travelers; may our meeting occur again and again.
There is indeed a cloud shining in the sky above the surface of the earth;
even while being consumed by the winds, does it ever sink into the subterranean realm?
A cloud that has taken its place in the sky, an ocean filled to the brim with water,
and one who is incapable even of supporting the weight of a cow's hoofprint—
How can that which is thus unreal be spoken of?
In this matter, behold how this great lake— the sole life-sustainer for the traveler— will dry up; its course blocked by the cloud of deluded intellect.
Has the caravan of your mind increased here?

Those who, regardless of their own interests, are ever-risen for the sake of pacifying the world— those clouds that pour forth water, whom those who do not grasp them fail to perceive, reveal themselves.
There truly are some of great majesty among them.
Where has the blind Bālāhaka ever seen, or smelled by the cow, such grass as was never grazed upon?
He is like a great tree that provides refuge for travelers.
He is free from poverty because he has mastered the nature of illusion.
Some [rivers] become turbulent with fierce waves by resting against the peaks of lofty mountains;
others, however, are merely the falling of water droplets, grass, and clods of earth.
For those who have abandoned deceit, their merits do not diminish even when they are in the midst of worldly affairs.
Where you have long remained without food, cold,
and naked, and where you are a debtor from the acceptance of gifts and the taking of wealth—
there, even upon the shore of the ocean, you roar shamelessly.
O Cloud, no one has ever been seen who is equal to you in boldness.
Having cast aside his pride with his roars and laughed for a long time, he rained down upon the various limbs of the peacock— who was like a *cātaka* bird—
just as a thick rain falls upon a peacock whose crest is curved and whose beak is long.
His inhalations and exhalations become merely a matter of jest.
Having ascended high, [the sun] dwells upon the heads of the lofty mountains that sustain the earth; yet even he, though drawing water from the ocean for the sake of allaying the world's torment,
casts a long shadow across the vast expanse of the sky.
"O Megha, who indeed would not envy you? For what reason is it that you have no desire for this vow?"
Having ascended high, [the moon] dwells upon the heads of the lofty kings of the earth;
yet even that water-giver exists for the sake of quelling the world's torment.
And its long shadow, vast by nature, forms a binding embrace within the sky.
"O Megha, who indeed would not envy you? For what reason is it that you have no desire for this vow?"
Excellent, O mass of clouds for the destruction of calamities! Excellent, O wise one! This should be meditated upon within the earth.
Who else is capable of performing this? This task is difficult even for the lords of men;
it is like a thunderbolt falling upon those few fields that are suitable for all crops.
In all those deserts of parched sand where no means of survival exist, may rains fall upon them.
In that dried-up lake, where frogs, *koṭarāsa* fish,
and tortoises lay motionless like the dead within the earth,
and where cranes stood with their broad mud-covered beaks repeatedly fainting, a cloud arrived out of season and brought it back to life.
Where herds of wild elephants, with their trunks submerged, drink the water.
By the virtues of his majesty,
even though they were slight, the roots of Daśaratha’s sovereignty were firmly established;
yet by [his son], the grasses suddenly caused his very life-breaths to be severed.
This is the activity of the cloud that releases a continuous torrent of abundant rain— the water whose course is difficult to determine.
One cloud, having received only a few scattered drops of water with great difficulty, thunders excessively; behold, it dances with extreme impetuosity upon receiving such a mere trifle!
Yet another, whose greatness is incomparable and whose ground is worthy of praise, I do not know how it dances.
With its vast expanse between the clouds, does the peacock-hearted Cātaka bird think that this is indeed a cloud?

O Cātaka bird, you who are distressed and blinded by thirst, why do you wander in vain? Those clouds have departed— those whose bodies are dark as a swarm of shimmering bees and whose splendor has even erased the distinction between land and water in this world.
"In this ocean filled with waves, where could even a single drop of water from you possibly be?"
"Let us see whether this one moves," [said they]; thus, by ministers who had achieved only minor feats, who were arrogant and negligent, yet impelled by powerful karma,
the thunderbolt was released when it was no longer possible to restrain it as it had gained full momentum.
Alas! This mountain village has been utterly destroyed by that dense enemy fire.
Having roared, completely obstructed the sky, and covered the circle of the quarters,
he assumed a body as beautiful and dark as a mass of crushed sapphire; yet,
even when the arrival of the clouds occurred, that water was abandoned by the rain-bearing ones.
And by him, the entire nest of the young pigeon was not even looked upon.

There, in that village— where the sky was overspread by sudden, dense clouds, where the ministers were absent, and where the natural activities of its inhabitants had ceased— it manifested itself in such a way that there was a vast interval between the mud flowing in the streets and the exceedingly pure, clear souls within.
Nor can it be known by ignorant people, just as the flow of water in the currents of a torrent cannot be discerned.
O clouds, have you not heard of the Buddha’s fame, which is heavy with the gift of his own body?
Or have you never heard anywhere of the conduct of the Pārijāta tree?
For by this [conduct], you roar as you give water that is so easily obtained.
Shame does not arise for those who, out of impetuosity, run wildly through the sky.
It rains in the proper place and does not thunder in vain;
it swiftly removes the exhaustion of the fields whose luster is withered by distress.
It brings security to the surface of the earth, and whatever intensity of goodness it places in the heart, it produces another kind of radiance.
May this cloud of the Sugata, with its skin as dense and glistening as an unfailing rain-cloud, continue to grow.

This ordinary man, by nature prone to despondency, has had his dejection removed by a mere drop of that water— the fame of which is spread by its activity in bestowing the objects requested by the Lord of the Three Worlds, the one who dwells in the ocean; he whose head is adorned with a single priceless jewel that is a shimmering flame of fire.
"Having discharged its water into the void, the cloud roars with pride like a torrential river whose destruction is imminent."
Just as the ocean does not overstep the boundary known as its shore, so too [the wise] do not transgress this other rule: "One must not assist those who are being harmed."
From cows and other such sources, milk turns into curd either on the following day or immediately;
but as for the ocean of salt water, even today there has been no transformation—how much less so for the great ones?
Although the ocean displays its jewels by virtue of its transparent nature,
nevertheless, do not think in your mind that it is only knee-deep.
Alas, even that ocean is merely called a "repository of rivers," for not a single drop of water from it ever falls into the mouths of those who seek it.
Let that greatness of the ocean be renowned upon the earth;
yet by it not even a single person afflicted by wind, heat, hunger, or thirst was ever satisfied.
When the ocean has been crossed by the gods who have escaped through the spreading flow of the nectar of immortality,
whose hearts on this earth tremble with the heat of the summer sun, O wretched ones?
Since he is Hara with the moon as his crest-jewel,
and since this Hari is also the consort of Śrī,
and since these gods are indeed immortals—
Therefore, these are but mere droplets of his sovereign power.
Indeed,
your very majesty is a virtue such that no one approaches you;
for you bear a form that strikes terror into the waters.
Why is the wheel-mark on the soles of his feet foremost?
Having disregarded the enmity arising from the theft of his splendor,
and without considering the churning of that mountain,
the great ocean gave refuge to Hari.
For the conduct of those with wise intellects is indeed free from envy.

The Lord of Waters, who bears the weight of the earth upon his head like blades of grass, and who possesses a luster surpassing that of the moon, is not truly the master of anything; in reality, there is no master over the Lord.
Jewels are [like] jewels, and grass is [like] grass once again.
In summer, let those wretched deer, longing for the arrival of the clouds, be filled with distress; yet let the foolish sapharī fish in the ocean be tossed by the shifting mountain-like waves.
The absence of trembling and the excellence of the body—both of these are inconceivable.
The pearls are its gems; the dolphin is its aquatic creature;
Lakṣmī is its water-born lotus; the multitude of pearls is its sand; the coral creepers are its seaweed; the water is nectar;
and upon its shores stand the wish-fulfilling trees—what else, indeed, could it be called but the "Treasury of Jewels"?
The elixir of immortality is far away for those who are distant from it; even when close at hand, it does not satisfy the thirsty.
Obeisance to the one who removes the exhaustion of those whose minds are scorched by forest fires far away, with the water of the ocean;
let this much suffice, if the tongue does not tire from the vessels of water.
It burns with double intensity, and craving does not cease.
O Abode of Makaras, O Sage, do not despise these jewels; for what indeed has not been bestowed upon you by the Kaustubha through the blows of its serpent-like body, tossed about by the surging waves?
And even the Supreme among Men, with his hands not yet extended, [bestowed it].
Alas, we are ashamed that even many Sāṃkhyas, though possessing great strength,
enter the ocean with their necks bound by ropes placed upon their shoulders.
When their tusks are raised, they are like dogs, clouds, and mountains.
O woman of great renown, for those who thirst for you,
the ocean— though visible from afar— would be as unapproachable as something undrinkable because it is infested with terrifying female sea-monsters.
Why are you afraid of the succession of waves?
Fie, fie, fie upon this ocean of the shameless,
in which travelers are utterly exhausted like those in a desert land,
their long tongues protruding from throats parched by the burning heat of thirst!
Wretched, they go toward the sound of wailing and lamentation.
Even if it were churned by the hosts of the armies of gods and asuras;
even if it were filled with the waters of clouds and rivers;
and even if it were consumed by the fire from the mouth of a forest conflagration—
The ocean did not become agitated, nor did it diminish in extent.

Wherein the Lord of the World, having hidden himself somewhere within a single part of the belly of this universe, remains while the mountains beginning with Maināka cower in fear of Indra; and from whom the Blessed One of fierce radiance rises, and wherein he sets.
Who among the wise is able to weigh the majesty of his profundity against that ocean?
By Upakṛtavatā, through the grace of the two Śrī-ratnas, the crest-jewel of Hari,
and the nectar of the fame of the enemy of Manasija (Śiva), may he remain unhindered by the weight of glory, surpassing even all the gods.
Otherwise, how could he endure?
If the wise ocean were not able to endure the exertion of being churned, [it would have perished].
Facing all directions, the ten quarters were filled with fierce [beings] resembling white coral and gems;
mostly consisting of deceptive allurements,
what indeed was not done by that ocean of fraud at the commencement of its destruction?
Even that was not tolerated by the gods, who were skilled [in debate], except for Amṛta.

O Ocean, since this time has passed away in its profound depth and greatness, yet the undertaking of unaccustomed virtues has not occurred— what is this that follows? Alas, O Sea, why are your waves still failing to reach their fulfillment?
Desist from this flow; not even a drop of this water remains.
Even while dwelling in the lap of this one whose face is turned away,
for even a single moment, his body blazes within; and yet, for that very moment,
he does not remove the thirst of the submarine fire (maurva-agni), despite the abundance of his wealth.
May the ocean of the non-Buddhist scriptures go to destruction, and may its greatness likewise perish.
Oh, how great is this ignoble form of the Lord of Rivers,
that he has allowed these jewels of radiant luster— their qualities long cultivated— to come from afar and find their place among the dull and useless!
Through the intense and powerful gaze of the Subhūti, he suddenly attained identification with that very state.
In this world, a certain person was born blind from birth; though he possessed all [the sensory organs], he was unable to hold even a single mouthful of water because he was parched with thirst.
Yet, he was completely overwhelmed by the deep and heavy thundering of his own self-praise.
O Ocean, why do you not fill the cavity of your ears with your own water, but instead distress yourself with impurities?
Having obtained here this salt water, which is unfit for drinking, one suffers greatly;
even plunging into it is not undertaken by one who is at ease due to the fear of seizing serpents.
Therefore, O traveler, why are you so bewildered by thirst in the desert, thinking it to be the ocean?
O fool, you run about while the impurity of your mental afflictions remains hidden within and unsheathed.

O Ocean, this supportiveness of yours toward all the three worlds is such; this splendor of yours in your watery abode is such; and this great magnanimity of yours is such—having served you alone, who possess a body fearful of many breakages, like the coastal mountain (velācala).
In the stream of the Dharma, whatever evil, suffering, and strife there may be is extinguished everywhere.
Let this [ocean] scatter its waves, rising from the playful sport upon the shore of the best of mountains;
or let it deafen the quarters with its sounds,
spreading far and wide, to cut through the excess of thirst in travelers whose bodies are scorched by the heat of the sun.
O Friend, what can the ocean do, even though it is vast and possesses the power to subdue the clouds?

To him who possesses a treasury of nectar that is peerless among all beings and who grants it to those who ask—though he is the illustrious Vāsava, the great Maṇi, the wish-fulfilling tree, the cow of plenty, and likewise the ocean of the essence of ambrosia—how wonderful that he has attained such [a state]!
