This world, with its one-pointed mind, perceives the ten directions as being devoid of the nine [intermediate] directions.
"Alas, what a tragedy! Seeing me, though I dwell here, as one whose previous efforts have been fruitless, these living beings go elsewhere every day, seeking the waters of the Vipāśā.
Thus, it is as if they have departed out of the intense distress born from carrying this useless burden of water."
I believe that the ocean daily offers its own form as an oblation into the fire of the submarine conflagration.
Whatever little has been obtained for a very long time by Madhusūdana through the preservation of his boundaries, the protection of the great and virtuous,
and through rest— [all that was gained] from the Ocean, who, though worthy of profundity, suffered the agitation of being churned.
O gods, that which was quickly established as the eternal truth has all been utterly destroyed.
The Blessed One is a wondrous forest fire, a wondrous ocean;
when one contemplates the excellence of his deeds, a trembling arises in the mind.
For that single consumer of its own support, drinking [the waters], no satiety was ever reached by the waters.
Not even the slightest fatigue arose in the body of that other great being.
O Ocean, if you do not feel agitation and if you lend an attentive ear for a moment, I ask you something;
having reflected upon it, give me an answer.
Why is it that you are seen sighing, sharpened by the mere latent trace of a desire for solitude?
How much greater would the suffering of travelers be from the heat of the summer than from the heat of the forest fire?
Here sleeps Keśava; here lie the kinsmen of his enemies;
and here rest the virtues of the mountains that provide refuge for those seeking shelter.
And here, moreover, lies the submarine fire along with all the clouds of universal destruction.
Oh, how vast, powerful, and capable of bearing the weight is the form of the ocean!
He gave the fresh splendor of Vaikuṇṭha to Śiva, and even the horse Uccaiḥśravas to the wielder of the thunderbolt; how can that be measured?
Yet, he gave even his own body to the sage who was tormented by thirst.
Who else in the worlds could become such a Bodhisattva, who is like an ocean?
If the ocean, its surface obstructed by the winds scattering golden sands shimmering with jewels,
were to turn toward him;
that indeed would be the misfortune of those who seek faults.
But even if the donor has a slight lack of faith, there is no such [lack] for the recipient.

The ocean clearly brings the drops of water to the state of pearl-jewels, as it constantly seizes them while they fall from the clouds— drops that were previously unobtained— and embraces them with its circling waves as they descend.
Even one who is humble is honored by masters if he has shown respect through his conduct from the very beginning.
May there be well-being for those who resemble coral creepers and flowers; may the row of pearl-oyster shells be auspicious.
I have obtained the entire fruit of the ocean.
That I have not been torn apart by the wood-dwelling aquatic creatures.
Having drawn water from the mouths of rivers on all sides,
what has been gained by this wicked miser?
It has only been turned into ash and offered as an oblation into the fire of his own speech.
And it was placed within the hollow of the Pātāla cave.
He who, out of pride, does not grasp a great jewel when the time has come,
later suffers upon seeing it in the hands of another.
It is split by entering within according to the limiting adjuncts of one's preference;
what kind of purity could there be for that insentient crystal stone?
That very quality which belongs to crystal becomes a defect;
for by its transparency, it assumes the reflection even of those things that are impure.
That the price of a mere fragment of stone is but a small amount of wealth for the Earth-bearer is a manifestation of that splendor whose essence never sets.
If someone takes the tips of the stalks of sugarcane for the sake of wealth,
fools nevertheless employ that very person to guard their feet.
Born from a noble lineage, possessing the virtues of the virtuous,
well-rounded,
and endowed with qualities that rival the moon, look, O beautiful one, how lovely this necklace appears!
She was drawn outside by her two high breasts.
If gold, though worthy of being grasped from the ground, is obstructed by tin and lead,
it neither cries out nor does it shine.
There is a restriction on the speech of one who employs [the means].
The excellent emerald, though soiled,
never abandons its own nature;
fie upon the impurity of the crystal!
He who has reached the limit partakes of form.
O friend, in this great abundance of jewels, why indeed do you worry?
O stone, become a gem; do not remain a mere stone.
For today, gems are indeed prevailing in the world.
For those whose very skill in grasping a blade of grass is their ornament.
Though falling to the ground, though covered in dust,
and though disregarded by wicked people who are blind from birth,
he possesses the supreme majesty of being worshipped by the three worlds.
For one who possesses a mind of reflection never abandons [the goal] at any time.
O Cintāmaṇi, if you have not been held upon the head by any deity on this earth, do not despair;
for there is simply no seed of merit for such an exaltation as yours.
In this world, the head of someone is worthy of good fortune.
The Creator fashioned both the wish-fulfilling gem and the wish-granting tree;
why then is the pride of being a "jewel" equal for both?
For the one is not exhausted by bestowing all desired objects upon those who seek them.
He took the tattered garment like a blade of grass, yet he was not ashamed.
Filled with hundreds of desires, yet honored by the crown of the Lord of the World;
rendered sufficient by mere blades of grass, having set foot upon certain rocky crags;
he who is the object of such a vision even for those possessed of consciousness—[to him I bow].
In the Luḥatya-cala-kaṇḍara mountain, there is this wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) Vidhura.
She gazes repeatedly at that which is supreme, desirable, and exceedingly delicate; she conceals it with incomparable joy, thinking it to be some great jewel.
Yet, having somehow acquired a surface resembling a smear upon a piece of glass, [she treats it as such].
Alas, the wretched fool indeed endures excessive torment!
O brother, having long filled the circle of the quarters with showers of pearls,
why have you manifested here in vain through this deception? Who here truly knows the ultimate, innate worth of your being?
In a village burned down by fire, where the lords and the commoners have been slain, [he is] like an emerald.
To some he is far away; even that person of unrefined intellect does not perceive his inner nature.
Some proud man does not beg, while another of meager intent merely seeks a trifle. Thus, for one who is addicted to the vice of giving when requested, the streaks of magnanimity do not shine forth.
Born amidst the difficulties that are hard to traverse, he remains steadfast in those situations that are like wish-fulfilling jewels.
Those who seize the heads of elephants, or even those who take heaps of jewels—
having been seen in every house for a long time as jewels burnt and their number diminished—
I do not know whether this is due to their absence or whether it is heard of here as being caused by fate.
Even the name of that [jewel] is not found here; yet he who takes up jewels in his hand [does not obtain them].
When those liberated from the ocean of existence are cast into the great Avīci hells,
they roll about at its edges with stainless radiance, appearing as if clearly laughing;
this is because that very ocean has been exhausted for them, and they have taken hold of other continents.
But there are indeed those who follow the path of the samyaktva, who are afflicted by the addiction of grasping at jewels.
"This ruby is of great value, honored upon the surface of the earth, radiant, and of noble birth;
surely, upon seeing it, some terrible misfortune will quickly depart.
Thinking thus, someone established it with various illusory displays for the sake of warding off calamity.
In that infinite [space], there is seen a certain fragment of stone, harsh with hundreds of wounds.
O Rohanagiri, may there be well-being for you from me;

do not even in your dreams think, "How, how will these [people] survive once they have fallen from their position? For if we, the jewels, have gained our standing through you, then it is your own glory.
Those kings, devoted to the deer-horned [bow], will place us upon their crowns.
Having climbed a tree upon the path for a long time, let him raise his voice loudly:
"Śaṅkha, whose fame pervades all directions, is here—the ground of honor."
"That which is agitated is indeed agitated; that which has ceased is dead. As for the fact that it breathes out with its exhalation—is that truly so?
Rather, it merely utters [a sound]; this is not its [actual] voice."
"That which is not worth hearing is not of true meaning."
Having abandoned their lives here, these conch shells— worthy of the quality of whiteness—
have attained union with the face of the world,
resounding with the sound of great majesty.
Those whose hearts are capable of giving up even their very lives for them are truly compassionate.
The wise man [thinks]: "Truly, the sound of the conch, which brings pleasure to the ear, is a supreme flavor and a source of great auspiciousness;
yet it is heard only somewhere in a village or a town during the midday hours, while the long necks of intoxicated, stout dogs are stretched out."
The *nāṭya* called *nāṭa* is characterized by gratitude for favors received and laughter born of rusticity.
Even when being reviled by those born from a mine of jewels,
or being mocked as one with "well-dried bones," or being struck by their sighs and huffs;
One whose mind is pure speaks only of auspiciousness; such a person is like a conch shell.
There are thousands of conch shells in the ocean, tossed about by the impact of the waves; they roll along the shores, their surfaces stained dark by the mud.
Yet, one certain Pañcajanya arose, a source of wonder for the virtuous.
The enemy of Mura is filled by his own breath-winds, which are equal to the winds at the time of universal destruction.
The perfection of all his aspirations was achieved through the pride of the syllable *huṃ*; even his birth was from the ocean of milk.
His body, which kisses the face of Govinda, is more beautiful than the orb of the full moon.
This is Śrī herself, innate to him; what else need be said of these virtues? For they are—
O Pañcajanya, that crookedness in your heart causes us great shame.
"Let there be the splendor of the moon alone, not the equality of the splendor of others"—
thinking thus, as the night-lily blossoms, the lotus closes its bud.
This form, which consists of contact with the rays of splendor, is certainly a blemish upon the lotus,
in that it turns its back toward the moon that is the jewel-cluster of virtues.
May there be many internal cavities and many thorns on the outside;
how could the virtues of the lotus stalk not be beautiful?
O Padmā, why do you cover yourself with white garments, even though you possess virtues that are exceedingly long? For if those noble ones were to see them, they would surely behold them.
Like one who is terrified, the Goddess of Splendor does not set foot there.
Heap up thorns upon the dry land with joy,
proclaiming them as born from a mass of mud;
furthermore, maintain your resolve when encountering the water.
"You are proceeding toward the splendors of those who possess horses and chariots."
Although these [lotuses] possess a natural addiction to the mud in their hearts, and their faces are thick with passion and intoxicated with honey,
nevertheless, they remain the supreme abode of beauty.
Indeed, that very wretchedness is what constitutes their misfortune.
Even lotuses and other flowers, though possessing many virtues,
do not perish when separated from the sun;
for they are born from a pond of water mixed with mud.
This world of the three realms is renowned as being surpassed by the elder [Subhūti].
O Lakṣmī, distinguish yourself by your skill in removing the thorns of distress;
O Jṛmbhā, abandon your yawning and your restlessness for a moment;
O Āśā, bring joy here to the swarms of bees that have arrived.
Since there exists a friend who possesses the proper means, you may accomplish this as you desire.

O Kuśeśaya, listen always to my words; out of affection for you, I shall say something to you. [I speak] because of this stainless beauty of yours, or perhaps because of your virtues, which attract like bees.
Why do you go to that which is most delightful, or rather, to the thicket of thorns?
"Contract yourself, abandon the lotus stalks!
Behold, O Sobhā, this fault-producing [state] now arises.
Having reflected upon it step by step, it prevails within the crooked self."
Concealment is itself appropriate for those who possess virtues.
Although it possesses many thorns, although it is full of holes, although it is born from foul mud, and although its splendor is enjoyed by bees— nevertheless, it is the lotus.
Upon the rising of the sun, it always attains full blossoming.
May the stalks of lotuses, which produce a deep, humming, and thick sound through their dense collision as they are greedily lapped by swarms of honey-bees, become objects of my desire—
stalks where even the Creator himself sings with a melody so exceedingly sweet to the ear.
He is that certain Bhṛṅga, whose lotus-feet are supported by the earth.
To you who dispel the heat [of suffering], whose heart is radiant and awakened,
who delight in affection for friends, who uphold a multitude of true virtues, and who gladden those who offer their own limbs with your sublime instructions—
It is fitting that your abode should be here, in every single lotus.
Neither birth from the mud nor a fondness for dwelling among the dull-witted would have occurred;
O land-lotus, if your body were not anointed with the radiance of beauty, like the luster of jewels,
you would not have instilled lightness in the hearts of the steadfast.
You alone shall become the supreme state of Lakṣmī in this world.
Innumerable clusters of lotuses have arisen upon the surfaces of the lakes,
resembling the lovely faces of the wives of the lords of night;
yet, in the navel of the enemy of Bhauma, there arose that one unique and great lotus.
He who has become the ground for the birth of the one who brings forth the manifestation of the three worlds.
Elsewhere, the space [within her] was skillfully cleared by means of the allure of fragrances;
though she entered into his own enjoyment, he did not grant her a loose embrace due to the absence of a treasury [of wealth].
Having thus been reduced to destitution at nightfall, this foolish-minded one, his path exhausted, departed.
Behold the bee, who, though intoxicated by the splendor of the lotus, is forcibly driven away from both sides!
Brother lotus, endure for a little while this closing;
that same splendor of yours shall shine forth at dawn when the sun appears.
Having reached a downward state, the lotus stalks are marked by mud;
though possessing virtues, they are dragged down by meritless alligators that reveal their own sprouts.
Then those lotus buds, endowed with virtues and worthy of being honored by the wise,
were placed upon the head by that dull-witted one, yet they remained closed.
In the desert there is no water at all; even if it is obtained with great difficulty, it is but little and warm, and does not alleviate one's thirst.
Even the hollow of the beak of a *caṭula* sparrow,
though it be as small as a single grain of rice,
has become the domain of intense joy today by virtue of its kinship with the arrival of the clouds.
Another was made [wet] with waters by the cloud.
O traveler, is this collection of materials necessary for the accomplishment of churning seen here in the desert named Sugṛhīta?
For indeed, everything there has been turned upside down.
There is a well there, and the water therein is obtained without effort.

What else in this desert is beyond the reach of words? O traveler, do not depart for a moment; be one who is compassionate toward those who have sought refuge. By you, who are so eager for even a drop of water—
A bed of sand was seen with its perimeter ablaze.
Those whose bodies were adorned with the excellence of abundant foliage and blossoms from excellent trees, who were weighed down by the burden of fruit,
and whose broad [limbs] were inhabited by hundreds of birds warbling with joy;
"Therefore, the deluded person searches for it in the desert of worldly existence; it does not exist there."
"The waters, trees, and grasses are empty for the weary travelers;
alas, I am truly unable to provide them with any assistance at all"—
thinking thus, the Blessed One did not indeed lie down until [the time had come].
He applies them for the attainment of the sixfold supernatural power (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
The earth was bewildered by the speed of his departure, and she trembled with longing; then, after sighing for a very long time, she stood there in dejection.
What indeed has not been done by this traveler? And yet, the desert remains thus deceitful.
It is miserable that [the mind] is by nature flavorless, since it does not attain even the slightest moisture.
From here the terrifying flock of crows; from here the gathering of hawks; from here the vultures and the like;
from here the family of herons and cranes;
in this desolate place, devoid of all virtues, where even the sound of a bird has been destroyed—
Furthermore, there were indeed two or three birds whose speech was not at all melodious.
Are you confused? Or have you lost your mind, that you are noticed in an instant? Yet again and again, you perform no action whatsoever preceded by a glance.
Even though you know it yourself to be waterless, you enter the desert.
O traveler, if you desire to obtain water that is cool and sweet—
He who experiences suffering for the sake of others is sweet even in his destruction;
indeed, every such transformation here is esteemed,
provided it does not fall upon a barren field and thus fail to reach maturity.
Is this not a worm living in filth? Yet, it is not through lack of merit that he has become a god.
O Desert, your heat is real; you are a forest of thorns for the trees and creepers that take refuge within you, and you are abandoned by travelers.
Your thirst is intense, and your treasury is the arising of misfortune.
Yet, is this not a very great benefit for those who possess a mere drop of water, as you roar with pride?
For that reason, even the common rain-clouds exert themselves to provide assistance.
If you have performed such service for me according to this method, there is no one to whom it is incomparable. Even if you have not served me, O Māra, you need not speak; remain firm.
Why do you produce this deception with clouds of water, like a deer-thirsting mirage?
O friend, you who cause thirst even in those whose minds are already fainting from it—how much more so others—are you not to be pitied?
Are these mango trees, beautiful with their heads bent low under the weight of fruit, being cut down by you?
Are these shady plantain trees, fragrant when in bloom, being destroyed?
Alas, they have been once again ravaged by the unchecked and fierce claws of wild elephants.
"O fool, why do you wander aimlessly in this windless desert, seeking in vain to die in the wilderness?"
Let the waters remain within the abysses or go wherever they may;
let the flow of the celestial river extend as far as the ocean, its source of jewels, during the rainy season.
Where is the end? Where is the utterly empty sound, and likewise where is the form of beautiful appearance?
These two were created as deceptions for those whose minds are empty of discernment.
He has no difficulty in carrying heavy loads, nor does he lack strength when pulling;
yet even so, the temple bull eats only what is wholesome.
A crocodile, having reached its own domain, can drag away even a lordly elephant;
yet that very same creature, fallen from its place, is devoured even by a dog.
Better a kick from the foot of a lion with its high, well-proportioned,
and beautiful tail than climbing upon a jackal.
A sandalwood tree, though its essence is fragrance, is served in vain;
serpents that feed on air are the attendants of the noble—a strange dispensation of fate!
Where has the deer gone that it does not live day after day eating various kinds of grass?
But for the lion, who feeds on elephants slain by himself, sustenance is difficult to obtain.
Even Viśvakarman himself would not be able to straighten out this difficult wood, which is crooked, lying in a disordered state, with its interior full of knots and many hard joints.
Not even slightly imitated by those who have long practiced [austerities] is that cold water;
on the contrary, my eyes are blinded by the lamps and filled with smoke.
When shall we, with stainless eyes, behold that city of Amaṇa, which is utterly destroyed,
where the Cintāmaṇi and Cakra are both devoid of their opposite qualities?
What else can be accomplished for him who touches a lamp, fearing it might be a radiant campaka bud,
other than the burning away of the stain of soot?
The ocean, with its mass of flames flickering like a cluster of firebrands from the crest of Mount Sumeru, is something to be leaped over by someone;
but this collection of city ruins is not.
O you whose many heads are more powerful than the sun and the moon, [the goddess] Se-Se,
lifting up the burden of the earth, prays to you with a multitude of piteous cries.
Who could perceive, even with effort, the path by which the food of peacocks enters their throats,
if it were not for the fact that fools dance when delighted by the roar of clouds?
In autumn, the night— though its mass of darkness is struck by hundreds of rays from the full moon—
is not even equal to the shadow of day, even when the sun is hidden behind clouds.
Even for one who delights in soft and beautiful ornaments, this single act of the God of Love is truly unbecoming:
that he has placed upon his banner a sea-monster with a mouth as formidable as a row of fangs.
O wise goldsmith, homage be to you! For it is difficult to examine many things thoroughly;
[only] with a touchstone can one distinguish them from an ornament of gold.
That which you are now placing upon the scale.
Even while that blind well of a potter was still active,
he was unable to remove your favor;
yet your base conduct has been sealed by you.
Let those who receive it partake of that water from his mouth.
If a hundred-footed creature cannot traverse even a cow’s footprint in a hundred years, how much less can a two-footed human being?
O you who possess the prowess of the ocean, we debate with you.
There is no delight in being attended by spiritual teachers or preceptors, nor is there any regard for gathering great disciples;
even when seeking [the Dharma], there is no talk of rewards or results.
O foolish hunter, why do you wish to seize me here now?
[The Buddha said: "O Subhūti, why is it said that both the blade of grass and the human being possess [the same nature], since they are both vast in their intention?
For those two, even by means of the minute particles of a single tip of the blade of grass..."
When the grasping and the counteracting have been brought to completion.
O goldsmith,
you who are skilled in the labor of fashioning various ornaments from gold and silver;
set aside your toil here today for this golden vessel.
For one who joins with a difficult-to-train [horse], there is the acquisition of great value.
Who here would not, for a long time, mistake a drop of water for a pearl because it is held upon the tip of a slender lotus stalk? Thus, one whose vision is perverted [regards the world as real].
In this world, we alone here possess consciousness.
O Daṇḍaśūka, even though it is improper,
your voice leads [us] to truth through its sweetness,
like the luster of anklets; for it has captivated the hearts of the assembly of listeners, who are now fainting with the intensity of their devotion.
"Why do you wish to make these marks on my body? he asked.
Goldsmith:
"You have come here to sell things worthy of being sold;
yet even today, nothing has been heard from this village."
The village headman was surely one whose ears were unpierced.
Is it not indeed a mark of beauty when one remains unagitated and cool even when struck by a blow?
When one's vital energy is crushed by the onset of a calamity,
is it right for the submarine fire to flare up in a fit of rage?
Even the blazing [fire] can be extinguished by churning the ocean.
How vast is this ocean, so great because it is filled by the flood of clouds and the flow of rivers; yet you, though like a small well, provide assistance to those who seek your aid.
For this greatness consists indeed in purifying the hollow of the womb.
Fie on the fire that approaches its enemy with such longing as to consume it; fie on the sword of an enemy who likewise seeks only to fill his own belly!
"One does not satisfy even the enemy with water."
"Desiring to prevent her young ones from falling into the water of the river,
the female pigeon, having seized the water with the hollow of her wings, reportedly sprinkled the forest fire again and again upon her head."
An affectionate person indeed does not consider even their own sleep.
A crow, though naturally fickle,
when it has obtained an offering, calls upon its own kin as well as others,
even toward the carcass of an elephant, which is full of skin, bone, and flesh.
"He hates his own [people] and strikes down others, for his nature is one of mercilessness."
The cloud that takes up water only to release it again in greater measure is the foremost among the dull-witted;
but he who desires to give back exactly what he has received is truly noble.
He is a stream-enterer, a ship’s captain free from shame.
Even though we conceptualize in many ways, we do not fully comprehend [the Buddhas]. By what names shall we designate those of great intelligence,
who are like gold that serves as the ornament for all remaining worlds?
The diamond is the supreme means of valid cognition for discerning reality.
The faces of those who possess all abodes have not withered;
there is no darkness for them, nor has any benefit been rendered to the world.
By what virtue do you think, "I am the son of the Sun," [and thus address] the worlds?
"You shall cause him to be restored to his seat without an oath."
The one who performs the act of protecting [the field] by means of the ploughshare—
behold this man, the very image of oneself! Indeed, he is steadfast because of his lack of activity, and free from pride.
The herds of cattle and deer will once again graze upon the grain.
Whose eyes are these that resemble the sun, unless they belong to a celestial being? For even having seized them, what is this [creature] with its mouth wide open that is swallowing them?
O fool, you have not seen the limit of this clear speech.
If you have indeed brought about a base birth for yourself, though endowed with virtue from birth,
then tell me this truth:
for what purpose was he raised by the driver Anala?
Therefore, O wicked one, bring stain upon this entire universe by doing that.
Even if one should fall from masculinity, even if one should go below,
even if one should be led away by the great [Yama],
such a person would uplift the entire world; this is the nature of this [compassion].
It was revealed by a certain Supreme Person who illuminated the directions.

One of limited intention who, while conceptualizing only the various forms of his own family and craft, stumbles like a goblin in a glass-shop— he is seized by the Kaustubha jewel, the gem that rivals the wealth of Indra.
The end of the single thread of the woven fabric occurs without effort.
Where is the Goddess who removes misfortune, the sister, the Mother?
Where is the Lord Hara, the husband of his sister, the kinsman of the distressed?
Where is that wretched state of having come for refuge to the ocean?
O Maināka, you must not speak this way. No.
But that string of the lotus-stalk,
though worthy of praise, O Daitya, is indeed useless for the sun as it seeks to set from the peak of its own lofty mountain.
Having approached him with fear, the Lord of the Maruts leaned upon him for support.
O Kubera, Lord of Wealth, you wear a house as your seat, an elephant hide as your garment, ashes as your ointment, and a bull as your vehicle; are you not ashamed?
This poverty of yours is a misfortune for your dear friend.
There is no cessation of activity anywhere in a single place; all phenomena are established in their own inherent natures according to their degrees of intensity.
Even when being consumed by the fire of the eon until the end of time—
The ocean of suffering is swallowed by a single mouthful of wisdom.

The Blessed Viṣṇu supports the entire earth; the serpent [Śeṣa] supports him along with that [earth]; and the ocean supports even him together with those two. Yet the pitcher-born [Agastya] indeed swallowed even him with ease.
There is no limit whatsoever to the greatness of the great.

Her youth has been mounted upon her broad hips; she is firmly embraced by the creeper-like arms around her neck; and this [chest] is intensely pressed by her lofty breasts, which are full as if with milk.
The pot eats the fruits of the kitchen.
If one were to place the tracks of the lord of beasts upon a wall of flesh, adorned with artificial garlands of pearls,
it would be like the footprints of one who is greedy for the temples of intoxicated elephants.
How could he not let out a roar like that of the Lord of Lions?
Even his face, from which radiates such splendor,
swallows the sun and the moon as if they were mere morsels;
for had his entire body been manifest, [what would have become of them]?
What indeed, what indeed could Rāhu not have done at that time?
O parrot, because they are deluded by the similarity between flowers, sprouts, and fruits,
they do not know whether you are perched or not;
therefore, you do not abandon this tree out of a desire for fruit.
One who is distressed by a matter does not take account of the harm [caused] by the withdrawal.
Is it not better that I have been crushed here by the heat of the sun in a thicket of shrubs,
or scorched by forest fires until my entire body was consumed? For I have not been trampled by the throngs of heartless people who are ignorant of the value of stalks and leaves.
O Mālatī, you are woven amidst other flowers.
What is this appropriate [question]: "O Śuddhodana, for you who are pure, clearly elevated by your kin, and endowed with the ripening of fruit, it is fitting to attain the excellence of virtue;
for a moment, [the words] have reached the vicinity of your ear as you stand before another."
O fierce one with disheveled hair, you who destroy those who are far away from the human realm.
That golden ornament,
once the praiseworthy glory upon the head of a king,
was reduced to such a state of wretchedness by the dust clinging to the ground that it was indistinguishable from a mere lump of iron due to the confusion caused by its mistaken perception as such.
Having observed him, the world avoids him out of fear of the touch of his feet.
Among the lowly and the noble, a mosquito is not distinguished from a great elephant;
whether dwelling in the midst or at the head, it does not surpass the luster of jewels. Even a firefly does not tremble to move among those who are radiant.
Fie upon this insentient generality, which, like a master, has not realized the inner reality of things!
If such is the inherent nature of the lake, why this dullness?
If there is indeed natural straightness, why these knotted stalks?
If the root is so beautiful, why this flow of mud from the lotus? If these qualities exist, for what reason [are they thus]?
"Friend lotus stalk, we do not consider it to be the truth that you have holes."

O friend, whether you are a wealthy man, or Kuṇḍalī, or a serpent—if you wear a crown adorned with jewels, O snake, may it be well with you; what does that matter to us? If you cast off your skin in an improper place, we have no desire for it here.
But what cruel flame is this, O brother, that you burn me; what is this obsession?
On one side, there is the head as the dwelling, the mountain cave as the home, and the shedding of the skin of the self as renunciation;
sustenance is provided by winds that arrive without effort, and such is the conduct in one place.
On the other side, the path is crooked, speech is a mere mat, and poison is seen in the very look.
O friend Bhogin, why does this lamp burn even without oil? What is this?
There will be many more mouths for him; indeed, you already know his great-souled nature.
Kadru, this is his first birth; considering that the world is now provoked, one must reflect on how his conduct, such as this, is a marvel to the three worlds. By means of this, she— [is overcome].
Even when the pure knowledge has been turned back as if straightened out, the stubborn stain remains difficult to remove.
Of what use is that mountain of gold or that mountain of silver,
by whose support trees remain merely trees? We consider only the Malaya mountain to be such, for it is upon that alone that they depend.
"Even the *sahā*, *hotanimba*, and *kuta* trees are sandalwood."
How much more blameworthy is that misconduct which is committed through deliberate intent?
Even those serpents who watch for the vulnerabilities of innocent people in order to kill them,
these very creatures, though deluded regarding the true nature of good and evil, wear jewels upon their heads.
For those endowed with virtue, there is no error anywhere due to propriety; therefore, enough with anxiety.
He was maintained out of necessity, not because he was created;
though perfectly independent, he was not pampered at will so that, being healthy, he might not strike back.
Let this bull, though standing here, remain mute while he performs his service.
"Householder, what more need be said? At this very moment, thieves are prowling about in your house."
If you do not give away what belongs to yourself, why do you cry out when others take even a little for the sake of another?
O wicked one, is this out of malice toward a hidden treasure and such?
This much is enough; I ask you another thing: for what reason am I [being treated thus]?
With roars as heavy as the force of a blazing fire, they burned the people.
Those who are devoid of essence, exceedingly light by nature, and unfit for any task—
those whose limbs, such as old grass and reeds, are now falling away, having reached a state of independence—
alas, fie upon that wind which, turning its back on the inner core, treats them thus!
Behold how the paths of the great, set upon the sky, proceed with extreme instability.

Look, my friend, at those who are light by nature and have never before entered into any calculation— those who were long buried in the earth, trampled daily by feet alone; now they have been tossed into the sky by the restless wind.
But these particles of dust, remaining above those who stand upon the earth, cause them to be elevated.
Subhūti said: "Listen, O Stream-enterer, if I speak my own words.
One should fear much from one's own faction, but not so much from the power of an opponent;
for even those possessed of light are but few when enveloped in darkness."
Objects appear according to their own capacities when the sun exists, but they do not appear otherwise.

Indeed, this pair of eyes of the Lord of Consciousness, which possess the power of vision, leaves aside contact with other limbs— claiming they are stainless— and leads toward the collection of objects present before it; meanwhile, the nose, delighting in fragrance, remains fixed in the middle region between the two eyes, as beautiful as a bamboo stalk.
"O weary one, do not let your eyes be constantly closed while you lie here; release your sighs!"
From his mouth [he spoke]: "How much of this is on the lotus leaf?
O dull-witted one, you considered that which was recited from the text to be a *muktāphala* (pearl). Listen to something else even more than this:
while it was being slowly removed by the slight action of the tip of a finger..."
Having departed from there, he sleeps day after day with the cry of "Alas! and finds no end to his sorrow.
Alas! How many hostile factions have gathered right here at this very lake!
Yet the mind of this swan does not turn even slightly toward the lotus, the abode of beauty;
having slept, it awakens only now. Therefore, let us wait for him from here.
The bees consider the time of dawn to be their beloved, while the moments of dusk are indeed their food.
Having been comforted by those who sustain the world through the diet of air,
they were in turn devoured by peacocks practicing the severe vow of subsisting on drops of water from clouds;
and even they were brought to destruction by hunters clad in the skins of fierce tigers.
Even though people recognize it as a manifestation of hypocrisy, the deceitful person still pursues virtues here.
Even the name of another tree was closed [to him], yet it was opened for him; the hand of Fate, faltering on its own path at the time of his departure, was seized by others;
and this world was rescued from the state of not seeing what was unseen through the power of destiny.
"O wood-gatherer, it is proper that you do not eat this mango from the *ālīma* tree."
He who formerly, when the great burden was upon him, always traveled alone on a perfectly level path; he who never once let out the lowing sound of his own herd of cattle;
and who was the very ornament of that very herd of cattle—alas, it is now he!
Alas! The cow of Dhavala, now that old age has come upon her, is being driven out for sale.
When the black serpent’s face was made harsh by the croaking of a frog,
he raised his hand without fear to slap it with the flat of his palm;
and while the serpent stood there covering its eyes with its lowered head—
All of that was merely the playful manifestation of some Blessed One, acting as a counselor.

O Fish, having observed all this clearly in this world by the simple folk— that you dwell eternally at sacred fords, that your nature is exceedingly tender and charming, and that your conduct is indeed divine, like pure drops of water fallen from the sky upon your face— [they have concluded this].
Your excellence has been demonstrated; by whom were these thorns, both internal and external, perceived?
Death has drawn its bow like a gaping mouth; these arrows are the fanged serpents.
His training has surpassed that of Arjuna, yet his terrifying course is one of total surrender.
Alas! There is cruelty within the heart of this rogue, yet sweet and captivating song flows from his mouth.
I think that this forest will become devoid of deer, just as it will come to be for this hunter.
Let the greatness of the sky be cursed; let the foot of Indra fall high;

let the course of fate be blameworthy; or let there be [the state] of non-existence or emptiness for him by whom, with hands upraised, his light is lost, and he is exhausted, tormented, and suffering.
Even for a friend, if left without support, no handhold was made for the sake of stability.
O you who cause the burning of the quarters and bring an end to the forest, these flames of yours do not please me;
people do not desire the growth of one who has risen against their own support.
This fire was created by ill-fated destiny to destroy the very roots of that great mountain.
O wretched one, who indeed would not fear you, who bring such distress to the world? Alas!
With a body somehow sustained through the suffering of hunger, emaciated and devoid of nourishment, he wandered from house to house seeking the crumbs left by householders;
yet, having found only a fragment of bone fallen by chance, he perceived these three worlds as empty.
Thinking thus, he said: "Alas, fie! That very son of a slave now acts like a lion!"

Even a cow’s bone—foul-smelling, worn away by time, covered in grime, and devoid of flesh—when obtained by itself, satisfies its hunger; yet that [bone] does not bring it peace. A lion, even when a jackal has approached, abandons it and slays an elephant.
Even when fallen into every kind of hardship, a person desires a fruit that corresponds to their own nature.
Having observed that the swans have slowly departed from the lotus pond, their plumage now worn by the water and their beauty dimmed;
and seeing that the lotuses, whose filaments are shattered by the currents, have sunk into the water;
and that this path, which serves as an entrance to the happiness of all seasons, is now covered with fresh grass.
Even that lake, though naturally pure, has perished through its very growth.
For those whose minds are awakened by the happiness of tranquility, that [state] is as close as a clod of earth;
but for those whose intellects are cluttered with greed for wealth, it remains far away for men.
For whose sake, then, was such a station of perfections created by the Ordainer?
Mount Meru, whose golden majesty is fully perfected within itself alone, does not please me.

For those with broken intentions, there is the overturning of the high and low status of substances, the sowing of seeds in the depths, and the seeking out of one's own natural flaws; while the children sleep in ignorance, those who have cast off fear arrange the formation of the cosmic array.
"Alas! Having found an empty dwelling, what—indeed, what—has not been done by the monkeys?"
When the great elements have dissolved into one another as if out of fear,
at the end of the eon, that single supreme tree alone expands with its mass of trunks;
it is by this deity that the three worlds are placed within the hollow of his belly and he remains there.
On the tip of a tree branch, like a swan weary from the playful sport of bathing in the water, the beloved of Lord Viṣṇu—
whose mind is intent on benefiting the three worlds— was born in the lineage of the mountains, gladdening the gods with her excellent and cherished qualities.

The Mother of her own abode, who is intent on granting the desires even of the Mlecchas, increases the height of the Vindhya; what power of fate is not innate? (By Amṛtadatta) O foolish-minded plowman, do not, do not wield the plow that has destroyed its fruit! (By Hāla)
The field does not exist here below, nor has hardness ever been seen by you there;

no impression is produced there—cease from affliction! Is it not seen or heard that many have gone forth, bearing only the fruit [of their efforts], while remaining perpetually seedless? Of whom is this [the teaching]?
O Wind, what kind of delusion is this of yours, that you establish a mass of dust— born from a place of refuse and clouds—
in the sky frequented by hosts of radiant beings?
Let alone the affliction it causes to the paths of people's eyes when it is stirred up!

By what means can this impurity of sin upon your body be endured? It was born from you alone, O Bhānu, as the tortoise Amṛtadatta, by whom his back was offered for the sake of supporting the vast burden of the world.
Dhruva’s birth is praiseworthy, for there the circle of the luminaries revolves, held fast by his command.

Having abandoned their vain factions, other beings—like moths caught within a fig tree inside the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)—have perished while attempting to do what is beneficial for others; they have neither risen above nor descended below. O elephant among men, why do you take such pleasure in this bitter [speech] against the ears?
O you whose own intellect is well-known, what is there that is not known? [It is said:
"The elephant herd sank into the hollow of a mosquito's throat, while its frontal globes were split open by the tip of the sword-blade."—of whom?

O arrogant one, do not be proud, thinking, "I shall agitate the ocean with the flow of my river," when you are but a mere drop upon the tip of a blade of grass. If you desire your own existence, then wander instead in the desert sands.
Or even if a forest fire is far away, it is here that you are being tormented by great beings.
O Lord of Waters, you who possess a lofty crest for the sake of the world’s stability and who are bound by the shore like a great mountain—
why do you vainly desire to cross over this [ocean] with your swift movement? For from that, nothing would come to you but the destruction of your supreme jewels and your very essence.
Surely, even after being struck by the soles of his feet, he will perish right there at the end of that very spot.
O virtuous one, you cause the sun in the sky to tremble incessantly,
as well as the hosts of stars,
the moon, and other luminous bodies such as the radiant fire and so forth.
Even so, you do not abandon that internal blindness which perceives variety.
Now begins the *Śṛṅgārapaddhati*.
Therein, first is the *vipralambha* (love-in-separation):
"This is that Śaṃkara, whose self-restraint is renowned throughout the three worlds... [Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra 1038-1]

Afflicted by the pain of separation, the god of love, laughing within himself, supports his beloved with his beautiful body; and thinking, "By him we have indeed been conquered," he causes the lover’s hand to be pressed against his own hand.
Those eyes of women—whose pupils are drawn by the bow of the eyebrows and released like arrows, whose lashes are the bees and sky-like glances;

which have dark pupils that pierce the hearts of men like cruel iron shafts; which have long side-glances for feathers and smiles for poison; and which are thick with lashes—are the very swords of women.
