the Five-Arrowed One,
In that regard, first, concerning the path of departure of the beloved in the context of *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (love in separation):
"Go, go, O beloved, if you must; may your paths be auspicious.
May my rebirth also occur in that very place where you have gone."
"What is so wonderful about your departing by force after having seized me by the hand? But if you depart from my heart, then I shall credit you with true manliness."
As she embraced her beloved who had asked,
"I am going," a struggle ensued between her speech and her life-breath as they vied for precedence.
When you have not been seen, there is longing for the sight; when you have been seen, there is fear of separation. Neither by not seeing you nor by seeing you can happiness be obtained.
"You should remember me, my beloved; I shall not forget you. For by that [love] which has stolen your heart, I shall remember you."
Casting aside her modesty, she wept; she held up the hem of her garment; "Do not go," she cried, placing her fingers over her mouth.
While the Lord of Life was departing, what did that slender-limbed woman not do to turn him back as he stood before her?
To them she said: "Enough, enough! It is no remedy for the grief of first separation to follow after the Lord of Life who has already departed.
'A journey to Rāma is for our welfare,' saying this, she was as if restrained by Kāñcanī, who rushed forward with cries of distress and prostrations at her feet."
Having spoken thus, "O you of practiced and sweet conduct," she spoke harshly out of anger; as her lover departed, intent on wrath by rejecting her prostration at her feet,
she sighed deeply and, placing her hand upon her breast, cast her gaze— veiled by tears— upon her friends.
“O beloved, will you come here at the end of the watch, or at midday, or even later? How much more so when the entire day has passed?
With such childish talk, full of playful jests and bashfulness, she prevents her lover from departing for that place which can only be reached in sixty days.
"Do not go"—this ill-omened word spoken out of affection;
"Go"—this command of authority; "Stay"—this indifference according to one's own whim. (All these are merely words from Kṛṣṇa.)
"Is it possible or not that the words 'I shall not live without you' could be uttered? Therefore, O Lord, as you depart, please instruct me in what is appropriate for you to say."
Let some [proponent] of the Dākṣiṇātya school indeed fix the resolve "I go" in his heart; however,
how can it be possible for one who lacks compassion for those whose life-breath is equal to his own to speak in such a manner?

It has been said that it is "merely a name"; yet, alas, even upon seeing the face of my beloved, with its tears flowing profusely, the desire for the acquisition of a mere fragment of wealth still causes me to wander!
That coral which possesses the beauty of a bimba fruit even in a dream— I have never seen it;
can the splendor of her smile be attained even through austerities by means of pearls?

O traveler, even if gold were to be purified by falling into fire, how could it ever become as beautiful as this? Why do you abandon your beloved wife, who is made of jewels, for the sake of what wealth?
O Śrī Śivasvāmin,
when the beloved’s departure had come within the range of hearing,
the innocent woman, standing at the edge of the bed, gazed for a long time at his stainless face.
Pressing her own face— tearful with heavy sighs and washed by tears flowing from a throat choked with intense grief— against her husband’s heart, she wept silently.
O beloved of the intoxicated woman, do not go; you have been told by me many times with hundreds of endearments.
O young girl, when you have come before me with your body bowed low, you shall attain the highest perfection.
Moreover,
our house is daily filled with ill-spoken words, even though we exert ourselves to endure the pain of the heavy burden of our breasts, while the lattices of our bodices are falling apart.
O slender-limbed one, you have been seen; the travelers have departed. Knowing that my arrival will be in just a few days, do not grieve.
Having suddenly disregarded such beloved words as these,
he has acted in a way that has caused another person to suffer the distress of all his efforts coming to an untimely end.

In the presence of my elders, my restless-eyed beloved did not turn her face toward me in any other way; out of shame at our conversation she could not speak, nor could she be consoled by my most piteous entreaties as I,
ready to depart, stood before her with tears streaming incessantly from that charming girl.
An unbearable affliction of passion was experienced through long inhalations and exhalations.
In this moment, O traveler’s wife, having cast your gaze toward the path of your beloved as far as the range of vision allows, you have become despondent;
when the paths were cut off by the spreading darkness at the turning of the day,
you took but one step toward home with great sorrow.
O Blessed One, do not look back again with your neck turned slowly in this manner.
Her vine-like arm was not clung to the hem of her garment, nor was it placed upon the threshold; nor did she repeatedly fall at his feet, nor were the words "stay" spoken.
At that time, when the sky was darkened by a mass of clouds, her husband was about to depart, but he was held back by his slender wife with the flood of a river filled by a torrent of tears.

Held by the sprout-like hand at the hem of his garment, and gazed upon for a long time with tears, he was entreated with palms joined in a gesture of deluded compassion, crying, "Do not go! Do not abandon me! But when, even though she stood there thus, that rogue proceeded to depart, he cast her aside.
Previously, his life was cherished by his beloved; thereafter, she became his most cherished possession.
If it is indeed certain that you must go, alas, why this haste? Stay for just two or three steps so that I may behold your face;
for life is as fragile as the water dripping from the spout of a water-clock in this cycle of existence.
Who knows whether there will be a meeting with you again for me, or not?
With tearful eyes, oaths, and prostrations at his feet, other wretched women tried to turn back the departing lord of their lives.
"May there be auspiciousness, blessings, and a fortunate day for you as you set out in the morning! they cried.
Having departed from your beloved home, you will hear that which was desired by those who were full of affection for you.
It is possible that you have already gone and reached the end of this life's journey;
yet, even those various pleasures which were once present before your eyes are now beyond your perception. However, this pain of separation is known by you now as you set forth.
"What indeed will the mind do?"—this being unknown, it is not correctly ascertained.
“O charming one, send me; travelers are departing, and time must be kept within its limits.
Why are you so anxious? Why do you remain silent for no apparent reason?
Having spoken thus, the lover embraced his beloved who had approached him, and she acted in that manner.
By him was given that drum which brings an end to the lives of all travelers who have departed.
"O beautiful one, you have gone far from the city; that tree over there is full of sap.
Turn back from right here," the traveler said softly to his beloved, as her bodice quivered against the expanse of her breasts, which were heavy and slow from the deep embrace.
With eyes filled with tears streaming from his chest, he brought about the abandonment of his departure.
I have heard these words from some people: "I shall go. An end has also been established in my mind:
"You must remain ever vigilant in the house. This is what has been arranged.
When her husband uttered the word "Sucī," the young woman looked at his face, and her gaze remained fixed for a long time upon her infant son, who was drinking from her breast.
Then, the state of separation of the steadfast elephant was exceedingly beautiful, bringing joy to the eyes with its intensely red hue.
With her mind she embraced her beloved, and with her hand she touched his lotus-like face.
As she was distressed, her face was dejected; as she wept, her eyes were filled with tears.
Before her, the circle of her friends appeared like a mere reflection.
Even as the heart of the deer-eyed woman was being consumed by the fire of love,
that her affection remained exactly as it was then became, as it were, a marvel.
The sandalwood paste applied between her breasts, which cools the heat of passion,
shone like the ashes of the mind consumed by the fire of love.
Even for someone,
the lotus stalks of that lady with arched brows— capable of allaying the heat of passion—
did not suffice; for how can that which is sought from long threads ever be obtained?
O venerable lady, desist, desist! O friends, [cool her] with the breeze from lotus leaves and palm-leaf fans;
this fire that has entered her heart might suddenly burst into flames at any moment.
"Remove the thick paste; make the necklace far away; what is the use of lotuses?
Enough, enough with the stalks of lotus fibers!"—thus the young woman speaks day and night.
The young woman,
her cheeks washed by a flood of tears, neither writes nor counts the lines [of the letter],
fearing that the day appointed as the limit might pass away. (Daṇḍin, *Daśakumāracarita*, 10.72)
The two lotus-hands of that long-eyed woman, which had been placed upon a bed of blooming lotuses, became visible as they were drenched by a continuous,
spreading flow of tear-water mixed with collyrium.
The heart of Gaṅgādhara possesses neither hardness nor delicacy when separated from her;
though pierced by the arrows of Love, it neither attains firmness nor does it break asunder.
Separated from Ratnākara, her life sustained only by a necklace of sandalwood-paste beads, the young woman clings to the lotus petals on the prince’s head—
petals jagged with the edges of his moving locks— as a swan clings to lotus leaves rough with the tips of trembling stalks.
The divine lotus garland placed upon Bāṇa’s body to soothe his increasing fever shines like a polished sword-blade wielded by the five-arrowed god [Kāmadeva] against the liberated Śunā.
The breeze, fanned by the lotus petals that serve as the seat of her heart,
does it perhaps alleviate the burning heat, or rather, does it kindle the fire of love?
O lotus-stalk necklace, having fallen from the midst of the weight of Devagupta’s breasts, why have you come here? There is not even space for your thread there; how then could there be room for you?
O Śrīharṣa,
with a mind scorched by the fire of love, why do you smear your body with sandalwood paste?
Do you not know that the internal ordinance is far more powerful than the external application?
Whatever part of her body her friends place upon a lotus petal to alleviate her fever,
that very spot instantly withers, as if out of shame at her lack of remedy.
O hero compassionate toward the people intoxicated by the pain of separation from their beloveds, Śrī Vibhākaravarman, you discharge your arrows;
O Manmatha, if you come within the range of the eyes of the Lord of Beasts (Śiva), I shall become your slave.
"What is the use of this talk? Tell me: shall I come, or shall I not go? Or rather, shall I go?
Thus was the high-minded woman made utterly restless by the god of love, wondering, "Shall I sleep? Shall I sleep?
Though nectar was held in her hand, she did not drink it; though the moon, a delight to the eyes, was present, she did not look upon it.
Even though her husband had departed, his wives, who regarded their husband as a deity, did not find pleasure even in hearing [the news of his arrival], nor did they sing.
These women bear white powder of camphor and sandalwood, and their every limb is anointed with fresh sandalwood paste,
as if it were a mass of ashes from the great fire of passion burning within them, consumed by its own exhaustion.
When he was somehow made to loosen his grip on her neck, he who considered death itself to be the means for attaining happiness—
him, as he was departing, they released, saying, "He is not being held back by force by you two," while his bracelets seemed like her own creeper-like arms.
As each line that the sun, glowing with coppery radiance, drew upon the earth with its hand so that Kaṅkaṇa might remember his beloved from whom he was separated,
she wiped it away with tears possessing the luster of pearls, released from the tips of her trembling eyelashes like those of a female crane.
How shall that fire of passion be extinguished— [that fire] for which necklaces, garments moist with water, lotus petals, dew-dropping snows of beautiful luster,
and fresh sandalwood are the fuel?
O Bāṇaka,
although the god of love exerted himself with his entire being, the long-eyed maiden displayed supreme skill;
her glances were filled with the playful movements of loveliness and charm, and she caused her body to become exceedingly slender.
Bhaṭṭa Āvalokita [says]:
Having abandoned her—who was terrified by the fear of this first separation—all those ungrateful delusions of the minds of the mindful have departed with ease;
yet, thinking thus, they surely remain hidden, firmly and repeatedly pressed against the throat of that wretched woman by her vital breaths, which are gasping out of deep affection.
When the sun had set,
when the trees were covered by flocks of birds seeking refuge, when the twilight glow was shimmering, and when the moon was slowly rising— there,
at that time, the slender maiden, her eyes burning with a longing for her beloved redoubled by his rejection, made even death a festival.
When the hunter,
in the presence of his elders, forcibly raised the gaze of that slender-limbed woman,
the flame of passion arising from their separation was ignited by those tear-drops falling within him.
I imagine that this column of smoke arising from his mouth,
under the guise of a swarm of bees drawn by the exertion of his sighs, is the very smoke of his expiring life-force.
On the face of someone,
she bears a decoration of musk-paste as if it were a heavy burden;
and on her thick breasts, the sandalwood paste, though applied, feels like a weight.
Even on her, whose very limbs are exceedingly delicate, he has placed another burden of grief with such effort; alas, what kind of ruthlessness is this on the part of the Creator!
The heavy burden of her hips has not yet reached the limit of the waistline; the waist is slender,
and it still seeks a little more thinness even than that.
The slight fullness of her breasts, though not yet fully developed, shone with grace;
and the slender-limbed girl appeared as if vibrating with life and yet as if resting in tranquility.
Long ago,
a certain woman separated from her lover gave water to a *navamālikā* plant for the sake of its growth; that very plant,
having blossomed, somehow brought peace to her grief by offering water in the form of tears during her separation.

Then, when questioned by her friends, she concealed the suffering born of separation from her elders; [the friend said: "O charming girl, why do you restrain this flood of tears flowing from your eyes?"
Night after night, your bed has been moistened by the tears from your eyes; its state, being offered to the rays of the sun, reveals this.
Your face has lost its radiance, your pair of eyes is white with tears, your body is exceedingly emaciated, and your fortitude has vanished;
O fool, having abandoned your shame, you speak words that lack substance—by which state of yours, my friend, this condition has been brought about in a mere moment.

O Subhūti, who indeed has rendered your vision empty by this scrutiny? Who here bears the supreme burden of those of virtuous deeds, whom you do not release from your mind—even while holding his lotus-face in your hand with eyes closed, as if he were but a painted image?
O charming girl,

tell me, who is this fortunate man that you gaze upon today with glances that are languidly turned away, moist with love, repeatedly half-closed, for a moment directed toward him, flickering with shyness, and then averted by winking, as if pouring out the intense longing of passion stored within your heart?
Another [has] a face empty with world-weariness, its petal-like lips trembling with a sigh, resting upon both hands whose fingers are interlaced and bent.
"Whose tears—whether of one praiseworthy or blameworthy—fall from the corners of your eyes like water; whom do you remember daily with such firm affection, even though he is so wretched?"
Supporting herself with one hand on a nearby *kesara* creeper, radiant with merit,
the weary woman placed her lotus-hand upon the slope of her hip with her left hand.

Speak with your neck uplifted on this cloudy day; raising your feet, whose path is now being gazed upon by you, O child with eyes like those of a bewildered deer, tell me: whose meritorious deeds are these that are being beheld?
“O Lord, why do you distress this child? Why does fever arise from unwholesome food?
O lotus-eyed one, nothing that is digested is ever prepared by me;
tell me now, without shame, about that other lover of his.”
His face was like a couch swaying with a cushion, and his body was as beautiful as Kandarpa.

Even on these familiar slopes of your hips, your gait is weary with fatigue; your glances are slightly averted, their range limited by the lashes of your eyes. Therefore, I think that today you have firmly held some beloved person within your heart.
Otherwise, how could these sighs of yours have become twice as intense?
O lotus-faced one, even for them, the face has become pale with a wan luster, the curls are disheveled, and the pride rests in their hands;
their gaze is vacant and wretched, their bodies have grown thin as their garments have slipped from their shoulders.
Your intellect is dull from one-pointed meditation, O mother of intoxication; you take delight in solitude and do not engage in virtuous discourse.
What indeed is this charming malady of yours, O slender-limbed one? Tell me, for are you not truly ill?
O friend, who is fortunate? Who has been fashioned by the Creator with a well-composed mind? Who is the beloved of Love? And for whom has the tree of past karma borne fruit?
Thus, for whose sake you bathe with unremitting day and night, with eyes that blink like water-jars faltering at the door, your two breasts embraced by the hands of silence.
Now, these laments of a certain woman separated from her lover: "I do not know how to weep; I do not know how to grieve."
Tears fall of my own accord; it is true, it is true, I am not weeping.
Even today, my son, the day of your father, the lord of men, has passed; the path is shrouded in darkness. Come, let us go to attend upon him.
O foolish eye, why do you tremble? When you are wretched and shedding tears, how can he who departed after abandoning me return today with such agitation?
O you who have transgressed all bounds! Remember, remember the fire of Śiva; it is not right for you to burn this person, who is already consumed by the agony of separation.
It is not surprising that one who has not personally known suffering should feel pain;
but what can be said of you, who have attained the state of a burner, yet still burn?
I shall not perish through pride; one should avoid quarreling out of pride. Having fallen into conflict with a lover, O beloved, one suffers no remorse.
O Heart, remain steadfast; why do you grieve thus? That person who was dear to you is no longer yours; he is not your beloved.
When love arises through the power of fate and is dependent upon another,
where in that situation can there be straightforwardness, shame, or even life— let alone happiness?
These two [eyes] of Vīrabhadra have come to rest upon me;

neither sleep prevails over him, nor does his mind perceive faults rather than virtues. The night does not cease, his longing for union does not wane, and his physical emaciation does not diminish his passion.
Either this day is better than the night, or indeed the night is better than the day;
or rather, let both come to an end where there is no reunion with the beloved.
"O son, do you perhaps remember your pitiless father, whose limbs were covered in the dust raised by the chariot wheels?
Having spoken thus at the end of the day, the traveler’s wife, with her long eyes, wept piteously over the child who lay upon her lap.
This is a falsehood, a lie, that the moon— the source of nectar—
has emerged from the mouth of Rāhu;
for this cruel and heart-burning event could not possibly be otherwise.
Tell me, friend, from where does this power of delusion regarding sweetness come to him?

"O friend, you weep excessively day after day; indeed, you bring upon yourself this reproach from me in vain. This heart of mine, melting away from contact with the embers of the bodiless god [Kāma], flows out as water; it is not tears, O well-composed one."
O friend, it does not distress me that he is so fortunate and possesses but slight affection for me;
for every person enjoys happiness as ordained by fate.
But for me, there is this constant torment: that even when people turn their faces away, my heart, though its pride is destroyed, does not for even a moment attain detachment.
O friend,
imagine that the moon’s orb is a lamp placed before you;
indeed, my eye has been obscured by this very thing, which is like a ball of charcoal in the form of a dark cloud.
Alas, this moon, though possessing a thousand rays, bears a veil of darkness under the guise of a spot;
for, like those who are blind, it robs the sight of people when they are separated from their beloved lamps.
In this world, people revile Kālakūṭa, by which Śambhu himself became ageless and immortal;
yet they praise Antaka as a nectar-like boon for women separated from their lovers—for indeed, discernment is rare.
Alas, O Moon, you still carry the form of the mark of Kālakūṭa in order to destroy it;
for out of fear of it, Rāhu quickly releases you even though you have entered his throat.
O Maker of Night, surely the moonlight has been fashioned from fragments of young *ketaka* flowers;
for it pierces our bodies with its exceedingly white radiance as if with thorns.
Surely it was a mass of ashes from the submarine fire that emerged from the ocean in the guise of the moon;
for its thirst could not indeed be quenched by the rivers of water in the eyes of people who had been tormented.
O King of Night, whose body is so delicate, who could endure your rays?
For even these moonstones melt away instantly upon receiving their touch.
It is fitting that my beloved calls my face a lotus during private dalliances and playful conversations;
for it undergoes an indescribable pain upon encountering even a slight resemblance to the moon.
O Padmanābha, show compassion once more;
satisfy Rāhu with your physical form, so that this moon, its brilliance eclipsed by that [Rāhu], may never again cause distress to the night-lotuses.
These are the darkened forms of Maṅkhaka’s wives,
turned to ash by the sin of devouring their husbands; this is Rāhu appearing out of a desire to consume the moon-like faces of women separated from their lovers— it is not the night-maker (the moon).
Speak, O Śiva, wearer of the crescent moon! Why do you abandon your enemy with such haughty gestures out of fear of the King of the Twice-born?
Does he perhaps return to heaven? If he is of such a nature, then let him fall; for he must indeed serve the daughter of the Ocean (Vāruṇī).
Could it be that the moon-eclipsing demon (Rāhu) swallows the moon because he is distracted by the beautiful glances of Svariputīkṣṇasudarśanā?
Otherwise, how could he let go of his own hand, which has fallen into her mouth and resembles a ball of sacrificial oblation?
O friend, fashion a heavy mace for my hand and provide me with a mallet outside;
as soon as the moon enters there, quickly strike him down so that he may be destroyed.
If the agony born of separation were not so great as the intense heat produced by fire,
how could women, being so reckless, enter the flames to follow their beloved who has departed this life?
O Sun, you who possess the splendor of deceitful brilliance, sit upon your seat and torment me, O sinner;
for I shall behold you again tomorrow, when your pride has been washed away by the lord of the day.
Like you, no one else was seen to be so intent on the destruction of others, nor did the God of Love flow forth from him;
for he, with his own self ablaze with the fire of passion, embraced the worlds in order to burn them.

At an improper time, how many times does she open her eyes? For this moonlight, once it has departed, is surely held fast in the hand; O friend, having been bound and set aside, the face of the Creator shall never be seen again.
Although he perceives his beloved to be naturally simple-hearted, even so, that dear one does not speak with longing or sweetness as before, nor does he engage in jesting.
O friend, although he presses me with a firm embrace around my neck, he does not love me; and although he treats me thus, I do not live.

Falling at her feet, speaking soothing words, charming chatter, a firm embrace with my body bristling with thrill, and even the forceful seizing of her hair— though such undertakings of pride yield many fruits, I still find no courage to pursue them.
What beloved object of desire can I provide here for you, who are so dear to my heart?
These two are Puṇḍraka’s;
this black one is indeed most dear to Kṛṣṇa. Now, what shall we do with the white one?
Let there be Yama; let there be going. Or rather, let there be going.
O friend, he by whom this path of my mind was followed for so long in the past has himself become another; for whose sake are old acquaintances?
O friend, I did not embrace anyone out of fear of my elders, nor did I say "stay" with a throat choked by tears at the departure of my beloved.
"I am departing in haste," [she said], "O dear friend;
though I have seen you, I did not gaze upon you fully, for the range of my vision was obstructed by the tears from my eyes."
The sun,
having reached the eighth part of its course, now scorches the herd of cows; O brother, sleep happily with your companions, for this is the conduct of the virtuous, like that of birds at evening.
How will he, who departed while I was weeping with eyes clouded by tears out of affection for him, now depart from you as you lament?

When the bond of affection had passed away and the high esteem in his heart had faded, and when the state of true intimacy had ceased as he walked before him like a mere stranger— Śivasvāmin [lamented].
And having thus reflected, dear friend, for all those days that have passed, I do not know what reason there is why my heart does not shatter into a hundred pieces.
My hair has been bound into a single braid, and I have donned a garment of white cloth;
I have even heard the words of my grieving kinswomen and friends.
Those friends of his who have turned back, seen him depart, and followed after him—
even though they are thus following their beloved life-breaths, they do not feel pity.
"O friend, somehow he is departing because of his anger at my bashfulness," I said;
then that hard-hearted man, leaving the bed, departed by force.
Thus, what can I do? My heart, having violently destroyed affection and abandoned compassion, once again feels desire for that which has its shame destroyed.
Of someone.
O traveler, if your brother goes toward that direction, O fortunate one, you should speak thus to that person whose heart has been described to you: "How is he?
When she was thus questioned, that young woman did not at all say what was desired.
Meanwhile, the lotus-faces of all were choked by streams of tears.
O young woman,
has any traveler on the road been encountered by you who is like your brother Darva?
O beloved, tell me what he is like, for there are hundreds of such men.
Seeing you, her eyes filled with wide joy,
she thought, "He must be my beloved," and having thus informed the traveler, she fell into a swoon.
Lifting up with her hand the thin wick of the oil-soaked lamp that had fallen upon her cheek,
and hurriedly covering her full breasts with half a garment trailing down, the young woman,
weeping, spoke thus according to her age: "I shall give you whatever is dear to you."
If my beloved approaches slowly from the tree with blossoming filaments, then [I shall go].

The days are full, and the sky remains dark with clouds; though I am resolved to die, my life-breaths do not leave me. Where indeed was that belovedness, and where now, in separation from him, is this life sustained?
O friend, that is the truth; I am ashamed by these false tears.
Although I am trusted by my friends and know the essence of the intentions of this person,
I am unable to cast my own gaze upon him there because of my modesty;
for even this world is clever at mocking others and is quite capable of discerning the subtlest gestures.
O Mother, to whom shall I go for refuge? The fever of passion is wasting away within my heart.

Blessed is she who, even in separation, casts aside shame before her circle of friends and remains at ease; she who does not even let out a sigh, much less weep, even when speaking. May that wicked woman—who is always agitated by the fear of elders—be filled with anxiety.
By means of the cause that is the kindling of the lamp, there is supreme liberation from sighing for a moment during the night.
While the circle of her friends was preoccupied with arranging auspicious items for the departure, while the elders— with eyes clouded by tears— and likewise the circle of well-wishers stood by,
the Lord of my life, his gaze fixed upon me, withdrew with great difficulty.
Why was the noose of my vine-like arms not placed around your neck by me, overcome as I was by shame?
The departure was made with bracelets, while her dear friends constantly wept;
she did not sit for even a moment, but resolved in her mind to go ahead.
When the beloved one had decided in her heart to depart, they all set out together.
Since one must go, why are life, dear ones, and wealth not abandoned?
For some of these, even a tremor is truly a trembling within the heart; even a thought is filled with anxiety; even sighs are indeed sighing; and even tears truly act as tears.
For one whose mind is afflicted by passion through the remembrance of a beloved, what indeed is the state of one who is attached to the self?
Like trees growing from within, the pangs of suffering emerge from the heart; fie upon the lover!
To him who was preparing to say, "I shall go to [the rescue] of everyone," he spoke with confidence;
yet as he went, he was left far behind, and though he turned back again and again to look, he was disregarded.
Having returned to that empty bed, my vital breaths remain there; O friend, stay, for I am facing the calamity of death! Out of hypocrisy, I weep.
Produced by the very arrows of the flowers of Spring,
increased by the cool rays of the Moon, nourished by the breath-winds cooled by the proximity of the Snowy Mountain (Himālaya),
and nourished by the cuckoos with their speech consisting of the essence of supreme nectar— [so was he].
"Among my various methods for alleviating suffering, which one is this 'procedure for the application of cold'?"
There was a certain person who always took exclusive delight in not looking at me;
his mind was never attached to anything else, even to his own life-breaths, for I was the sole object of his focus.
"Friends, look! Now not even a report of him is heard.
It would be a marvel indeed if he were still alive; otherwise, how can there be talk of him?"
For both of us, the arrows of Love are difficult to resist; the beloved is far away; the mind is intensely longing;
love is profound; youth is fresh; life is exceedingly fragile; and the family is stainless.

"O friend, womanhood is opposed to fortitude; the time is a friend to the god of love; Death is impartial; and our friends are not clever. How, then, can this separation be endured? Thus [I am] deceived."
The sighs of Bhartṛśaṅku burn his face; his heart is uprooted and utterly tormented.
Sleep does not come, nor is the beloved’s face seen; day and night he weeps.
Having fallen at his feet, she attained the embrace of her beloved, who had previously looked upon her with indifference.
O friends, considering what fault or virtue, have we caused our beloved to practice such pride?
Trembling in my heart, my words falter, and my mind is restless with agitation; my limbs grow weary, my eyes are clouded by tears, and anxiety withers my face.
O friend, since this former display of physical grace has vanished, that pride of mine has been abandoned.
Even those eight goddesses are to be worshipped, who are the beloveds of him who is honored upon the surface of the earth.

O beloved, if from this day forward I should again become the mistress of another man— whether he be of noble birth or otherwise, whether he be handsome or even one whose very name causes agitation in the heart of a deceitful mind—
then, without him, the night will be devoid of the pure, bright laughter of the moonbeams.
Or even a single day, turbid with clouds, during my rainy season.
"I am now oppressed by the malady of pride; I am unable to go into his presence.
There is no clever friend who might carry me there by force. Even that proud man, O Mother, does not come to me himself for fear of appearing humble."
Time passes and life is fleeting; thus the minds of the wise are weary with such reflection.
"O simple girl, why do you begin to pass all this time in such simplicity? Assume pride, maintain fortitude, practice straightforwardness, and cast aside [all affection] toward your lover.

Thus exhorted by her friend, she, with a frightened face, gave this reply: Subhāṣitāvalī 1161–1 to 3. Mugdhe mugdhatayaiva netum akhilo kālaḥ kim ārabhyate | mānaṃ dhatṣva dhṛtiṃ badhāna ārjavatāṃ dūrīkuru preyasi || sakhyevaṃ pratibodhitā prativacastām āha bhītānanā || 1161_3 ||
"Indeed, the Lord of my life, who dwells within my heart, will surely hear my low-voiced plea."
O friends, why do you release such harsh words? Let his transgression be forgiven once;
this fickle man will never again do me harm. He who was dear to me shall not act unkindly again.
Thus, terrified by the conflict arising from her grasping at pride, she is instead mocked by her own attendants as she becomes agitated, having begun to employ conciliatory gestures.
O King of Birds,
go quickly and speak before the range of his eyes reaches you;
tell him that today his beloved has assumed a display of jealous anger.
But when that beloved, whose movements were those of a rogue,
is seen, my face inevitably becomes smiling, even though my body is completely drenched by the obstruction of perspiration.
Placing his face upon her face, he draws her mass of hair— dark as a swarm of bees—
from her head; with his own neck locked to hers, he exerts a deep embrace upon her breasts.
O girl, he whose feet fall upon my hips with boundless attachment—he is such a beloved of mine!
O simple one, shame has been cast aside; no, no, for what cause for shame is there in a bodice? It brings modesty!
For some mother there exist in that place breezes carrying the spray of the hair-tuft, winds that bear fragrance;
or there are masses of clouds, white-limbed with flashes of lightning, pouring down abundant rain.
Or like the cry of peacocks or cranes perched upon the peak of a great mountain at midnight—
by that sound, the Lord of Life remembers this suffering retinue of his.
Now, that friend of Vikramāditya,
who was touched by the hand of her lover, did not appear as if her purpose were yet accomplished.
Why is she not grazed upon the grass, like a cow tied to a tree?
O timid one, abandon this softness that causes confusion through anger at inappropriate times;
for one who is always sweet-natured and dear may be rare, or perhaps not so, O simple-minded one.

If that merciless one has departed, leaving behind this high hip with its disarrayed girdle and this face with its pupil wandering toward the corner of the eye— O fair-thighed one, surely he alone is the one who has been deceived!
O beloved, whose speech is tender with affection, since you, in your excessive anger, did not yield your resentment when I bowed at your feet—
now I believe that very resentment, melting away through intense remorse, flows forth from you in the guise of this abundance of tears.
Without reflecting out of affection, and disregarding the advice of friends, O simple one, why have you now maintained pride toward the sky?
For these [arrows] have been drawn back, possessing crests as brilliant as the fire of universal destruction.
With his own hand, he [offered] coals, eight-petaled lotuses with honey, and his tears.
O friend, for some of them, the heat of passion increases while their bodies have grown thin; O hard-hearted one, by the abandonment of fortitude, their gait has lost its natural grace.
Tell me, does this mind— consumed by the creeping flames of the fire of passion— not endure that same agony of uneven internal burning?
Why was the door not bolted for long after placing [the child] on the couch? Or why did she not remain clinging to it, weeping with her upper garment tucked up?
For at this time, the season of flowers, the passion of lovers is redoubled.
O beloved, as he was departing, you released him right in front of you, yet he remained fixed within the core of your heart.
If my beloved has arrived suddenly, adorned with a garland of flowers, and has not yet come forward to meet me,
nor has she firmly embraced me, her high breasts adorned with ornaments; [then I am lost].
O simple one, you have been destroyed by your own wicked deeds— whether by embracing my arm or by words tender with affection, when you were addressed with such high expectations.
"O son, Ratnamitra was killed by a wild beast; you did not fall at his feet.
You were bound by this girdle, your companion in secret dalliance, and you did not even hiss!"

What shame is there in being robbed? What is the use of these strange smiles revealed? Alas, O wicked woman! These are not the flames of the fire of separation; you know them to be the arrows that pierce the vital organs.
For some woman,
that emptiness of passion arises when he stands within the range of her vision;
the lover, though having already attained the goal of pleasure, does not yet feel satisfied and longs to embrace her.
Fie on that unworthy woman whom he seeks even beyond his own attachment;
does not even an animal, having come within the range of hearing, obtain the fruit of pleasure?

O you of wicked conduct and fickle heart, why did you treat with such indifference that dear one who came to your house of his own accord, fell at your feet, and was drenched with the moisture of love?

Therefore, from now on for as long as you live, enduring the fruit of your anger— the source of ill-fortune that has cast out the arising of happiness and whose only refuge is weeping— bear it with patience.
O angry one,

why do you weep, repeatedly casting away the tears mixed with saliva with your fingernails just barely reaching [your face]? O angry one, you will weep even more as you cast them away further and further.
He whose mind has reached the highest stage through the words of the Teacher’s instructions will become weary of attachment and will attain a state of equanimity toward his dearest friend.
O friend, what is the use of those bracelets which slip off when one is separated from a beloved, and which shatter when reunited with him?
Indeed, no mortal person desires association with those who have no utility whatsoever in times of both adversity and prosperity.
Now, regarding the dispatch of the messenger by the lover of *utprekṣā* (Subhūti):
"Today is Tuesday; truly, truly, it is irrelevant for you. (Subhūti 1179-1)
Nevertheless, O messenger, you must go; a woman does not wait for the right time.
Prosperity is as flickering as the waves of water, and youth lasts but three or four days;
life is as fragile as an autumn cloud—O messenger, go and say this quickly!
O friend, it is said that for both [parties] there is a restriction of speech; a virtuous woman should not speak harshly to her husband.
Therefore, having entreated him, bring him here; how could one who causes displeasure be entreated?

"The eyes are at the door, the hands are on the cheeks, and life itself resides in you; whence then can there be strife for her?"—this speech of lovers, though repetitive, attained a fresh novelty for his delight.
With the binding of the thread of her waist-braid fashioned from the fibers of her own hair, marked by the seal of sandalwood paste upon the face of her bud-like breasts—
she has become the very target for the arrows of the hunter Smara.
Indeed, it is said that even a letter, though not yet opened, [conveys its meaning].
Belonging to someone,
marked by sighs that were pure due to the cessation of reproachful speech, with the external syllables [of the name] washed away by the sandalwood paste from her cheeks raised by tears—
A letter, its lines of characters blurred by her hand as she wrote with fingers whose tips were sore,
though composed by a messenger, speaks of the pain within her limbs.
Vajravarman.
There is no leaf in her ear, no collyrium in her eyes heavy with tears,
no passion remains as before in her lower lip, nor is there lac-dye on her feet; thus,
you falsely imagine her to be harsh in her abandonment of love.

Deprived of her writing materials, by what means can she now compose a letter? If that woman in separation were to write here the story of how Amaruka lived, it would be a tale of circumstances [of his own].
Today, tomorrow, or perhaps he will die—what is the point of wasting time on death?
O friend, my hope that you would come here has proven fruitless; brother, depart now. There is no letter for you; tell me what else you deem appropriate.
Lothitaka,
whose gaze was not fixed on accomplishment because it was agitated by tears and trembling,
and who did not remain still while being embraced by a hand with its bracelet turning;
O messenger, since you have not brought about the destruction of the lotus-heart of that woman,
what are you able to say, even having gone there, to this heart made of flesh?
O messenger, you are young; he is a youth and fickle. The directions are dark with gloom. The instruction is strictly secret: his place of rendezvous is in the forest.
Again and again these spring breezes carry away my heart elsewhere; go for a meeting with your lover at the proper time; may the deities protect you, O clever one!
"O friend,
you who have been instructed by her— she who, though disregarded by her own kinsmen, does not forget this [love] because she is carried away by the attainment of virtue—
you must make an effort to depart toward your beloved, as if it were a refreshing bath in the cold."

One whose mind is filled with resentment should be treated with measured kindness by one seeking a purpose, just as a Brahmin who has come for a meal is welcomed; for the movement of Time is swift and unforgiving.
Now, the lamentations of those separated from their lovers:
"O wind, blow! Having touched my beloved, touch me as well.
This is much for one afflicted by love; can I live by this alone?"
This is much for one who is driven by desire, and not at all small for one who understands:
that I and you, O fair-thighed one, have both resorted to this single earth.
Not even a necklace was placed upon my neck, for I was afraid of the touch of enjoyment;
mountains, rivers, and trees have arisen between us.
"Suffering is neither dear to me nor far from me; suffering has not entered my heart.
This alone I grieve for: that youth is passing away there."
When indeed shall I, having slightly raised my face, behold that well-tamed, lotus-petal-eyed countenance,
which is like a supreme elixir?
Having recollected the beloved face of the blessed sage Vālmīki, with its long and beautiful eyes,
one's mind does not split into a hundred pieces; therefore, it is neuter.
Fools treat their life-breaths and their beloved as equal;
yet the beloved leads to pleasure when she is at one's throat, while the life-breaths lead to death.
"O Subhūti, today a thought concerning the separation from my beloved has entered the heart of both of us. Thinking thus, sleep departed; for who honors a person who is ungrateful?
The word of the Sage is true: that the entire world is momentary and subject to destruction;
for who else could endure the agony of separation from those with eyes like Hari’s?
Experts in that field declare the eternity of sounds for someone:
"The words spoken by my beloved still remain in my heart even today."
Having attained the supreme perfection in grammar, speech,
and logic, the gaze of this learned man is truly desirable, like that of a doe.
O slender-limbed one, we have been worn away by that single, slender waist;
yet I do not know what that pair of elevated breasts will do.
Surely it was for them as well that very person whom I saw became the cause of this obstacle;
since even in a dream such a one is difficult to find, how, my friend, shall I live today?
The heart of the slender maiden is pitiless; the arrows of Māra are irresistible; her life is as hard as adamant—alas, alas, what a succession of sorrows!
My heart longs [for him], yet the young woman is very far away; my youth is fresh, fate is adverse, and desire is my enemy—alas, alas, what a succession of sorrows!
These words of Rairūpuka,
uttered with a gait heavy and slow due to the fullness of her hips,
have planted a step in my heart even as she walks away from me.
The mind is by its very nature fickle and difficult to perceive;
nevertheless, how has it been pierced by the Bodiless One with arrows equal in number to all [the gods]?
When these two— the curved, flickering eyes of Śrī Hārādevī that creep toward the ears, and a wicked person— are seen within the span of a month, how can there be happiness?
To someone a divine eye has arisen, even though their mind is not free from passion;
by means of which, while staying here, I may see my beloved who has gone to another land.
For the cause of creating an image that surpasses beauty is Dhairyamitra; what must the Creator have looked upon when fashioning those with tremulous eyes?
If sweetness were created by the Creator for the eyes of the deer-eyed woman,
then why has such towering loveliness been produced in contradiction to that statement?
Alas! The glance of the lioness, which steals away my life, makes me helpless;
oh, how wondrous is the conduct of women!
Those [women] are intoxicated by the pride of the Yavanas, while we are of unsteady mind; thus,
the burning heat arising from the beauty of her limbs spreads within us.
Whichever way the large-eyed woman casts her glance, right there the sharp-witted five-arrowed god hurls his arrows.
Thinking "this is lovely, this is lovely," she wanders through all her limbs with the guidance of her dwelling-place; I believe that Love himself wanders there like a fool.
Furthermore, by those traveling from the Middle Country to certain other regions,
her form was made the object of their gaze, as if she were the very destination for the eyes of the world.
May there simply be the sight of the Beloved; what need is there for other forms of vision?
For by that [vision], even with eyes still possessed of passion, nirvāṇa is attained.
O slender-limbed one, some unprecedented path has been shown to me by you,
by which passion itself increases even as I contemplate yoga.
For one whose beloved stands far away with her nine swelling breasts,
neither the pond nor the clouds can alleviate his torment.

It would be better to touch two snakes with gaping mouths than the breasts of that slender woman, which are soiled by the marks of her lover's enjoyment and from which the bodice has just been removed.
If this monastery, protected by the Sugata,
were like a den of deer and birds, how is it that Smara dwells right there with his bow strung?
"Friend, while all my senses were withdrawn in equanimity,
my mind was captivated by the slender-limbed woman for some desired object."
Whoever perceives that [object], in their eyes it becomes as pleasing as a lotus;
yet in the eyes of others, it does not become pleasing at all.
O bewildered one, how are your eyes curved for your beloved?
How are they red with passion for people, and how are they the ruin of people?
How will that slender girl, who dwells in my heart pierced by the sharp arrows of desire,
not cause me burning anguish?
When remembered, she leads to torment; when seen, she increases madness;
when touched, she brings about delusion—how, then, can she be called a beloved?
Alas, having encountered this wretched fate, even the words of the Sage have proven untrue,
since the destruction of life in an instant through separation from loved ones is not being seen [by you].
Surely that fortunate one whose banner is the sea-monster must be a messenger of hers,
since he proceeds toward those places indicated by the movement of her eyes.
"Come! Go! Fall down! Stand up! Speak! Observe silence!"—who has not been deceived by her whose eyes are like those of a frightened doe?
He in whose hair are the Jīmūta clouds, in whose every joint are rivers,
and in whose belly are the four oceans— he shall conquer the fire of separation.
May he who, having attained the commonality of the eyes from Maheśvara,
proclaimed the entire Vyākaraṇa, describe the qualities of that slender [speech].
If indeed what is inside this body were to become outside, then,
O slender-limbed one, it would be visible at all times without any effort.
Knowing you to be a eunuch, this was sent by me to you;
my mind delights in that very [man], and we have been struck down by Pāṇini.
With her heavy breasts acting as Jupiter, her radiant moon-like face as the Sun,
and her feet as Saturn, she shone like the personification of the planets.
The teacher, burdened by the weight of her breasts,
instructed her in such a manner that at that very moment she attained a state contrary to the proper way.
While there is a lamp, while there is fire, and while there are the stars, the moon, and the sun,
this world has become shrouded in darkness for me without the eyes of the fawn-eyed one.
With her face like a moonstone, with hair as dark as sapphires,
and with hands like rubies, she shone as if she were composed entirely of jewels.
Even when her lotus-eyed form is seen from afar by another,
that very same image does not depart from the heart of one who has committed sin, as if it were a persistent suspicion.
For both of us,
that which is evening is indeed evening; that time is called "time" because it possesses faults,
being devoid of union with the slender one.
One heart is pervaded by longing, the other has been stolen by my beloved;
how many hearts does my consciousness possess?
If fate, naturally hostile to us, had not been so cruel as to bring this man of variegated beauty within the range of our vision for even a moment, would the moon-faced one have been led away?
O Govinda,
if that beloved of mine, with her beautiful limbs, dwells within my heart,
then how is it that I am empty-minded? Alas, what a reversal of fate!
Of someone.
In all directions, on the earth, and likewise in the sky, it is everywhere clearly perceived;
when there is doubt regarding the vital breaths, it is remembered as becoming subtle and attaining the state of Nārāyaṇa.
Oho!
What a day for me! Homage to me, since I have been beheld by this young girl with eyes as large and tremulous as those of a frightened doe.
As long as it remains within the range of vision, it consists of nectar;
but once it has passed from the path of the eyes, it exceeds even poison in its harm.
On one side a young woman counts the days, and on the other side stands Death;
we do not know whose presence we shall reach first.
Even if we are indeed proponents of destiny, being struck by the dart of death regarding both [past and future],
why could there not be other means [to avoid it], since the "deer-glance" has been shown?
O Venerable Kambalaka,
even those days that pass for me while separated from that slender-limbed woman,
Yama will likely count them as acts of cruelty.
In her absence, O fawn-eyed one, I have been favored by you alone,
since the thorn of longing for the embrace of another woman has been extracted.
The foolish desire union; I declare that it is separation.
In union there is only one [moment], but in separation the entire world is absorbed in her.
For some, this young woman is the sole object of union; when separated from her, the entire world consists only of her.
Since separation is thus a source of benefit, by whom could it be censured?
If I remember her of the slender limbs, whence can I have any hope for life? But if I live by forgetting her, what is the use of such a wretched existence?
"O lamp,
depart from my heart, or come into my left eye;
the pain of longing for a separation that is not far off is difficult to endure."
For some,
that month is equal to an eon, and that eon is equal to a month—
for him who passes his time with a weary mind, and for him who passes it with one that is not weary.
Four syllables:

"Those by whom that [truth] of the Eternal One has been seen, and those by whom it has not been seen—they are equally robbed. The hearts of some have been stolen; for others, the very fruit of their eyes has been taken."
If even Sakra-deva weeps so piteously upon separation from his beloved,
then to what use will this burnt city of the gods go?

O traveler of the mind, do not wander through that forest of women belonging to the deceased, which is impassable due to the mountain-like breasts; for there dwells the thief of memory known as Desire.
O mind, O parrot, desist!
You who are like the cheek of a lustful woman, there exists a net of hair placed there by the hunter of desire.
O bee of the mind, O Rājanaka Āhlādaka, turn away from the lotus-face of this amorous woman;
now that the moon of passion has arisen, you will surely be caught in its snare.
O heart of Rairūpaka!
Have compassion for me; restrain your fortitude until you have seen the fawn-eyed one.
Whether it be "alas! or "it is done," let this burst forth suddenly—there is no other way.
O friend, you rest upon a white stone at night, yet day after day you do not diminish your thinness;
like us, O anxious one, are you perhaps thinking of that very same woman?
The beloved of the one whose throat is green (Śiva) bestows intoxication; intoxication brings incomparable torment;
and torment, alas, leads to death. Nevertheless, she alone is the refuge of men.
The glance of the slender maiden, like a virulent poison, lassos the body, causes the mind to whirl excessively, spreads a burning heat,
and repeatedly induces delusion.

When he is weary, she is weary; when he is joyful, she is joyful; when he is agitated, she is agitated; like a reflection, the beloved is exactly like him—except that when he is enraged, she is merely terrified.
A wife who is capable of enduring the exertion of desired sexual union, who avoids incompatible unions,
and who is skillful in complying with her husband's mind, is born only to those who possess merit.
This separation from my beloved, surely a curse brought about by the ocean of passion,
how else could you have made me endure days exceeding a thousand years?
Even a mere glance brings happiness to one whose eyes are as beautiful and tremulous as blue lotus petals;
how much more so, then, the impetuous embrace of that slender woman, which possesses the luster of the mountain of her tresses?

For one whose mind is captivated by love as he recollects her lotus-face— with its bee-like eyes devoted to the nectar of sweetness, and with lips for petals and teeth for filaments— whence can there be sleep?
With breasts so exceedingly lofty, a sunken waist, and hips so well-raised—
who, indeed, would not stumble upon the body of Hari’s consort, which is like a newly formed landscape?
Is this a calamity, O Princess, or is it a flood of moonlight, or perhaps a thunderbolt’s fall?
Enough of that; for she alone is my life, or else fie on me, as I am the only one who has achieved his purpose.
When the fire of passion blazes and burns intensely in the hearts of people by their very nature,
what further use is there for those skilled in useless things who offer the oblations of bad poetry?
"It is a well-known truth on earth that the renunciation of even some [pleasures] destroys all calamities;
yet, by the renunciation of this girl with the innocent eyes, I have come to know all calamities."
For Śūdraka,
even a moment’s delay in speaking of the time of death was like separation from her;
for even the blinking of his eyes, which were languidly longing for the face of his beloved, became an obstacle.
Perhaps the face of that long-lashed-eyed woman— its lower lip repeatedly pressed by his fingers,
its speech faltering with words of refusal, and its flesh turning away— was somehow raised up, yet never kissed.
O fair-thighed one, you who have extinguished the lamp of Love— if you have indeed departed from the range of my vision,
tell me, how will you ever depart from my heart, which is pinned fast by the arrows of the peerless archer?
Whom on earth does this beautiful woman not bring under her sway— she whose body is marked with streaks of saffron paste, who wears necklaces hanging from her fair breasts,
and whose lotus-feet resound with the tinkling of anklets?
It is not so wonderful that even a tree, though insentient, blossoms when its roots are touched by the feet of noble women dyed with lac;
but it is truly marvelous that a man does not melt away when his body is touched by the essence of their limbs.
The moon acts like the sun; even a gentle breeze acts like a thunderbolt.
A garland acts like a cluster of needles; an ointment of sandalwood acts like sparks of fire.
Light acts like darkness; by the power of fate, even life itself acts like a burden.
Alas! This moment of separation from my beloved stretches out like the time of the end of an aeon.
Even now, I remember her—her banner of triumph won in love, with long, dangling locks and a face pale from separation;
her restless eyes, vanished in an instant even in my dreams, like a magical lore mastered through grace.
Upon the heart of my beloved— pale with the rows of flames from the great fire of separation and heavy with breasts—
these drops of tears surely fall with a *chamaccham* sound, as her piteous eyes are fixed upon the trees along the path to my dwelling.

Even now, those sweet syllables of his— uttered with a "chamacchami" sound as he was half-closing his eyes in sleep, slow with intoxication, words that were neither meaningful nor meaningless— resound in some inexplicable way within my heart.

When that beloved of mine, her body as delicate as the interior of a lotus, had hidden herself against the neck of Kalaśaka— her arms trembling from the embrace— she surely entered my heart at once through the channels of the wounds inflicted by the arrows of Love.
The sharp glance from the corner of the eye of the illustrious Goddess of Fortune,

falling upon me with her charming face, does not so much pain my vital organs as does her withdrawing it out of anger with trembling; for a shaft, once extracted, is indeed more unbearable than its mere fall.
When, indeed,

shall I drink from the face of my beloved— her half-knot of hair loosened and pulled by him as he seized her by the tresses, her eyes trembling with shame like a water-pot, and her lips agitated by the pain of being forcibly grasped?
O long-eyed one, having entered the heart of Vasunāga— which seems as if fashioned from the shimmering mass of all the digits of the full moon—
his form burns it, as it were; for indeed, when fate is adverse, there is surely no path that does not lead to calamity.
Ever since I, thirsting for desire, drank the abundant nectar of my beloved’s lips, from that time forth my craving has doubled; since her beauty is so great, what is there surprising in this?
She is both a child and one who understands the wiles of the five-arrowed god of love; she is slender yet her frame is burdened by the weight of her breasts.
She feels bashfulness at the conclusion of lovemaking—alas, she is someone extraordinary! What can I say of her? How can I describe her?
O Bhaṣa,
those excellent poets must surely have had their speech inverted, who always say that women are weak;
for how could even Śakra and the other gods be conquered by those women with the falling glances of their most tremulous pupils?
O heart, as you meditate upon the face of my beloved— its locks hanging down, its cheeks pale with the pangs of separation, that charming and lovely abode of the God of Love,
its temples moistened by thick tears falling from the edges of her eyelashes— you do not go to pieces, bit by bit.

O heart, why do you not shatter into a hundred pieces as you remember at the end of love-making the beloved’s face— smeared with the fresh sweat born from the exhaustion of the sport of passion, eyes closed and pupils trembling in ecstasy?

I constantly remember that pair of eyes of that slender woman—eyes which were heavy with tears, clouded by impatience, yet opened wide for those who were utterly wretched; eyes that were slowly reddened and closed firmly after a deep sigh whenever she was in the presence of her elders.
Even now, I remember the face of my beloved during our inverted amorous dalliance— fair as the gleam of her swaying earrings,
and sprinkled with a profusion of large, glistening drops of sweat from the exertion of tossing about, like a scattering of fallen *muktāphala* pearls.

The fortunate man, exhausted by the fatigue of love-making, places his chest within the cage of his beloved’s arms— arms that are as round as the frontal globes of a rutting elephant and moist with saffron—
and, having found sleep for a moment, passes the night.
O Smara, why do you, harboring resentment, discharge your bow and arrows at me alone, having uprooted the very foundation [of your power]?
Cast your shafts repeatedly upon her whose eyes are like those of a doe; let your passion be directed toward her, lest you yourself become truly loveless.
When the summer season has arrived, she whose limbs are so cool extinguished for me the heat of the fire of passion;
yet that tremulous-eyed woman, dwelling within my heart, now burns me—though she was my beloved, she has become an adversary to me, like the moon on an inauspicious day.

Gazing at the sky with eyes clouded by tears like rain clouds, she somehow managed to say half a verse: "If you are traveling abroad, my beloved... and then, clutching my garment, she began to scratch the surface of the earth.
Thereafter, she ceased speaking there.
O deer-eyed one, the fire of passion, fanned by the force of the wind of separation and flickering with its flames, burns my body; depart from me,
for I am being consumed.
You are being burned from the very house where your heart is struck, as long as you do not [realize this].
Of whomsoever.

My heart has no refuge from the side-long glances of those with long-lashed eyes— glances that are languid, turned away, innocent, tender, and slow-moving, yet whose pupils are bright with a smile of inner wonder suddenly blossoming.
It has been carried away, cast aside, drunk, or uprooted.
O Bhavabhūti,
for those such as we, both your state of being one whose arrows are flowers and the coolness of the moon are seen to be devoid of reality.
The moon dispels the fire with its frost-filled rays,
yet you, moreover, turn even flower-arrows into diamond-hard shafts.
Gazing with most enchanting and playful glances,
she walks very slowly out of fear of her elders;
having taken only a few steps, her mind is already filled with longing for me.
The young woman gazes again and again with her neck turned, making a "jhaṭiti" sound.

Whom does the conversation of that fair-browed woman not enchant— she whose smiling face is concealed by her hand raised in playful sport, yet whose blossoming teeth are slightly visible through the gaps between her fingers;
she who scratches the earth with her big toe while slightly bending her neck, casting sidelong glances?
The words of those children—

whose faces possessed the beauty of laughter mingled with tears because they had feigned anger at the clever, playful speech that was full of intent, which was pleasant on the surface yet concealed a secret meaning within their hearts— are [uttered].
Whom do they not inspire with longing, even when they are pale, yet possessing unimpaired and gentle splendor?

Where the creeper-like neck attains uninterrupted continuity, as if covered by a dark garment; where the lower lip, dripping with the essence of passion, bears a form that is as if already well-drunk;
and wherein the entire system of the God of Love has been thoroughly mastered and forgotten.
I believe that for him who has savored the flavor of that delight, the fruit of birth has been attained.

The proud woman, her lower lip trembling like a fresh sprout as she shook the tips of her hands with agitation, her creeper-like brows dancing with the angry words, “No, no! Do not leave me, you rogue! and her eyes filled with hissing sighs—she who was thus impetuously kissed.
The nectar has been obtained by them; the ocean was needlessly churned by those foolish gods.

The face of the slender maiden at the conclusion of sexual union— its eyes languid with the end of lovemaking, its almond-shaped earrings swaying as she wears a disheveled mass of hair, and its forehead slightly smeared by fine droplets of perspiration— is [the very image of beauty].
May that Reality protect us for a long time; what need is there for deities such as Hari, Hara, Brahmā, and the rest?
Due to his long practice of celibacy, he delights in a widow;
due to his youth, he delights even in a maiden; and due to the power of fortune, he delights in a married woman.
Without these [qualities], however, a courtesan possesses the passion for enjoyment with many people.
Indeed, that man for whom she is dear must surely be called fortunate.

That which is renowned in the world as the inseparable union of Kandarpa and Vasanta is clearly manifested, alas, in the bodies of lovers who agitate the mind; for it possesses breasts as charming as a blooming lotus, and arms that sway like creepers.
Her line of body hair is like a swarm of bees, and her rows of nails have the form of young sprouts.
O beautiful one, it is wonderful that the weight of your breasts attains such indescribable loftiness;
that upon those lofty breasts, the radiance of your face shines with a pleasing luster;
and that upon that face, the pair of your lotus-like eyes possesses the splendor of blossoming.
That does not lead to delusion; for whom is this wondrous nature of yours not a marvel?
With his heart agitated by anger, the Lord of Beasts (Paśupati),
having assumed a form for the sake of a curse, burned with great effort that [sage] who was performing penance,
as he fell down with a playful and languid grace, his eyes half-closed in laughter.
The third part of the day produces the limb of darkness with a flash.
I praise those victorious, beautiful-eyed women of Virūpākṣa, who, by their very glance, restore to life the God of Love who has been consumed by fire with their look alone.
Hara, hara! This Creator, turned away from compassion, counts even those very days upon which young men do not rest for even a moment between the breasts of lily-eyed women.
For some,
there is a youthful, beautiful woman who provides exceeding delight, intoxication, exhilaration, and constant pleasure;
if that beloved dwells within the heart, where is recitation, where is austerity, and where is the practice of meditative concentration?

For someone who has been brought by a dream to you every night, her glances are immersed in the beauty of your limbs, her ears in the ocean of the nectar of your song, and even her skin in the delicate softness of the blossoms of your slender body.

O slender-limbed one, your tongue has never tasted anything but nectar in its own dwelling; your heart has never been fixed on conduct other than yours; and by no means whatsoever have you ever been led astray from your path by the snares of the senses.
O Śrī Hara,
do not place this mango-arrow in your hand, nor string your bow; O you who have conquered the universe in play,
what is the point of this manliness that slaughters people already rendered unconscious?
Even now, my mind does not even slightly kindle when I direct my attention to that very doe-eyed woman, whose series of sidelong glances has shattered me.
This is not a serpent-king with a broad hood resting upon my heart;
this is not the luster of poison upon her neck, shimmering like the petals of a blue water-lily;
this is not ash, but sandalwood powder, for I am bereft of my beloved.
O Ananga, why do you run away in anger, as if out of delusion, having struck me?
These two [verses] are by Jayadeva.

O slender-limbed one, grant us your own lower lip, which provides protection from the death of our passion even more than the nectar of the moon and more than the essence of the best elixirs; for that [moonlight] is not even equal to it.
Have mercy! Why do you cause us to be slain by these invisible arrows, O cruel one without a body?
It would be better for us to be pierced by the sharp, fierce darts of your love, which are purified by the essence of love.

O fair-faced one, if you are indifferent toward me, whose body is agitated by the disease of separation, then why do you maintain pride? Tell me, how can this wretched man endure the arrows of love, which strike at every vital spot with unabated arrogance?
O young girl, may I become a bee that relishes the lotus of your face, which possesses lower petals of lips and is adorned with the filaments of teeth.
O wise ones, what can the clusters of lotuses that are the words of the slender maiden say to me, whose mind is swooning from the poison of separation,
other than that this [separation] is worthy of being bound with fetters?
Why does the mind, having abandoned its flight, become bound to the feet?
O lovely one, this unprecedented lamp of your face shines for a long time;
O fair-limbed one, it dispels the darkness of those who behold you most effectively,
beneath which, alas, lies this mass of fragrant smoke.
If even this mere report inflames people like moths [into a fire], then what need is there to speak of seeing it?

How could there be delusion regarding the moon’s face, which possesses the radiance of a lotus, even though it is the moon that shines by day? For who would mistake a woman for the moon, when her face possesses the splendor of a lotus?

How could the moon, which shines by day, be confused with her face? How could there be such an error regarding her lotus-like countenance? How could the moon, which possesses the brilliance of day, be mistaken for her face? How could there be delusion concerning her lotus-face, even though the moon shines by day? These two,
Rairūpaka and Prasādaparatantra, who were long ago cast out by me— devoid of intoxication with honey and their modesty abandoned— now move about with slackened smiles and effortless gait.
O friend, what can we say that is sufficient regarding that which was experienced within my heart at that time by Priyā and Anayanā, which is beyond the reach of words?
Before Kālaśaka, I, a wretched man cursed by fate, with my face bowed and terrified by a slip of the tongue regarding his lineage,
have begun to write something out of sheer embarrassment.
The arrangement of the lines was clearly manifest; somehow she became so transformed that the very same young woman appeared once again through her limbs.
Then, with her cheeks radiant from the glow of her supernatural vision (*abhijñā*), the noble lady, her voice faltering with the weight of deep-rooted affection, exclaimed through tears:
"Oh, how wonderful! How marvelous! It is clear!"
O beautiful one, this left foot of yours, the weapon of desire, has been placed upon my head.
Worn out by the burden of carrying [him], exhausted by the heat, clad in soiled garments, bowed down,
not having been seen for a long time, she wept with her breasts trembling.
Having reached an indescribable state of intimacy and affection,
this heart of mine has become as one with the heart of her who has eyes like a deer's.
Whose daughter are you?
By whom were you made? Are you not indeed my own nature, O limb, naturally soiled with the grey dust of impurity? Why then do you act as a cook in the house of your elders?
"Did you remember us? "No, indeed, no, no," she replied;
thus, falling upon my heart, the young girl wept with a trembling born of longing.
Sometimes, out of delusion, I perceive her with her long tresses disheveled; sometimes my imagination places her before me as if she were a friend.
In some cases, the hope of seeing [a loved one] brings joy for a brief moment when pursued;
homage to that [hope], whose very separation delights the heart.
"My body would become withered in the absence of the pleasure of embracing my beloved; my eye would be filled with tears for even a moment if she were not seen.
You have never been separated from that lady with the deer-like eyes.
Since liberation has been attained, why do you carry such anguish in your heart?

You constantly gaze upon that form fashioned by conceptual construction; you always address it with equal speech and embrace it at all times. You drink from its face, which has eyes like budding joy, and you cause it to drink as well.
Nevertheless, O heart, why do you yearn day and night?
Be gracious, O mistress of my life; heed my words, O lady of beautiful countenance.
Abandon this heart of mine, scorched and consumed by the fire of passion, as well as my youth and my naturally delicate limbs.
These [fires] carry away the suspicion that the fire of passion might even burn one who has already been consumed.
O friend, this is the truth, the absolute truth: for some people, a certain fire of separation blazes within the heart, yet my mind does not grow weary even by day or night.
Enough! The thought that my beloved, whose body is as tender as a lotus bud opening at dawn, dwells here for so long burns me.
The teacher who composed the commentary [has described] a flower never before smelled, a sprout not yet touched by fingernails,
a gem never before worn, and honey whose flavor has never been tasted.
Like the flawless fruit of merits, that sinless form—
I do not know what enjoyer it will attend upon.

That this heart of mine— whose secret intentions were never disclosed, whose outward appearance remained unaltered, whose inner torment was never spoken, and whose resolve was buried deep within— is now uprooted by my slackened limbs as it yearns for the state of a dog toward that sinner who treats me with such indifference; this is what rends my heart.
O lady with bracelets upon your arms, why have you placed this lotus-face of yours upon your lap?
This anger is not fitting for one who is devoted, even toward a person who has done no wrong.
While I was speaking thus, at that moment, the doe-eyed woman’s only reply was the tears from her eyes, which caused her breasts to tremble in unison with her own sighs.
Due to the constraint of her vow, she suppressed her heavy grief within her trembling pair of breasts; for when the elders gathered there said,
"Stay," what indeed did she not do but cast away her tears?
His three-eyed gaze, long separated from me and now drawing me away, is fixed upon me with unflagging attachment.
May the glance of the Lord of Yaśas— dark-bodied, with eyes like those of a startled doe, casting its shadow upon her cheeks,
and with hair like the plumage of peacocks— be upon you.
I perceive the play of your eyebrows in the slender ripples of the river;
alas, O timid one, you possess no beauty anywhere that is not concentrated in a single place.
Having painted you on a stone slab with mineral pigments as one angry in love,
I wish to depict myself fallen at your feet;
meanwhile, my vision is repeatedly blurred by the accumulation of my own tears.
Cruel as he is, even in this matter, Fate does not tolerate our union.
O you with eyes like those of a restless cakora bird, these two [eyes] of mine have not seen your vision even in a dream— alas, it is difficult to obtain— and thus I remain sleepless.
Although the path has been shown to me by the Blessed One,
adverse fate does not permit even the slightest ease.
That greatness of my own evil deeds is indeed what has caused you to treat me with such disregard;
for if the cātaka bird does not obtain water from the cloud, the blame lies with the silence of the cloud-dweller.
The eyes of Rairūpaka were closed, his lower lip was pale, both cheeks were emaciated, his two arms were limp,
and the mass of his hair was disheveled in every direction.
O brother, it is impossible that she who was even entrusted to me as the final command of my mother should now say, "She lives," while I am alive.
Her hips,
bent by the weight of her long strides, bear a pair of breasts as delicate as golden lotus buds; her speech is beautiful with smiles, and her glances are familiar with the play of her eyebrows.
His youth proceeds, delightful with the unfolding of his teeth that have just begun to emerge.

“O beautiful one, do those who have departed not meet again? You need not worry for my sake. While I was speaking thus, she looked at me with eyes whose pupils were slow with shame and which fell as tears were drunk away.
Having seen you, my smile revealed your eagerness for the state of death.
Where is my unworthiness, and where is her noble lineage? Might she not be seen by me once again?
Ah, I have heard that for the sake of pacifying my transgressions, even in anger, her face remains lovely.
What will those of purified intellect and perfected minds say? She is difficult to find even in a dream.
O mind, attain composure; for what fortunate youth indeed shall behold her lower lip?
Her chest, fragile under the weight of her swelling breasts, was left without an upper bodice; yet,
as for the arrangement of the rest, the entire lower garment was not loosened, remaining exactly as it was.
"Where indeed might our meeting take place again? Why was it not spoken of thus?"—by you, agitated, hurried, and as if terrified by love-play, we have been deceived in this way.

She who, though wearing a garland of jasmine flowers for a long time, becomes weary; she who cannot endure even thick ointment applied to her limbs; and she who is unable to look upon even the flame of a lamp within her own dwelling— Subhāṣitasaṃgraha 1345–1347.1. She who, though wearing a garland of jasmine flowers for a long time, becomes weary; she who cannot endure even thick ointment applied to her limbs; and she who is unable to look upon even the flame of a lamp within her own dwelling— Subhāṣitasaṃgraha 1345–1347.2. She who, when her husband is away, does not even sleep on a bed, but rather lies down on the bare ground; she who, when he is present, does not even speak to him, but remains silent; and she who, when he has returned from afar, does not even embrace him, but stands with her face turned aside— Subhāṣitasaṃgraha 1345–1347.3.
