How will she be able to endure that heat, which is like the great fire of separation?
She is young while we are of unpracticed speech; she is a woman while we are timid. She bears the weight of full and swelling breasts, yet she is weary, while we are burdened.
She is overcome by the heaviness of her hips, yet she is unable to walk, while we are likewise unable to move.
It was a marvel that those who were previously devoid of power became powerful by relying on others' strength.
"You are going away; I am consumed by separation, my heart is ruined, and my life-breaths are cruel in their action.
This fire of love is tormenting me; I am submerged in the midst of this perilous fear.
Having spoken thus, the beloved, her breath shattered by the blow of his hard breasts, [fainted].
From that place where she lay weeping, her creeper-like arms hanging down from my neck.

If you have indeed abandoned me, overcome by passion for her, then why do I experience this inexplicable and intense longing within? O heart, compose yourself for a moment and tell me your true state!
O Subhu, does a two-fold conduct arise for you who have been shattered by torment?

This body, which was once turned with the neck uplifted and languid with shame when in the presence of her friends, and which spoke something indescribable as she departed— O my life-breaths, why have you departed through separation? Why has this cruelty been resorted to?
If, by recollecting that, it is right for me to remain here, then, oh, you are my authority!
Having heard these harsh words, "I shall go," from Śrī Kalyāṇadatta, she bowed her face and,
with the surface of her big toe, began to scratch the ground that was moistened by the tears from her eyes.
When she was asked, "O lady, where are you going?", she turned her face away; that [silence] of hers is like a thorn piercing my vital organ today, the ultimate cause of my death.
Having bound them firmly with the noose of her creeper-like arms, tender yet trembling with anger,
and having led them to the chamber of their residence before those friends,
she reproached them for their misconduct with faltering, soft words, saying, "Never do this again."
The fortunate one is indeed struck down when, intent on concealment, he laughs while his beloved weeps.

With both eyes he shall behold forms close at hand; his chest shall embrace [his beloved]; his tongue shall be fully satisfied; and he shall drink the supreme beverage, the taste of the fresh lower lip.

O foolish heart, you will hear with your ears a voice that is faltering, stammering, and slow, speaking measured words; even though it has reached you, what indeed will you gain? For what object of thought remains for you?
When I am afflicted by suffering, that lady of the Sānudeva clan becomes sorrowful; likewise, when I am joyful, she is delighted.
When I am dejected, she falls into dejection; and toward me when I am harsh with anger, she speaks words that are wholesome.
She knows the proper time, she speaks with skill, and she takes delight in praising me;
my wife, my excellent minister, my friend, and my retinue—all these have become one, yet they have attained multiplicity.
Let her rolling eyes, heavy with the weight of her breasts, and her trembling, playful brows,
along with this sprout-like lip presided over by passion, indeed cause me pain; for she has turned away from Bhāsa.

Why does this line of hair on my abdomen cause such intense heat, even though it stands in the middle? It is as if it were a garland of the essence of good fortune, inscribed there by the Flower-Armed God himself.
O Lord, may the elements that constitute the body of someone attain dissolution;
O Creator, having bowed my head to you, I beg of you once again today: "Make me [yourself]."
In its waters, it [placed] water; in its sprout, light; in the space of its own abode, space; on the path of its trunk, the earth; and in the hollow of its fibers, the wind.
This lotus plant bears a pair of buds for some unknown southern drama;
the mango creeper bears a fresh sprout tasted by the male cuckoo.
Having heard these words of her friends spoken in secret, she, standing by the long pond, concealed her breasts with the hem of her garment and covered her bimba-like lips with her hand.
May the arrow of her glance, fixed upon the bow of her brow, create agony in the vitals of someone; may even the mass of her curly hair, dark as Time, bring about the destruction of his efforts.
O slender one, your delusion has become thin, and your bimba-like lip is full of passion;
how then can your well-rounded breasts play with my life-breaths?
The moon,
beloved of the night, forcibly assumes the guise of an army defeated by her lotus-face;
and the bow of the Love-god, threatened by the play of her eyebrows, bows down in submission.
Surely, having attained detachment upon reaching the forest ground, the Bimba fruit now clings to the earth, tormented by that lip which possesses the luster of tender sprouts.
Even for one who is weary, the Malaya breeze brings no delight; for one staying in a palace, the moonlight brings no joy;
and a pond with full-blown lotuses stirred by bees leads only to exhaustion.
For one whose conduct has been consistently free from error throughout,
how is it that this mental birth is seen to proceed toward a visible form that is uniform and consistent?
I saw that noble girl, terrified of her elders and distressed by separation.
When we were in a secluded place, I asked her, "Why are you so emaciated? What has happened?
Looking at me with both affection and fear, she drew her body close to mine; when she spoke with a sighing voice, my heart was pierced with pain.

That face of my beloved, which I beheld at the conclusion of our lovemaking—with its pair of eyes languid and tremulous, its creeper-like brows arched, and uttering soft, drawn-out cries of "Hā! Hā! as she moaned from the pain of her bitten lip.
By what can that state be forgotten—the state where the body is moist with sweat, fragrant with the scent of blooming lotuses, and covered in horripilation?
Today in a dream, I saw my beloved turned away in anger; weeping, she began to depart, saying, "Do not touch me with your hand!
Before I could embrace her and comfort my dear one with hundreds of sweet words, [I awoke].
"O brother, by that very method, I have been made destitute of sleep."
O red Aśoka tree,
you whose slender trunk is like that of a woman, where indeed has she gone— leaving behind her devoted lover?
Why do you cause my head, already trembling from being shaken by the wind, to tremble further with the thought, "I have not seen her"?
O Eight-Petaled One, whose eight petals are struck by the jar-like bodies of bees longing [for you] and pressing against your vessel;
from where would this flowering of yours come without being struck by your feet?
O Vasunāga,

you are enamored with fresh sprouts, and I too am enamored with the praiseworthy virtues of my beloved; friend, arrows discharged from the bow of Love come toward you, and they come toward me as well.
The touch of your lovely soles brings joy to you; likewise, it brings joy to me as well.
In every respect we are equal, O Aśoka; the only difference is that I have been made sorrowful by the Creator.
That man alone was truly possessed of the armor of glory; he was a man of vice who, while crying out, "Alas,
my beloved!", had his life-breaths departed simultaneously with his final gasps.
But other beasts, failing to obtain food, cast themselves into calamity through the tears born of separation from their beloved ones,
produced by the dejection and exhaustion of anxiety.
O beloved, that blue lotus which possessed a luster equal to your eyes has sunk into the water;
and the moon, which imitated the beauty of your face, has been hidden by the clouds. Alas! Alas! [I am lost].
Even those royal swans who followed you out of affection for your departure have gone;
fate does not permit me even the mere diversion of beholding you.

When that pleasure-reversal had occurred through those various commands of hers, he, the illustrious Sūryavarman, mistakenly dressed himself in her own garment as she stood there, slow with bashfulness.
Wearing that very same silk headband, standing as I am now, I have been told:
"This attire alone is indeed fitting for you"—this must not be forgotten.
Though she has embraced me, that beloved makes my body long for her embrace; though she is seen, she of lovely aspect causes my eyes to desire to see her again.
Even though she dwells within my heart, my beloved enters it ever more deeply; despite our reunion being firmly established, she assumes a newness in me day by day.
While Gopāditya’s slender lady,
her face clouded by words even more difficult to endure than the pain of her own departure,
stood with me looking on, and while the attendants, out of mutual examination, maintained a silent smile;
Seeing me agitated by the impulsive urge to prostrate at his feet, that deer-king spoke these words, "Do not be afraid," and thus I was comforted by him.
Though she was under my own control, I did not kiss her; though her lower lip was full, I did not drink from it out of thirst.
Her gait was not observed, nor was her laughter witnessed, nor was she embraced with effort.
Even when she was enraged, that most beloved woman was not appeased by me, a fool, for so long.
O friend, how have I been brought to this separation by the cruel power of fate?
"I must go," she said with longing; seeing me ready for my journey, her eyes clouded with tears yet smiling, she whispered words foretelling my welfare.
At dawn, hearing the morning drum struck by the early breeze, she was awakened.
"Alas! The night has passed so quickly," saying this, the beloved wife fell upon the chest of her husband.
For some of these [women],
the striking of the lotus-like hands with graceful movements constitutes a certain form of binding;
for others, the obstruction of a playful embrace causes anger, which they express through a silent rebuke.

O wrathful one! Having suddenly forgotten what was previously agreed upon here, why do you, out of a burden of anger, feel such longing for me when I have gone beyond the range of your sight? Alas! Subhūti 1372.3–4. Subhūti 1372.4.
Where can my gaze find rest, accustomed as it is to drinking the nectar of her form?
Whence can my ears hear anything else, intent as they are on the practice of listening to her speech?
And how can my limbs endure, saturated as they are with the intense flavor of her embrace?
Alas! Now, in his absence, we have fallen into a miserable state.
The earth bears fruit only when it supports the feet of one whose eyes are innocent and who has attained the state of a perfected sage;
blessed is that expanse of the sky which comes within the range of his vision.
My own heart is even more fortunate than those, for it exists as being composed of that very [Buddha-nature].
"Let us see what she intends to do"—thus did I maintain my composure;
"What is she saying to me? This man is surely a rogue"—thus did she resort to feigned anger.
In that state, we were both agitated by the mutual exchange of our shifting glances.
I laughed with feigned innocence, but she shed tears that robbed me of my composure.
If a servant commits an offense against fate, he is then tormented or bound;
by this silence, so skillful at manifesting pride, he is reduced to servitude.
Thus did I speak to her, even though her tremulous glance was fixed upon the circle of my shoulder.
The tears from her eyes, possessing a white luster like a string of liberated pearls, were beyond description.
With her toe, soft as a young sprout, she draws patterns upon the ground at every step; again and again she casts her eyes, white with dark pupils and flickering, upon me;
and bearing a face bowed with modesty, her lower lip slightly quivering, she holds within her words a hidden meaning.
That which he did not say, even though it remained in his heart, pains my mind.
Even now that remains revolving in my mind: when I was asleep at night, the princess, having first uttered the auspicious word "Live! to me, afterwards placed a golden lotus-leaf upon my ear.
When I had departed from Bilhana’s presence and traveled a long distance, she wept for a long time with her throat unbound; then,
having wiped her eyes, she approached me with a prostration, her slender body trembling.

My beloved said to me: "In this time when darkness is bound by the thundering of clouds at the end of the world, even a skull-bearer (kāpālika) travels abroad; that my heart is not pained [by his absence] from home."
Is this childishness of someone's, or is it their very nature? Is it ferocity, or perhaps anger?
Or is it restlessness, or a high resolve, or the pride of the onset of youth?
O Noble One, by these [arrows] of yours— whose points are the corners of your eyes, whose tips are your smile, and which possess the grace of your lovely breasts, eyebrows, and waist—
the world, though previously composed, is consumed when they are placed within the mind.
With her cheek resting in your hand, her eyes on your path, and her mind fixed upon you— where is there any occasion for her pride? (Amaruśataka 138)
Vararuci reveals that all things are subject to momentary destruction; seeing the entire world as empty,
he acts beyond conventional memory, like one whose intellect has become awakened to the Buddha’s teaching.
With its excellence of qualities, its elision of letters, its compounds, its irregular formations, and its mixture of prefixes,
this [work]— with its difficult words and meanings— is like the grammatical system of Vyākaraṇa itself.
Excessively maintaining silence, having abandoned garlands, ointments, and bathing,
and having cast far away all sense of shame, she was like the composition of a Jain scripture.
With her attachment to sense objects extinguished, her lotus-like eyes closed, and her breathing gentle,
she meditates constantly on something indefinable, as if ever devoted to yoga.
With her eyes encircled by the threads of tears falling incessantly from her eyes,
the young woman separated from you mutters your name as if it were a mantra for conquering death.
O handsome one, in your absence, this girl of delicate form, whose eyes are but this much in size,
has suddenly reached such a state in merely these many days.
The wind scented with the fragrance of night-lotuses, the warbling of cuckoos, and the humming of swarms of bees—
by fate, all this array has been brought together for his destruction.
It is better that love has never been felt at all than that it should be born only to be frustrated;
for one whose eyes have been plucked out suffers in this way, whereas one who is blind from birth does not.
The tears of Ravigupta’s wife,
entering her throat again and again as she endures the onset of suffering, seem to block it as if out of fear that her meager remaining life might escape.
O friend, because she has been pierced by the arrows of the God of Love, she travels a very long distance toward you;
meanwhile, O friend, she weeps piteously before her companions as they travel along the path.
While Andhaka remained silent, she sat down, having performed extensive protective rites; with her matted hair clinging to her body,
that poor woman, intent on meditation for your sake, has undertaken the great vow of the skull-bearer (Mahāpāśupata).
Desirous [of her goal], smeared with sandalwood ash, her forehead marked by lines and drenched with tears,
wearing a garment of lotus fibers upon her breasts, she performs the vow taught by Smara.
Having cast her gaze, languid with fatigue, upon the two of them and beholding the excessive beauty of the clouds, she—
slightly comforted by the prospect of imminent death— breathes once more; do not be afraid.

Having offered herself even to you for the sake of happiness, she has obtained as its fruit a continuous state of fainting, gasping, lamentation, wakefulness, trembling, and yawning—O Sakacella! O mine of jewels,
you are most dear to her, and she is most worthy of being dear to you;
for the day does not shine without the sun, nor does the night shine without the moon.
That which,
having been seen by a woman with beautiful eyes, is not seen again all at once, is better left unseen;
for such a thing, being exceedingly rare, attains the status of a beloved, like nectar mixed with poison.

Having perceived you within her dream, she awoke with her arms still clinging to you in a false embrace; seeing you there upon the bed today, the bewildered girl closed her eyes again and again in feigned sleep.
You remain constantly upon the heart of your beloved, which is scorched by the mass of flames from the great fire on Mount Śikhara;
yet that compassionate young woman does not dwell for even a moment upon your own heart, which is as cool as a spray of snow.
Where are those cruel, double-tongued, and deceitful men who burn others even with the mere sight of their breath? And where are those playful lovers?
O serpent-like man, this certain form of Cupid’s artifice—which is not a snake—enchants us merely through the poison of its glance.
"Let this slender,
delicate girl be spared here; she is but a child"— with such apprehension,
a certain cluster of blossoms was seen by Bhaṭṭa Vāsudeva, its flowers crushed by the weight of bees.
Therefore, you must press that [grape] mercilessly in secret;
for a vine overcome by dullness never yields its juice without being pressed with force.
"What is the use of asking her whose hips are so broad? Let us go from here more quickly;
that beloved of yours has been seen by me alone, brother, for the entire day with tears."
To every traveler she looks with her neck craned in haste, crying "It is you!";
yet, as soon as he is seen, she turns away, weeping incessantly, saying, "It is not you, O Bhava!"
Unable to endure the suffering of separation from you, she has released her life-breaths;
by her, this final message has been sent to you, O hard-hearted one:
"O cloud, my only child is young, and I am struck down by fate."
Just as this [teaching] is given to one who delights in the addiction to service, so too [is it here].

Having meditated upon you, the Lord who is the very essence of Brahman, in a secluded place, he suddenly breaks through his physical wall; having reached a state where consciousness is destroyed, how did that pitiless one go, and what does he say to each individual?
Or rather, what can fate do? You, however, are an authority; for you have abandoned that madwoman and stand among others who follow the conduct of the virtuous.
With her cheek resting upon her hand, her neck turned sideways, and her limbs drenched by the streams of tears from her eyes fixed upon the tip of her nose,
she uttered half-syllables with a voice faltering and choked by the paralysis of grief.
That which was intended by you with such restraint and compassion cannot be expressed.
In summer, the beauty of spring is like a woman with thick, continuous streams of tears falling from her heavy breasts; in autumn, she is like one whose hands and breasts are cold;
and in winter, alas, the splendor of spring is like a woman whose lotus-face has fallen away due to perspiration.
Out of affection for you, she showed him all the seasons, even though they were not present during her separation from you.
The tears of Hari’s beloved were shed upon her kinsmen, the heat of grief was inflicted upon her friends, wretchedness was cast entirely upon her attendants, and anxiety was entrusted to her elders.
Today she is indeed departing for her own nirvāṇa; she is now greatly distressed by her own breaths. Be confident, for the sorrow born of separation has been shared by her.
Was a bolt not fashioned from the broad palm-leaves of the *bāhulata* tree?
Was the hem of her upper garment not held fast? Or was it not falsely cried out? (Amaruśataka 1408–1)
When you have departed from home, O beloved, what else can the world of women do but fall at your feet, weeping piteously out of longing?
O traveler, brother of Śrī Dāmarasvāmin, go to your home very quickly; I have seen your beloved wife, who is eager to hear news of you.
Meeting a traveler on the road, she has approached him with respect.
Unable to speak due to her throat being choked and agitated by sobs, she weeps for a long time with deep sighs, her lips quivering and her neck turned away.

The eyes of someone are restless with longing for your path; their lower-lip petals quiver, weary from the exhaustion of labored sighs, as they greedily gaze upon your lotus-face, which is formidable with streams of falling, languid, and shimmering tears.
Or perhaps your entire mind has been fixed upon her; or else everything has already been taken away by you.
That grief, though its limbs are withered, still strives to give even this to you, though fate has struck it down.

The body of the venerable Govindarāja— burning with the fire of passion (*dāha*), melting with the flow of water (*ambhaḥ-prasṛti*), thick with accumulated moisture (*pracayavat-bāṣpa*), observed through the channels of his eyes,
with sighs as flickering flames of a lamp, and its form submerged in the palm of his hand— [is thus described].
Moreover, what else shall I say? Throughout the entire night, she remains by the window of your path, her moonlight obstructed by the parasol of her hand.
O virtuous Mādhava, while this month of Madhava is sweet with bees intoxicated by the fragrance of the filaments of the *rajaśekhara* flower, let this poor girl remain here for now,
lest she be consumed from afar by the fire of separation.
O you who are as fickle as lightning, why do you look upon this, your own body, which is as delicate as a flower? O Subhūti, what is this obsession with pride?
Do as this messenger says; go!
O Lord, even in her dreams, Śivardhana’s wife does not obtain the sight of your face which grants happiness; distressed by her young son, she remains sleepless due to separation from you.
The supreme happiness of investigating your path was indeed hers,
yet it was obstructed by a flood of tears.
The mango tree is a thorn with its garland of blossoms; this bank of the house-lotus is a nest of crows;
the creeper is a spear made of frost; and even the pond is a cauldron of heat.
To her who is being crushed by the harsh wind of the *śarabha* deer, the lotus stalk is a mere blade of grass;
alas, during her separation from Rāma, even a necklace is a blow to the doe-eyed one.
Regarding food, she has somehow become restrained; there is a seal of silence upon her mouth,
her eyes are closed, her slender body remains motionless,
she stays in solitude, and her mind is one-pointedly absorbed in meditation.
Therefore, O fortunate one, I think that for your sake she must be performing intense penance.
Then, as she was conversing with her female friend,
questioning her about her lover, and arranging the ornaments for her husband, the bride spoke these words.
A certain serenity arose upon her face—was it from the splendor of her attire, or perhaps from the pleasant news?
Śiva touches his vital points, speaks what is pleasing, remembers him with love, and watches for his weaknesses; yet,
even when such a person acts with many strange transformations, no treachery is perceived in him.
Enough, enough with the name of that cruel man; that very same time has come once again.
Speak, speak, O messenger! Even the reply of an enemy is to be respected.

Upon that beloved woman whose eyes were fixed upon him, whose beauty was acted as a messenger by the glances from the slightly trembling eyes of Vāsudeva, and who was adorned with necklaces, girdles, and waist-bands—
upon her, the splendor of the bracelets and anklets being transposed, appeared as if it were a brand-new radiance.
"Tell me, O skillful one: where was Govindarāja seen, how, for how long, what did he desire, what was said by him, and when will he come here?"—
such conversations concerning their beloved, expanded by various expressions of affection, do not cease to be cherished even in dreams.
O friend, if that merciless rogue has not yet arrived, why do you suffer, O messenger? He is self-willed and has many lovers; what fault is there in that for you?
Look! Today, as he is being drawn toward union with his beloved by her virtues—as if by the weight of her longing and anguish—this heart of mine will go forth of its own accord to burst open.
Having observed him to be crooked and accompanied by others, you bit your lip in anger—unable to tolerate his denial of an offense witnessed by your own eyes. Alas!
Why were you, so fickle, sent by me into this deluge of sorrow, you who, though distressed by the exertion of sighs, do not even cease the trembling of your breasts?
O messenger who speaks falsely,

you have gone from here to bathe in the pond— having wiped away the sandalwood paste fallen from your breasts, having rubbed redness from your lips, having removed the collyrium from your eyes, and this slender body of yours is covered in horripilation—
but you have not gone to the presence of that base man, even though you know the suffering of his kinsmen.
"Whose messenger are you?
"I have gone to that lover, O fortunate one. "Was he seen? "For a very long time. "What was he doing? "He was occupied with playing the lute.
"Was he proud of his good fortune? "He gave no answer at all. "Was it out of pride? "No, because of his voice being choked with tears. "Is that a trick of a rogue? "Indeed, it is."
Then Upahāsa said:
"Since neither conciliation nor bribery has been successful, it was well that you inflicted punishment upon this ill-behaved man, even though the possibility of division had been shown."
O messenger, this monastery is merely a throat-torment; your eyes are red with passion, and your face is devoid of desire—why have you gone forth into the religious life?
O messenger, by this passionless one, who is like the Buddha himself,
emptiness (*śūnyatā*) has been declared without artifice regarding all things.
"Why do you hide your breasts and face with your hand, O messenger?
Only when wounded by a lover's teeth do the lips and breasts of beautiful women shine so brightly."
Messenger, what is the use of that sin committed by one who transgresses the scriptures,
since you have been devoured by him who [devours] five of the five-clawed animals?
With your two thighs scarred by wounds and lacerated from blows, O messenger,
you are fit for the field of battle, not for the work of a messenger.
"O messenger, you must keep my nails, teeth, and bones;
eighteen akṣauhiṇīs have met their destruction for the sake of a friend."
"O messenger, you have performed a deed that is difficult for another to do:
you have struck down the one who destroys those who have come for refuge and seeks out their vulnerabilities."
"Your body is emaciated, your gait is weary, your eyes have tremulous pupils, your speech is indistinct, and your garment is loose; O messenger, why are you feverish?"
O messenger, what need is there for much speaking here? For the sake of accomplishing my purpose, even my own flesh has been given; what then to say of other things?
O Vararuci,
with your curly locks of hair, your forehead of rosy luster, and your pair of cheeks,
this body of yours trembles; I know it must have been struck by your lover.
O lotus-eyed one,

how shall the fever— having reached its full intensity throughout your entire body— ever leave you, as you lie intent upon your bed, trembling all over, with a throat swollen by sobbing, your gait faltering,
and uttering soft moans?
On a certain night,
my garment— which was improper for another woman due to its association with sexual dalliance—
was somehow taken by that friend of mine.
This was brought back by you through the gift of your own garment; O messenger, from where else could one so skilled in the means of pacifying transgressions come?
O messenger,
if my beloved is like that seed which has not yet sprouted, even though he has made such an oath,
why then have you, in your anger, bitten the tip of your own lower lip with your teeth?
Abandoning this trembling that causes a flow of perspiration, attain composure;
for who, O friend, will understand the inner state of one whose nature is perverse?
"Whose horripilation do you cause? Having resorted to some extraordinary meditation, your gaze wanders, O fiercely fickle one; and your hissing sound is clearly manifest."
Having seen that man who is indeed as skilled in the arts of love as a courtesan, O messenger,
are you feverish with passion, or do calamities arise from touching a sinner?
"Whose sister are you?
Why have you come so hurriedly? Why has this favor been bestowed upon me? Your braid is disheveled; why do you fall at my feet, coming and going?"

O messenger, with your face moist with perspiration melting away from the heat of the sun, what will you say when your lip—possessing the luster of a withered lotus—is parched? What is the use of excessive words?
"O you who cross over by means of virtue!
Why do you come? Your own lip has been moistened by the rapid turning [of your tongue], yet why has the passion for your sake fallen away from the petal of your lower lip despite your entreaties?"
This body is already wasted; what is the use of gnawing at those [other] feet?
Tell me, how can his dwelling be for the sake of your own conviction?
Why is there sweat upon you on the road, caused by the defect of the burning heat of mental anguish?
O friend, does your lip become parched from the anger of a thwarted request? O lady, has your forehead-mark vanished because you weep at being addressed by your name?
Is the man’s garment pure, yet soiled, in order to protect himself from the wicked?
O fair-faced one, why have your bracelets been broken by the traveler? Why is your face, covered in dust, washed clean and devoid of its usual adornment?

"O Subhūti, has your passion perhaps been dissolved by the gusts of breath from my sighs of distress? Or was it stolen because of my greed for your garment? "Indeed, it was taken by me out of a desire for your clothing."
O Śrī, alas, as you were proceeding along the path to accomplish the purpose of Bakasura, a man-like wind appeared before you;
for it caused this arrangement of your braid to become disheveled, its locks of hair tossing about like those of a woman in agitation.
O friend, why have you ventured into that pool which is the sole kinsman of evil deeds?
For your limbs remain drenched, and you wear your forehead bare of its tilaka mark.
O beautiful one, by what sequence did the second [letter] become even more beloved than that? For even now, the lingering tremor has not subsided for you whose eyes are agitated.
O Kaśmīra-born one, surely your very own flaw is the stain of saffron dye upon your limbs;
for you bear body after body—fragile though they be—covered by swarms of bees attracted by its fragrance.
Has a nail-to-nail struggle been initiated by someone with him?
For you have suddenly entered here for the sake of water, only to fall within the range of his scratching claws.
Now, regarding the observation of women by Pañcika:
who would not be made sick with love by even the sweet sound of the word "woman"?
How much more so, then, his speech, which is sweet with the grace of nobility and eloquence?
By whom were women created? They are like jars of nectar, like reservoirs of happiness, and like treasuries of delight.
Her fortitude has already dissolved simply because she is a woman; what more need be said of her being so beautiful?
If she is compassionate, it is a hardship; if she is full of desire, it is exceedingly difficult to endure.
Is my beloved hidden, or dissolved, asleep, or even dead?
Embraced as she is, she causes me a hundredfold doubt.
The deer-eyed one is the essence within this worthless, burnt-out cycle of existence; she possesses the flavor of unartificial love and moves with a languid grace.
Practice produces true skill in actions;
it is practiced according to rule until the gazelle-eyed woman is created.
Of all those who possess this beloved form, which surpasses every comparison,
only one might attain such beauty: one's own reflection resting upon a mirror.
As she, Maṇibhadra’s mother,
treated this innocent person with such contemptuous disregard,
her gait was undoubtedly like that of an elephant.
If the Creator were not all-seeing, by whom could this world have been fashioned? On the other hand, if He possesses sight, what reason is there for Him not to take possession [of it]?
Whose [is this]?
The moon, which is the essence of the nectar of ambrosia, the entirety of the Makara-bannered god of love,
and the bringer of joy to the eyes of all people— how has it risen during the day?
O Śiva,
how wonderful! Though bound and tightly restrained by the limbs of this female serpent— limbs that are pale and wan from the pervasive heat arising from the fire of love—
she extends life to him who has never experienced it before.
O Govinda-svāmin,
for this [creation], Prajāpati is not considered capable of every kind of arrangement; nor is the moon,
nor the god whose weapon is flowers (Kāmadeva), nor is the sweet-smelling Madhu, nor even the lord Viriñci (Brahmā) who stands afar.
This is my opinion: when the ocean arose from untruth, she herself was given by it to Hari after being churned by Mount Mandara, and having been given, she was protected as Śrī.
With a radiant form, dark hair, and a face like the moon,
with a slender waist and an auspicious appearance, she is composed of all the gods.

Surely it was by the God of Love, acting with excessive impetuosity, that the very name "woman" was here established as a sword-blade raised against Kalhana— who, though unconquered, desired to conquer him by casting aside his bow of fifteen sharp arrows.

With her lotus-eyes cast down, the young girl weeps only with tears that flow from the base of her clear cheeks, falling like shimmering water.
No knitting of the eyebrows was made by Līlācandra; the story was not interrupted, nor was he indifferent to the agitation;
nothing disagreeable was said, and his left side was not even made to bristle with hairs.
By that beloved woman, who had ascended his lap and was embraced deeply,
his grief was communicated through restless tears that fell within the intervals of his gaze.
Beholding the marks of her own husband’s teeth upon her lower lip, Dharmakīrti’s [heroine] suffers from jealousy;
seeing the nail-marks placed by herself upon an improper place, she is tormented by shame.

O deluded one! By remaining in that state of pride which robs one of all discernment, you have rendered even your own self—though it is naturally free from vain conceptualization—a mere companion to your husband.
When his foot became copper-colored at its sole, when his lotus-like hands were crushed and their bracelets shattered,
and when his palms were scarred by the blows [he received].
A certain weak woman, desiring in her mind to kill him who had never before experienced the touch of a beloved, weeps again and again in utter agitation.
Fearing that someone might perceive her affection, she respectfully covers her feet even though they are exposed;
she conceals her smile under a pretext when it appears, and does not look clearly at him.
Like a conversation between friends, she appears with her husband even when he is angry; for this slender woman, there exists an intense affection in which even indignation has a lovely emergence.
The face of Bhīma,
with its lower lip quivering with anger, was not shown to me; nor did that charming girl utter even a single word, however slight, for more than a hundred steps.
Her intoxication was signaled by her spirited movements that inflamed the state of his mind, while her anger was communicated by this girdle whose knot of cloth was tied with extreme firmness.
O sages, listen as I relate this wonderful account of what occurred in this world-age of Nārāyaṇa, during the time of the dark clouds that bring joy to the peacocks.
1592.1–2. What transpired in this age, hear it from me! 1592.2.
Alas! Out of fear for the loss of their good fortune, those two proud women, beloved by their husband, have undertaken the vow of exile for the entire night in this single dwelling.
Then, for someone, there was this conciliation:
"Alas! With these very lives now in my hands, like balls," Subhūti 1593-1.
O deluded one, how much longer do you wish to play with that which has no end?
O Śivardhana,
what remains for you to do with your hand toward this servant who has fallen at your feet?
O passionate one, who will bring anger upon you, you who are already so prone to wrath?
O frail one, this face of yours, resting upon the palm of your hand, its edges blurred by drops of water falling incessantly from your eyes— how is it that it does not cause you pain?
O fair-thighed one, look at both of them together; what is dear to you? Behold them without hesitation.
For water held on the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass never satisfies one’s thirst, even after a very long time.
Upon this lotus-stalk of the face of Vṛṣṇigupta, the dancing girl that is your creeper-like brow performs a playful dance;
what a charming metaphor for beauty!

O slender one, you have indeed been brought to the final stage of the ten stages by your glance, which is like a pair of scales. Tell me, O beautiful one, what is the purpose of this smile, which is like the light of the moon—this grinding of flour?
O Lord of Wisdom,
if we are not dependent on others, then why, O friend, has this cheek been reduced so suddenly to the state of the moon— marked by tears from the eyes like the dark collyrium of bees?
O fair-limbed one, abandon your pride; behold me prostrate at your feet. Indeed, never before has such anger as this been yours.
While the Lord was speaking thus,
she, with her eyes cast down, shed no small amount of tears, yet it seemed as if nothing at all were released.
O fierce woman, why do you bear such harsh words, eyes copper-red with anger, a frowning face, and even a body that is vainly devoid of ornaments?
This [joy] brings only excessive self-exertion to you;
for me, however, it clearly results in even greater sorrow, if it should manifest so vividly.
"Venerable Lord Tathāgatendra-siṃha, please be gracious.
If one says this, it is not appropriate when there is no anger;
[one should say: "I shall indeed act in such a way that there will never again be such an admission [of fault]."
"You will surely know this as well—that I have no fault—yet you speak falsely. O beloved, I do not know what it is that you are fit to say."
O Śrī Hara,
by virtue of his close contact with his lips, even his face has become reddened; and due to the crookedness of his hair and eyebrows, even his mind does not abandon its downward inclination.
Alas! My anger is long-lasting; what else could it be but for the union of my eyes?
O fierce woman, because of its proximity to your breasts, even your heart must be hard.

For someone, her own eyes are like blue lotuses through their radiance; her face is like the orb of the moon through its beauty; her hair is like bees; and her sweet words are like the songs of cuckoos.
O deluded one, through your rivalry you have brought us to a state of humiliation; O wicked woman, cease your harassment, for it is not fitting for you toward us who have sought refuge in you.
"O charming girl, what is this sudden aversion toward your left foot, which has been attached to it for so long?
When a lover is intent on jesting, there is no room for anger, reproach, or obstruction.
Thus, as her surge of anger was softened by the gentle words of her attendants...
Immediately thereafter, due to the sudden bursting forth [of the sprouts], it neither remained stationary nor did it proceed.
O fair-limbed one, the fire of anger within both of us shall surely be extinguished after a long time; moreover, your face, having attained its own natural splendor, will abandon its sorrow.
"The stations of worldly existence are empty for you, but these days pass by for me;
there will be no returning to them again, yet my mind is still pained."
O Bhaṭṭārikā, he is not of wicked conduct, nor indeed is he devoid of virtues;
beloved by you, having cast off his ornaments, he has fallen at the base of your feet.
O charming girl, let the moonstone attain the state of being cherished around your own neck; there is no other remedy for the pacification of the fever in your heart.
When her pride had withered away,
when her face was lowered in shame, and when she— having no other means remaining— held me by the hand, with prostration as her sole resort;
With her eyes half-closed and her eyelashes slightly drooping, she suddenly spoke with a voice that was soft and faltering at the base of her breasts.
With a pair of eyes tremulous from the heat of anger and her creeper-like brows arched, her face copper-red with sighs,
do not exert yourself in vain by cutting your hands with your nails;
for this pearl necklace is already clinging to you through the clear streams of teardrops from your eyes.
O Caṇḍī, you shine with wrath as you fashion your entire mass of hair into a crest-lock.
O Beloved, having fashioned your eyes with two blue lotuses, your face with a water-lily, your teeth with jasmine, your lower lip with a fresh sprout,
and your limbs with petals of the *campaka* tree— how did the Creator fashion your heart out of stone?
"O slender one, though you are thin, you are beautiful; truly, you grow more and more radiant. Desist, be gracious, O lovely one; youth, once gone, does not return."
For someone, the night has almost passed; the moon, whose body is like crystal, seems to be sinking; this lamp has fallen under the power of sleep and seems to be flickering.
O fierce one, though you bow down and abandon pride, you do not likewise abandon your anger; alas, O cruel one, even your heart has become hard through its proximity to your breasts!

O beloved, that you are harsh toward the affectionate, rigid toward the one who bows, hostile toward the passionate, and turn your face away from the one who looks up to you— [all this is directed] toward him.
It is fitting for you, who act so perversely, that the application of sandalwood paste is poison;
that the rays of the moon are a scorching heat; that snow is fire; and that the joys of play are torments.
Jayadeva’s Dialogue and Response:
"O child, O lord, abandon this anger, O proud woman; what has been done by you that is born of wrath?"
"I have no weariness toward you; your honor has not offended me—it is I who am at fault for everything. Why then do you weep with a faltering voice? Before whom are you weeping?
Is it not this [fact]: 'Am I dear to you?'—it is because of this that you weep."
In the speech of Bhaṭṭakumārila,
anger flashes forth on all sides; his eyes are fixed,
the lines of his eyebrows are knit, and this surface of his cheeks quivers.
Indeed, this mass of bristling hair on the face betrays a secret longing for you; O beloved, such is the state of one who feigns anger while harboring a harsh reproach.
O you who uphold the treasure of honor, go; may your paths be auspicious today.
By this man with joined palms, my entire heart has been poured out.
Let it be known to someone; enough with these useless words, my dear, let us go.
There is not even the slightest fault in you; rather, it is fate that has turned its back on us.
If such love for you has brought her to this state, then what pain is there in the departure of that wretched life, which is by nature so fickle?
O gazelle-eyed one,
may no cloud ever arise to obstruct you;
may not even for a moment the five arrows of the god of love strike you in separation, O frail woman— even for a mere blink of an eye.
O hard-hearted one, release your anger which obstructs happiness;
O proud woman, Yama indeed writes down every day that passes by.
In youth, this is not appropriate; and when a union is fleeting, as long as there is quarreling, O fortunate one, so long should one engage in pleasure.
O hard-hearted Bhasa, abandon this delusion based on false arguments; it is not right to lead these people to suffering with malicious words.
"What is this, or rather, O charming one, what have you now resolved upon? Having made that which is held in your heart known to me, my beloved, remain at ease."

By your arrival here so early in the morning, sleeplessness has been brought upon my eyes; by removing my sluggishness, lightness has been produced in me. What is there that you have not done? Since I have abandoned the desire for death, let us go.
"You remain in suffering; now that you have departed, you will hear what is beneficial."
Thus it was that this body of ours was once indivisible;
then you became my beloved, and I, cursed with ill fortune, became your most cherished wife.
Now you are my protector and we are your wife—what more can be said?
This is the fruit of my having attained mastery over these lives, which are as hard as adamant.
Better is it for you to display a frown that reveals the power of intense anger;
better are words faltering with reproach when turned away from affection;
better is the practice of showing disregard, forcefully enacted out of the heat of pride.
O you whose heart is hard, this concealment is not anger toward one who has reached the end.

A steady, unwavering gaze from the corners of your eyes, a soft and indistinct voice, and a most timid touch amidst the throng of people— these very things were observed by me at the onset of your love.
When those very beings with distracted minds are seen, they become dispassionate.
If even their gaze has been fixed upon the void, why is there such steady curiosity?
If an effort toward silence has been undertaken, why does the lower lip quiver?
If the mind is fixed in meditation, how can there be the bristling of hair?
Enough with these dramatic gestures; look, for pride has been subdued—be gracious and release me.

That which is accessible to a friend through profound respect, that in which they find an opening due to courtesy or out of fear, and that which arises suddenly from playful jesting— [if such things occur]... (Amaruśataka 1626–1628)
That which restrains shame and in which conviction is produced by means of oaths—is that called love? And even in that, is there not anger?
A row of decorative leaf-patterns on her cheek has been crushed by the pressure of her palm;
the nectar-like essence of her lower lip has been squeezed out by her sighs;
and the tears repeatedly clinging to her throat cause her breasts to heave.
O you who are devoid of compassion, anger has become dear to you, but we are not.
I have been utterly deceived by you through various feigned acts and illusory friendships; yet I too have perceived this through your most artful and hidden words of business.
Let it be known to you; do not trouble yourself in vain on my account. For I am impatient, while you are devoid of affection—thus has equality met with equality.
O Bhāsa, abide in grace; manifest your joy and abandon your anger.
O beloved, your limbs are withering; let your words sprinkle them like nectar.
O charming one, turn your face toward this moment, the treasury of all joys;
for the time that has passed cannot be recovered.
In Candaka’s case, anger consists of knitting the brows; restraint is silence; conciliation is a mutual smile; and favor is a glance.
Behold, this very affection of yours has now turned into a calamity;
you fall at my feet, yet there is no release of my wrath toward you, O wicked woman!
Thus, as you have said, all my faults are yours; O lotus-eyed mistress, who would persist in being at odds with their own master? Here I offer this salutation with joined palms—please restrain me.
The servants are running about; what opportunity is there for the arrival of the hour?
"You are indeed beloved by many; you are a young man, handsome, happy, and pitiless.
O one of deceitful mind, you do not know the suffering of another, and therefore you yourself do not feel pain. But ask someone else about this unbearable agony caused by the arrows of Love."
Be our protector, so that you shall not be called a "Kāpālika" by virtuous people.
May this perverse Kāma, who is like the pain of separation for some, emaciate the body; and may that Yama, who is skilled at counting the days and devoid of compassion, do the same.
O Lord, you too are subject to the malady of pride; consider this: how can people intoxicated by passion live, when they are as tender as young sprouts?
O you who ferry me across by means of your virtue, I did not consider the arrows of the hunter of desire when I remembered you as my life-restoring herb;
nor was I burnt by the fire of separation when I suddenly tasted the nectar of union with you.
This day has been spent by me in drawing various forms according to my imagination;
what else remains? You indeed dwell within my heart, and you yourself are the witness therein.
Suvarmaṇa,
having abandoned his pride and possessions along with his circle of friends and his minister, said:
"Having been deprived of the grace of your feet, I am unable to live for even a moment."
Behold this body of yours, O plowman, and the various states it has passed through; I have fallen at your feet, O Lord—be gracious now!

Behold me with eyes that rival the petals of the blue lotus; O fair-browed one, let your face, which sheds a flood of moonlight, be raised toward me. Let my two arms, placed upon the region of your neck, become a necklace.
Upon attaining you, let this pain of separation depart like a woman who has gone away in anger.
Having myself made nail-marks upon the bodies of both [lovers], I shall show them to my clever friends, saying, "These were made by you."
Thus I remember you, who were frightened by me in secret,
and who are capable of enduring the breaking of the seal of the fragrance of love.

O Destroyer of Mura, I recognize your two eyebrows as the two bows of Rati’s son and Śara, which, having distinguished between male and female, are capable of conquering all who have considered propriety, and which are bent like the bow of the God of Love.
O Lord, you are the two-nailed arrow hidden within the quiver of the chest for the sake of releasing the shafts of those two;
you are the wind-weapon born from the sweet-sounding breath of their sighs.
If a mango tree grows in a parched, saline soil through the nourishment of rainclouds,
and if a lotus rises in ploughed earth through the application of manure and a ball of milk,
and if a plantain tree bears fruit by being sprinkled with grape juice— then [only] by the words of yours would such things occur.
Then, for the sake of instruction, there arises from that sweet foundation the suffix -tama.
If Smara were to produce nectar from the fresh ocean of milk by means of the rope of his eyelashes— which are like fine threads—
and by churning the mountain of sugar that is the wealth of the Vedas, he might perhaps win over the tongue of Your Majesty; yet, for my ears, it would only bring about their ultimate exhaustion.
That rustic fellow, though clever in society, always goes to the end of the row;

yet, O charming girl, even the arrows of the God of Love turn away in disdain at the mere thought of touching him. Why do you not call your lower lip "honey," and why do you not call your body "gold"?
"What is the name of this 'good lady'? he asked, yet she gave him neither word nor answer.
These are the *Sambhoga-śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment of enjoyment) of Śrī Harṣa;
therein is the description of the six seasons.
In this regard, it is the behavior of the cuckoo, blinded by the intoxication of spring, that women themselves go to meet their beloved during the autumn.
This is the activity of one who is dazed by the passion of spring.
On the peak of the great-souled one’s mountain, the cuckoo, adorned with a crest of blossoms and robed in the hue of flower-clusters,
makes its song intelligible through its cries, as if by the gestures of one of noble birth.
This sweet-voiced female bee is not crying out in intoxication;
this is the sound of the bow of Kandarpa being drawn.
Having climbed a tree under the pretext of gathering *kiṃśuka* flowers, Bhaumahasya,
like the fire itself, gazes everywhere upon the forest, both burnt and unburnt.
The lotus stalks within this very water, their throats constricted by joy, have risen up as if to hear the sweet song of the cuckoo.
The bee, thrilled by its first union, kisses the delicate flower-stalk after embracing it, just as a lover, overjoyed by a new encounter, kisses his beloved.
Not seeing her beloved in the forest, the female cuckoo, having searched for him long and being afflicted by separation, entered a red *aśoka* tree as if it were a funeral pyre.
The flowers of rivers, the blossoms of trees, and the digits of the moon may all diminish and yet return; but the youth of embodied beings does not return once it has faded.
"Abandon your quarrels and mental strife; rejoice, united with those you love"—thus did the cuckoos, with their sweet warbling, speak to the people.
Freshly adorned with tilaka marks, immediately seeking the honeyed lips of their lovers,
and possessing blossoming flower-arrows, the women set foot upon the garden grounds.
In the garden groves—
which were as cool as the breezes from the waves of the Vararuci lake—
and which served as fortresses for the spring, the season gradually conquered the winter by means of its power aided by the sun of burgeoning heat.
Like a twice-born man who, having abandoned the south and once delighted in the abundance of honey and flowers, gradually undergoes suffering again;
so did he.
Having wandered thus,
the sun, having reached its southern course, extended its rays everywhere;
then, like a sacrificial priest whose ritual has ended, it departed toward the abode of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) to obtain riches, as if sighing in exhaustion.
The ear-ornaments of Kumāradāsa,
their stalks covered with clusters of blossoming flowers,
shone brilliantly like rows of lamps with their wicks smeared with collyrium.
The lotus ponds, their throats marked by the contraction of their petals due to long dwelling in cold water, rose up as if to enjoy the heat bestowed by Indra.
Because he found no delight in one place, as if casting it aside in anger,
the bee kissed with devotion the lotus-face of the lotus-pond— her face which was trembling and agitated by her sighs, and whose red petals were fragrant with honey.
With her face bowed down and her body covered by clusters of pollen newly shaken forth,
the *mālatī* creeper shone like a youthful maiden breathing heavily.
The campaka flower of Vyāsadāsa was filled with a mass of golden filaments, its interior brimming with beauty like the unfolding of a smile;
it was like the golden casket of the God of Love, prepared for the purpose of writing his royal edict.

Whose dispute did not increase with life-breath upon seeing the blossoming *karṇikāra* tree, which, by its qualities of color, touches the vow of the panegyrists who are eager for the fragrance of its pollen?
Fearing these two— Karṇikāramañkha,

whose claws were wet with the blood of his enemies, and Vasantaka, who roared like a lion— the elephant of pride fled from the women, as if casting off its iron chains under the guise of the streaks of tears mixed with collyrium.
The sun in the southern quarter was unable to dispel its heat because of his presence; even he [the sun] was always of little heat.
I do not know what slanderous report was circulated between them at that time.

Those winds, who travel through the lineage of the lotus-like eyes of the travelers, whose spreading rain-clouds are like the collyrium on their eyelashes, who are adorned by the trailing hems of the garments of women languid with the joy of union, who dwell within the cave-dwellings of the sandalwood mountains, and who possess the power to bestow grace upon the deer with their leaping leaps— those winds have grown strong.
Seeing this mango tree ablaze with the radiance of its blossoms, the wife of the traveler,
as if out of fear of being consumed by fire, drenched his heart with the water released from her eyes.

Like a beloved wife, the flowering mango creeper— whose seat was fresh sprouts and who had bathed in the auspicious waters of the essence of the coldest season— was seen by Diviraya Soṣarvadhana as she turned toward the fruit.
In the springtime, when the quarters of the sky are made faint with the fragrance of the heavy mass of filaments from the flowers of the Sahakāra tree,
and when the bees are intoxicated by sweet honey— who would not feel longing?

The sweet honey, intoxicated by its sweetness, delights the earth— the earth which is adorned by the warbling of the black-throated cuckoo, who is rendered passionate by the Malaya breeze that dallies with the Malaya mountains, and who is like a lover to Kapila-Rudraka.
O Rudra,
that forest region shines like a beloved woman, its beauty enhanced by breasts as white as pale sandalwood paste,
and with Madana playfully aroused by her amorous gestures.
O Bhartṛhari,

why is it that you, like a traveler seized by a rutting elephant with a goad of *kiṃśuka* flowers, are constantly struck on the head by the wicked words of one whose seed is impure, as they fall down red as blood?
The hearts of travelers were excessively pierced by the falling arrows with their flickering feathers,
which revealed a deep redness like that of intense passion.
At the same time, the fresh sprouts— juicy and covered in thick redness—
tremble in the wind, as do the hearts of passionate men.
With her girdle of bees as a waist-belt and a garment of scattered flowers, her beauty possessing eyes like trembling lotuses, the Fortune of Spring shines like one intoxicated.
The foliage, curved like the young crescent moon and lacking the quality of expansion, appeared intensely red,
like the hundreds of nail-marks on the forest grounds immediately upon their union with Spring.
Rooted deep, possessing the crimson hue of coral and bearing clusters of flowers along with new shoots,
the *aśoka* trees cause the hearts of those whose beloveds have departed to become sorrowful as they gaze upon them.
The cooing of the cuckoo,
though its sound is exceedingly sweet, brings distress to those who have transgressed their commands;
likewise, a sweet voice causes pain to one whose authority has been overstepped.
The lotus plant, though frequented by him along with his beloved, cannot endure it without her;
now she remembers him, who was placed within her heart by Spring, day and night as the very essence of delight.
O Rudra,

that season of spring has arrived like Hanumān; its beautiful filaments are kissed by the breeze, it is led by the bright orb of the moon, and it is gazed upon with longing eyes by women separated from their lovers.
With its *kiṃśuka* groves everywhere ablaze with the likeness of fires at the end of an aeon, their leaves fallen away, and their clusters of flowers bent low,
this earth, now that the spring season has suddenly arrived, shines like a newlywed bride clad in crimson silk.
Having cast off her garment of leaves, the trumpet-flower tree (*pāṭalā*) shines forth, adorned with blossoms upon her own bark;
yet even so, the bee does not abandon that beloved— where indeed is the capacity for discernment among the passionate?
The tree, its branches shaken by the wind from the south, as if agitated, seems to cry out "Do not,
do not! to the flock of cuckoos in order to ward them off, looking with compassion upon the woman distressed by separation from her husband—
[thus says] Śrutadhara.
O mango tree, you were nurtured day after day by my own hands with water and the exertion of providing its sap;
yet now, in our separation, nothing is done that is equal to this, for the cluster of blossoms you bear is the very bowstring of the God of Love.
O cursed doorkeeper! What is this wicked mango blossom that has been nurtured by the tree?
For even when it undergoes the slightest change upon blooming, terrible fevers of passion break out.

O friend, by me— whose hips are trembling, whose vision is blinded by tears, and whose constant sighing has been fanned by the breeze— the blossoming *mañjarī* clusters have not been beheld, nor have the fragrances wafted from them been smelled.

By the stream of tears adorned with bees and *āmalaka* fruits, neither song nor weeping was heard; fortunately, the sweet voice of the young girl has today been transgressed by her distress, which destroys her fortitude.
O Śrī Vibhākaravarman, what should be done with the throat? Should it be pierced for long by the eye that has no eyelids? Or should the cool, sweet-smelling wine be drunk at the proper time?
One should enjoy the self even more through this nectar of the pleasure of touch;
thus has my mind been captivated by this fresh white creeper, like a bride.
The accumulation of effort for which you have nurtured me with such great hardship—
now these very life-breaths of mine, distressed by separation from what is dear, depart.
May these days of yours, O Spring— the foremost of the Lord of Pleasure— be auspicious, with their trees humming with bees in their bowers and their limbs filled with birds.

In the month of Kārttika, which increases the joy of the black cuckoos and the Śiva-devotees, when the minds of men boil with passion stirred by the playful warbling of the cuckoos, and when the god of love expands through the deep humming of the female bees; Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra 1686–1; Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra 1686–2.
O Lord of Life, tell me, how can I continue to breathe at this time when you have abandoned me— a time when the wind is intoxicated by the white dust of the pollen from blossoming flowers?
If, while on the road, this wife— distraught by the separation from her husband— should give up her life while remembering him,
whose great sin would that truly be?
[It would be the traveler's,] as long as he has not yet placed [the fruit] upon the heart of the tree.
The cuckoo repeatedly utters its loud cry, "Thine, thine! many times over.
If, at the onset of spring, the companion of someone who has been distressed by long separation should give up her life, tell me, who would be the partaker of that sin?
Deliberating whether it was the wind, or moisture, or the flower-arrowed god [Kāma],
he clearly heard the warbling of a multitude of cuckoos.
O traveler, do not go to your own home; let the season of spring be enjoyed. O proud woman, abandon your pride toward your beloved; what is the use of persisting in anger?
"The spring has arrived; it destroys the lives of those distressed by separation"—thus does the cuckoo, with its flood of melodious notes, speak as if by the command of Love.
In this springtime, when the ground is whitened by the abundant pollen fallen from the swarms of intoxicated bees clinging to creepers shaken by the wind from the forest groves;

when the firm-limbed women, their arms moist with the sweat of passion and their bracelets jingling as they loosen their hair-partings— even a gentle embrace of the neck causes the heart to languish, so what need be said of separation?
Is this the twanging of the bowstring of Madana as he practices his constant discharge of arrows?
Or are these, alas, the manifest fainting fits of Spring, the friend of the one who sings?
Are these the loosened girdles of the forest deities themselves, resonant with the tinkling of their ornaments;
or are they perhaps rows of bees, sweet with the sound of their humming, feeding upon the flowers?
Could it be that the series of mantra-syllables belonging to her, having performed intense austerities, has attained the power to bestow beloveds,
the immortality of the gods, and even physical form? Or perhaps she has employed that very series of mantras for the purpose of adorning the Blessed One with garlands of jewels?
Why indeed does that swarm of bees hover about, seeking to drink from her?
Then, during the summer,
when the intense heat was oppressive and the interiors of the streets were deserted,
the sun appeared like the moon to two young lovers who found happiness in their conversation with one another.
Like a deer scorched by the rays of the sun who has taken refuge in a thicket,
a virtuous man, when his fortune is exhausted, sinks low as if having reached a pit.
The mountains, scorched by the fierce heat, no longer flow [with water],
just like the hips of aged women now that their youth has passed.
With hands resting on the ripened *udumbara* fruits and even the cuckoos uttering their cries,
the woman seated upon the chest of the elder does not appear to be intent on her purpose.
Just as a tree, having been entered by a fire that has reached its core, is consumed by an internal burning after first performing what appears to be a virtuous act; so too does this [person] burn.
These shadows, like noble women filled with modesty, now enter the interior of the house at the mere touch of the tips of the hands of this great man, the Sun, who is like the Supreme Person.
Now that the sun has reached the meridian out of fear of the unbearable heat and distress,
even the shadow, as if seeking shade, has departed from the foot of the trees.
Upon seeing the multitude of supplicants who had approached him with joy, the surface of the lake belonging to the illustrious Avantivarman burst forth,
as if it were his own heart, from the heat of his compassion.
The forest is empty like me; the waters have become thin like us;
and the days are long and scorching like our sighs.
The thick,
hot, and burning expanse of summer, which brings distress even to noble-born people when it appears before their eyes,
causes suffering upon the earth like wicked men.
Scorched intensely on all sides by the rays of the sun, who increases the nectar [of life], and being burned on the path by the hot sands, the serpent—
moving crookedly with his head cast downward and sighing repeatedly— sits beneath the peacock.
The serpent, whose crest-jewels are pierced by the radiance of the sun, whose breath is licked by his flickering double tongue,
and who is scorched by the heat of the fires of poison and the sun’s glare— even when tormented by thirst, does not kill the family of frogs.
In the vicinity of this earth whose surface is so difficult to traverse, these clouds appear to us like wretched, hopeless men— futile in their efforts and clinging to something unattainable.
Just as my own efforts have resulted in this vast manifestation of fruit and splendor,
so too do these countless rivers reach their full development within their own respective domains.
Having drunk water from a pond that had become tasteless, boiled by the midday sun, and having looked all around at the forest refuge enveloped by a forest fire, Jayavardhana—
Completely hemmed in on all sides by a terrifying heat,
the king, his body reduced to a mere circle of skin and bones, enters his own shadow.
The measure of his nose has been distorted by those dear to him; it has been made to gape wide by lotus stalks; it has been treated harshly even by a friend; and it has been stretched long by thirst.
Fools have attained a heavy fondness for that which is a mine of faults; alas, time has arrived as the age of Kali, for indeed, that season of heat has not yet come.
In the forest of Ratimitra,
where all creepers were scorched, where deer were ever intent on hostility,
where the shoots of the *kṣāmakṣama* tree sprouted, where bees were faintly intoxicated, and where the *kunda* trees bloomed at will;

O traveler, how do you survive as you journey through the summer month when the sun’s heat is intense, the flowing streams are parched, the dust is thick with scorching heat, and the air is searing like flames?
The añjali was made from afar, not because of a desire to drink water;
the hair stood on end continuously out of affection, not from the coolness of the water;
the head was moved in wonder at the sight of his form, not from thirst for relief.
A traveler, having seen a woman guarding a water-station, devised a clever stratagem.
With bodies covered in drops of perspiration, they long for the touch of cool breezes; with mouths parched by excessive thirst, they crave the drinking of clear, cold water;
and with limbs unable to endure the exhaustion of the long journey, they seek rest in the shade.
Why does the fortunate one wander all around Kāśmīra at this time of the summer heat?
These clever water-girls at the temple of Bhaṭṭabāṇa are not merely pouring water from their jars; by blocking it with their fingertips, they extend it into extremely thin streams.
O traveler, you too surely know how to drink water with a hand whose fingers are splayed, slowly biting the lip, while keeping the eyes motionless and gazing upward.

O woman with trembling dark locks, if you desire to go quickly to someone's house, or if you long day after day for your own beloved wife who is at home; ||| Subhv_1712-2 ||| or if you wish to see your own household members; ||| Subhv_1712-1 ||| [then come here].
O brother, even though she is a mere water-girl at a well, avoid her from afar— she whose glances cause travelers to falter, their eyes becoming dazed and sluggish by her beauty.
In the summer heat, when the winds caused the rows of enemy soldiers to collapse with a crashing sound,
and their bodies were scorched by the fierce rays of the sun,
those whose exhaustion was dispelled by the moonlight of the faces of the beloved women imagined upon their minds felt no distress.
Even at midday, travelers go forth with joy, longing for their own country.
Then, the gazelles— whose bodies were moistened with the juice of sandalwood, who wore locks of hair adorned with jasmine flowers slightly opened by the heat,
and whose majesty was exhausted by the scorching rays of the summer sun— [sought refuge].
Once again, it slowly causes her limbs to sprout forth, including even those that were previously hidden.

In this lake, whose waters have become almost entirely mud due to the summer heat, and which possesses but a little water now that the travelers have fled in fear of the cranes, these [cranes] have wallowed about.

Having repeatedly dipped his worn-out tattered rag into the water and squeezed it over his head, the thirsty traveler continues on his way, even after finding water, crying out "Alas! Alas! in his thirst.
O child,
this garland of clouds does not reach so high as to pervade the sky;
why then do you vainly soil your face with streams of tears that fall from the edges of your eyelashes?
A streak of smoke, resembling a multitude of stones from the trunks of rutting elephants that have emerged [from the forest],
has arisen from the forest fire and now defiles the circle of the directions.
"Which parts of Mount Dhārākadamba have been burnt? Which regions remain extremely dense with forest?
Or what portion of the grove still stands?"—thus [he asked], his splendor made manifest by contact with the wind.
The forest fire, with its rows of fierce flames and the laughter of sparks bursting from the knots at the tips of the trees,
seems to gaze upon the dense mountain peak covered in dry grass.
Then, during the rains of Bhīma, having beheld the sky filled with the shimmering glow of lightning flashes at the arrival of the clouds;
Those who live apart from [worldly attachments] have no fear.
The earth shone with the Indragopa insects of the sun’s rays,
as if strewn with the drops of blood flowing from the hearts pierced by the arrows of the Bodiless One (Kāma) for those dwelling in exile.
Heavy with a womb of water filled with dense currents,
a continuous line of thundering clouds settled upon the mountain ridges.
O Vararuci, the glowing,
tawny-hued Indragopaka insects on the earth shine like travelers' wives who have vomited blood and are clinging to life.
The earth was filled with tawny *harigopaka* insects, which, like fallen fruits from a sun-like tree crushed by the blow of a cloud-elephant, were as bright as the sun itself.
Seeing the solar disc covered by untimely clouds,
a pair of *cakravāka* birds cries out, fearing the onset of night.
O cloud, thunder or rain, or discharge your thunderbolts;
men facing their beloveds take no account of cold or heat.
The sky seems to laugh with its flocks of cranes, it seems to dance with their outstretched arms, it seems to weep with streams of rain, appearing like one who has gone mad.
These riches, as fickle as the hearts of women, do not remain for long with those who are like the hollows of clouds, having come to them like prosperity that has reached an unworthy vessel.
Nowadays, everywhere, all water is turbid yet sweet,
just like the artificial and deceitful speech of dishonest people.
These two great men,
accompanied by Indra’s bow [the rainbow], appeared like mountains with clouds clinging to them and waterfalls cascading down;
they shone like rutting elephants draped in blankets of fine wool.
That which was never seen before by us is now being seen: the poison has been drunk by those who bear it as their very nature,
and the wives of travelers have fainted.
For someone,
the quarters were beautifully adorned by the white Kutaja trees,
which, with their dark trunks, appeared like stars descending from the sky whose path was blocked by clouds.
O Venerable Śamavarḍhan,
when the jar of the year was shattered and struck by a flash of lightning from a dark-blue cloud,
drops of water fell as large as clear, released pearls.
Like a blazing fire fanned by winds that have suddenly arisen and intensified its force,
the flaming radiance entered the hearts of the travelers' beloveds in an instant.
When the sky was covered by dark clouds in autumn, as if out of fear of a heavy rain,
the heat of summer seized the hearts of those separated from their lovers.
In the rainy season,
the bow of the Lord of Gods (Indra) is perceived as unstable, possessing many colors, devoid of virtue, and eternally crooked and difficult to grasp—
just like the mind of a young woman.

Travellers are terrified upon seeing a rainbow, which lacks the quality of a firm foundation, is devoid of the excellence of stability, and is merely a collection of vanishing fragments— just as one is alarmed by beholding a wretched desert.
The earth, darkened by the passing of time, was excessively moistened by clouds discharging a continuous stream of water, like the hearts of proud women softened by the departure of their lovers.
Now, Kāma has been inflamed by the beloved Nīlakaṇṭha, who dances with his charming serpent-arms and whose beautiful moon-beams flicker like flames.
With the dust and agitation gone, and the light of the stars obscured by thick layers of clouds,
she is like an aged woman in the rainy season, burdened by the weight of her hanging breasts.
These clouds, composed of smoke, fire, wind, and water, have indeed been fashioned by the Ancient One;
for otherwise, how could they blind, burn, agitate, and strike one down during separation?
Bhaṭṭa Ānandavardhana says:
On the roads, a traveler remembers the playful gestures of his beloved’s fingers as she threatened him, while a bee, trembling, perceives a sprout that is not yet red.
Whose mind is not delighted by the clouds, which possess the grey hue of thick dust and are as restless as children who, having seized the sky, have made it turbid? — Vararuci.
Beholding the quarters of the sky covered by dark clouds— like black dogs following the tracks of a seed-sower—
the white swans, like virtues, have abandoned the world and departed for some unknown place.
A certain traveler gazes at the cloud, dark blue with its fresh burden of water and resembling his own dwelling,
suspecting it to be the rising smoke from the funeral pyre prepared by his beloved.
Above is a dense mass of clouds, the mountains in the distance have peacocks dancing upon them,
and even the earth is white with *kandali* flowers; where, O traveler, can you cast your gaze?
A mass of clouds has appeared above my husband’s head; my beloved is far away—what calamity has befallen me?
On the Himalayas there are divine medicinal herbs, yet the serpent, overcome with rage, has placed them upon his own head!
"My dear friend, for those living abroad, what time indeed is more painful than this?
Thus spoke the wife of the traveler, and the crane replied, "It is the rainy season."
Even at other times, separation from a beloved causes distress;
how much more so on days when the clouds rumble with deep and incessant thunder?
"What is the use of going for those [who remain] if she does not live? And even if my beloved is still breathing, what then?"—
having thus gazed upon the garland of fresh clouds, the traveler does not return to his own home.
Having destroyed the strength of their enemies, pure, and being the cause for the removal of the mud of the world,
those clouds— whose conduct was humble and who were supported by the virtuous— attained equanimity.
Overpowering his friend Mitra through his dark nature, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who has come from a lowly state,
seized the sky with clouds, just as the earth, driven by the wind and covered in dust, is seized by fear of the waters.
Having drunk the pure water from hundreds of rivers, its belly filled with an incessant burden of water,
the ocean, as if experiencing exhaustion born of excessive drinking, sank down upon the mountain slope.
I have created this darkness that obstructs the vision of the world by suppressing the rays of the sun;
yet it is repeatedly destroyed by my playful power, just as a cloud is shattered by the wrathful Indra with his lightning.
With their copper-hued eyes fixed upon the sky and their locks of hair stirred by the fresh breeze,
the wives of travelers shed copious tears for a long time along with the spray from the rain-clouds.
The bee, nestled within the heart of a ketaki flower as enchanting as its fresh awakening,
remained for a long time in happiness with his beloved, having no fear of the arrival of wind or rain.
Even when the forest fire was extinguished by a timely rain and the rows of trees were covered with swarms of bees and dust, the female deer—
though their own luster was equal to that of the embers— did not abandon their fear upon seeing him.
Even these virtues of Kumāradatta, consisting as they do of the essence of Kamalākara’s poetry, sometimes appear like a fault:
that the minds of people were deluded by them, even though they arose from a collection of clouds that dispel the world’s weariness.
When the wind carrying the spray of the Śīśira (winter) season blew swiftly, as if out of fear of the cold,
the god of love entered the hearts of women separated from their lovers like a sacrificial fire fueled by grief.
Then, following the sound of the clouds' kettledrums resounding with the proclamation of the Mind-born One’s conquest of the quarters,
the *kadamba* trees— those who live by him— seemed to don armor under the guise of their intoxicated bees.
