The sky is darkened by clouds as black as the smoke from a soiled fire;
the earth, with its newly sprouted kandaḷa grass, is dark with dense rows of hair-like blades.
Surely that very season, so delightful for amorous play, has arrived.
Death is the refuge in which these [beings] become separated.
In the palace of King Citrāṅgada,
the moonlight shines intensely as it bears the nectar of its beams; yet, in this flickering light of the lightning that flashes again and again,
I think that she— turning her face away out of wretchedness and sleeping before her elders— is weeping with deep, heavy sighs.
O clouds, desist! Why do you discharge this rain in vain? Depart from here toward some other quarter that is pleasing to your heart.
This is not that forest, nor is this the path, nor is it that stone slab,
since it is not filled with the tears shed from the eyes of the slender maiden in her separation.
Having gazed for a long time with bewildered eyes at the sky, which was covered by masses of clouds that had reached the peaks of the mountain ridges and were casting shadows,
the deer-eyed woman then remained still for a moment during her first separation.
By whom the water-offering of departure was given by travelers in this world.
The winds from the *kuṭaja* trees have been smelled; the deep thundering has been heard.
O fool, night after night you have exerted yourself in vain, making your bed upon the empty floor.
You have covered the walls of your house with lines of calculation for counting the days until death.
Indeed, your vital breaths have not departed, nor have you come here.
Having forcibly seized the water of the rivers, having scorched the entire earth,
and having withered every dense forest, even those lords were brought to ruin by their own kṣapaṇas.
Intent on searching for where the warm-rayed sun has now gone,
these clouds wander here in every direction, illuminated by the light of lightning.

The cloud scatters showers of water—showers that are like a mass of snowflakes for those wandering in impurity, and like charcoal for the bodies of women separated from their lovers.
The peacock cries out for someone, the cranes shriek, and the thunderclouds subside without agitation;
the clouds roar, and the flock of cranes wails loudly.

The winds scatter his body, and showers of rain fall before him; having abandoned his beloved during the rainy season, the traveler for whom the singular joy of passion was his only motive now departs.
Even though he knows that his beloved is separated by regions, by the streams of rivers, by mountains,
and by forests, she does not come within the range of his vision even with great effort.

With his neck upturned and his gaze fixed upon the tip of his snout, blocking the earth, and with eyes filled with tears, the traveler nevertheless gazes at her again and again, meditating on something indescribable.
In the *Narasimha-purāṇa*,

some manuscripts have a slightly different reading: "The old, dilapidated, and impoverished houses, once gazed upon by the flocks of peacocks as they flew up, are now shattered by the winds of their sighs."
These drops are falling from the fresh cloud, beginning their heavy downpour;
they are the droplets that have rendered moon-like the faces of separated women lusterless.
For someone, rows of flowering forest trees are being cut down; for someone, serpents are being driven out;
and for someone, the wind is being woven together with the fragrance of blooming *kardama* flowers.
"Alas, what misery! Woe, oh woe! Is there not even one who will silence these clouds for me?
Having heard such lamentations from the wives of travelers, the sky itself seems to weep.
O traveler, no lodging is now given here in this village of Nabhuvaka; O traveler, this youth has fallen asleep at night upon the floor of the monastery’s pavilion.
Then, as the cloud thunders with a deep roar,
the people stand still, remembering their beloveds and fearing that the thunderbolt will fall today just as it did for them.
Having previously heard the sound of thunderclouds, a certain young woman with tremulous eyes, though terrified and clinging firmly to her husband's chest,
embraces him even more tightly.
How indeed will that young woman now behold the row of clouds during our separation— she who, having removed it from my face, fastened it around my own neck?
While Durgasena’s dance was being performed,
where the moonlight flickered like a swarm of bees, the day turned dark as if by a cloud of collyrium,
and the lightning flashed like a streak of crystal amidst the rain of the steady drum-beats.

At the onset of the rainy season, when the winds blow cold with showers and the clouds arrive, the traveler cries out, "Alas, alas! The innocent young bride will surely die! Subhū 1773–3; Subhū 1773–4.
O King, at night, a traveler— distressed by the sound of clouds heavy with rain and shedding tears due to the sorrow of separation from his own wife— sang that song out of such intense longing.
The very mention of his departure was like a thief of life;
the world impetuously offered a handful of water even for his honor.
If the movements of these swans have been captivated by her, let them cry out with longing;
or if the splendor of their plumage has been stolen by her locks of hair, let these peacocks dance.
“May this heat of the scorched-rayed sun take away his beauty;
O clouds, it is not right for you to thunder thus against me who am innocent.”
The cries of someone,
born of separation from you, are equal to the thundering of clouds with their unceasing streams of tears, and to the flickering flames of the fire of grief with their shifting glances.
O Cloud, my friend, having reached the face of my beloved within this interval, our state of union has been completed; why then, O cloud, are you intent on burning me?
The sky is filled with clouds bearing fresh water, the earth by the lightning-vines,
the quarters by torrents, the heavens by rain-showers, the forests by *kuṭaja* flowers, and the rivers by cities.
O you whose life-breath is destroyed by the rainy season, why do you display such false ostentation to kill this single, wretched, and pitiable woman who is distressed by separation?
May the clouds,
heavy with the weight of fresh rain, release their roar with enthusiasm;
may the winds blow, fragrant with the scent of *kadamba* groves, and may the enemies of serpents (peacocks) dance.
O merciless lightning, though our womanhood is equal, why do you flash upon me— who am miserable with a downcast face as I am plunged in the ocean of grief from separation from my beloved?
On the horizon of the sky, the sun, bearing its rays like a staff, stands ready for the attainment of its station;

then, like a cloud of terrible roar, it proceeds with the giving of its light toward the acquisition of that place. Afterwards, as if through the discipline of remorse, it spreads forth the sun with its brilliance.
The moon was surrounded on all sides by stars, like a crane by its young chick with its beak.
The god Jhaṣaketu performs a fire-oblation (*homa*) for the wise Pañcapātajaka upon the hundred-peaked mountain in the sky;
indeed, his thundering is the recitation of mantras intended for the banishment of women separated from their lovers.
In the peaks of the abundant clouds that serve as the crowns of the mountain-like kings, the paths are made white by the god of love;
those very paths bear the graceful appearance of sparks from the fire rising from their friction.
O slender-limbed one, as the onset of the rainy season brings sharpness to the weapons of the god of love like a blacksmith,
so too, amidst the clouds that possess the luster of glowing embers, there stands a blazing crest of fire within them.
Let the winds blow fiercely, let lightning flash, let the clouds thunder,
let the serpents release their harsh cries like the shafts of the God of Love who delights in beholding the clouds;
yet she who, shameless in her separation from the Lord whose life has just departed, continues to live— [may she be spared].
If she were to become attached [to him], she would be destroyed in intellect and become the abode of all calamities.
One cannot go outside from the palace with those dear ones who are as unsubstantial as a dream; for the sake of shivering from the cold, she is embraced tightly with eyes closed in delusion.
With nets of spray, the breezes are cool and dispel the exhaustion of intense passion;
indeed, for the fortunate, even a foul day becomes a beautiful day upon union with their beloved.
O brother cloud, whose throat possesses the splendor of a blue lotus, a tamāla leaf, and collyrium,
and who has draped around your neck a garland as beautiful as Indra’s bow—
thunder at will for a moment; show mercy to her whose eyes are flooded with tears.
A young girl with a body as delicate as a lotus stalk is not able to endure hardship.
O sinful one, previously in the spring season I was scorched by mango sprouts and cuckoos; now, during the rains, I am tormented by your thundering—what else remains for you to do?
Wretched and distressed by the pain of separation from my beloved, my body has become emaciated.
O Cloud, you pour down rain upon the parched earth while life remains as a mere residue.
O traveler, brother to some [of us], be gracious and desist; it is not fitting for you to depart for the Akāṇḍa forest, leaving behind your beloved wife whose face is drenched with tears.
O Householder, when you were away from home, you saw these kinsmen of your beloved coming out to offer water for the deceased, crying out in lamentation as they passed through the village.
"Bhadra, you live in this village of Madraka; you are familiar with it.
Do you know whether any woman on this road—eager for the sound of the clouds—has perished?"

Thus, O traveler, fearing the loss of the remaining days until the end of your journey, you do not go to your own house even though it stands nearby, being preoccupied with asking after the welfare of your beloved.
Bhīma,
having made the sky beautiful with clouds accompanied by thunder, having fashioned a palanquin with elephant tusks, and having covered it with chowries resembling moonbeams—
Having smeared the ground with camphor and musk, he lies there; O Pulinda, you are our beloved, with your arms as a noose for us who are eager for you.
Let the clouds rain down torrents; let the winds of that day blow cold;
yet this beloved, who destroys all fear like a great jewel upon my breast, remains here with me.
Then, for both of them,
there arose a coolness like that of autumn, radiant with bracelets of lotus stalks, which allayed the heat of their grief.
The autumn season is like a longing woman, possessing breasts as firm and pale as sandalwood powder.
The flowing rivers slowly reveal their sandbanks,
like women whose hips are gradually revealed out of shame during a first union.
The breezes are fragrant with the pollen of lotuses, delightful with the scent of *vaṃtīka* flowers,
and as slow-moving as a lover approaching a young bride languid with fresh passion.
At night,
breezes blow that are scented by the fragrance of jasmine flowers from the swaying hair-braids of young women, whose hearts are weary with the fatigue of love-making.
Those who harbored doubts regarding both the lake and the sky— the water and the heavens—
fell into the water like *caṭaka* birds, while the *cakravāka* birds flew into the sky.
Just like fresh butter, the autumn season has now produced an intense heat; having exhausted the abundance of clouds, the sun has made the sky his sole domain.
These two are the white blossoms of the *kavṛddha* tree; the *saptaparṇa* trees have the color of the cream of curd;
the moon resembles fresh butter; and in autumn, the moonlight has the luster of buttermilk.
Then,
when the thick darkness was dispersing and the time for colors had arrived, Gaṇḍoṣapāla brought light to the quarters of the sky,
like the dawn of autumn.
Empty, pale in spirit, silent, and rendered light,
the clouds departed from the quarters of the sky like your defeated enemies, having laid down their bows.
The sky was like water and the water like the sky; the swan was like the moon and the moon like the swan;
the night-lotuses had the appearance of white water-lilies, and the white water-lilies had the appearance of night-lotuses.
Subhūti 1802–2: Essenceless, devoid of merit, crooked, yet endowed with a variegated form, the rainbow soon met its destruction, just like a wicked man.
Whose mind would not have been captivated by the rows of white birds,
beautiful as they were, appearing like the moonstone faces of women at night?
The autumn moon, which had been made turbid within by Śakra’s armor, was cleared by her; likewise,
the sun, its radiance reddened by the intense heat of the ordeal, was restored to its brilliance by her service.
Due to the extreme weight of the burden of its fruit, the *kālāma* tree bowed slowly,
as if wishing to smell the lotus that had emerged nearby.
"Vararuci, [I thought] he who has been nurtured by me since birth and has now attained perfection— where indeed will he go?
As if out of fear of separation from Śāli, he has gone to the fields and waters of the Kṛṣas."
Like anger itself in the form of heat during the summer, or like weeping during the rains,
the autumn brought a serene clarity to the night-maidens of the moon.
The field-ditch, having gradually dried up, became helpful;
out of compassion, the rice plant turned pale and its face appeared withered.
O Vararuci,
having vomited forth all the water of the ocean of milk,
the clouds once again assumed a whiteness like that of cows who have just drunk their fill of milk.
His feet shone in the grove of blue lotuses like the darkened rays of the sun released from the bonds of the clouds, appearing as if stained by the darkness.
The forests and waters of Bāṇa’s realm, with their flowers like eyes and lotuses whose bees were settled within them,
gazed at one another with wonder, as if out of reverence, through the garland of Śrī.
Bhaṭṭasvāmin:
The young crescent of the moon, submerged by the splendor of the reflection in the jewel-lights,
was not pursued further by the royal swan, whose mind was deceived, as if it were a lotus sprout in the waters.
This pair is exceedingly equal for Kumāradatta: on the one hand, the status of being of low birth;
on the other, this [earth], in which the fruit is gathered from the fields and deposited in threshing floors.
Scorched by the autumn sun’s smile and exhausted by the excessive heat,
the great rivers appear as if feverish, fit only for the treatment of fasting.
These two breasts of Jayagupta’s wife,
bearing with their hands a rainbow that shone like a series of moist nail-marks,
surpassed the heat of the sun while pleasing the moon, which is marked by its spot.
The beautiful woman did not wish to touch with her hand a lotus that was like a sharp-thorned staff.
That very same [woman] tore apart the cluster of blue lotuses;
fie on her softness, which is the abode of all insults!
Bearing their blossoming red petals and drawing up their stalks from the waters,
the lotuses shone like ascetics who have cast away all attachment to worldly pleasures.
Then, with a face like the bright moon, clad in white garments, and eyes like the petals of a blue lotus, she approached—
like the Autumn Goddess herself, accompanied by her attendants and a fly-whisk, coming to dwell upon the earth together with the splendor of the lotus.
For that great-souled one, there was no water that did not possess beautiful lotuses; there was no lotus that did not have bees clinging to it;
there was no bee that did not hum its time; and there was no humming that did not captivate the mind.
The teacher said with hesitation: "The blue lotus is the opposite of the eye of Akṣi; that which the maiden, the protector of Kāla, wears."
Furthermore, that very same [hostility]—
the firm enmity of those who have attained high status— is directed toward their adversaries, not toward those they have defeated;
the sun burns fiercely like a man of recent wealth when he is in a low position.
The horn sheds its skin as a thankless person abandons a friend;
the water becomes clear like the mind of a sage within;
and the mud dries up like a poor man who falls into debt.
Bhāsa’s [work] has been brought to me by him, who has constantly joined it with a great increase of water and a weighty fruit;
that field of *kāla-māṣa* rice, bowed down by grief as if from excessive anxiety that the sun-maker [the author] might wither away, has turned pale.
In some places rich with crops, in others with blooming beds of lotuses;
in some places with clear waters, and in others with the cries uttered by cranes.
In some places with the expanse of the sky, and in others with the white discs of the moon and stars, oh,
this autumn captivates the hearts of men with its many forms!

Half-asleep at night, his limbs slackened and weary from the exertion of impetuous lovemaking, he awoke on the palace terrace as the unbearable heat of the springtime intoxication subsided; then, with a low moan, he was embraced by the vine-like arms of his beloved, who were relaxed from the fatigue of their union.
The unfortunate man does not drink the autumnal water, which has its flow indistinguishable from moonlight.
For both [of them],
their bellies were filled by the onset of the rainy season;
heavy with the burden as if pregnant, they became unfit for service.
Now these rivers shine forth, stainless and beautiful with bodies as fair as the moon, like women who have given birth, their waters drunk by young cranes crying out.
Śrī Bhogivarman,
having spoken in order to enjoy, does not eat out of the suspicion that the moon’s curved lotus-stalk might be a snake; and,
distressed by the stars appearing as scorpions, he does not drink the thick drops of water situated upon the lotus leaves.

The bee perceives the shadow of the lotuses as a twilight filled with darkness and variegated by swarms of bees; and the cakravāka bird, fearing separation from its beloved, regards even the day as night.
Śrī Śivasvāmin:
Now, the winter season. Subhāṣitāvalī 1827-1: [He is] the beloved of the moon-like face of his beloved, who is exhausted by the heat of the autumn season.
Winter has suddenly arrived, the vassal of the King of Love.
In the expanse of the sky, the stars, shimmering with their flickering luster,
appeared like the fresh sprouts of seeds sown during the rainy season.
As if apprehensive due to reflecting upon the pride of Kandarpa,
the breast of the intoxicating-eyed woman was not touched by the cold [wind].
Thinking, "This is my enemy, the son of Maṅkīra,
the source of my affection," the lotus pond was scorched by the intense heat [of his anger], as if by a thunderbolt.
Even the lotus bed was withered by the sun at midday;
what can even those possessed of brilliance do when the power of time has arrived?
With these moonstones as her teeth white as snow, and the stars as her dim glances, the night—
with its vast darkness doubled— slowly, slowly passes away like an aged woman.
Are there any trees who, having always been naked, enduring the cold, wearing matted hair, and now casting off their leaves and fruits,
have begun ascetic penance out of a longing to attain the bliss-bestowing Mādhava?
"This one that causes trembling is a thief of the cool season; it withers the trees—will it now seize us?
Thinking thus, as if out of fear, the grass on the ground has become parched and turned pale white.
Does he carry away the mass of ashes of those whose nature is scorched by autumnal heat? Or does he purify the moonlight with clouds reduced to the state of winnowed chaff?
Does he vomit forth a cluster of flowers and *sundarī* grass from his throat, having swallowed it entirely?
Does the winter scatter about the heaps of frost?
O Śrībaka,
when you have departed, I shall remember two things during this winter:
water that is cool without effort, and nights equal to the time of sexual union.
Although it is deep, at this moment, as if pained by heavy grief,
the throat of the well is choked with tears at the departure of night.
Even when called by his companions,
even if he has shaken off sleep, and even though he desires to depart, the traveler does not loosen his contraction, saying, "I am coming."— Bāṇaka, verse 1838–1839.

The time has arrived when there is contact with frosty, cool breezes carrying remnants of snow; when flocks of bees are sated by the nectar of blossoming *kunda* flowers; and when women bear the weight of their high, full breasts, tawny with saffron paste.
In a small grass hut at the corner of a field, upon a bed of fresh barley stalks and straw provided with a pillow— this is the *doharā* verse.
He avoids the pair of plowmen who are well-guarded,
yet his essence is marked by the lines formed by the great weight of her breasts.
At the end of the night, on the borders of the barley fields green as parrots belonging to Kamalāyudha,
the female curlews, their sleep suddenly dispelled, shone with the luster of frost.
They produce a lovely sound where the letter *ka* rises up,
and the letter *ra* is broadened by the jar-jar sound from the straightened tube of the throat.
O traveler, are you unacquainted with the flames of the fire of separation from a beloved?
Or is it that you have no beloved? Or perhaps you are devoid of intelligence?
For [here is] this [place], heated by the sun and suffused with the reddish glow of saffron.
At that time, he emerged from his house into a multitude of six-legged bees delighted by the jasmine flowers.
At that time, when the brilliance of the blooming priyaṅgu flowers was intense, when the bees were humming amidst the bursting kunda blossoms,
and when the sky was adorned with a garland of wild mandāra flowers shaken by the wintry winds—
those deer-eyed women whose eyes, moist with frost-like tears, did not remain for even a moment upon our necks; [how could we endure it?]
Truly, this night, which is like the abode of Yama, passes away as if it were the arrival of the morning.
Even for them,
the pearl garlands, their strings snapped, scatter their loosened pearls;
the sandalwood dust, parched by the heat, stings the breasts that have grown weary from their burden.
"Whatever coolness,
gentleness, and equanimity they brought forth, these divine women now abandon it under the guise of frost."
The inhabitants of the earth, adorned with garments as pure and exceedingly white as falling showers of blossoms, perceive the directions as beautiful, radiant with clusters of shimmering pearls,
and bearing the splendor of the circle of the earth.
Do these cloud-like mountains not produce the great winter frost appropriate for the season?
The activity of departure obstructs the falling of frost;
by its vastness, it expands the time for enjoyment as it darkens the atmosphere;
and with cool breezes, it brings about a dense embrace.
This winter brings about some benefit for the young trees.
These [verses] now belong to Śrī Bhartṛsārasvata; next,
for those who delight in words that are not derived from roots, like women, there is the *Śiśira*.
This arrival of winter has come to provide the practice of making the sound "siit."
Even though her anger was not produced by any cause, now that the clouds have arrived,
she firmly embraces her beloved under the pretext of the cold night.

This cold rain falls everywhere upon the poor, threatening them on all sides with the heavy garments of the great man, with embers in the form of the inner chambers of their homes, and with the moaning of their beloveds.
With his two hands folded together, his body bent forward as his nose-string slipped away,
the traveler stands as if painted in a statue, weary from descending into the river.
Behold the majesty of the winter season: even the two breasts, though white as snow and appearing to shrink under the guise of parched skin due to the fear of cold,
have been seized by the waters.
At the beginning of his hands,
feet, face, and so forth, he draws them in, making them turn red; then,
like a tortoise, he withdraws his limbs, which have been made heavy by the cold.
The door of the seed-vessel is closed;
at the side of the house, outside the bed,
a heavy cotton cloth is burning on top.
Does he who possesses such wealth act in this manner toward his wife, who is devoted and full of affection,
while he himself sleeps?
Tearing at her hair,
clouding her eyes, forcibly casting off her garment,
causing a thrill of horripilation to arise, and manifesting a trembling of agitation— thus did she act as she departed.
Repeatedly pressing his lips with loud,
cool sighs, this autumn wind now generally behaves like a lover toward the withered creepers.
Kissing their cheeks adorned with curls, emitting "siṭ" sounds upon their faces;
causing the bristling of the hair on their breasts as they pressed against the bodices covering their heavy bosoms;
making their thighs tremble and causing the silken garments to slip from their broad hips.
The winds blow from the Śīśira mountain, manifesting as the conduct of beloved women who have abandoned their customary behavior.
For someone,
the Creator has at times fashioned the moon— possessing the luster of a fragment of a polished rice grain— to be eternally risen;
yet, for another, He makes its body drip from the impact of the jar-like clouds.
Surely, out of a desire for the welfare of the world, he scatters from all sides this satisfying rain:
beautiful, abundant, and excellent like a shower from a cloudless sky; lovely as the light of the sun, yet more substantial than the heavens upon the earth.

In the fire of the merit of Pañcaśikha, which has long since been extinguished, the traveler— having slept at will during the night upon the trembling body of the village goddess, whose hair is her crest— now finds himself in the first stage of a burning that was previously beyond calculation.
The half of the skull trembles as the aged body decays;
while a wind blows with great force, its sleep is shattered by many cracks, and the curved nose, struck by the frost, moves from one curve to another.
Then, while gathering flowers,
the proud woman was offered blossoms by her beloved, who belonged to a rival clan;
she said nothing at all, but with eyes clouded by tears, she merely traced patterns upon the ground with her foot.
With its clusters of flowers being pecked by parrots and its young sprouts on the branches of the *aśoka* tree,
the grove was seen by the young women to mock their own vigorous shaking of their lower lips and hands as they bit them.
O proud woman, do not exert yourself in vain by shaking your hands that resemble fresh sprouts;
how indeed could this row of bees, having approached with the suspicion that they are a *kalpalatā*, now be terrified?

A certain woman, her mind agitated, struck her beloved on the chest with her high, full breasts, while he was attempting to remove from his eyes the pollen of flowers that had settled there by means of the breath from his mouth.
O Bhaarava,
why does he offer this bud, as if repeatedly mocked by the cries of the cuckoos? O rogue,
by entering that dwelling today, you have given him nothing but a great *kalir* (discord/conflict).

Leaving behind creepers that had shed their flowers, the bees placed their feet upon young women wearing delicate garlands; for those who are attached to noble families, intimacy with the base-minded is not the primary concern.
The beautiful woman, with a breeze carrying the fragrance of flowers, guided her lover toward the peak of passion;
at that moment, she immediately filled both eyes of her rival young woman with the dust of her wrath.
Having first gathered a mass of flowers from the tree-shade where she stood, the deer-eyed woman desired to climb it;
as she reached for the root of the *aśoka* tree with her foot, that very tree blossomed once again because of her.
"Right here on this vine-creeper of celestial pleasure, there is a lovely *mālatī* flower that has not been plucked by another.
Having said this, a certain rogue took the hand of the innocent-eyed girl with his tender sprout-like hand and led her away into seclusion.
These two,
bent low by the weight of clusters of beautiful, full-blown blossoms, are this lovely mango creeper held by the deer-eyed woman;
I suspect that she has used it to fulfill the desire of Kāma, who is intoxicated by the slaughter of those separated from their lovers, serving as a counter-bow to his own flowery shafts.
Even though the spring possesses countless flowers, it gives only five of them to the mind-born god of love for the sake of his arrows;
thus, as if realizing its own worthlessness, the spring’s wealth was seized by the women.
When mud had been produced everywhere by the water of perspiration and the heavy burden of floral pollen,
the God of Love made his dwelling upon the firm and elevated breast-mounds of women.

Then the floods of water attained the state of being beloved by the young women: they brushed aside their garments, disarrayed their locks of hair, clung to their necks, touched their hips, and struck their breasts.
The clusters of lotuses trembled with great agitation as their stalks, covered in thorns, touched the slopes;
they appeared like the bodies of women whose dense throngs of horripilation arise from the embrace of a lover.
Thinking that the saffron tilaka on her heart had been rubbed away by these [fingers] which had found an opening,
the two breasts, closely joined together, did not then allow any space between them for the water.
These rows of bells on Jayavardhana’s waistband,
appearing like moonlight partially veiled by clouds upon the slopes of his own powerful hips,
remain silent as their cords are filled with water.
For those intent on splashing the water with their mouths,
as the spray droplets vie with pearls and rise toward the clouds, even a broken necklace is not noticed by one who is being scorched by the sun.
A certain charming young woman, having gazed upon a lotus leaf shimmering amidst the water,
quickly and agitatedly stretched out her hand as if in a flurry, mistaking it for a pearl.
The fruit of the lake’s asceticism, ripened by the constant winds of the Malaya mountains,
was such that even a woman of no strength embraced its water with her arms as if it were a lover.
Alas! Even though her eyes were closed by the spray of water sent by her lover Saṅkhaka,
she was seized all the more intensely by the pain arising from the unbearable fire of love within her heart.
Shaking her hands, which were like fresh sprouts, as if she had suddenly become agitated by the depth of the milk, the jealous woman—
afflicted by an inexpressible lack of composure caused by the cries of her friends— attained the embrace of her beloved’s lap.

Out of affection, she did not discard the garland—though soiled by water—that her lover had woven and placed upon her full breasts in the presence of his rival; for virtues reside in love, not in the physical object itself.
The faces of the young women, with their locks of hair spreading out as they plunged into the exceedingly turbid waters,
attained a likeness to lotuses hidden by swarms of bees.
As she was being led away by her pair of breasts, which possessed the beauty of the frontal globes of great elephants, the union of the two wheels of the chariot came to an end;
for who, when his own prosperity has been overturned, brings happiness to others?
When the beloved Śyāmā sprinkled her face with water from her hand, Ānanda felt joy;
yet the face of the other woman, though not sprinkled, became bathed in copious sweat born of envy.
"The blue lotus has surpassed even the eyes of beautiful women in its splendor; it is not my own face alone that possesses such luster.
As if singing this with the humming of bees, the great blue lotus danced upon the water whose waves were tossing.
These lotuses have obtained the fruit of their existence through association with the lakes, for they have stolen the beauty of lovely women’s faces;
indeed, it is as if these blue lotuses were the very eyes of those fair-limbed maidens.
Then, as if to test the natural beauty of those lotuses whose feet were the lake's lotus-blossoms,
the waves drew away the red lac-dye from their tender shoots.
These two are the setting of Bilhana’s poetic splendor:
the departure of the hand from the sky [the manuscript] and the loss of light as the autumn has arrived.
Even the sun experiences the state born from the contact with the clouds.
Beholding the union of the sun with the western quarter, which possesses a fragrant crest,
the face of the eastern quarter has been made dark; for women do not endure a rival.
The sun, its rays dissipated, departed as if exhausted, leaving the lotuses scorched and the women separated from their lovers distressed.
What difference is there between a master who does not recognize excellence, who robs one of all splendor,
and who is devoid of discernment, and the darkness?
The sky seems to smear darkness upon my limbs, and it rains down collyrium;
my vision has become fruitless, like service rendered to a wicked man.
In one place the sky is filled with Orion, in another the Kṛttikās are hanging down,
and in another the Śravaṇa is shattered; thus the heavens appear like a hunter's dwelling.
The orb of the sun fell into the ocean, red as the blood of twilight passion;
was it not suddenly the head of the day, severed by the cruel sword of Time?
O Upamanyu,
when the thousand-rayed sun had ascended to the delightful heights and began to redden the eyes [of the world],
the scorching heat departed from the earth, leaving behind the pairs of *cakravāka* birds.

At the end of the day, even the sun, the source of light, assumes a form that is like the ripening of poison; who else here would not undergo a transformation when his body is surrounded by such terrors?
It was not fitting for me to abandon my friend, who has cast off all faults, nor to reveal my inner state;
yet, having thus disregarded him at that time, I closed my heart like a lotus.
Having abandoned a friend who was free from malice and devoid of pride, yet whose greatness was not recognized through his own disposition—
by such a vast sky, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) was revealed with extreme clarity.
As Jayamādhava approaches,
the sun sets quickly as if out of fear, gazed upon by playful women afflicted by love and eager for their tryst,
their lips quivering.
Then the king of men, whose splendor was irreproachable and who had cast far away death for the sake of his people,
reached his end as if to teach this very lesson: that every thing subject to birth must inevitably perish, just like myself.
When the sun has set, the lotus closes its petals; well done by the lotus!
For even after seeing the entire world with her eyes, the fruit for those eyes is merely the sight of one who is dear.
Thinking, "May we not suddenly see this sun— the benefactor of Pāṇini and our dear kinsman— falling down,
deprived of his rays," the lotus-eyes of the wives of the Nalina-lake were closed, as it were.

Whether pure or turbid, stable or moving, and endowed with qualities of crookedness or straightforwardness—all of this is rendered uniform by darkness; such is the "greatness of intellect" of the ignorant, which destroys all distinction.
Some declared that when the day was exhausted, the fierce-rayed sun entered the ocean; others spoke of his departure to another world,
while some described his union with fire.
O dear friend, it is false that this sun is without a witness;
for I believe the sun presides over the hearts of travelers who find delight on the road, even as its heat is intensely manifest before our eyes.
Like the sun,
who, though assailed by great floods of darkness, remains undeluded in mind even in the face of fear, and who,
stationed in every house with the light of his lamp, shatters the body into many fragments; so too does Indulekhā [shine].
When the sun is eclipsed by the splendor of the Buddha, the Blessed One illuminating the worlds with his own majesty, even the sun becomes destitute of light.
Oh, how fleeting is prosperity! Oh, how great is the power of the Mānava! Indeed, all ten directions are touched when fortune undergoes its reversal.
For this lord of light, having scorched the worlds with his intense brilliance, has gone to his setting; indeed,
the splendors acquired merely through one's own prowess do not endure for long in those who scorch others.
The sun,
by whose spreading rays the darkness of Saṃkāragaṇa was utterly destroyed so that it did not remain even at the ends of the quarters—
he, that very sun, is now overcome by darkness; whom do calamities not touch through the power of time?
The pair of cakravāka birds, languid with passion, carry a pair of lotus stalks placed between their two beaks; these stalks,
resembling the pins of a door that has been excessively jammed together, appear as if they were a barrier erected out of fear of separation.
"O lotus-eyed one, since I have departed, this is the time for me to awaken her from sleep;
as if to reassure the lotus-lake, the sun places his rays upon the summit of the setting mountain."

At dawn, the celestial splendor appeared like the orb of the sun resting upon the peak of the mountain of sunrise; and at evening, it was seen as the full moon rising from the crest of the eastern mountain; thus, by day and night, the sky was adorned as if by two bronze cymbals held in the hands of Hara during the performance of the twilight rites.
While the quarters were obscured by this moon whose beauty was clearly manifest, we passed the night in a happiness so subtle that it remained unnoticed;
meanwhile, the women going to meet their lovers bore up against the darkness for a long time with their heads, lovely with the tight binding of their braided hair, as if out of love.
Having been entreated with palms joined like unopened lotus buds, how has that Aśumālin now departed after being dismissed?
Thus, as if with the humming of bees trapped within her, the lotus pond slept through the night in a deep slumber.
The rays of the sun approached the eight surrounding mountains, wondering whether they were the hot-rayed one or the risen cool-rayed moon;
meanwhile, like scouts dispatched by the darkness of night, the flickering shadows moved for a long time across the grounds where he had walked.
At the close of day, the houses attained a state of embrace by means of lamps whose flickering crests were blackened with soot;
these lamps, glowing with affectionate persistence and possessing hands of crimson hue, seemed like the twilight children who have come to hold them in their laps.

These [birds] of the jewel-mine tremble, wander, weep, and fall into a swoon; they gaze at their beloved, cry out most piteously. For when the sun has set, the female cakravāka bird thinks: "Alas! Even in life, separation from one's beloved is death."
“May my beloved, who has come from afar, reach the end of this unbearable separation by embracing me most intensely while I am filled with longing”—
having reflected thus, the Blessed One, the sole kinsman of the three worlds, departed as if out of compassion.
With one eye, reddened by the *pāṭala* flower and matured by age, she perceives the sun as being situated in the west; with her other eye, pale as a water-lily, she sees her own beloved.
At the end of the day, like a bold dancer, the female ruddy goose—fearing separation from her mate—manifests two blended emotions.
While the sun,
glowing like the flame of a sacrificial oblation, stands upon the peak of the western mountain, the bee, thirsting for nectar, enters the lotus; meanwhile,
the person seeking wealth does not notice the obstruction within it— the twilight— and, thirsting solely for the fruit, he does not consider the impending loss.
Viṣṇuśarman perceives the moon as equal to glowing coals, sees a blooming flower as a firebrand, and beholds a lotus stalk as fire; he regards the host of planets as being like sparks from that fire.
Even at night, when it is cool, Cakrāhva is tormented by water;
for those whose minds are scorched by the pain of separation from their beloveds, the world generally takes on the singular form of fire.
The one called Cakra, though struck in the heart by an arrow, did not give up his life for a long time; being devoted solely to the meditation on the bliss of union with his beloved,
he beheld his own reflection in the water and, perceiving it to be his dear one, [continued to live].
O brother, having failed to inform him of that [news] upon his departure, he has now died in misery.
Distressed,
he gazes repeatedly at the orb of the sun and cries out;
with his beak, he repeatedly wipes the eyes of his companion standing before him, who is sluggish in her efforts due to grief.
The sun will set; this Āditya, who agitates the mind at his rising, does not find happiness even by day, like a cakravāka bird. Fie on those afflicted by desire!

At the time of sunset, the bird named Cakravāka—whose orb is already turning crimson out of compassion—performs various actions with a distracted mind: it flaps its wings, falls upon the earth, scratches its breast with its claws, and gazes repeatedly at its mate with upturned eyes while meditating on her.
By these acts, the sun does not set.
When fate has turned adverse, even great effort becomes fruitless;
the thousand rays of the sun were not enough to prevent its own descent.

The western quarter, her abode the sky, banished from the dwelling of the heavens the sun— who, though possessing a body that brings joy to the eyes and is full of affection, was now devoid of wealth (light).
When their radiant lord had departed for the next world, his exceedingly pure rays entered the fire;
for otherwise, how could that very same husband be easily found again in another birth?
When the orb of the sun has set, the sky shines with a light that cannot be discerned and is not seen;
when the clamor of people has ceased, the darkness shines forth. Indeed, even in the absence of qualities, the very lack of qualities becomes a quality for one who is devoid of faults.
Even on a day when the sun’s rays have ceased, he did not succumb to the pervasive darkness;
for even the light of the minor planets, though naturally bright, becomes dim when resting upon a dark source.
The night of Māgha is the time for the Kirāta; the clear lotuses are the slain deer; the two days are the hunter’s arrows;
its twilight is the beautiful stream of blood; and the stars are the pearls from the frontal globes of elephants.
This day, acting as a companion to the crow-colored [sun], like an enemy of the king, falls into the western ocean with its head severed—the orb of the sun.

what is this unprecedented stream of water that is seen by you?
For it pierces hearts with its very virtues, and not with arrows.

This Lord of the Night, standing before you with his hands raised as if to hiss, has had the entirety of his splendor stolen away by your words; he now rests upon the peak of the Sunrise Mountain.

take this moon— who consists of digits— from elsewhere for the purpose of measuring the moments;

O Mañjūṣā, on which mountain peak, for how long, and by what name did that ascetic perform his penance,

O lady with tremulous, long eyes, since this ocean of water— this very sea— does not attain even the slightest beauty when your smiling face, now filling the quarters of the sky with its loveliness, is present, I consider it to be clearly evident.

One who is proud cannot endure being insulted by another when there is a ground for pride.
This weight of your breasts causes exhaustion to both [shoulders]; why then is there this additional burden of a necklace upon your waist?

You are already adorned by your own limbs; why do you carry ornaments that only lead to suffering?
Be gracious; let the swan of those who have abandoned their refuge go happily.
Let a smile be released, radiant with the luster of a kunda flower. Close your eyes, and let the blue lotus on your ear become captivating.
Cover your face with your hand; let the rising of the moon shine forth.
At the rising of the moon, she was silent; in separation, she was pale; even in playful jests, her speech was charming;

I know that her slender body was rippled with waves of anger against some other man, yet by him I was embraced; my breasts were touched without restraint, and even the necklace was placed upon his side.
O friend, I remember only this much:
that which follows from it is the supreme destruction of my fortitude, equal to the dissolution of the body; even after reflecting upon it, I do not know what else it may be.
When one is overcome by fainting, the eyes do not perceive; the body is scorched by heat;
trembling seems to announce the departure of life; and the mind sinks into delusion—this occurs due to powerful past karma accumulated in previous births, or by Time, or by Desire.
Who knows by whom this serpent, which robs me of my composure, has been placed upon my neck?
These two [verses] are by Kṣemendra.
Now, at the break of dawn:
Then, his body adorned by the shimmering rays of the dawn, the Moon—*Subhāṣitaratnakośa* 2153–1.
He assumed the pale whiteness of the cheeks of women who were longing for him yet restrained by their vow of celibacy.
As I gazed upon the moonlight,
which was like a woman who had stolen away the veil of darkness from my heart, the moon reached a state of shadowlessness at dawn,
as if by the rays of the sun— so said the sage Bhagavān Vālmīki.
As long as merit kisses the beauty of the moon’s splendor,
so long does the shadow of the dark spot remain hidden once its lord has arrived.
The row of stars,
like a stream of tears shed by the dark sky separated from its beloved,
gradually vanished from sight as it was wiped away by the hand of its young friend, the moon.
When all prostrations have become futile, the moon, possessing cool rays and a full orb,
supports the night as it desires to depart toward the edge of the sky.
The sandalwood paste on her bimba-like lips was rubbed away by her rival’s collyrium, and the thick mascara was smeared;
yet at dawn, though angry, the fawn-eyed woman was satisfied with her guilty lover.
As soon as she had approached me, that chaste lady, adorned with ornaments of frost, vanished like a vision;
and the sun, with its unceasing rays, swiftly scattered her various star-like jewels.
At dawn,
as the night hurriedly led away the moon— her paramour, soiled like an unfaithful mistress— from before the sun, her anklets, resembling lovely *kalahaṃsa* birds, resounded sweetly.
The young women wear upon their breasts a fresh, shimmering circle of cloth that reveals the curve of their shoulders;
this ornament of their garments makes their natural beauty even more radiant.
If this young woman, dwelling between the arms of her beloved, has performed some service for the venerable Kumāra,
then let the bride be restrained by her voice in the presence of her elders, as if she were a *śārikā* bird.
When the sun, whose rays are like a spread-out cord of light, rises for someone, and the moon, the storehouse of cold, goes to its setting,
this mountain bears the grace of the Lord of Elephants encircled by his two long, dangling tusks.
Ghaṇṭāmāgha’s form was shaken by the morning breeze, like a lotus stalk upon the bank of the Kumudvatī; yet,
like an angry and proud lotus plant, she did not tolerate union with another, even though the bee was devoid of hope.
O Blessed One,

what is the use of ornaments fashioned from gold, or of collyrium and other pigments applied as special decorations? Are not the moist nail-marks, glowing with the hue of saffron, the true adornments upon the limbs of playful women?
This cool-rayed moon,

with its mass of rays, opens the swarm of bees from the lotus-pool as if it were the seed of darkness, which had been hidden within the lotuses for the sake of being sown by the cowherd-woman who was traveling to the assembly of this bull among kings.
Moving slowly around the region of their udders, stumbling slightly at the center where the bells were clearly sounding,
and obstructed by the broad expanse of their heavy hips, these horses— whose fatigue from the passion of lovemaking with their mates had been dispelled—
neighed repeatedly as they sought their fodder in every direction, their sleep having long since departed.
Moreover, this sweet-voiced copper-beaked bird, being heard by those filled with desire, warbles most melodiously.
For both [the sun and the moon],
the stars— casting the shadow of their faces like ripe pomegranate seeds—
now slightly sprout the rays that are the very life-breath of the rows of lotuses.
The moon, bearing this orb which is round like a shuttle woven from the threads of the night, kisses the western mountain as it rises from the expanse of the sky at dawn, radiant with its first rays.
O enemy of Mura,
at that very moment the night-lotuses closed, and alas, even the night— bereft of its stars—
came to an end.
Thus, brooding over his beloved wife,
the moon bears a body that is like a corpse, its beauty vanished as if in grief.
You hide your limbs marked by fresh nail-scratches with your fine garment;
you repeatedly cover with your hand your lip bitten by teeth;
and you spread about in every direction the marks of contact with other women.
Tell me, by what can a fragrant scent be prevented?
Thinking of the events of the night as they were known to her friends, she said many things before him, "I was indeed intoxicated," and she even acted out four [verses] for that master of poetry.
On a day when intoxication has vanished, the innocent bride is filled with bashfulness.
Having gazed with curiosity all night long at the impassioned lovers engaged in their ever-delightful and fresh amorous sports,
this palace has its abundance of light rendered indistinct.
The flame of the lamp flickers like an eye heavy with sleep.
Casting their rays even more swiftly upon the mountain of the branches, they produce deep sounds like the ocean; these [beings],
like hosts of gods, act to extract the essence, as if from the moon.
The cowherds milked the cows, which were as heavy with udders as the ocean at the time of the new moon.

Having failed to follow his advances, the woman— who was feigning sleep and turned away— somehow turned over in her sleep at that moment upon hearing the cry of an owl, though she remained truly blinded by slumber.
With eyes half-closed, she embraces her lord of life.
With his neck-loin cloth loosened and his eyes closed,
having experienced for a moment that dream while still standing upright,
he desires once more to sport with her as she lies before him with her hair disheveled.
A horse with nostrils that quiver and twitch, its lips moving restlessly.
That moon which, upon meeting me, attains a radiance of rising joy— were it not better that he fall? Having gone elsewhere,
he now appears as a mere luster, like the glow of a smile, instantly eclipsed by the brilliance of her presence.
This beautiful radiance flashes forth from the woman in the eastern quarter.
Bearing a single,
partially severed head with its face bathed in water, and possessing another head of great sages whose flesh was still quivering, he bore a clear sound as it was sung by a multitude of sages.
A state equal in form to that of the white water-lily and the lotus.

The gentle breeze blew, blinding the swarms of bees with the fragrance of blooming lotuses; it was perfumed with sweet nectar and was skilled at dispelling the sweat born of the exhaustion from the impetuous amorous play of men unrestrained by youth and intoxicated by passion.
Having kept watch throughout the night with a beauty even more radiant than that of a grove of fresh white water-lilies due to his dalliance with laughter,
this moon now casts himself upon the lap of the western mountain with drooping hands, like one exhausted from sleep, his pale form languid.
As long as the female cakravāka bird, distressed by separation, remains on her wing, she beholds the sky free from the darkness of gloom;
and as long as she is driven by longing, summoned by the sound of chariot wheels, she has come from the farthest reaches of the western shore.
O noble one, you have spoken the truth when you say that "mine" is what is dear; for this fine garment, worn by a beloved person, should not leave my dwelling.
Indeed, the beauty of an ornament for lovers becomes fruitful only through the sight of the beloved.
When her husband, his limbs relaxed after embracing her with a necklace of heavy pearls that had snapped, asked for leave to depart,
the pair of breasts of the frail woman seemed to weep at that moment, as large drops of fresh tears like pearls fell from them.

Having studied the *Sāman* chants according to the prescribed rules, those preeminent Adhvaryu priests— whose darkness of past sins had been destroyed by their teachers— performed the oblations for those who had taken refuge in the stars, the moon, fire,
and the consecrated sacrificial fires.
The sacrificial fire, consisting of oblations, is well-prepared for the ritual.
Drawn from all directions by rays of light whose forms were like wide,
outstretched leather thongs, he was being led forth like a great jar amidst the tumultuous clamor of cuckoos and *kalaviṅka* birds uttering their cries.
The sun is drawn out from the midst of the waters of the ocean.
Having sat down for a moment with one foot upon the ground,
and having looked at the world with great affection and supreme reverence,
he will survey the entire surface of the earth.
The sun has risen from the peak of the mountain that supports the earth.
Resounding upon the very peak of the mountain of sunrise,
he was gazed upon by the lotus-ponds with the smiles of their lotus-faces,
while the birds warbled as his outstretched and gentle fingertips touched them.
The young sun falls effortlessly from the lap of the sky.
The lily grove loses its splendor, the cluster of lotuses abandons its beauty,
the nightingale loses its joy, and the ruddy goose loses its delight;
the Lord of Day rises, and the cool-rayed moon sets.
For the ripening of those who delight in forbidden practices is indeed manifold.
Having risen again before the sun, the abode of cool rays, as if to take the hand of the quarters in marriage,
that moon has now approached very swiftly from the western horizon, trailing his rays like a humble husband.
Having brought about the dissolution of the entire mass of stars in an instant, and possessing a splendor that surpasses even the goddess Śrī while maintaining his passionate glow,
this one radiant Lord alone presides at the end of the night-like cosmic age, like the sweet-natured Madhupuruṣa (Viṣṇu) over the ocean of the sky.
As Māgha was departing from the palace of Rati, he observed that the night was nearly spent;
though she had repeatedly offered him deep embraces and kisses, she remained unsatisfied.
Placing one foot upon the ground and resting the other upon the couch,
the slender-limbed woman, her body turned sideways, long kissed her beloved.
The eastern quarter,
the queen of Hari, bears a smiling face because she beholds the moon— the lord of the stars— approaching her; he who,
by the gradual descent of the mass of his rays upon her shoulders, has stripped her of her garment of darkness, and who, through the grace of his presence, appears as if looking at her own face.
With clear drops of water from the tips of young *kuśa* grass—
collected in the sequence of dew-drops, frost, and rain during the night’s chill—
a man skilled in hollowing out bamboo whistles [produces sound] by mixing them with the tips of pure reed-shoots.
Having reached a certain state, they disregarded even those who had attained the fruit of liberation.
The stars in the sky are raised aloft to serve as clear, stainless dots upon the letter *a* of the word *arka* (the sun), which is the beloved of the sun’s radiance;
they have been drawn upward by the high-pitched *udātta* accent in the arrangement of the musical notes.
The moonlight from the orb of the moon at dawn is like the light of the morning sun.
Upon seeing you, the lily wanders in delusion, as if its own eyes were covered; Nala remains far away, and the moon, the lord of stars, has its vigor destroyed—
just as Rāvaṇa did to the illusory wife of the Lord of the Raghus.
The sun, with its rays, destroys the night that seizes the hair of the darkness.
The host of planets enters the sky— the couch for the play of the celestial couples— bearing a mass of beauty from the portions of flower-garlands shaken off during their amorous dalliance; yet,
being gluttonous with its exceedingly soft rays, it swallows them up like heaps of cotton wool.
The moon does not remove the affliction caused by the application of a boil-ointment.
The rays of the sun now constantly adorn the vicinity of those whose forms manifest as the four Vedas and their thousand branches;
for from the cavities of their mouths rises that [Vedic sound] which is the very essence of sacred study.
On that very path, there arose an echo consisting of the words of sacred revelation.
Here, observing the hawk’s flight as it ranges through the sky— acting as a bird that dispels the dark specks of gloom with its great brilliance— the moon,
out of fear of the sun’s scorching rays, has reached the very last quarter of the night.
Because of the attainment of that, he rose up from the waters with his arms extended.
Having first offered the guest-water (arghya) with stars that were unbroken and firm,
yet made variegated by the rows of mountain ridges covered in dense darkness,
the sky then extended hospitality to the rays of the sun through its own wandering clouds.
He emits [the breath] through the sixteen channels consisting of the veins of the head, which are filled with water and flour.

Is the preceptor of the sons of Diti not capable of depriving even the Asuras— who have met with calamity arising from the Sun— of their lives, like straw? He recites the *mṛtajīvinī* spell, consisting of knowledge, upon the throat of Luṭhantī.
If he does not fall into the fear of violating his vow of silence during the twilight hours.
Just as the rows of birds in the sky are now [awakened] by the mango blossoms,
so too has the lotus in this lake emerged from its seal of sleep, with the nectar of her lips—
obtained from the face of the bride— dripping into its center at every interval.
The honeybee drinks the sweet nectar from the lotuses.
The quarters of the sky appear pale due to the departure of darkness,
with their stars grown thin; yet, what lake is not raised up by the laughter of lotuses, as it were,
through the bearing of the stream of light that destroys the gloom gathered in its depths?
The peak of the sky turns blue by its own masses of splendor.
In this world, those two who, like a pair of cakravāka birds, having reached the further shore of the ocean of passion, repeatedly enjoy each other after parting—
since their appetite for food and drink always arises from nectar alone, the powerful Lord Śambhu, the master of the nectar-eaters, consumed poison.
Does the people, blinded by the darkness [of night] due to eyes composed of their own buds, falsely accuse the moon of being unobservant toward the night-lily because she does not look at the sun?
As for those wives of the king who are merely the products of a poet’s imagination—listen, listen!—they are indeed not destined to be "unseen by the sun."
The rays of the sun, the lord of light, which move along the edges of the lakes, have become like young princes who, praised by their enemies, possess the splendor of a multitude of bumblebees;
these bees, greedy to seize the beauty of the swarms of bees, are agitated by the joy of the fragrance of the lotuses.
When her husband, the sun, had departed and the time for the subsiding of the day arrived, she, full of passion, was ablaze with a fire that did not consume her.
Having been forcibly drawn up from the lower world by the charioteer, she has attained the city of the Lord of the Immortals; thus, she truly embodies the form of a faithful wife.
This account told by wise men is indeed true: the dark complexion of the son’s body was, it is said, born from the food of his father, Śitikaṇṭha (Śiva), who is the color of a dark cloud;
for even from the body of the Sun, which possesses a stainless luster, darkness was produced by the waters of the rivers Saṃnaya and Yamunā flowing from his limbs.
The moon, seeking to destroy the state of the lotus-born Brahmā, drinks it up with its rays;

he who causes the disappearance of the multitude of stars and the conch-shell, now acts as a saw that cuts through the conch-like neck of the lover of the night, by means of half-closing his eight eyes, thereby turning his orb into the likeness of a wooden plank.
The sun, like the day itself, having used the rays of the gods as his own beams, stripped away the darkness from the crowns of the mountains;
thereafter, the surface of the earth shone all around with masses of hair-like shadows, which, being eager to fly away, certainly appeared dark due to the guise of their respective reflections.
Although she was previously freed from her husband by the moon, and although she laughed at the lotus plant— the wife of the sun—
the night-lily now contracts both out of fear of him and, as it were, out of anger toward the rays of Aruṇa, the charioteer of the sun, as he rises.
That which awakens the eyes of the lotuses when the sun rises,
and with which Hari filled his thousand lotus-eyes—
therein lies a true kinship between the lotuses and the eyes.
The poets regard the eyes of others as being like lotuses, yet they hold their own roots to be superior.
These [verses] are by Śrī Naiṣadhakāra:
"When, at night, in secret, lovers devoid of restraint act with passion toward one another, their conduct is filled with longing for the attainment of the pleasure they desire."
Then, his face meeting with Ānanda’s, having somehow remembered it before his teachers,
he remained for a moment, his pupils meeting slowly as they were restrained by the breaking out of a smile.
"O dear friends, today at night, out of passion, you have provided excellent assistance to me as I exhausted myself in amorous play," the beloved says to her friends in front of her.
Displaying a slight semblance of anger, the slender woman offered a smile hesitant with shame,
her face raised as she blocked it with the tip of her finger playfully flicked upward.
When the Mallaka couple were conversing at night within their home, the house-spirit uttered certain words;
as he repeated them in the presence of his elders in the morning, the bride was overcome with extreme shame.
Having placed a fragment of ruby, held in her beak, into the hollow of her lotus-like mouth,
she who is afflicted by modesty effects a verbal entreaty under the pretext of offering a gift of food.
On the forehead of a certain woman, there is a decorative mark (lakṣālakṣma) on both sides; on her neck, the impression of an armlet;
on her face, the blackness of collyrium; and in her eyes, the deep red hue of the *tāmbūla* leaf.
O you who cause my heart to tremble with anger, having seen this ornament upon your beloved for so long this morning,
the deer’s sighs have come to an end within his playfully copper-hued belly.
To that certain Daśanātha, who is like a flame, whose moon-like splendor is being consumed by the remaining [flames],
and who has fashioned this circle with the stars as its flowers— [salutations] to him, the fierce-rayed one.
"Ah, in order to bring about such a state [of darkness], at the very onset of night,
the one called 'Time' (Kāla) slowly causes it to rise, like a blacksmith [blowing on his bellows]."
Like virtuous people scattered here and there during the Kali age, the stars became sparse;
like the mind of a sage, the sky became serene everywhere.
And darkness departs from the mind, just as a wicked person leaves those who are virtuous;
night quickly vanishes, like prosperity from those who are indolent.
The eastern quarter became tawny like the Lord of Liquors (Fire) after casting forth its golden luster; the moon lost its radiance like a wise man in the assembly of the vulgar;
and the stars were extinguished in an instant like kings intent on idleness.
The lamps do not shine, like the virtues of those devoid of wealth.
The ruby-red glow of the eastern quarter has released the seal of contraction from the circle of lotuses;
the lily-thicket is drowsy, and in the lake, the female crane and the female swan are warbling.
While the attendants speak thus, her eyes are slightly opened as she awakens.
The earth, the earth, having been separated [from him], again suddenly embraces her lord of life.
These bees,

released from the interior of the lotus and freed from the bond of their beloved’s two arms, seem as if they have finally emerged after a long time from the womb of the quarters of the gods, having given birth to the sun, the son of Uḍuḍāmarā.
When the night, agitated by the throbbing of separation from the moon, has somehow reached its end,
and the beloved is beheld, she bestows such joy upon the birds separated from their mates that they cannot contain it.
Just as the moon, about to set behind the western mountain, with its rays scattering like fresh blossoms,
clearly brings about for its enemies a greater rise of misfortune than even its own splendor brings them joy— so too does one's own prosperity.
May the thick sound of the morning musical instruments, which shatters the pride of beautiful women toward their husbands,
bestows eloquence upon the city pigeons in the palaces, and confers the poetic gift of intuition (*pratibhā*) upon the poets,
fill the sky as it rises at dawn. It is like a cloud of dust rising from the earth.
By the tinkling of the chains of the excellent female elephants of men, who had not yet arisen from their very slight sleep;
Now, this is the mixed [verse] of Rājaśekhara:
"He who [is not the lover] of her whose brows are lowered by the play of long, dark side-glances..."
Salutations to that king of kings, who was under the sway of Priyāmukha.
O physician, tell me what medicine there is for one who is consumed by the fire of the slender woman’s glance?
It is the embrace of her pathyā leaves, along with a kiss accompanied by the seizing of her hair.
Because she who was beautiful even when angry suddenly becomes appeased without cause,
and because she is herself gracious, the lover bears the shame of his own eyes being unable to look directly at his beloved.
The playful arching of eyebrows with curved ends, glances that are tender yet overcome by amorous gestures, and smiles—
this movement of women, proceeding slowly with grace or coming to rest, is both their ornament and their weapon.
O son of a poet,

here has arrived that remaining heaven, where the beloved Malati— with her jasmine buds opening upon her head, sandalwood paste upon her body, saffron smeared [upon it], and languid with passion— rests upon his chest.
Casting aside stinginess and reflecting upon what ought to be done, let those possessed of wisdom speak this with propriety:
should one serve the hips of mountain ranges, or rather those of women whose eyes smile with passion?

When knowledge has been mastered, when pride has vanished, when wealth has been acquired, and while youth is still in its prime, one should enjoy the hips of playful women; thereafter, for that same purpose, the slopes of the mountains.
O people, I speak the truth; this is the reality throughout all seven worlds:
there is nothing else more captivating than women with shapely hips, nor is there anything else that is such a singular cause of suffering.
When the fire of passion blazes and burns intensely in the hearts of people by their very nature,
what further use is there for those skilled in useless things who even offer the oblations of bad poetry?
For some,
there is honey and the shoulder of a blooming lotus, and palace rooftops made verdant by the spray of moonbeams;
and women whose charms are stirred by passion— these are the fruits of wealth, while other forms of power are quite different.
O fool, traveler!
When the young and weak daughter of Menṭha was alone, so too am I; and the master of our house has gone abroad.
To whom can this poor girl here beg for shelter? Indeed, my mother-in-law is blind and deaf. O fool, traveler!
O Rudra,
how can there be any attachment for those whose lotus-faces remain bowed low with the weight of modesty, their glances slow and restrained,
toward the mouths of courtesans whose lips have been tasted by many men?
A smile slightly charming, a power of gaze tremulous and sweet; a movement of speech savory with novel and playful expressions;
a commencement of gaits accompanied by an emerging grace.
O King of Deer, what indeed in the forest is not delightful to one who is tranquil?

The intense scrutiny of each other’s faces, the sending of messengers by both, the joy and the serenity born from the thought, “Today or tomorrow there will be a reunion,” and the impulsive kissing and embracing even when the reunion has already occurred— [all these are the fruits of love].
For one who desires that, the fruit is that very same pleasure; it is esteemed even by the learned and the simple alike.

A maiden seeks union out of mere curiosity; a widow, for the sake of mere physical relief; a courtesan, according to the whims of her heart; and a housewife, because there is no other alternative. Thus, due to the influence of various causes, women desire union with men in these many ways.
"Another's wife, bound by pure affection, is obtained through supreme merits."

Bowing aside in a corner of the house, she appeared different from her usual self even while facing her husband; "Quickly prepare [the meal], daughter! Let her go to another dwelling on this auspicious day," so the mother-in-law urged the bride many times, as if in great agitation.
Seeing a traveler, she, with a smiling face, broke off half-cooked rice.
Where is the cloud, and where is the peacock with its shimmering plumage and fanning tail-feathers?
Where is the moon’s orb, pure with its lattice of rays, and where is a wave of the ocean?
Where is the rising young sun, and where is the lotus crowded with rows of intoxicated bees?
Whoever is desired by another, that person brings them mental happiness even from afar.
Even for those [poets],
she remains unassailable; though assailed by the bodiless god of love, she seems to shrink away from his impetuousness— she, whose mind is weary of the cleverness of Acaṇḍavaṭu’s compositions.
When one engaged in sexual union does not know internally, "Who is this?
or "Who am I?", then the enjoyer is the beloved and that very act is the enjoyment; otherwise, they are merely husband and wife.
First, my mind was filled with longing for the virtues of the future;
then it became distressed; thereafter, its exertion slackened and its fortitude vanished once more. (Amaruka 22)

Then follows the delightful conduct of a noble woman, characterized by unrestrained intimacy filled with the intensity of love and moistened by passion, and yielding a supreme pleasure through the uninhibited contact of her limbs.
One who has a body as tender as the interior of a white water-lily should not consume these: fresh clarified butter, milk, snow, black rice,
fresh meat, red saffron, mārūka, turuṣī, grapes,
wood-apple, honey, and *kīrī*.
I believe that for that person living in Kaśmīra, there is a drought upon his own face.

On the Himalayas— the most enduring of places, where the surfaces of the rocks are washed by the Ganges, where trees grow upon the shoulders of Śiva’s bull, and where caves are inhabited by perfected beings (*siddhas*)—
what honorable and wise person would perform an act of bowing down to another, which is soiled by servility?
If women were not like the eyes of a startled doe, they would not be the arrows of the God of Love.

In this essence-less saṃsāra, which is like the gateway to the palace of a wicked king, how could those of pure intellect apply their minds to the attachment of service, which destroys all steadfastness—
unless there were these lotus-eyed young women, filled with the mass of rising moonlight, with swaying girdles of bells, and with waists bent under the weight of their breasts?
For as long as one remains on the true path, a person retains mastery over the senses;
for that long he maintains a sense of shame and likewise adheres to discipline.
These blue-jawed birds, born in the paths of the streams and released from the earth by the plow,
fall as arrows of sight upon the hearts of those sporting in the Lilāvati, bringing them steadfast joy.

Mother, here lies my aged grandmother, her life-span entirely exhausted; and here, Father, lies my father, his body weakened by the toil of karma in the ocean of existence, free from all affliction; and likewise, here lies the slave-girl Kumbhī.
In this sinner’s abode, where the breaths of life have lingered for but a few days,
a young woman thus spoke to a traveler under the pretext of describing the dwelling.

O Rudra, for him who strives daily to attain union with you, his two messengers— exhalation and inhalation— are constantly being worn away as they mutually dissolve, while he extends his longing for the perpetual attainment [of you].
How can the happiness of two young people, newly in love, ever equal that which arises when, after a long time,
they finally meet face-to-face following their longing for one another?
The pure smiles of playful charm from his beloved serve as chowries;
her breasts, marked with sandalwood paste, serve as golden jars for the ceremonial sprinkling;
and her hips, possessing the beautiful luster of refined gold, serve as the throne of world-rulers.
This sovereignty consists of victory and defeat; the remainder, however, consists of anxiety.
The deer-eyed woman’s various eye-movements were not acquired by the deer through their vow of dwelling in the forest;
alas, even by the casting of many oblations of gold into the fire, that radiance was never attained due to the passion for its brilliant luster.
These two belong to Kṣemendra: the *Cūtodyāna* (Mango Grove) and the *Sārdūlavikrīḍita* (the "Tiger's Play"), which features fragrant breezes, dark ground covered in lush grass,
and jasmine creepers swaying with the sound of stringed instruments and wine.
In this world of living beings, which is as fickle as a circle of lightning, what else is there but clear moonlight, nights devoid of people, and eyes like fading lotuses?
May the laughter of those who strike down the frontal globes of intoxicated elephants bring auspiciousness!
For who, even with the strength of a single arm, could endure the defeat of another?
He alone is the radiant son of Siṃhikā among the enemies of the gods,
by whom the foes are not conquered except for their heads being severed.
For both [of us],
this is the market where fame is the price for the purchase of a husband;
this delightful time has arrived when celestial nymphs may be chosen by one's own hand.
Many men here, though born of the lineage of Śāṇḍilya, are lame and study the scriptures; rare, however,
are those who can endure the falling of the edge of an enemy’s sword.
O Prince,
on this earth crowded with a multitude of endless and wondrous beings,
if even those who are somewhat clever in the *śāstras* and *aśāstras* are but mediocre; how much more so are those like me?
Behold the difference in magnitude between the heap of refuse that is the world and the greatness of Śeṣa;
upon him, who wears a garland of a thousand hoods, the earth shines like a bee.
"Do not be afraid; these are not swords with the luster of blue lotus petals.
These are the playful glances of the eyes of Lakṣmī, who gazes upon heroes."
Of what use is the age of those born together with light?
Even the rays of the young sun fall upon the heads of kings.
Mount Meru does not have peaks that are too high, nor is the netherworld (rasātala) too deep; for those who possess resolve as their companion, there is no further great ocean beyond.
That the price of a mere fragment of the tooth-relic was less than the value of the earth itself—
that is the manifestation of the splendor whose essence never sets.
May these [misfortunes] not live for anyone; even one consumed by the pain of others' contempt may yet live.
But let there be no birth at all for that man who causes distress to his mother.
Since Rāhu swallows the sun after a long time,
while he swallows the moons at once despite their equal offense, that is clearly the fruit of his gentleness.
It is better for a king to be dust that, having been kicked by the foot of a living being, rises up and settles upon his head,
rather than the dishonor [of being insulted] while remaining at ease.
O Māgha,
these high-minded men do not tolerate the whip-stroke of their own horses, nor the roar of lions, nor being pointed out by the fingers of their enemies.
As long as a man is not deprived of his honor, so long is he honored by Fortune; so long is his fame stable,
and so long does he possess the splendor of a Vidyādhara.
That man’s birth is as useless as the birth of one who, while his own name is already present before him,
does not proceed to another when the fingers are raised for counting.
People do not leap into a blazing mass of ashes out of fear of being burned;
likewise, those possessed of pride do not easily abandon their status out of fear of being overcome.
It is a marvel that these mountains do not bow before Bhārava, who is mighty-armed and holds his bow; for what count is there of mere pebbles among enemies, which are like crows?
The sevenfold earth, the rivers, the oceans, the dry land, the netherworld,
the anthills, and Mount Sumeru— all these belong to the steadfast man who has exerted effort.
These two are the death of Bhartṛhari while he is still alive; for when people see his face,
they break their own faces in laughter and point at him from afar with their fingers.
For one who has been slain while facing the enemy, there is either victory or heaven;
for one who merely enjoys the pleasure of hearing the praise of both armies, there is no such worth.
Even the sun, the maker of day, becomes motionless when touched even slightly by the feet of the blazing Bāṣkala;
what proud man, then, would be able to endure his wrath?
In the vast and stainless sword-blade of Indrasiṃha’s arm, who else could endure the talk of prowess?
For even when his life has departed on the battlefield, that hero still cleaves the solar disc in two.

This is indeed the firm vow of me, the bearer of the *Svastyāyana* and *Sūktas*, as I stand upon my chariot: that the enemies shall not behold the rear of my horses in battle. In wars where fortune is fickle, it is not my vow [to determine] whether victory or defeat shall be by destiny.
"The entire army of Candaka was not slain by me; let there be no service rendered to my master through this body.
As if out of shame at having been struck by the tusks of the rutting elephant, Subhūta sank into the blood."
The chariot of the glorious Sun has but a single wheel; its seven horses are measured by serpents;
its path is without support; it is devoid of a driver, yet there is a charioteer.
The sun travels daily to the farthest limit of the western sky;
the accomplishment of great men’s deeds resides in their inner being, not in external instruments.
For him,
Laṅkā was to be conquered, the ocean was to be crossed on foot,
the enemy was Rāvaṇa, and his allies in the field of battle were the monkeys.
