Likewise, Rāma slew the entire clan of Rākṣasas in battle;
for the success of the great resides in their inner strength, not in external instruments.
The ocean was his birthplace, wild animals were his retinue, the earth was his garment,
dwelling in the forest was his home, and roots and such were his food—
yet Agastya, possessing such qualities, drank the entire sea within the hollow of his lotus-like hand.
The accomplishment of the deeds of the great resides in sentient beings, not in material resources.

The adversary [of love] is Śrīkaṇṭha; the lord of the earth is the minister; the season is Spring; the vassal is the flower-arrowed god; and the target is a woman. Even so, Madana conquers the three worlds, though he is bodiless.
The accomplishment of action by the great resides in the being, not in the instrument.
Even for some, a supramundane conduct bestows a firm standing; for lineage is certainly not the cause of nobility.
The birth from the water-pot of the sage Vāta-api was a mere play, whereas the drinking of the unsealed ocean was his true feat.
"O Earth, be firm; O Serpent, support her; O King of Tortoises, you must bear this weight.
O Elephants of the Quarters, maintain your resolve toward these three! The God [Śiva] is drawing the string of his bow, the weapon of Hara."
O Śūdrakas, flee together in terror; O monkeys, you who have shattered the temples of Indra’s elephant,
these arrows falling upon your bodies cause you supreme shame.
"O Saumitri, stay back; you too are not a fit vessel for my wrath, for am I not Meghanāda?
I shall seek out Rāma, who has bound the ocean with the mere play of his slight fury."
Shall I bring forth the elixir of immortality from the netherworld? Or shall I extract the nectar by squeezing the moon? Or shall I ward off the fierce rays of the sun?
Shall I not rather crush him into atoms, as if he were a mere blade of grass?
This is the speech of Hanumān:
"Those who are generally timid due to their extensive skill in diplomacy and stratagems— [it is said that] for the brave,
resolve alone is the supreme cause for achieving success."
Who are the ministers of the Lion, who finds singular delight in the sole activity of crushing the thrones of his enemies with the thundering roar of his two fangs?
If Rāvaṇa had not abducted the wife of the descendant of Kakutstha,
where would there be the ocean, where the construction of the bridge, and where the crossing and victory over Laṅkā?
If the enemy had not brought about the defeat of Pārtha, where would such asceticism have been?
Those who are full of pride are generally led by their enemies to a state of supreme downfall.
For both [of them], fire can be cooled and frost made to blaze; the wind can be restrained and water solidified;
the sky can be made corporeal and the earth raised up or brought to a state of prostration.
It is said that he alone is a king whose power it is to lift up the earth and to solidify the ocean;
all other monarchs are merely [earth-lords].
The fire of the forest does not cause distress to the venerable Vṛddha by its crackling flames, nor does the ocean suffer from the cool water of the snowy mountain melting away;
for those of profound mind, there is always an experience of equanimity, whether at a time of despair or at a time of joy.
Indeed, on the battlefield of victory, earthly beings abandon their bodies and attain a single celestial orb;
then they reach the fierce solar disc, as well as the desired orbs of the breasts of the wives of the gods, moist with love.

In this state, no pain arises from the thick, coarse, and intense heat within the continuum; nor is there sufficient distress to the vital organs when the life-breaths have moved away from the knots [of the channels]. Nor does one remain with a heart terrified by the wailing of kinsmen.
For this death is not at all a ground for the attainment of happiness, O fortunate one.
Then Kṛṣṇa laughed at those who regarded him with the intellect of cattle, thinking he was merely playing with cows;
"Ah! How devoted to her husband is the goddess Lakṣmī, who has fallen into his side!"
For one who seeks atonement for Amṛtadatta after being struck by the foot of his beloved,
his head should be washed with the wine of the beautiful Gaṇḍūṣasīdhu.
As you are about to cause the lofty tree of Śyāmāka to fall and lift up those that have fallen,
various wonderful manifestations are seen, like those of a creator.
Do the hairs of a tiger's neck commit an offense? Shave [your head] of the afflictions!
What is the use of saffron robes for a mind that is full of passion?
He was adorned with a crown marked by a crest-jewel, wearing a lower garment of fine cloth,
and his inner silken robe shimmered for the sake of a jeweled necklace.
Widows are occupied by heretics; wives of masters are brought to ruin;
courtesans seek out wealthy men; and students are devoted to begging for alms.
Whatever agitation women provoke with the side-glances of their lotus-like eyes and creeper-like eyebrows,
all of that falls only upon those who are free from other attachments— namely, upon their own hips.
At first humble, then arrogant, harsh at the time of business,
but humble again once the task is done— the merchant is like a fishhook.
The *ketakī* flowers are covered with thorns, and the lotuses are born from the mud; those who are devoid of passion possess envy—where, indeed, can there be a jewel free from affliction?
There is no cutting off of the tongue, nor is there fear from the falling of the palate;
one may speak without hesitation—who that is eloquent is not wise?
If there were not the deep caverns of the mouths of preceptors, astrologers, physicians, and Vedic scholars at that time,
where could the deer of corrupt words, terrified by the lion of grammar, roam?
The astrologer calculates in the sky the conjunction of the moon with the constellation Viśākhā;
yet he does not know his own wife, who is occupied with various tasks for her husband.
There is a fault in other women, but none at all in one's own;
for this very reason, among those of noble family, Karasundarī is praised.
The fair and exquisitely expansive vulva of the harlot, shaven clean,
shines like a golden plate struck by the rays of the sun atop Mount Meru.
Having practiced the mastery over the vital winds and explained all the *Sāṃhitās* of the Śaivas,
at the time of death, the vital breaths of the gurus emerged like secret mantras.
"Grain for me! Gold for me! Beans for me!
Beautiful lentils for me!"—thus, alas, making these "mine, mine," he was led away by Kṛtānta like a beast.
What kind of cleverness is there in that rule of one devoid of intelligence,
who did not apply oil to the tusks of elephants while they were still in the elephant-stables?
The tenth planet, the son-in-law (Jāmitra), is always crooked, always cruel, and always a destroyer of honor and wealth;
it is eternally situated in the sign of Virgo.
Yama said: "The earth laughs at the protector of his own body who has accumulated [wealth];
and a woman of wicked character laughs at her husband who is devoted to his sons."
With a single downward-facing fang that discharges venom and semen,
this world has been bitten by the one devoid of fortune, who is difficult to cure.
O one of evil intellect, having obtained the food of others, do not show compassion toward your own life-breaths;
for the food of others is difficult to obtain, as are life-breaths in birth after birth.
Even for a person afflicted by indigestion, food bound with clarified butter is given;
however, a piece of ātīka fruit is a great rarity even when it comes to food.
Greedy for the sake of heaven, fathers entreat their sons;
yet one who would offer his father milk-rice, as well as steamed rice, fried grain, and parched grain—[that son attains the highest state].
She was indeed Pārvatī, not otherwise, and he too was clearly Śiva;
for even while they remained thus united, they were capable of enjoying the delights of sexual union.
He might have been a mountain, or a goat, or even the lord of beasts;
he who, like a master of amorous graces, consumed the flower-armed god of love with his glance.

That which is not joined with the lower opening [of the vulva] by means of the kisses of the betel-bearer’s lips, which are the impressions of service rendered to another, is not equal to that [union].
Even for them,
water is drunk at the watering places, food is eaten even at the almshouses,
they sleep in the temples, and wherever something is obtainable, there they exert themselves.
In the summer season, while a brahmin was fast asleep beneath a tree, a dog urinated in his hand; he said, "Devasya tvā... (the Vedic invocation).
O Lord of Physicians, homage be to you, who have destroyed all diseases;
with the burden now laid upon you, this Kṛtānta (the God of Death) prospers in happiness.
Taking away the wealth of the sick and fleeing even from a deer—this is the physician's true medical skill;
a physician is not the master of life.
“I am suffering from the debility of a burning fever; tell me, physician, what medicine should I take?
“Drink liquor from a bowl! Bring me a skull-cup as well!”

The intentions of these— Māyā’s son, the low-born, those who live by the sword, those who subsist on faith-offerings, and wicked kings— do not succeed; it is because of this that the world is sustained.
Those ascetics who teach others freedom from anger while they themselves are prone to anger;
those who, though destitute, teach the extraction of minerals solely for the sake of wealth.
Who created the *kāyastha*,
having combined the first syllables of "greed" (*kāka*), "restlessness" (*caulya*), "Yama's cruelty" (*yama-krūratva*),
and "the constant killing of one's own father" (*sthāpaternitya-ghātita*)?
Even Yama was deceived by him with that stroke between the letters *na* and *ka*;
even the god [Śiva] fears him, whose weapon is the *kalama* (the bow).
Because of the presence of the fetus in the body and in the womb, the mother fears for her life;
that she does not consume her own intestines is due to the fact that they have not yet been fully developed.
One should not trust a scribe who has committed a crime, nor a clerk;
one might rather trust a black snake or a tiger in the forest.
Devoid of affection, cruel, and a companion in adversity who creates obstacles—like a lentil seed lodged within the body, whose presence in the body can bring peace? To no one.
One with light steps is not a cat; one who carries his own provisions is not an ascetic; one with a staff in hand is not Yama; and one who seeks out vulnerabilities is not a serpent.
Whatever has been spoken very rapidly and extensively by the wise Vyāsa, even though it is in many hundreds of stanzas,
find your delight in that very [work].
The wheel, the dead preceptor, the garment, the food, the prostration, the staff,
and the small bell— these are the seven means of livelihood.
That servitude which was performed for the low-born Niśeśvara by Daṇḍīnātha, the son of Damodaragupta— that is merely the manifestation of a belly that is difficult to fill and ungrateful.
The deer of corrupt speech that was slain by the lion of grammar—
that [deer] was not killed by those physicians who were mere practitioners of the *natas* (actors) and had pale, emaciated limbs.
[Subhūti] said: "How can this beggar, who is like a leper, laugh?
To whom do these [people] belong?"
Through slandering others, through excellence in dress, and through excessive pride in one's manliness,
men may attain the status of a prince by performing even the most trivial acts.
Out of fear that the crimson hue of her lower lip— produced by the fresh twigs of khadira wood used for the *prakāśavarṣa* rite—
might fade, the young woman does not drink water, even though she is thirsty, as she stands at the edge of the pond.
Daṇḍin’s *Kāvyādarśa* (Subhāṣitāvali 2337–2338):
"Alas, how very great is the high worth of this prince, even as he recites verses devoid of meter, swallowed by the poison of incorrect words!"
Listen,
friend, to this one curiosity created today by that rustic rogue:
while my eyes were closed in the bliss of love-making, he thought I was dead and abandoned me in terror.
The unrefined one said: "O Brahmin, you are a weary old man, difficult for a young woman to please;
you have escaped my untimely death by means of this ruse of love during the night."

By means of the nectar of her lower lip, Damodaragupta’s bile is destroyed; by the weight of her breasts, his wind (vāyu) is pacified; and by her incessant passion, the phlegm is subdued—the body of this slender woman thus balances the three humors.
Even a physician’s treasure is merely a matter of endurance; if he lives, that is a great honor for him.
Who would not become a friend out of fear of disease? Therefore, apply yourself to medical treatment.
Neither a couch with a fine spread, nor a comfortable and charming bed,
nor even a hundred thousand marks of wealth is equal to the pleasure of impromptu, clandestine love-making.
May I possess the *dvigu* compound, as well as the *satpuruṣa*, the *avyayībhāva* which is ever-present in my house,
the *tatpuruṣa*, the *karmadhāraya*, and that by which I may become a *bahuvrīhi*.
He causes it to be recited, but does not have what was written by another written; nor does anyone else cause him to recite what has been written by another.
This is another distinction of his: he does not even cause what he himself has written to be recited.
May this widow— a basket that shatters happiness— crush the excessive suffering of those whose faces are pale with passion and whose heads are shaven,
even as they wander through the forest of worldly existence.
The cloth was taken away by Raṇḍānanda through the snapping of his fingers; Sambhu departed even by the mere removal of his garment.
Śaura was defeated by the omission of a consonant, and Āśmālaka by the half-moon [mark].
For some,
there is suffering in the amorous acts involving the hair, lips, breasts, and thighs;
yet for others, there is pleasure in the moist marks of women, just as there is for the hosts of disputants.
For one who has entered uninvited, who is watched with angry eyes,
and who sits down of his own accord, death is better than a meal.
Bribery, flattery, threats, intimidation, the theft of property, and violence—these six must be employed at that very moment;
they are not obtainable at any other time.
If the lineage of marriage for one does not continue up to the seventy-seventh generation, he is surely unlearned;
for those [ancestors] live on through weaving and pounding, so why would he give fodder to the cows?
It is a well-known fact on earth that misfortunes multiply through the vulnerabilities of one who lacks discernment;
however, for those possessed by desire, it is quite the opposite: when they expose their vulnerabilities, it is indeed gains that arise, not misfortunes.
The letter *ta* is very small for those who are learned, wise, and of noble lineage;
yet this *ta* has become a *muṭṭha* (a fistful) for Bhaṭṭa—so what answer will that procuress give you here?
Of these two,

one is known in the world as an *agnihotrī* who maintains the fire, yet sells milk and offers water instead; the other is known as one who approaches his wife only during her fertile season, yet goes even by day to a prostitute who is in her menses.
The mountain-dwellers, beholding the golden gods who are free from grinding, cutting,
and heating, embrace themselves with their arms crossed and contemplate the higher goals among those who act for the welfare of this world.
O blacksmith, Iśvara-varman,
if I were to cut this [plow-shaft], what would be the use of my life as a fool, or what would it matter to the Lord of the Cow-pen?
If I sit with my legs stretched out while people laugh at me, then let there be toil for the plow through its heavy loads, its virtues, and its bulls.
O Ratnabhūti, the sky has become exceedingly light, its expanse slackened; and that lord of harlots is one who constantly cuts into pieces.
Even there, alas, the nights of the month of Māgha are cruelly destructive; oh, how can this array of calamities be endured?

One who performs meritorious deeds and places fish— well-prepared with ginger, black pepper, fresh ginger, cardamom, cinnamon, cumin, and salt, and seasoned with oil— upon a plate of cooled white rice, attains the world of Brahmā.
He weighs out food like Vajra, the lord of the gods; he extracts it whole, like a splinter lodged in a bone.
With a mind free from envy, he gives away the thick broth mixed with fine salt, which removes all burning sensations, just as one would give water.

Even after having thoroughly mastered the six systems of tenets (*siddhānta*), the four Upaniṣads, the fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), and all the arts (*kalā*), one who does not understand the manifold and diverse wheel [of dependent origination] remains light; whereas he who does understand it attains true weightiness.
Her waist can be grasped by a fist; her belly can be spanned by the arms of two men; her breasts dangle like bells; and her hips seem intent on departing.
Her smile has the sound of a kettledrum, and her face is terrifying; yet even so, this slut humiliates and torments me.
Clad in a pair of white garments, his shanks reddened by the friction of the leather sandals, wearing a garland withered from being worn for three days;
with his hair-knot loosened and disheveled, he searches in secret for another woman in the vicinity of the royal courtyard, his eyes fixed upon her.
For every living being in this world, two things are certain: prosperity and decline.
When an old man associates with a youth, he is abandoned by women;
yet, among his kin, he alone remains the man who is the refuge of their prosperity.
If a woman conducts herself like a man, know that the household is ruined.
He drinks the blood from the throat of the virtuous; he does not eat meat or liquor;
he steals the property of Viṣṇu; he observes fasts on the twelfth lunar day;
and having heard the Sāṃkhya philosophy, he seizes the livelihood of cows and Brāhmaṇas.
Sin, hypocrisy, and the companion of the Kali age—the official (niyogin)—is the friend of whom?
Frequent questioning and varied conversation; scratching oneself while pulling at the hem of one's garment;
looking at the sun to determine the time of day; excessive laughter; flicking away mosquitoes and gnats;
going out often; quarreling with one's own kinsmen; and breaking water-vessels.
And "the extinguishing of fire"—these are the twelve activities of goldsmiths.
Exert yourself constantly if you have the power; for day by day, O beloved, youth passes away.
Who will give you, once dead, a funeral offering of sesame water upon a bed of *darbha* grass, along with the hairless vulva?
Straightforward gaze, laughter free from coarseness, gentle embraces, aversion to jesting, effort in traveling to distant holy sites,
delight in ascetics, and a body that has indeed abandoned the desire for pleasure, with full and long-hanging breasts— [these are the marks of one who has attained the goal].
May that slut, who is adorned with a garland of bones and dwells upon the great seat of a corpse, be for your happiness!
For courtesans whose minds are intent on securing the next world and who are utterly absorbed in their devotion, this alone may sometimes be a flaw in their asceticism:
that with mouths bold with the thick redness of betel juice and the fragrance of wine, they kiss even Brahmins while uttering the impure "Hūṃ" of greeting.
With wealth, one knows a courtesan who resembles the god of love, as well as those afflicted by leprosy and worn out by old age;
yet even without wealth, one knows the passion of love, as well as those afflicted by leprosy and worn out by old age.
O moon-faced one, this single dīnāra coin belongs to Kṣemendra; it is bound by a knot at the end of my girdle.
It was acquired through many hardships; grant me the favor of giving half of its half.

In the season of Śiśira, may those thickets of *karambhaka* plants abound—thickly packed and densely crowded with roots of lotus shoots that cast the shadows of the moving tusks of great elephants; filled with the essence of all the flocks of birds, and bursting forth amidst the clusters of *vaṭīkā*.
Tearing at his teeth with the juice, causing his palate to split in two through numbness, chilling his throat and contracting the openings of the gullet—
thus [is he] like a stainless water-jar struck by an unbearable blast of frost.
The fortunate ones drink the abundant water day after day, released in a continuous stream.
Bearing hundreds of wet nail-marks on their hips, yet not on any other part of their bodies out of fear,
they kept their eyes fixed motionlessly upon the surface of his lips, languid with sleep.

A woman who, through the signal of her eyebrows, brings about the union of her lover according to their private convention, attains success like a wish-fulfilling creeper; yet a slut does not achieve this without merit.

When an old man, with limbs weakened by age, engages in the arduous act of lovemaking with a young woman who is distressed and filled with shame—wherein his efforts at raising her are merely for the sake of a momentary effort, while his own remaining strength is exhausted, his skin wrinkled, and his hair thinning and falling out; when he embraces her with a futile exertion that causes his frail body to tremble—is it right to laugh at such a sight, or rather, is it right to weep? It must be reflected upon.
O venerable one, you possess limbs yet are not supported by many; you know for yourself what is appropriate;
you travel on foot and speak with your head; you are able to move about.
O wonder! You show no aversion toward food, nor do you feel thirst; today we see you, free from the sickness of servitude, alive once more, filled with joy.
O serpent, you who with supreme devotion gaze upon this abode of a courtesan— filled with the scent of cooking meat and wine, and crowded with *ceṭīs* and *tiṣyas*—
it is here that the household deity resides, acting as a grinder for the long duration of your life.
She whose daily offering consists of the sacrifices of her own beloved husband, well-performed according to the sacred vows.
I am a vulture among those who are deeply deluded; a fierce bee amidst the honeyed [pleasures];
a tigress among those with rows of sharp claws; a female serpent among those with various kinds of fangs; a scorpion amidst the upward-turning [spines]; and a mouse under the guise of wealth.
She remained in the house, assuming many forms to deceive the paramour of the courtesan.
Loud recitation of the Vedas, ancient tales, conversing with women,
delighting in their children’s play, praising their false merits,
and proclaiming one's own good fortune and fitness for the company of fathers, brothers, and kinsmen.
The twelve rules for a monk’s conduct regarding his own observance, speech, and salutation.
"O beloved, why do you scold me today when this house is already ruined? Why do you not do it yourself?
"O wicked woman, you prattle back every day; your father is a sinner!
"Fie on you, O wrathful-faced one! Who is more prone to anger than even you?"
For a husband and wife, what happiness is there when their constant quarrels and afflictions never come to an end?
In the onset of dense darkness, there is no pleasure in glancing with knitted brows; sweet conversations do not arise spontaneously from mutual speech;
for thus, when the heart is filled with fear, no attachment to joy is produced.
And though it is a strange act of theft, there is nevertheless some indescribable and delightful aesthetic flavor for the mind.
Desire for one’s own wife, like medicine purchased at a price, is merely a labor due to one's mastery over it;
any desire other than that is *manmatha*, like that of an artisan.
Independently achieved and exclusively beneficial, this covering of ignorance was fashioned by the Creator;
specifically, silence is an ornament in the assembly of the all-knowing, yet it is a disgrace for the unlearned.
Taking up the works of the authors, engage in discussion with the learned teachers; become a diligent recipient of these books, and vie with the wise,
laughing loudly and repeatedly while moving your various hands in diverse ways.
If one who is utterly foolish and even extremely dull-witted should desire to be foremost among the wise;
Speak loudly without hesitation; distort your face out of pride in your knowledge. Boast of yourself and mock others; laugh suddenly after uttering some vulgar word.
Recite impure, broken food-offerings; engage in dispute, exalting the world of fools.
If you desire the state of being a wise man even before a crowd of fools, then even a lowly fool among the multitude of fools [should speak].
Mocking Vyāsa and other poets with improper challenges,
shouting loudly while closing both eyes, and reciting verses with pride— appropriate yourself to poetry composed by others and compete with the wise!
If you request that one who is devoid of learning may attain wisdom by force;
In his speech he is like a cuckoo, in kissing like a pigeon,
in his gait like a swan, and in the crushing of passion with his beloved like an elephant;
thus is my husband served by qualities that are praiseworthy among all young women.
If it were the case that for one who has passed away there is no married husband, then this fault would not exist.
My husband is endowed with many qualities of a leader;
if he alone were my lover, my life would be fruitful.
"O each and every puppet, do not weep! Where have they not caused you to whirl about?
What need is there to mention those who, by a mere glance from their eyes, seize you by the hand?"
Among them, a certain Brahmin, accompanied by his wife and wearing the sacred thread, was skillfully deceiving people for the sake of his own wealth with the sound of his own hand:
"I am a student; I do not weep, nor do I recite the Vedas."

O King, O Ānandavāmin, I swear this solemn oath: I hold in my hand the supreme, most sacred *yajñopavīta* (sacred thread). There is nothing else that captivates the mind, nor is there anything that is a cause of singular misery, other than women with shapely hips.

May the fortunate Bhaga protect you—he whose unprecedented deeds are auspicious; for even as he emits [his seed], he brings delight; though struck, he causes joy to the heart; and even when his virility has been spent, he produces a festival for the eyes.
Even when deprived of his topknot, he maintains his splendor during sexual union.
A fool, even when engaged in adultery with another's wife, spreads the verbal sin of claiming it was for the sake of purification;
he casts away the lotus leaf uprooted from its stalk in order to conceal his theft within the lotus pond of the sacrifice.
Just as the sick have a longing for unwholesome food, just as those in extreme poverty long for wealth,
and just as the wicked long for the infliction of pain upon others, so do women long for the festival of thievery and sexual pleasure.
Those seeking wealth endure the exhaustion of a long journey like servants forced to bear a heavy burden;
those afflicted by disease endure bitter medicine like wives enduring the house of their own husbands.
The first [the wealthy] always bear fruit for the Īśvaras, Cāraṇas, and Gāyanas like wish-fulfilling trees;
but the virtuous, with mere words, bestow something upon the good at evening, like camphor for a lamp.
Her own sister-in-law pushed her away, and her husband’s brother pushed her away;
yet she rejoiced, O dear friend, for she had found an equal in the house as a husband.
The distinction between the sounds *gha*, *jha*, *dha*, *dha*, *bha*, *na*, *ṇa*, and *va* cannot be perceived from the speaker’s mouth;
rather, the distinction of those [sounds] is perceived by means of the teeth and the cavities of the mouth and anus.
For whom is this moon not censured? From whom is the sweet speech of a messenger not heard?
Whose sighs do not burn the heart? And whose body does not undergo emaciation from the cold?
While he sleeps, embracing his own wife who is submissive to his will and adorned with her own garlands, Bhṛṅgī bears a body that is nothing but bones, rough and bound together by dense sinews.
Our mother was born from a family as radiant as that of the true Vedic scholars;

indeed, I have married a certain maiden from such a lineage, and for that reason, O father, I am superior [to others]. Yet our sister, the daughter of my sister’s son, has been falsely accused by enemies.
Out of devotion to him, she abandoned even her own beloved wife, though she was dear to her.
The child cries out at the sound of the house collapsing; the young woman emits a gasp;

the mature woman releases incomparable grief for her son, struck as if by a staff of nectar; and the old man becomes a churning mountain for the violent agitation of the deep ocean of his profound fortune.
May the letter *la*—which has the appearance of Indra’s thunderbolt and the tusks of Airāvata—be victorious for you!
O monk, your neck is indeed slack; do you not catch fish with a net for the sake of killing them? You drink wine like those intoxicated by liquor, and you go to a courtesan as if she were honey.
Having placed your foot upon the throats of your enemies, why do you say, "I am the breaker of their walls"?
You are a thief; for the sake of gambling, how have you become a gambler, by which I have become the son of a slave-girl?
The talk of milk is far away; for what other distinction is there among kings?
By means of a staff-cake, curd may indeed be obtained, but where could buttermilk possibly arise for me? May the whey be auspicious, yet the very mention of the essence of cow's milk is fruitless.
It is my good fortune that I have been deceived by mere fragments of gold, rendered devoid of all pride.
Enough with these afflictions fashioned from hair that must be removed; her mind is to be captivated.

Even a rustic man is desirable to her—what more can be said of this woman whose cleverness has been burnt away? Go out at will, my son, to where young women are obtainable through their own affection.
May that which was spoken by the courtesan—this public display of the lofty demeanor of a soldier—protect you!
At first, those who are engaged in business become exceedingly arrogant—proud, intoxicated by pride, and obsessed with seizing the wealth of others;
they become extremely cruel.
Then, when they fall from those businesses, their feet are bound with fetters and chains, and they are tormented by whips.
With long tufts of hair and dejected faces, they become exceedingly gentle, like sages who have attained equanimity through the nectar of immortality.
"Others may enjoy these pleasures, but we must endure the pain of being crushed by them"—
as if saying this, the two breasts of the aged woman moved toward the root of the vulva, which shares their common suffering.
Then Jāti,
having risen from beneath a heap of ashes like a cat, stretches her long limbs and shakes her body,
which is rough with dust, at the end of the night.
The traveler, longing to go home, sings, laughs, and dances, yet he thinks only of his beloved held within his heart;
and though he seeks it, he finds neither peace nor composure.
With bodies grey with dust,
their forms fashioned solely for the sake of play,
and making various sounds with their mouths, children play with unrestrained joy.

Whose heart would not be captivated by the face of Rudra— the moon of his forehead, its cheeks and chin joined as he covers his nostrils with fingers splayed like a lotus, while the sound "da" issues forth from it? It is like the light of a fine lotus fiber.
Covering his entire face with his hand, whose fingers are slightly spread apart,
this moon, emitting the sound "Daka," produces a captivating radiance.
These two verses were composed by Vallabhadeva:
Roaring in a mountain thicket filled with water, Hari, having heard the sounds made by echoes,
composed a verse in anger as he intended to step forward, suspecting it to be the roar of another lord of elephants.
At night,
in the palm groves where the clouds are discharging their water, the elephants—
sitting with their trunks near the millions of water-drops falling from the tips of their tusks and with eyes half-closed— listen attentively with their ears fixed like cymbals.
Of someone else,
who was taking two or three faltering steps while holding onto his nurse’s hand,
and who was once again practicing crawling on his knees with fearless gait;
O friend, that joy which arises in one's heart from a son— whose mouth is like a budding flower of uneven teeth and who speaks with indistinct words— that joy cannot be described.

Hearing suddenly that his father had come from the house of Bhaṭṭa Janārdana, he abandoned the dust-covered playgrounds where he had been engaged in play with his friends, and departed with cries of "Sire!
(Śi).
With a face beaming from afar, the boy extends his two graceful arms and approaches the presence of Bādhana with supreme affection, making a loud,
joyful sound.
"O Mother, devoted to the Dharma, show compassion toward me! O Princess of Videha, I am weary; today at night, having gone secretly to the corner of the porch near the door, I shall sleep there.
Having spoken thus, he was suddenly rebuked by the words of the fierce Gṛhiṇī.
The traveler, his fistful of betel-nut powder lost within the [five] aggregates (*skandha*), set out once more,
while Ravidatta sat upon a seat spread with grass, his face turned away from the fire.
Overcome by winds as piercing as poison blowing through the openings of their throats, whose knots have been loosened,
travelers— bent double with knees drawn up like those who are exhausted—
have with great difficulty reached the night, which stretches out even further due to the doubled intensity of their inner, irresistible suffering.
Having shaken off the sleep of some person by tossing up his wing, his limbs expanded as he spread his entire plumage;
even before dawn, with slumber dispelled, he gazes at the sky illuminated by the shimmering rays of the sun.

Having risen early in the morning, with his body standing firm yet slightly swaying, the cock stretches its neck high and, with its forebody raised and its crest disheveled, crows out a loud, gurgling sound.
The horse of Nandūpa appeared as if drawing the earth toward him, as if treading it with his hooves, as if abandoning its hindquarters,
as if appropriating the sky, as if drinking the quarters of the horizon, and as if devouring the winds.
As if touching the earth covered in embers, as if entering a shadow,
with his face fanned by waving yak-tail whisks, the illustrious horse gallops forward.
After extending his right leg and stretching his body high with the triple-joint (trika) bent and expanded, Śrī Siṃhadatta,
with his neck curved, struck his face against his chest and shook off the dust that had turned him grey.
The horse, its long snout incessantly flickering and thrusting out of greed for mouthfuls of fodder,
rises from its bed and, making a soft sound, scratches the ground with its hoof.
Terrified by the light and filled with fear at the sight of the women, the serpent fled as the flood of people occupied the doorway with a loud clamor that paralyzed his vision;
struck by blows from stones and harsh shouts of "Seize the staff!", the frightened snake, finding no hole in the house, slithered from corner to corner.

Sniffing again and again at the scent of Divīrakiśoraka, his mouth and nostrils distorted as he bared his rows of teeth, he ran while letting out a loud cry, repeatedly and impetuously seizing [his prey] from behind.
Drawn by a longing for sexual pleasure that is twice as intense as a kick from a she-ass, the donkey mounts with impetuosity; then, his desire frustrated, he descends after a long time, fainting.
Having smelled the pervasive scent of Śrīmayūra’s urine, which caused the contraction and bending of his nostrils as he stood facing it,
and having gazed at the sun with wide-open eyes, he struck the ground with his hoof.
Moving his pair of eyes,
which resemble a cluster of blue lotuses, the goat makes many goats dance like a clever man blinded by passion.
Having roared like clouds, Bhaṭṭabāṇa first slowly formed his body into a circle, then,
supporting himself on his two horns, he began to tear the earth before him with the tips of his hooves.
Moving very slowly together, planting their feet firmly and striking one another with their horns,
these two great bulls fight like lotuses, repeatedly shaking their curved tails.
O cow, whose calf, having repeatedly struck its mother’s udder with its head, drinks the flowing milk quickly; whose single hump is slightly bent and whose beautiful tail is constantly swaying.
Having crossed over, because he was the beloved son of the boatman, he gave a *huṃkāra* seal;
with his mouth smeared by the spray from the streams of milk flowing from the relaxed [udder], he licked his mother’s limbs to satiety.
O illustrious Peacock,
may your enemies fall upon you, deprived of the enjoyment of your feathers.
They are like the breasts of noble women consumed by the widowhood of their young children.
O Lord, you who resemble Nārāyaṇa and who hate hell,
it is fitting that even a single "Si" (the syllable of command) was established by you as a protector against the host of enemies.
Having ascended the scale, when the sun places its foot in Scorpio,
it is effortlessly placed upon the heads of those who enjoy worldly pleasures by you.
How can the Dharma of the Single Path be practiced in this Kali age,
were it not for this lineage beginning with you to serve as its support?
In this age of Kali, you alone have accomplished the task of establishing the next world by bringing to fruition the pure paths that lead to the accumulation of virtuous qualities.
What is the use of that place where you are not, and what is the use of that time when you are present?
If your birth occurs during the Kali age, let it be so; what is the use of lamenting?
For logicians, there is indeed no proof without that which is to be proven;
yet, alas, for you there is no object to be proven, and yet there is still proof—how strange!
The wise declare that valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which is non-contradictory with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
how then can this flood of qualities of yours not be considered valid cognition in this world?
The cause is in one place, yet the effect is seen elsewhere;
great is the majesty of the Lord, while the burning of his enemies occurs within their own hearts.
You alone are the king of those dwelling in Pātāla;
you are the foundation of the wind-gods of Cāmara; and you alone serve as the support for the three worlds.
With its rays difficult to behold and scorching the people with its heat,
the sun, whose orb is crimson for but a moment, is not equal to you.
This much can be said by us: that you are virtuous.
But as for discerning the mass of jewels within a mine of gems, who are we?
Their bodies withered by the intense heat of the circle of friends, they have now become like days of the summer heat; thus,
the popular maxim that "the effect is similar to the cause" is proven false.
O proud one, it has come about that you have become free from pride and possess fame upon the earth.
Even by you, who are free from pride, all these people, through virtues such as generosity and honor,
are made equal to yourself.
Even these servants of yours enjoy happiness;
yet, how could that attainment of happiness which they possess through your favor belong to you?
The enjoyment that is partaken of by those in need is truly fruitful for you alone;
what is the use of enjoyments for other men, which are like the hoods of serpents?
Duryodhana, you are like a thorn in the hearts of your kin; Śalya, you are the dart of your enemies.
You alone are Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the elephant, yet you act as a mere jackal among the Kauravas.
You are Yudhiṣṭhira in steadfastness, Bhīma in prowess, Arjuna in your conduct;
you are Sahadeva in wisdom, and you possess Nakula’s eloquence of speech.
Inflict a firm tax upon the self-arisen ones who follow the excellent path;
remove the tax from the self-arisen ones who follow the excellent path.
Some among the Kanādas have departed, others have taken up residence in the Vindhyas;
still others have become servants to the Śabaras, while yet others have become authors of treatises.
Obeisance to your arm, which causes trembling and burning pain to the enemy—the arm that is the battle-ground for the world’s fierce kings and the crusher of their pride.
May there be well-being for you.
O Śrībhūti, you who have reached the end of hell and sport as the lord of the earth,
your birth— born of devotion to truth— is as praiseworthy as that of Hari.
O King, this poverty, like a passionate woman, does not tolerate even a single moment of being disregarded; it quickly abandons him as if out of jealousy.
Surely the Creator did not realize the vastness of your mind;
otherwise, why would he have fashioned [the earth] with its four oceans as its boundaries?
He who does not leave the shadow of your feet is a vessel for prosperity;
otherwise, if you are acting perversely, why do you not look at the lotus?
"You are always, everywhere," so you are falsely praised by people;
yet even your enemies could not reach your back, nor could others embrace your chest.
The Sarasvatī resides in the mouths of some, and Lakṣmī in their lotus-like hands; but has Kīrti departed to another land because the king is angry?
O King, when your drum was struck, the jars of your enemies' hearts burst open;
that it flowed out through the eyes of their beloveds—this is a great marvel!
"From where did you learn this unprecedented science of archery? A multitude of arrows approaches, yet the bowstring reaches the farthest horizon."
These seven oceans, possessing the luster of rice-pudding mixed with honey,
are the cage for the deer of your fame, which has been born from the moon, within the three worlds.
O Lord of the Earth, your fame has indeed been born from plunging into the four oceans;
it has gone to the orb of the sun to provide relief from its heat.
Who has performed this glorification that pains you?
Yet, when you are praised, even Maghavan is delighted.
Neither the moon nor the sun attains equality with this Amṛtadatta;
for the giver whose hands never grow weary by day or by night.
Viṣṇu himself,
declaring "I am the letter 'A' among all letters," was indeed rendered insignificant by you through that very letter 'A'.
Although these two arms of Bhaaskarasena are languid from the embrace of lovely women,
they are nevertheless capable of piercing the armor of elephants in battle.
People are made to undergo penance for approaching those who should not be approached;
yet that which is unapproachable leads one to glory and is purifying everywhere.
O glorious one, how wonderful is your benevolence!
For you have brought even your enemies to a state of purity, just like yourself.
Although you both possess an equal number of virtues, there is this great difference between you:
the bowstring snaps when it reaches the bow, but you, whose virtue is unbroken, remain unsevered.
What can your flood of virtues do, which— like a lamp within a jar—
is its range restricted by the boundaries of the earth and the sky?
Pāṇini, though he knew the proper times for peace and war and had accomplished his purpose,
is not to be compared to you, who inspire conviction in others.
It is the consensus of Pāṇini that prefixes (*upasarga*) are used in connection with a verbal action;
how then can your enemy, though devoid of action, always be "possessed of a prefix" (*sopasarga*)?
In that regard, both the verbal roots and the suffixes are subject to grammatical derivation;
they are modified by means of prefixes and prepositions, as well as by the addition of *guṇa*, *āgama*, and *vṛddhi*.
For those led astray by wicked poets, like the verses of enemies, there shall be stumbling at every step due to the occurrence of difficult constructions and connections of meaning.
I do not consider it surprising that you give away what you possess;
yet, since you have no fear even in a dream, how is it that you have given [this] to your enemies?
Your sword is without blemish, firm, pure, surrounded by a scabbard, endowed with excellent qualities,
well-proportioned, heart-captivating, and truly beautiful.
For the most part, all those who are subject to destruction perceive everything as perverted;
yet you, though fair as gold, have become the very death of your enemies.
How can there be skill in the family of those who are at odds with you?
For their dwelling must necessarily be in the forest, which is filled with the skillful.
O enemy, your Buddhist doctrine is self-contradictory:
it asserts momentary destruction in the case of conflict, yet maintains emptiness in all its constituent parts.
Due to his attachment to the enemy's army and because of the multitude of deities associated with it,
Jayalakṣmī (the Goddess of Victory) departed from the mouth of the great king into the mouths of his enemies in battle.
O Pāñcika,
today snow does not fall upon the city of Puṇḍravardhana, which stands as the sole essence of the three worlds and is adorned by the moon of your fame.
By you,

who are pre-eminent among those who are not pre-eminent, the quarters have been conquered in battle as you struck down the army of certain enemies who were themselves pre-eminent among those who strike.
O King, as if out of fear of sinking into the ocean of your fame,
the sky now holds two water-jars in the form of the orbs of the sun and the moon.
Oh, what an indescribable flower of pure fame has blossomed for you,
of which this young moon, dripping with nectar, is but an external sprout!
O Jayavardhana,
when you, who bring the joy of sight, have risen like the moon,
the faces of women become like moonstones, raining down incessant drops of water.
The moon, waning by itself, resorts to but one friend for a month;
you, however, resort to hundreds of friends and attain increase at every moment.
The pair of breasts of your enemies' wives, moistened by tears and situated close to the fire of grief in their hearts, undergoes a fast as it were,
abstaining from food.
The fame of the venerable Bhattabāṇa kisses the quarters of the sky, embraces the earth whose throne is the ocean,
and rejoices in the groves; it has grown old, yet its actions remain ever youthful.
That seed of a Great Being, which was seen by Śrī Kalla as a mere sprout when sown by Arjuna, is now seen here by you, O Creator,
to have blossomed and borne fruit through your manifestation.
Like the syllables of a verse belonging to Ānandavardhana—
separated by vowels (*ū*, *u*, *sm*), devoid of *vṛddhi*, lacking conjunct consonants, and even light at the end—
his enemies become heavy upon reaching the end of his quarters.

O King, how is it that you are not the supreme among men? For even in your childhood, you were the leader of the cowherds, your body radiant with the splendor of the rising sun’s orb; endowed with strength, you protected the herd of cattle.
The enemy’s wife is mocked by the autumn season: her breasts have lost their luster, having become pale from the extreme heat of the fire of grief;
and her Bandhujīva flowers, tasted by the arrows [of the god of love], have been consumed by the shafts of the enemy.
Having beheld the sun, which kisses the faces of the quarters like brides and possesses great radiance, the day becomes weary;
therefore, it is embraced by him [the moon], who displays the rising of his broad breasts [the lunar crescent], and thus the entire night is encompassed.
Though addressed, she remained intent on her pursuit and did not manifest any overt gestures of physical affection;
like a young bride unable to lie upon her husband, the army of the enemy was incapable of resting atop you.
For this woman of broad hips,
during the festival of the earth in times of financial distress, and as a lamp in the darkness of fear arising from enemies,
there exists some rare jewel like you— a true gem capable of bearing the weight of manifold assistance to those in need.

O Bhalla, you always captivate the minds of men by your possession of such great excellence; yet even so, you are not of many minds, for who would reveal another's stolen property? Or rather, who would disclose what has been taken?

Sudyumna was born of the lunar dynasty; that king Daśaratha was also a protector of women and exceedingly auspicious. He was the son of Dharma and possessed of the Nakula [lineage]—by what comparison can you be likened to this sovereign of all?
On both Airāvaṇa’s temples, where the earrings remain motionless as they hear the sighs of celestial women embracing him,
swarms of bees drink the ichor without hindrance; whose endeavor does your auspicious activity not bring success?
O you who have conquered pride,
on the lofty peaks of the snowy mountains, hosts of kinnaras together with their beloveds sing this of your fame: it is as white as a conch shell,
the moon, the petals of the kunda flower, a young lotus stalk, a lotus fiber, frost, and a pearl necklace, and as bright as the laughter of Śiva.

O Subhūti, the battlefield shone as if with the heaps of matted hair of enemy elephants, whose temples were split open by the sword-blade of your staff-like arm, and from which streams of pearls had fallen;
it appeared like a mass of flowers from the tresses of the smiling, beautiful women captured by you.
O Harṣadeva,
if these four quarters— now in their season, sprinkled with rain, clad in washed garments, with the expanse of their breasts in the form of hands quivering,
and possessing flowers for the sake of offspring for their lord— desire union with you, then let it be so.
By him, the sun-like Maātangadivākara, whose hand was like a terrifyingly shaped sword-blade,

the heads of the foremost warriors on the battlefield were severed; thus, through his respectful swallowing of the enemy’s splendor as if it were the moon, he appeared like a succession of Rāhus in combat.
O Prakāśadatta,
what is this unprecedented web that you have fashioned with qualities that are truly a source of wonder?
For it binds even the mind— which is formless and fickle— and that which has entered the ear is indeed something never before seen.
O Ratnākara, even though you are not the ocean, you have never failed to provide for the wise through your efforts;
you do not always move about here wearing a garment of wet hide, nor are you a lord of all creatures dwelling in the midst of a lotus.
O Lord, to what can your fame be compared? It cannot be likened to the jasmine flower, which perishes in an instant; nor to the orb of the moon, which is stained by its dark spot;

nor to milk, which is subject to change; nor to a flock of swans, whose association with the dull-witted is a blemish; nor to necklaces, whose bodies are riddled with holes, despite their white luster.

In the city of Sinmādana, your enemies—the tribes of Pulindas—have their feet firmly planted upon walls of various colors; with one hand they hold a leather shield, while with the other they perform the caresses of love.
By your virtues you are Purūravas, by your fame you are Rāma, Nala, and Bharata;
you are Satrughna in the great battle, and you stand as Janaka upon the earth— thus,
through your noble deeds, you bear the renown of the ancient rulers of the world.
O King, how is it that you, though a conqueror of the three worlds, are not a sovereign?
O King, though your anger is proclaimed by a frown as you suddenly desire to march against the enemy, you might indeed crush the rainy season;
yet those elephants of yours would not, on the contrary, turn the paths into mere mud with their incessant streams of rutting ichor and their cloudy days.
The quarters of the sky, darkened by the dust raised by your own vast army surging with impetuous force,

were gazed upon by circles of peacocks— even those whose hostility toward the stalks of lotus fibers was due to the festive agitation of their minds at the untimely arrival of the rainy season— known by the name of hunters,
Vikrāntivarman.

Even though they are unarmed, even though they are deprived of all their followers, and even though they are on foot along the roads— how is it that your enemies still roam about with weapons, with their attendants, and with their horses?

These two—the moonlight of the son of the Sun (Kṛṣṇa), who is worthy of being beheld; the garland of the flowers of his fame; the beautiful crest-jewel of the treasury of virtues; the lotus-pool for the lilies of the arts;

the thunderbolt for the coral-stalks of his graceful form; the moonlight for the darkness of his enemies; the magic wand for subduing the hearts of excellent playful women; and the slender body that brings praise—are all [manifestations] of him.

An untainted family, an auspicious form, an intellect enriched by learning, abundant strength of arm, widespread prosperity, and unimpaired sovereignty—these states are indeed naturally pleasing and are the causes of intoxication; yet those very things by which a man falls into madness become for you the goads that restrain him.
He who displays his back to both [sides] in battle amidst the ranks of enemy hosts,
he who maintains crookedness toward you alone, and he who cruelly scatters [his arrows] upon the path of violence— [he is the one].
O Sage, as you partake of the virtues of such a person as he,
you alone are clearly renowned as the foremost among those who perceive excellence.

Having beheld with the strength of his teeth this entire earth whose body is embraced by garlands, that King Pṛthu— moving amidst the rows of gods who have bowed down out of curiosity to see the joy of battle, and who create the illusion of a multitude of moving mountains on the battlefield—
is once again setting his mind upon uprooting the mountains.
O Lord,

having heard that Your victory— which dispels all fear, is protected by intense majesty, has traversed the circle of the earth, and has brought about the destruction of enemies— Śrī Hara, the sovereign of the gods,
flees in secret; he does not wish to offer a reply, he asks his preceptor with affection, he longs for protection, he faints again and again, and he keeps his eyes fixed upon his bed.

O King, today my heart’s desire rests upon none other than him—whether he be Śiva, Rāma, Indra, Airāvata, the elephant of heaven, Viṣṇu, the lord of serpents, or even the bull; for my preference lies in his garment, his belly, his emblem, his intoxication, his throat, his glance, his matted locks, his calf, and the path he treads.
As for others, my interest lies in their sky, their bellies, their insignia, their pride, their necks, their eyes, their manes, their vehicles, and their tracks.

At the time of your arrival here, when the army of the Lord of the Entire Earth was moving with an exceedingly difficult-to-restrain pace and trampling [the ground], even the pair of eyes on the head of the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa) were instantly blinded by the dust;
yet that dust did not cause the failure of his vision, nor did the clamor of the foot soldiers reach his ears.
When you, with all the components of battle assembled, fixed an arrow upon your bow, O King, whatever was suddenly encountered by whatever [means]:
the bow met the arrow, the arrow met the enemy’s head, that [arrow] met the circle of the earth, the earth met you, you met stainless fame, and that fame met the three worlds.
O King, among the gods in heaven, among men in the city, and among those who enjoy pleasures in this world, there have been some, there are some, and there will be some;

yet among them, there has never been, there is not now, nor will there ever be, one equal to you—who are bowed to by kings, devoted to poetry, praised by the learned, and who have struck down his enemies.
O King, who among those born of the lineage of Śaśibhāskara have not been subdued by you?
Yet, O Lord, we consider you alone to be the true sovereign of the earth—
by whom [the enemy] was touched on the body, then his hair was pulled, and finally his long [arm] was cast down.
Having reached Cola and now the Middle Country, my hand has fallen upon Kāñcī.
You traverse two or three steps of the peacock; your enemies leap over the earth.
You discharge eight or five of your own arrows; they discharge their weapons.
O Lord of the Goddesses, those lords have their weapons placed by you; you are the lord of human women.
How can there be blame in them, and how can there be praise in you? O Śrīkarṇa, let this be resolved.

O King, when that Kalpavr̥kṣa (wish-fulfilling tree) ceased to grant boons to you, it somehow became bent over under the guise of the heavy burden of fruit produced by the constant wandering of supplicants; but how could the Mountain of Jewels (Ratnācala) remain— exalted by the emergence of its inexhaustible wealth of gems, yet overcome with shame at the unbearable pain of rejecting the throngs of beggars?
O Moon, you who act as the victorious mark upon those filled with pride by their own white virtues, today the night-lily wanders about, fearing sleepless nights as you approach.
Does the jasmine flower hide within its braided hair out of fear? The cool-rayed moon shines forth, bearing a hidden terror under the guise of flowing nectar.
With his body submerged up to his neck in the waters of the army of your scent-elephants,
white with foam that rivals the fatigue from the sport of conquering the elephants of the various quarters,

the ocean— appearing as if he has four tusks due to the reflection of the pair of [the elephant’s] tusks— extinguishes his separation from Abhramuvallabha (Airāvata) under the guise of the water upon his trunk.
This belly of Dāmodara’s mother, having supported the three worlds,
was now unable to contain them due to the weight of their vastness; yet today,
through the path of her navel, those very abodes of the two-legged lion (Viṣṇu), which had emerged from the lotus-hands of the Destroyer of Madhu as if to fill that very belly, have now departed.
"Stability is attained through humility alone, while the very quarters of space are transgressed by arrogance"— thinking thus, you,
wielding your bow and discharging arrows, became a teacher even to your enemies in battle.
O Lord, you who have taken a vow to delight the people have not gone forth even after encountering enemies;
for, having made even those who were intensely disaffected appear as if they were deeply attached, you exerted yourself and released them in battle.
O Lord, the gaze of men is not fixed on the uplifted bow, nor on the joining of the arrow, nor on the drawing back of the tip of the ear; it is not in the sky, nor on the target, nor on the ground.
Yet, O God, although the arrow is nowhere visible, its presence is inferred by the holes made in the chests of the fallen enemies.

"Protect me! Protect me!"—because you spoke thus, it has come to pass that you remain silent. O enraged one, have you perhaps been wounded by the heads of enemies, that you bite your own lip with your teeth?
Even as his right arm recedes, he offers a boon to the Great Archers who advance before him;
with great joy, he desires to grant an embrace of the bow to his left arm as it moves forward in battle.
The Chapter on the Enemy of the Gods: "O Lord, when both arrows fall upon you in battle, they do not produce a whistling sound as they descend, nor do they cause you to tremble;
this is fitting, for the liberation of both is such that there is no returning."
In that regard, it is a marvel that one person there breaks with a friend while another breaks with an enemy.
I recognize him as the creator of the vast expanse of the sky, the sun, and the earth; I suspect that he is the forest fire within the depths of the ocean's waters,
the enemy of the king of serpents who pervades the sky, and the one who eclipses the splendor of the stars.
O King, that scorching heat of his majesty cannot be fathomed by words.

These verses are by the author of the *Naiṣadha*, Śrī Harṣa: O King, you whose lotus-feet shine with the splendor of the presence of Śrī, who hold the conch, discus, and mace in your hands, and whose activity is the protection of the gods;
though you are devoted to Balabhadra, you are the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) of inconceivable deeds, who has conquered many years.
The distinction between the fire of Kapiladāmodara and the fire of your majesty is clearly evident:
that which is burnt by the former does not sprout again when subjected to this [latter] fire.
O you who are truly devoted, though you gave away your desired wealth and abandoned your home,
your fame— like a woman unfaithful to her husband— has gone naked to every quarter of the sky.
Therefore, O delighter of the eyes, I have beheld this entire earth as a marvel,
since even you, the Giver of Wealth, avoid contact with the fierce.
This is another most wonderful thing: that while you are being ravished by thousands of young women, there is an increase rather than a decrease in the splendor of your good fortune.
How can that Piṅgala be equal to you, O Noble One, by whom the lowly caste has been brought to a state of dignity through natural lightness, and who [composed] the Jaghanacapalā metre?
This wretchedness that you commit is a sin even for a Rākṣasa who is not his equal;
he did not create such power by night, yet you now forcibly enjoy the fortune of your enemy.
These have been released by Damodaragupta: the jasmine flower with its burgeoning pain, the *vicakila* with its agitation of trembling, the *ketaka* with its anxiousness,
the *madana* with its wretched lassitude, and the *atimuktadruma* vine.
O Lord, why did you not release [the elephant] at the time of your departure from the city, when his enemies' wives were overcome with grief?
At that moment, the *kesara* tree—possessing beautiful filaments (*satkesara*) and having completed its transformation into a *mādhavī* vine—was ready to liberate him.
O Lord,

when you— who are the source of prosperity, the foremost among the generous, preeminent in majesty and splendor, and the one upon whose shoulders the burden of the earth rests— were created by the Creator in the abode of the gods;
Was the moon fashioned? Was it created by a man? Or was this wish-fulfilling gem produced? Alas, why were these mountain kings created in vain?
What is more substantial than fame here? Not wealth. What is to be done? Noble conduct, not misdeeds.
What is an unobstructed eye? Intelligence, not the physical organ. Who other than you knows how to distinguish between the existent and the non-existent?
He who was utterly dark is you, yet you are stainless; he who was dwarfed is you, yet you are exalted in every way.
Since you, O Hero, are Viṣṇu—the benefactor of mankind and one whose nature is compassion—how can there be any comparison for you?
O illustrious Bakā,
when the royal sage Himamīṣacchiras was upon this earth, did his palace not shine even more brilliantly?
Yet, from that time until now, in this spring season, your own [palace] has quickly burst forth upon the ground under the guise of flowers.

If the clouds [conceal] the sky and the atmosphere, then our beauty is destroyed; yet by that sun with its sharp rays, we are constantly oppressed during the day. Thus, as if out of sorrow at being struck by the rising of the cloud-laden sun, our lord has come here.
O Lord of Men, those devoted to serving the gardens are, in fact, thieves under the guise of flowers.
That this summer possesses the majesty of radiant splendor,
that this rainy season is exceedingly prosperous and abundant, and that this autumn is fruitful and pure as a river—
all this is due to the hope that winter and spring, wearing the garment of dense clouds, shall come through your service.
O Lord, what need is there for a multitude of flowers? Is not the springtime itself intent on serving you, desiring your steadfastness?
O glorious Lord, the Goddess of Speech dances before your face;
seeing this, Lakṣmī has arrived, bound by your virtues. Your fame is like the moon, the rays of Indra’s elephant, the white water-lily, and the Milky Ocean.
Having leaped across the ocean of fear, you have not yet come to rest even now.
O King, having perceived some person of wicked conduct elsewhere on this earth as a cause for the obscuration of the splendor of the *Dākṣiṇātya* [Southern] tradition,
your white fame proceeds toward all directions as if out of anger to expel him.
Paṃ:
"What news has come from Śrīvaṅka? However, I am not able to remain silent;
for I am naturally talkative and possess the disposition of a Southerner."
Alas, your beloved Fame wanders like a madwoman from house to house, at crossroads, in taverns, and in the company of drunkards!
They say that the fame of Mātaṅgadivākara, though it does not even enter the interior of his home, is a virtuous wife;
yet poets declare your fame to be a virtuous wife who wanders at will through the three worlds.
O Lord, your paternal grandmother was the Earth, and immediately after her,
your mother was Saṃbhūti. Now, for the sake of your victory,
she herself shall become your irreproachable daughter-in-law once again in a hundred years.
It is indeed fitting that this [work] belongs to the Lords of the World, who are masters of all the scriptures.
In the springtime, they delight in idleness like elephants; in summer, they are fond of sexual indulgence;
in the rainy season, they are intent on the waters of ponds; and in autumn, they loathe the water of wells.
O Lord of Men, may your enemies— who are languid with autumnal fevers and sluggish with winter sleep,
and whose bodies are being wasted away by their own vices— not survive.
[He saw] the slender wife of the physician Haricandra, who had abandoned her household duties, whose voice was faltering, who bore horripilation,
who was trembling, whose lips were wounded, who was naked, and who was emitting long-drawn sibilant sounds.

And with both arms, as if out of fear of the falling essence of their own teeth, they embrace their own forms tightly around the neck— forms that are like beloved wives to those who hate you, and which are intensely passionate.

O Lord of the Earth, it is truly marvelous that your generosity is more firm than the fame of a cloud that has shed its water, and your majesty is greater than the heat of a sword that has lost its edge.
O King, you bear no outward mark, nor do you boast; you do not signal your desire to give, yet you release the fruits of goodness like the silent rain of a cloud.
Your favor will surely be made manifest through its very fruit.
This Indra of Mātṛgupta is one whose wrath is restrained; he is the burner who is yet a purifier, and though he is the Ender, he is the giver of wealth;
he delights in celestial chariots, he is the wielder of the noose, and the lord of the waters.
He who is the wind that carries away desire, and he who is the Rākṣasa Nairṛta— O Guardian of the World, there is no one else on earth who could be equal to you in virtues.
O Lord of the gods, Indra, the glory of Śrībakas, which was prepared for sovereignty over the eastern quarter,
has extinguished the pride of the white splendor of all the mountains, shining upon every limb.
Is that reflection of the conch shell perhaps the beauty of a row of autumn clouds? Is it a synonym for the waters of the ocean of milk? Or is it a complete restatement of all [the white things]?

O King, by whom has this hand not been seen? It stands upon the peak of a mountain fortress whose ramparts are shattered by the blows of swords and whose water-jars are the heads of enemies; it scatters heaps of pearls from its position atop the turrets.
On the earth where horses have fallen in battle against the fourfold army, it seems to scatter seeds of fame, as if sowing them in the fertile soil of the battlefield.
The boatman crosses the waters of the ocean filled with fierce crocodiles;
he wanders in the supportless sky; and he ascends the difficult-to-traverse peaks of the mountains.
O Lord of Men, since your fame travels alone to the underworld (pātāla), crowded by swarms of serpents,
I consider the fear of women to be something artificial.
From the inner palace of Karṇa— whose face was eclipsed by the blinding darkness censured by the unrestrained clouds,
whose tresses were disheveled by the fierce and auspicious marks of one who stays awake at night,
and who was like a forest fire to the fresh water-clouds that were his enemies— [the messenger departed].
O lotus-eyed one, you have arrived; I believe this fear of women is feigned.
She is renowned throughout the three worlds as the River of the Gods; she is the crest-jewel of the Sambhu family, possessing virtues as stainless as the essence of the moon.
That [glory] would be fit for comparison with Your Majesty’s fame; otherwise, it would be constantly reduced to a state of constant downward motion due to the weight of the marks of a sovereign.
At the mere sound of Kṛṣṇaka’s name, the mountain range of the quarters trembles, the golden mountain shakes, the earth quivers,
and all the oceans in every direction are struck with fear.
O crest-jewel of kings, while you hold aloft the blade of *darbha* grass for the sake of giving, the Lord of Treasures approaches Laṅkā with trepidation and falls into deep apprehension.

O Sun, when the forest fire— having reached the sole refuge of the dense forest of clouds— takes hold of the mass of smoke in whichever direction it may be; at that time, [the world] becomes like the state of one who has entered the southern hell (Dākṣiṇātya).
This, however, is merely the proper conduct of those two who were already conquered by the splendor of your arms;
fie on that forest fire which, out of fear, entered the water only to emerge from both sides again!

O Lord, your enemies—whose limbs were drenched by the rain of arrows discharged from the bow—crossed the ocean of existence in battle; having first caused the destruction of their boat, they reached the shore after sinking it without even a rudder.
"O King, these two are always like my own life-breath to me, and that monarch always regards me as equal to his own eyes"—
it is as if the golden ornaments on the ears of supplicants exist merely to proclaim the king's own exhaustion.
Misfortune abandons those whose bodies possess a reddish-brown luster from contact with the beautiful golden ground beloved by you,
as if out of fear of the rising heat, just as it flees from those who seek fire when it blazes.
O Bilhana,
you bear this entire moon upon your face, yet it is without a single mark;
whereas that cruel double-tongued serpent does not fall upon your ear nor upon your crest.
Although this abundance of yours produces no prosperity for those who are harsh,
from where does this unprecedented and faultless universality of yours come?
May the mark on the moon, the throat-base of the conqueror of Tripura, the chest of Murāri,
and the temples of your elephants, beautiful with the flow of rut-fluid, [grant you prosperity].
O tilaka of the earth’s circle, even today these regions appear as if smeared with the darkness [of night]; tell me, have they been whitened by your glories?
O *kurabaka* tree, you shall be separated from the pleasure of being struck by the breasts of the King’s crest-jewel; O *bakula*, the sprinkling of wine upon your face must be remembered by you.

"The world will become empty of moving beings and vessels; he who departs shall be the cause of grief for those already grieving"—thus did the wives of his enemies lament at his departure from his own city.

How could there even be the possibility of this sun, with its intensely red rays, arising from the Jewel-Mine (the ocean) even in a dream? This is surely a ruse devised through an affection for the morning waters.
By you, whose noble self is white with the cool and sweet activity that produces intense bliss,
this shattered world has surely been restored to its former state this very day.
Śrī Kallaṭa,

whose intellect was drawn toward the ultimate meaning, who composes verses with a mind focused on the Word (śabda), and whose soul is occupied with the process of discerning the junctures and the rules for their emergence— [to him this salutation].
May that fear which arises for a poet— like that of a thief who looks about repeatedly with apprehension, thinking, "Let no one here catch me"— be yours, O enemies!
For one who is full of apprehension, whose mind is utterly bewildered, whose luster has completely faded, whose limbs are exhausted, whose heart trembles, whose veins are prominently visible,
who abandons shame, reflects upon the sequence [of events], and perceives many obstacles;
The affliction that arises in those who desire wealth when they wish to speak—that shall be yours among your enemies.
“O good poet, friend, please recite again this verse of mine;
its meaning is repetitive, and there is yet another such construction here, O sir!”— thus,
by these clever words, the excellent vine of his pride was completely severed.
O King, let your enemies meet with that very suffering which poets say comes upon those who go astray.
The gates are guarded by staff-bearers, and even outside, the grounds are occupied by elephants with temples flowing with rut;
within, the floors are presided over by chamberlains wearing shimmering jewels;
and the bedchamber itself is occupied solely by the queens of those who hate you.
O King, this very long-standing principle remains the foundation for the stability of the kingdom, even in times of emptiness.
"Why do you not come before me with a smile? It has been a long time since I last saw you.
O heartless one, by whom have you been driven away, this love for wandering? These were the words of yours in dreams, when your throat was clasped by the embrace of your beloved."
Having realized this, she weeps: "The enemy's women have become as empty as my own pair of arms."
"O fickle one, why do you now weep with a heart torn by remorse, having abandoned that very Rañjanakamaṇḍa as your beloved? Thus,
with eyes like torrents of rainwater, [you weep] in the empty city of your enemies."
Beholding you depicted in a painting before them, travelers obtain a vision of your splendor.
O King, because they have been struck down by you, the lord of the opposing realm, and are terrified, these kings do not display their various great weapons in battle; rather,
with their crowns bowed low from afar, they merely present themselves before you.
The rainbows on the earth were formed by heaps of jewels of various shapes and actions.
Why was this form of Hari, which is without beginning, middle, or end, not described by the Sage, the son of Satyavatī?
For the sky-dwellers, seeing the sun of the battlefield thus engaged in uprooting the army of the thorn of the universe, feel great trepidation.

These [qualities] belong to him who, by bestowing his fortune upon some, dispels the darkness of the night with his splendor, overcomes the fire of poison and other such things through his power, and possesses various other virtues such as these.
"O King, you touch with your feet those jewels which all [other] kings bear upon their heads because they are worthy of praise;
oh, what a fruit of policy has been obtained by you!"

O God, is he not like the ocean, the abode of beings from whom nectar is bestowed; is he not like Mount Mandara, the source of beauty; is he not like Mount Sumeru, whose nature is auspicious; and is he not like the gods, who are the refuge for the celestial drink?
O Kalpavṛkṣa, although you possess shade and are not like the *rūdhadustara* creeper,
and although people compare you to them, the intellects of foolish poets nevertheless [strive] against yours.
O Lord, your desires are never frustrated even in dreams; you never cause suffering to those who seek your favor; the double-tongued serpents are not dear to you;
you do not possess many bodies, nor is your single form ever preoccupied with favoring the ignorant; your vision is never partial, and yet you are renowned on earth as a sovereign lord.
O King, prosperity is adorned by your intellect, and that intellect is further adorned by your learning;
your learning is distinguished by supreme knowledge of policy, and that policy is graced by your valor.
Your valor is enhanced by your glory, your glory by your deeds, and your deeds by your majesty.
Fire has arisen from its own family, and that family too is praiseworthy because of your birth.
Having roared from afar and risen high, the clouds release their water;
even for a noble elephant, a state of rut arises at the time of musth;
and by shedding their floral garments, trees generally yield their fruits.
For you who are engaged in giving, there is no pride, no intoxication, and no squandering.
The boundary rules of these two are maintained by both;
this earth is supported by both, and both are followed by beings and by serpents, like two oceans of jewels.
Thus, between you and the ocean, who possess equal qualities, there is one great distinction:
by virtue of your extreme loveliness, you are charming, whereas he is merely distasteful.
Some were bound; others were led face downwards; some were impaled;
and even those who had amassed great wealth were forcibly stripped of everything.

Others, having somehow escaped from their bonds after a long time, are now without support; yet these enemies bear upon themselves the mechanism of your discus, which is like a machine for pulverizing iron jars.
They were brought to ruin by the torment of your hand, cast down from their thrones,
struck as if by thunderbolts; they were scorched by the eternal fire of your majesty,
which has made even the elements its abode, and bound with coils of ropes around their necks, they were forced back again to the earth.
O Lord, the earthen jars have now been shattered; what is the use of looking at these shards?
Some become crows fed by others, some wander the earth as vultures;
others take on the form of weavers' birds, while others are born as quails in the forest;
some indeed become wagtails through their perilous journeys along the roads—alas!
Even when your enemies were reduced to the state of animals, they did not achieve the elevation of their wings.
Now, as they walk, their faces are washed by tears falling like water, and the ground is strewn with darbha grass by their feet from which blood drips from toes tender as lotuses;
these wives of your enemies, terrified, now hold onto the hands of their husbands.
They wander all around the forest fire once more, as if their wedding ceremony were being performed anew.
That the ocean has become composed of salt is a supreme affliction;
that this earth, though adorned with all auspicious marks, appears as a mere spot;
and that the wish-fulfilling gem of Brahmā, which grants the fruits of every desire, has become heartless.
The mind that does not realize reality acts with a well-guarded intention.
It is no wonder that Fortune dwells in a lotus where the pollen-dust is stirred by breezes laden with the fragrance of spring blossoms, for that is beautiful by its very nature.
But it is truly marvelous that she should cling to the sharp sword-blade, dripping with the blood from the throats of her enemies.
She has been dwelling with you for a long time; even though she is a woman, she remains joyful.
Slender-bodied, free from blemishes, adorned with pearls, possessing excellent hips, walking with the gait of an elephant, her skin bristling with thrill and illuminated by the luster of her teeth;
