dark-complexioned, with beautiful breasts, most radiant, she captivates the hearts of men.
O Desire, may your words fall day after day upon the edge of the sword of your enemy.
They go to a great station; supreme prosperity arises upon the earth for them.
Their own family is adorned by them; by them alone is the land won.
At their gate, throngs of horses neigh daily, fully caparisoned.
Those who have been seen by you, the Supreme Lord, whether in a state of pleasure or anger.

In that garden-ground of battle, where the earth was tilled by the hooves and mouths of horses, it blossomed with showers of water from the streams of blood flowing profusely from the throats of heroes when struck, and with pearls scattered from the splitting of the frontal globes of intoxicated elephants.
O Victorious One, the Glory of Victory has become the fruit upon the creeper of your sword, possessing a heart-delighting taste of incomparable flavor.
In a vast celestial palace, reclining upon an excellent couch illuminated by radiant jewel-lamps, he—
his body bristling with horripilation from the touch of his beloved’s pair of high breasts—
stirred his hand, eager to release her garment in a dream.
Meanwhile, he was awakened by the tip of a bamboo staff that had pierced the edge of his mat as it lay at the end of the couch.
The splendor of the honey-colored luster of the madhūka flowers resting in jeweled bowls has not been attained,
nor has the brilliance of the stainless earrings adorning the cheeks of celestial nymphs;
thus, in the pleasure-pool of the palace of your enemy, the forest elephants have been uprooted.
The blue lotus seems to weep aloud with the humming of bees wandering among its filaments.
I am not equal to him who forcibly brought the world under his control without guile; I am not the Lord of the Tretā age, for I have never been one who seizes the wives of others.
What rivalry could I have with the Dvāpara age? I am no god who slays his own kin, sons, friends, and relatives.
O King, thus does the Kali age mock the Kṛta and other ages under the pretext of your glory.
Sarasvatī always dwells within the lotus-face of some; your lower lip is such [a face],
while your right arm is the ocean, skillful in evoking the memory of the prowess of Kakutstha.
O King, these mares, accustomed to carrying you and long familiar with you, do not at all cease their constant neighing; yet, since your inner mind is so pure, how can you have a desire for water?
In every direction, the splendor of the sprouts of his emerging hair is like that of young elephants;
here, in the depths of the netherworld (pātāla), the exceedingly white hoods of the lord of serpents have sprouted forth from their roots.
O Lord, in this expanse of space, this orb of the moon— moist with nectar—
is the fruit that the creeper of your fame bears, appearing as clusters of blossoming stars.
By their deeds, which extended from the world of the gods down to the city of the underworld, bringing new splendor to the earth, how was whiteness not brought about?
Moreover, for these women who hate their lovers during separation from their husbands,
those very nail-marks have been turned into ornaments that possess a pale whiteness.
Whose heart has not been pierced by that very same arrow of love, whose limbs are bathed in passion, which is firmly fixed,
and which was seen falling even upon elephants from the hands of other men?
"Attached to him, this man reckons nothing; let it be known to you that I have been given by him to his servants.
Thus spoke her fame, as if departing for the ocean through its connection with Śrī.
O Lord,
this sword is the power within your pair of arms; O mine of faults,
this magnificent scimitar dwells by your side like a great female companion.
O noble one, your fame shines forth before you, reaching everywhere; why then do you speak thus to me with such anger? For by your fame, the quarters have been rendered white as conch shells.
O Father, that lack of support of mine, my lack of familiarity with others,
my envy toward others, and likewise that innate fickleness arising from the playful movements of my eyebrows— all of which were censured by the world—
have now vanished through union with a virtuous husband; I am no longer to be pitied.
Your fame has gone to the ocean as if to speak with Lakṣmī in private.

"You were created by the Creator with joy and curiosity, through concentrated meditation that set aside his own Vedic recitations and completed all his ascetic penances— for the sake of subduing the arrogant, for the victory of the world, for the prosperity of those who beg, for the honoring of the virtuous, for the welfare of the great, and for the distress of kings."
This [Lord] is a poet of the highest order, possessing a splendor devoid of the letter 'a', free from destruction, partaking in the delight of yoga,
valorous, equal to the universe, and one whose form is elevated by the playful grace of eyes like lotuses.
O God, may you— who possess various pure and perfect fame, whose body is pervaded by the elephant-goad, and who are composed of the essence of bliss—
become likewise for us enemies, starting from the very destruction of our first letter.
The glorious Bakasura,

whose noose was adorned with the splendor of the sun and the moon, whose flowers were clearly manifested as pearls from his union with the elephant-faced one (Ganesha), whose arms were like serpents emerging from the waters, and whose slough-like fame rested upon the peaks of the mountain ranges.
The sword in the hand of the Lord is like a cloud at the dissolution of the host of enemies, formidable with its wide-spreading torrent;
out of affection, it is the eye of the goddess Lakṣmī and the conqueror of the blue lotus.
Blinding the gods with the dust of someone’s hooves, deafening their ears with the sound of those hooves,
paralyzing the wind with the speed of his gallop, and silencing the virtues of the bards— [such is the horse].
O King, under your governance,
even a horse neighs joyfully as it touches with its hoof the earth, which is like a fresh lotus, for the sake of the world engaged in the acquisition of merit.
In the city of Vidrāṇa, where the squares and streets resound with battle cries and all are terrified,
even if some warrior, exalted by his fame, should turn back in anger,
he merely turns his face away as he approaches.
O King, by the stroke of your dagger, their heads were instantly severed and fell away.
His face, overwhelmed by extreme agitation, does not even glance at her; his body, devoid of a single hair, does not produce a row of horripilation—the very root of bliss;
and fearing a tremor of the knees, he does not move his head; we do not know why this is so.
O Śrī Kīrtipūṇa, how is it that the Lord of Serpents manifests his joy upon hearing from you?
O you who were born from the lineage of the Śubhus, dwelling in the caves of Giribila;
as you emerged, you were entreated by the auspicious words of your mother, whose mind was clouded by the grief of her own labor.

You cried out loudly, and as the reflections of the crescent moons of your eyes met with the tears of your weeping mother, she was both comforted and consoled by the smiles of her son, which brought relief through their close proximity.
In the arena of battle, the Gaṅgā—consisting of the stream of the fame of your two arms—met with the Yamunā, which was the river born from the Kalinda mountain of his ill-repute.
Then, having plunged into that [confluence], many warriors began a grand display of eagerness for the forest sports of the Nandana grove, which is the abode of the bliss of embracing Rambhā.

O Hero, who else is more valiant than you—whose fame is adorned with the application of sandalwood paste from the Malaya mountains upon the expanse of the earth bounded by the seven oceans; whose prowess as an archer is celebrated by the dense throngs of people dwelling beyond those seas; and whose moon-like nails rejoice in the service of the hands of the wives of the kings who have simultaneously fallen at your two feet?
These are the trees that provide shade for travelers on the ground of the far bank, in the Himalayan forest of Mālaya—
trees that are exceedingly tall and difficult to climb.
Ah, your mature glories wander upon Mount Mandara, amidst its great peaks and dense caves of the gods,
yet they do not fall!
O Earth,
bearing as you do the faults of all beings— such as the bowstring and the like— your exhaustion brings about some indescribable act of sport;
for we, the tortoises, having performed our assembly for the pleasure of grazing upon the tips of the sprouts of moss on your surface, find relief.
The noble elephants drink from the river of tranquility and wisdom flowing equally.
"O Menakā, why this silence? O Sacī, why do you bear such distress? Who is this Ghṛtācī?
And what is this, Rambhā?
For, apart from your own conduct, the lotus-faces of the women of the gods have not come within the range of my hearing."
Thus, O King, the words of her friends were released, like the fever of a harsh recollection.
He who was Nala by his roar of enmity, a Nala who was a lamp for the earth; he who was Dilīpa, a protector of the earth;
he who was Pṛthu in his pride, yet Pṛthu (vast) in the world; he who was Rāghava, free from all levity;
he who was Bharata, delighted in fame; and he who was Śantanu through his royal virtues.
O Lord of the Earth, once you were born, whom among them all have you not forgotten?
Alas, O Lord, when the interior of the quarters has been flooded even by day with your glories— as if with camphor, as if with mercury, as if with streams of nectar—
the moon,
having donned its armor of constellations and placed Mādhava [the sun] before it as its charioteer, [emerges].
Desire rushes forth, shaking its bow with the thought that it is the rising of the moon, the friend of the night-lotus.
O Lord, today, as your moon— white as the crescent moon, having washed away the orb of the sun, and beloved by the world— pervades the expanse of the sky and dispels the dense darkness,
the mountains become like Mount Kailāsa, the serpents like Śeṣa, and the oceans like the great sea.
The rut-fluid flows from the elephants of the divine islands, and the male cuckoos act as swans.
O Caitra, do not remember; forget the memory of Rati; what is the use of Cupid’s arrows? O simpleton, why do you bind the lizard? And cast away the bow, firm as it is with its string-fastened grip!
For when this God is remembered even for a moment, there is neither thought, nor memory, nor stability.
For those with beautiful brows, there is neither attachment, nor steadfastness, nor even peace anywhere.
How is it that this wife of your enemy, who was once a marvel as she walked upon her own ground with her feet adorned by jeweled anklets,
now crawls along the earth, bristling with thorns?
In solitude, with a well-defined line, he drew his own likeness upon a blank canvas; and with a mind full of conceptualization, he fashioned many elaborate mental constructions.
He beheld the doctrine of another creator and undertook a rigorous vow.
How much did the Creator not exert himself in the process of fashioning you?
When those stories of your beauty were being recounted by the gods— who showed contempt for Kandarpa, Nalakūbara, and even the lord of the night-lotuses— and who listened with curiosity,
Urvaśī grew weary of passion, Rati was ruined, and Rohiṇī was struck down.
And though her body is as slender as a plantain stalk, she has become one whose onset is the heavy burden of a fever of harsh longing.
Though full of longing, exerting effort, and intensely yearning, the gaze of the deer-eyed women does not go anywhere else, even toward the vicinity of their own pleasure-groves;
for today, by the sudden stroke of fortune, it is eclipsed by a complexion like that of a fresh elephant tusk.
The darkness has come to an end—that darkness which was as black as the mass of hair of beautiful women.
He perceives his own excellence in speech, masters supreme eloquence,
composes perfect verses, and gains familiarity with the path of resonance;
he discerns the manifold variety in the art of expression in the presence of Vācaspati himself.
O King, for the sake of praising your virtues, what indeed does the Goddess of Speech not perform?
Your glories flow as streams of sandalwood paste upon the heart, stream as waves of nectar upon the body, and flow as elixirs of rejuvenation within the ears;
they spread as a carpet of pearls across the expanse of the earth and shine like the moon at the heights of the sky.
O ornament of the three worlds, is it that the night has dawned with the rays of the moon, or has it risen with pearls?
Is it that the jasmine buds have blossomed into smiles, or have the *mālatī* buds opened?
Has the earth been covered by the playful laughter of beautiful women, or by the flowing streams of nectar? For there, where your fame wanders, these things appear as such.
The faces of the quarters are not unrestrained, nor is the expanse of the sky like a forest grove;
the surface of the earth is not elevated, nor is the earth itself the floor of the netherworld.
O King, how is it that these [directions] have become as white as the tusks of an elephant severed by you?
And his glories, which pour forth streams of the nectar of sacred revelation, move and play at their own will.
Magnanimity is the way in accomplishing one's purpose; modesty resides in the virtuous, as does it in a woman of noble family;
refined poetry dwells in the mouth; intoxication in the elephant; the male cuckoo in the forest;
the bee in the lotus; and the scratching of fingernails upon the cheek of a beloved.
O Lord, you who are slender upon the surface of your bed are likewise an ornament upon the surface of the earth.

The throats of your enemies' fair-browed women are choked by the exhaustion from the rays of the sun, their eyes are narrowed by the swirling clouds of dust, and they utter cries of "sīt" as the tips of their white garments are torn away; thus, out of fear of the forest-dwellers, there arises a flood of sighing waves.
"O King, such is the manner of amorous play appropriate for desert lands."

If that splendor which exists in the moon, that depth which exists in the ocean, that majesty which exists in Mount Meru, that loftiness of power which exists in the lotus-stalk, and that quality of valor which exists in the lover of Lakṣmī—were all these combined in one place; ||| Subhv_2624-3 ||| ... [then he would be like that]. ||| Subhv_2624-4 ||| If even such a person were to become angry with me, what need is there to speak of others? ||| Subhv_2624-5 ||| For this reason, O King, I am not afraid of anyone else. ||| Subhv_2624-6 ||| But I am afraid of you, who possess such a nature. ||| Subhv_2624-7 ||| And because of that fear, I have come to you, O Lord of the Earth. ||| Subhv_2624-8 ||| Therefore, O King, grant me protection. ||| Subhv_2624-9 ||| For one who has sought refuge, there is no other protector than you. ||| Subhv_2624-10 ||| Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the King's Majesty. ||| Subhv_2624-11 ||| Then the king, having heard those words, spoke thus to the sage: ||| Subhv_2624-12 ||| "O Sage, I do not know the cause of your fear. ||| Subhv_2624-13 ||| Tell me truly, by whom are you afraid? ||| Subhv_2624-14 ||| Then the sage, having reflected for a moment, spoke these words: ||| Subhv_2624-15 ||| "O King, I am not afraid of anyone else. ||| Subhv_2624-16 ||| But I am afraid of you, who possess such a nature. ||| Subhv_2624-17 ||| And because of that fear, I have come to you, O Lord of the Earth. ||| Subhv_2624-18 ||| Therefore, O King, grant me protection. ||| Subhv_2624-19 ||| For one who has sought refuge, there is no other protector than you. ||| Subhv_2624-20 ||| Then the king, having heard those words, spoke thus to the sage: ||| Subhv_2624-21 ||| "O Sage, I do not know the cause of your fear. ||| Subhv_2624-22 ||| Tell me truly, by whom are you afraid? If you desire to see him, behold this god, the jewel of the three worlds, appearing here from this very place.

He is celebrated in the world as Trivikrama because of your three strides; by him alone was Bali slain, whose hundred arms were shattered. Who in this world does not know that Vaikuṇṭha? You, however, are unimpeded in conquering even the earth.
There is indeed a great difference between you and that god, the enemy of the Daityas.
O Lord, the wish-fulfilling creepers bathe [the assembly] with showers of nectar; they provide a continuous stream of water dripping from the sandalwood trees,
and they adorn the Mandāra vines with thick drops of moonlight.
Today, the celestial maidens in the courtyard of heaven do not sprinkle [themselves with sandalwood water], out of fear of the fire of your majesty.
O King, wandering through wildernesses, forests, and riverbanks, amidst the laps of the earth’s expanses, in cities, and on the shores of the ocean—
those who possess the luster of the inner buds of *ketaka* flowers wander like you, O Lord of the Earth.
Your glories grow upon the lovely outskirts of the Nandana grove, amidst the young sprouts of its trees.
"Is this the rising of the moon? Or is it the white mountain, the Guru?
Is this the ocean of milk? Or is it the serpent sporting in its play with the Triple-City destroyer?
Or do I think this is the Manyā mountain, washed by the waves of the ocean of nectar?"
In your fame, embodied beings dwelling in the cities and palaces of the earth have become filled with doubt.
These poets— who bathe in the wondrous flood of the pure, victorious fame of Śambhuka, which is like the ocean— what [others] would not be constrained by silence?
He who, having entered the water, surpasses the moon in the beauty of his drops and remains invisible to the eye—
he is the Lord of Speech, the deity of the waters, who awakens upon the crystal ground.
O you whose fame has washed clean the entire three worlds, even all those who have become dark with the soot of worldly existence find rest in their conversations about your renown; yet, alas,
from my own infamy, there has arisen a burden of existence consisting of that very same fame!
Yet this [shadow], with its soiled appearance, remained fixed even upon the path of his speech.
He is the protector of the virtuous;
moreover, he alone takes singular delight in supreme merit.
He is a planet in its proper place, devoted to the path favored by the Guru.
His hand constantly touches the necklaces of hundreds of millions [of people];
he gives away his entire wealth as if it were a blade of grass; thus he triumphs over the Lord of the Gods.
O Subandhu, this Kṛṣṇa causes me daily the pain of churning; what is the use of serving him while he sleeps?
I must serve another who possesses supreme wisdom through inner knowledge and is eternally awake.
O King, having observed this and seeing that your fame has thus reached such a state, the ocean itself has come here, as if under the guise of the moon, solely for the sake of serving you.
This verse was composed by me, Śrī Baka, for the sake of Jainaullābha and others, and it is dedicated to Āturi;
it was written in the month of Vārīḍa during the winter season.
In the sky, at the time of the auspicious festival of the autumnal clouds, there appeared a cloud as beautiful as a lovely woman;
as it wandered through the firmament,
it was like a rain of flowers from the celestial nymphs in the world of heaven.
It pervades the earth with the guise of frost, like the moon.
O illustrious Bhūramaṇendra, it was precisely this [Rāhu] that, arrogant with the poison of your fame,
instead of approaching you with devotion, became enraged and attempted to swallow the moon when it had come within his grasp.
This very person, having consumed excellent food, is seen to be emaciated by its digestion in his stomach;
I think that because of this, he has gone to the abode of the two rivers of beauty and modesty.
The completion of the verse with three quarters is as follows: "Is it out of fear of the consequence of meaninglessness regarding the words of Śrī Baka’s heart, or rather,
out of a desire for the purpose of creating a young woman?"
O Lord of Men, at the beginning of creation, Brahmā exerted himself to establish his own consciousness as more highly esteemed.
While the illustrious Lord of the Earth protects the netherworld (pātāla), the hooded serpents protect it;
while Indra rules the celestial realm, the immortals enjoy the sacrificial feast.
While you, whose fame is renowned, always protect this earth, O Subhūti,
all people obtain soft food, fine garments, and great happiness.

O King, may the lord of serpents, his body rippling with joy, sing your fame in the musical assemblies of the serpent queens; for that fame which exists within the range of their eyes is sufficient to satisfy even a hundred eyes.
While being sung from all sides by passionate celestial beauties, he whose two ears are like moons will not hear it; for how could he, who possesses a thousand eyes, have ears that function as eyes?
O Murāri,
while standing near the churning mountain and bearing the celestial river (Gaṅgā) upon his head, you, the beloved of Śrī,
remained hidden in the ocean even as she flowed along.

O Hero, I believe that the lotus-born Brahmā, seeing that your future prowess would be exceedingly great like a fire, has submerged himself in the mud of the lotus-pond while carrying her [the Earth] in his water-pot.

O King, the sparks from the explosion of the mass of fame— which has been shattered by the intense heat of the flames of your majesty arising from the pride and weight of your staff-like arms— are these:
how many Śeṣas, how many stars, how many oceans of milk, and how many snow-mountains,
conch-shells, pearl-oysters, camphor, jasmine, and moons?
These two belong to Śrī Hanumān.
Now, the Path of Ethics:
If it is not possible to follow the entire path of the virtuous, one should at least follow a small portion of it; one who stands upon the path does not come to ruin.
Supreme is assistance; supreme is the Dharma; supreme is skill in action. Supreme is giving to a worthy recipient; supreme is desire; supreme is liberation through detachment.

That which is without substrate is the Dharma; that which is not contradictory is the meaning (artha). That which is free from attachment is desire (kāma); that which is non-rebirth is liberation (mokṣa).
Ignorance is the enemy of knowledge; mental cultivation is the enemy of worldly existence.
Generosity is the destroyer of poverty; ethical discipline is the destroyer of miserable rebirths.
Even when one has reached an advanced age, knowledge should be grasped with all one's being by the wise;
for if it does not bear fruit in this life, it will bear fruit in another birth.
Fortune does not approach one who is excessively noble, excessively generous, excessively devoted to vows,
or who is arrogant in his wisdom, out of fear.
Those who are not lazy attain their goals, nor do those who are impotent or arrogant;
nor do those who fear public rumor, nor those who are ever-opposed.
He who restrains anger and pride as soon as they arise,
and he who is not bewildered in times of adversity— he is the vessel of prosperity among men.

Prosperity attends one who has conquered the senses, who has mastered himself, who wields the rod of punishment with firmness toward the fickle, and who acts only after careful deliberation— such a steadfast man she serves most devotedly.
Fortune dwells with that man who provides for the future, who is vigilant, free from anger, diligent in his undertakings, and undaunted.
While living, the enemies within the body, such as the eyes and other senses, are difficult to conquer;
once they are conquered, indeed, this entire world has been conquered by you.
If you wish to bring the world under your control by a single deed,
ward off from those who speak ill of others the cow as she grazes.
Even a friend is an enemy to him whose self is ill-governed; wholesome food, when indigestible, leads either to disease or to death.
Even if a coward is fleeing, he should not be pursued by one who is stronger;
for he may sometimes attain valor when resolved upon death.
One should not practice excessive harshness toward those who are radiant and endowed with splendor;
for fire is produced even from the friction of sandalwood.
What can a spirited person accomplish, even if capable, when lacking companions?
Like a fire blazing in a windless place, it will extinguish itself.
He who, having created enmity with a powerful person, does not protect himself,
will find that it leads only to his own ruin, like unwholesome food that has been consumed.
One becomes dear for a reason, and one becomes an object of hatred for a reason; this world of living beings seeks its own interest—no one is dear to anyone by nature.
By nature, there is no such thing as an enemy, nor does a friend exist;
it is through the application of circumstances that friends and enemies arise.
Without causing distress to others, without resorting to the behavior of the wicked,
and without abandoning the path of the virtuous— even that which is very little is much.
Just as unwanted sufferings come upon embodied beings, so too do pleasures; I consider that in this matter, only wretchedness exceeds all else.
What has not been, will not be; what has been, cannot be otherwise.
Why is this medicine, which destroys the host of anxieties, not drunk?
Those beings who are destined to exist within me shall come;
I am to be followed by them, but their path is not that of the common multitude.

Trade is based on the thought "there is wealth"; agriculture is based on the thought "there is something [to be gained]"; service is based on the thought "there is nothing [of one's own]"; and courage is based on the thought "I do not exist."
The ocean does not become needy by its lack of water, nor is it filled up by waters;
rather, the self must be made into a worthy vessel, for prosperity comes to such a vessel.
One should destroy mental suffering through wisdom and physical suffering through medicines;
having understood this capacity, one should not equate it with that of fools.
For a man who is separated from sons, friends, or kinsmen, or deprived of wealth,
or submerged in calamity and hardship, fortitude is what brings about his ultimate welfare.
One who is suffering should look upon those with greater suffering, and one who is happy should look upon those with greater happiness;
one should not subject oneself to joy or sorrow as if to enemies.
Even a man who is wise and brave is deluded by supernatural power;
it is my view that everyone, being immersed in present pleasure, does not perceive this.
Those goals which are achieved through the affliction of the body or by transgressing the Dharma, or by bowing down before an enemy— do not set your mind upon them.
Effort should be made toward virtues; what is the use of external remedies?
Cows devoid of milk do not produce it simply by being struck with hammers.
Virtues are indeed virtues alone; they are not the causes of wealth.
For it is destiny alone that brings about the accumulation of riches.
Indeed, qualities are merely qualities; they are not the causes of results.
A bow with its string is without fruit, while the arrow without a string bears fruit.
When the bestowal of virtues depends on oneself, there is blame for a lack of virtue; but when wealth depends on fate, what blame indeed can there be for a man?
That Lakṣmī should show affection for even a moment toward one who lacks self-control is, according to the sage Bhagavadvyāsa,
merely the fickleness of womanhood, occurring by the logic of the "falling of the crow's eye" (a rare and chance occurrence).
A eunuch does not even know how to enjoy accumulated wealth;
a rustic man becomes detached even while seeking to please a passionate woman.
That they sometimes disregard an evildoer even though they are capable of uprooting them completely is not due to folly;
rather, it is a strategic means.
If the kind of understanding that arises in one who has experienced suffering were to exist previously,
for whom would the arising of the fruit not occur?
Even the ignorant attain the state of the wise; even a mountain is gradually worn away. Even a mouse eats a great tree—behold the power of persistent practice!
Blessed are those tigers among men who, by means of their intellect, restrain rising anger—
just as one quenches a great, blazing fire with water.
Knowing "I am great," one should not transgress against a Mahāsattva;
for does not the lion seize even an elephant with his two paws?
The wind is a friend to the fire that consumes the forest;
yet for that very same fire when its fuel is exhausted, who shows it such kindness?
Even one who is like the Omniscient One in virtue remains solitary and without support;
even a priceless ruby requires gold as its setting.
Having observed the decline of Ravigupta,
the exhaustion of añjana, and the accumulation of an anthill,
one should make each day fruitful through acts of giving, study, and virtuous deeds.
Whoever desires a certain goal and strives for that goal will certainly attain it, provided they do not turn back out of weariness.
A crawling ant may travel even hundreds of yojanas,
while even Vainateya, though flying, does not go a single step without moving.
For indeed, the remedy for calamities must be sought at their very onset;
it is not appropriate to dig a well once the house is already ablaze with fire.
A person recognizes the true essence of friends, kinsmen, and relatives, as well as of one's own intellect and fortitude, when they are being crushed by the weight of misfortune.
For one who stands firm in all circumstances, a friend and kinsman in times of distress is difficult to find;
those who offer kinship in adversity are true friends and kinsmen.
That friend assists one who is distressed and has failed in their purpose;
he is not skilled in finding fault with the past actions resulting from one's misdeeds.
"Even hair, which has been constantly held upon the head and protected with affection, becomes discolored;
how much more so that which does not undergo such transformation?"
Insult is constant suffering, and enmity toward the harsh is constant pain;
therefore, having abandoned these two, one should resort to the middle way.
For even by gentle means, one's own goals are accomplished through action;
the slender-limbed leech drinks blood for her own satisfaction.
Indeed, no such enchantment exists within the three worlds as generosity,
loving-kindness toward all beings, compassion, and sweet speech.
But one who has conceived enmity toward a powerful person always sleeps in misery,
with an uneasy mind, like one in a house with a snake.
He who gladdens the world through four means— by deed, by mind, by speech, and by eye— the world in turn gladdens him.
One should engage in eating together, conversation, inquiry, and social gathering with one's kinsmen; one should never harbor any hostility toward them under any circumstances.
This alone is the essence of life, which is fragile by its very nature and perishing in an instant:
that one remains unrestrained in the company of those who are affectionate, innocent, and wise.
Wives have been shown in the home, food has been eaten without hesitation, and secrets have been told; what greater sign of friendship could there be than this?
It is a vessel for joy and confidence amidst sorrow, distress, fear, and terror;
the secrets have been told—what greater friendship could there be than this?
The kind of trust that men place in a constant friend is not found toward a mother, nor toward wives,
nor toward brothers or other kinsmen.
Even toward those who are not kinsmen, the state of kinship arises through affection;
yet even toward one's own kinsmen, that state of kinship is lost when they lack knowledge of the world.
One who is honored by one's own kin here is highly esteemed even by others;
for a man who is despised by his own kin may be overcome even by an outsider.
When those who know [the truth] desire to speak words that are bitter and harsh,
the wise person should pacify them with gentle speech, even when their hearts are full of anger.
An enemy who is beneficial is a kinsman, while a kinsman who is harmful is an enemy;
a disease born of the body is harmful, whereas the medicinal herbs of the forest are beneficial.
Even a mouse born in one's own home must be killed if it is harmful;
yet a cat that provides milk is sought after from elsewhere as a benefactor.
One should abandon a wicked person who has cast off affection and is devoid of love—
even a uterine brother, let alone an ordinary stranger.
But if there should be one who has been a benefactor in the past, even when a great injury is committed against him,
that offender should be forgiven for the sake of that previous benefit.
But if, having spoken what was born of the Buddha, they should say it was not born of the Buddha,
he would strike them down for even a slight evil, even for such a transgression, because they are upright.
The former is great among the noble, while the latter is found among the ignoble; since this is inverted among the ignoble, do as you wish.

One should always sit with the virtuous, one should associate with the virtuous, and one should form marriages and cultivate friendship with the virtuous; one should never perform any action with the wicked.
Even those who are at odds with one another must dwell together as virtuous people who perceive the Dharma;
for even the faults of the virtuous are equal to the virtues of the wicked.
One's own nature (svabhāva) is to be observed with effort, and not other qualities;
for having transcended all qualities, one's own nature stands at the summit.
One should extract the essence from everywhere— just as gold is extracted from us— whether it be from the ravings of a madman or the crawling of an infant.
One who speaks kindly is not ugly; one should be a hero without being boastful. One should be a giver who does not rain gifts upon the unworthy, and one should be confident without being harsh.
"What would happen to me by doing this? What would happen to me by not doing it?"—having reflected thus with the mind, the wise person should either act or not act.
An action that has been scrutinized and examined by the wise is not only beautiful in times of prosperity,
but shines even in times of adversity.
A six-syllable mantra is never broken; a four-syllable mantra likewise is never broken. But as for a two-syllable mantra, even Brahmā cannot reach its end.
For those of firm resolve, success is unfailing when there is good counsel, courageous exertion, well-executed action, careful deliberation, and a successful undertaking.
A wise person should not undertake undertakings that are fruitless, those with disastrous consequences, those whose results are merely equal to the effort expended,
or those that are impossible to accomplish.
Whatever task is to be performed here by a man who is resolute, that task should be done without hesitation; for success rests upon destiny.
Prosperity that has been attained through the conjunction of fate, yet lacks the foundation of a firm vow, perishes quite suddenly—
just like an association with the wicked.
A self-possessed person should not abandon effort, thinking that it is all destiny;
for who can obtain oil from sesame seeds without exertion?
Where there are many leaders,
all of whom consider themselves wise, and all of whom desire greatness, that group perishes.
O Bhārata, when the father has died, the eldest brother is equal to a father;
for he shall be the provider of their livelihood and he shall protect them.
All, following his will, should pay homage to that youngest one and should depend upon him alone,
just as they would upon a father.
What is the use of that cow which neither yields milk nor bears calves?
What is the purpose of that son who is neither learned nor righteous?
Between children born dead and those who die at birth, sons born alive are better;
yet while those two cause some grief to their parents, the fool causes extreme grief.
It would be better to be childless than to have a son who is twice as wicked.
Even while living, one who is undisciplined is as good as dead; of this there is no doubt.
What is the use of a hundred sons devoid of virtue, even if they number a hundred? A single moon dispels the darkness, whereas a thousand stars cannot.
He whose fame is not celebrated for generosity, austerity,
or heroism, nor for learning or the acquisition of wealth, is merely his mother’s burden.
Whether it be water obtained without effort or food that is delicious yet fraught with fear— I truly perceive that happiness alone to be true happiness wherein there is liberation.
That which is separated suffers through affection; that which is united is broken by suffering. But that joy which consists of being both separated and united is not joined with affection.
One should not trust the untrustworthy, nor should one over-trust the trustworthy.
Danger arising from misplaced trust cuts down even the very roots.
When servants have increased their wisdom and valor yet act with deceit, the master,
trusting them and losing his vigilance, is deceived and oppressed.
Whose actions, whether proper or improper, are always the same— what wise person would place their trust in such a foolish one whose soul is devoid of integrity?
The thought "I have committed no offense" is not a ground for confidence;
for even those possessed of virtue may find themselves in fear of human beings.
Some have the faces of deer while being tigers, and some have the faces of tigers while being deer;
indeed, such a perversion of one's true nature is a path to calamities.
Praising others, lack of diligence in one's own duties, and resentment toward those who recognize merit— these three are indeed the paths to calamity.
Whatever can be swallowed as a morsel, and whatever, once swallowed, is digestible;
and whatever is wholesome during digestion—that is what should be eaten by one who desires well-being.
A wise person moves with one foot while keeping the other steady;
without having examined another place, one should not abandon one's former abode.
Indeed, the combination of many things that have little substance is difficult to overcome;
a rope is entwined with blades of grass, and by it even an elephant is bound.
If one wishes to do what is unpleasant even to many enemies, one should endow oneself with virtues; that is what is most deeply disliked by them.
What can the combined forces do to one whose body is protected by wisdom?
They are like torrents of rain against one who holds up an umbrella.
"That which is impossible cannot be accomplished even by one running with great speed;
yet the dull-witted man thinks, 'In a mere moment, I have been deceived.'"
When was it that our hair, once thick, became thin and fell away? For calamities indeed befall those whose very nature is to grow.
"Father, do not act rashly, for you are deluded by your riches;
even one's own limbs become a burden when they lead to calamity."
"O father, do not oppress this pitiable person, saying 'I am powerless';
let not those with eyes of compassion burn you like fire consumes fuel."
My dear son, do not place your trust in the thought, "I have now reached the pinnacle of prosperity," for a fall from such a high ascent is indeed terrible.
The man whom gamblers praise, whom spies praise,
and whom harlots praise— that man does not truly live.
Whoever, having generated the [vows of] abstinence and so forth, desires a reconnection [of the precepts],
for him no reconnection exists, just as there is none for a broken earthenware vessel.
Even when trumpeting, an elephant kills; even when smelling, a serpent kills;
even when laughing, a king kills; and even when showing honor, a wicked person kills.
Adopting the contraction of a tortoise, one should endure even blows;
at the proper times, however, the wise man should act like a black cobra.
One should carry this enemy upon one's shoulder for as long as time permits;
then, when the right moment has arrived, one should shatter him like a jar against a stone.
One should fear fear only as long as that fear has not yet arrived;
but having seen the fear that has arrived, one should strike it down like an enemy.
He who sleeps peacefully with full confidence, having made a secret pact with an enemy,
awakens like one who has fallen after sleeping atop the branch of a tree.
But whoever, having once committed an offense, desires to reconcile again, he embraces death just as one enters a womb for an uncertain duration.
One should not expect that all trees in the forest are exceedingly straight; go and see for yourself, where the straight ones are cut down, while the crooked ones stand at every step.
One who seeks to find what is unpleasant for another should always speak what is pleasant to them;
hunters sing melodiously and heartily in order to kill deer.
Fire destroys, fire destroys, and likewise the enemy destroys;
these recur again and again—therefore, one should practice the destruction of fire.
For no one perceives an agent apart from an action;
therefore, one should cause all actions to be performed with their respective results remaining.
The wise should not overlook an enemy, even if he is small, out of contempt;
for even a small fire, when it grows, reduces everything to ashes.
One should extract an enemy with the help of an even more formidable enemy,
just as one extracts a thorn embedded in the foot with another thorn held in the hand.
Some have perished through ignorance, some have perished through negligence;
some have perished through pride in their knowledge, while others have been destroyed by those very [faults].
A wise person should not trust someone who is at odds with him, thinking, "I am far away from him.
Long are the arms of the intelligent man, with which he strikes even from afar.
O King of kings, women are like cooked food, common property for all;
therefore, one should not be attached to them, nor should one trust them, nor rely on them.
O King, I do not believe that Maṭhara could be an ascetic, nor that Śūra was free from wounds, nor that a woman could be a drunkard.
One should cause an unfaithful wife— who has overstepped her authority, who is defiled, who subsists on mere alms, and who sleeps on a low bed— to dwell in a state of humiliation.
O King, the Creator fashioned four means [of restraint] out of silver;
he did not create even a fifth by which women might be held in check.
The minds of women are more fickle than the tip of an elephant’s trunk, than a sprout of the Pippala tree,
and even than the flickering play of lightning.
They converse with one man, look at another with amorous gestures, and think of yet another dwelling in their hearts; what indeed is dear to women?
That which is within is not on the tongue; that which is on the tongue is not outside. Women of diverse conduct do not reveal what is outside.
Neither by gifts, nor by honor, nor by honesty, nor by service,
nor by weapons, nor by scriptures are fickle women ever captured.
Women possess an incomparable purity; they never become defiled. For month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their misdeeds.
She is a wife who speaks kindly; he is a son where there is peace;
that is a friend in whom there is trust; and that is a land where one truly lives.
She should always remain joyful, skillful in her household duties,
keep the utensils well-maintained, and always be open-handed in generosity.

One should not indulge excessively with women; one should eat what is wholesome and avoid what is unwholesome. Being free from arrogance, one should honor those worthy of respect and serve one's teachers with sincerity.
One should not engage in sexual intercourse with women; wives must be protected with great effort.
If one does so, one becomes short-lived and contemptible; therefore, one should avoid them.
Women must indeed always be protected from even well-behaved and affectionate men;
for if they are not guarded, they will bring ruin upon two families.
One should not sit in seclusion with a mother, a sister, or a daughter;
for the assembly of the senses is powerful, and even a wise man may be deluded in this regard.
Women desire that man who seeks them out, approaches them,
performs services for them, and acts with devotion.
As soon as a husband realizes that his wife is devoted to the power of mantras,
he should tremble before her as if from a snake that has entered his house.
There is no sacrifice for women, nor any vow, nor fasting;
yet she who serves her husband well is exalted in heaven because of that.
One may enjoy drinking, gambling, women,
hunting, singing, and instrumental music with moderation, for addiction to these is indeed harmful.
Those for whom favor is fruitless and anger is likewise useless— such a person people do not desire as a master, just as women do not desire a eunuch as a husband.
Unrealities appear as realities, realities appear as unrealities, and various phenomena are seen as both real and unreal; therefore, investigation is appropriate.
O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, those heroes who act toward Brahmins, women, kinsmen, and cows as if they were mere straw—
like ripe fruit from a tree, they fall.
A person goes lower and lower or rises higher by their own actions alone,
just as a digger of a well or a builder of a palace [descends or ascends].
Even Bṛhaspati, if he speaks at an inappropriate time,
incurs only contempt for his intelligence and sheer disrespect.
What can even one with eloquent speech accomplish by instructing those who are unworthy vessels?
Even a carpenter with a sharp axe is frustrated when faced with rotten wood.
When one who has not heard the Dharma becomes negligent, that is not a deception;
for this is the very nature of the blind that they stumble even upon the wicked.
While these [fires] burn, the blazing fire of the sage Śrī Vyāsa protects the roots;
the gentle and cool torrent of water uproots them entirely.
One should recognize a friend in times of calamity, a hero in battle, and a pure person in private;
one should recognize a wife when wealth has diminished, and a beloved guest during a famine.
Having acquired [the kingdom] through merit and the sixfold approach, and protecting it with justice, he performs that which is superior to all other gifts: the protection of his subjects.
As if thinking, "There is no space within the hearts of virtuous women for anyone else," the Creator fashioned her two breasts so perfectly round on the outside.
O great sage, what fault is there in the darkening of a cloud at the onset of the rainy season? Tell me, where is the whiteness of an autumnal cloud of any use?
He who, transgressing the opinion of the virtuous, abides by the opinion of the wicked,
falls from his station due to that lack of distinction and comes under the power of the twice-born enemies.
Thinking "this is me," one should not cause even the most lowly person to suffer;
for even when struck mercilessly, a diamond emits sparks of light.
No one among the kings is dearer than Candakauśika;
even the fire, when it touches the Hotṛ priest while he is offering oblations, burns him not.
What is too heavy for the capable? What is distant for the persevering? What is a foreign land for the learned? Who is a stranger to those who speak kindly?
"For one who is indifferent to the body,
skillful, and persevering, and who undertakes his task according to the proper method, there is nothing whatsoever that is difficult to accomplish."

Neither doing a favor is a sign of a friend, nor is doing harm a characteristic of an enemy; rather, a mind that is either corrupted or uncorrupted is the defining characteristic of a friend or an enemy.
Through appearance, gestures, gait, movement, and speech, as well as through changes in the eyes and face, the mind within is known.
One should reflect again and again: "What is the time? Who are my friends? What is the place? What are my expenditures and income? What is my vehicle? And what is my capacity?"
It is better to uproot from the very root a thorn that has pierced, a loose tooth,
and a wicked minister.
If you will be devoted to the company of the virtuous, you will flourish; but if you fall into the assemblies of the wicked, you will perish.
He who,
being himself free from fault, casts blame upon others for their faults, and he who, though not deluded, becomes angry— he is considered the most foolish of fools.
Everyone is always skillful in criticizing the speech of others;
however, they do not know their own faults, or even if they do know them, they become deluded.
Whatever a person of small intelligence might say, the wise man should endure it all;
for what can mere worldly praise or blame accomplish?
That man who praises [the teacher] to his face but reviles him behind his back should be abandoned by one who desires to attain sovereignty in this world.
Generosity, patience, fortitude, wisdom, tranquility, steady speech, modesty, non-violence, freedom from addiction, and ritual bathing— these bring about happiness.
One should indulge in that pleasure which, even while being pursued, does not cause one to fall away from virtue and wealth;
one should not practice the conduct of a fool.
In every respect, wealth has its root in the Dharma, and the Dharma is bound to wealth;
know that these two are mutually dependent, like a cloud and the ocean.
O Brahmā, he who constantly pursues only sensual pleasure and does not attend to the other two goals is fit to be slain by the whole world and is loathed by the gods.
One must acquire wealth, increase it, and likewise protect it;
for even the Himalayas waste away if they are consumed without being replenished.
He who has wealth has friends; he who has wealth has kinsmen.
He who has wealth is a man in this world; he who has wealth is a wise man.
When a king behaves without distinction and treats his servants with equality,
then those who are incapable of exertion lose their enthusiasm.
Happiness belongs to those who distance themselves from a friend who is like an enemy, from a wife who speaks unpleasantly, and from a husband who lacks discernment.
O King,
a master who is a knower of the scriptures, a donor, one who appreciates merit, and who is compassionate is difficult to find;
likewise, a loyal servant who is well-behaved and pure is also hard to obtain.
A master who can distinguish between the essential and the non-essential is rare;
likewise, a mindful servant who carries out his master's instructions as they were given is rare.
One who is of noble lineage, endowed with ethical discipline, eloquent, skillful, pleasant in speech,
a speaker of what has been said, mindful, and swift— such a person should possess these seven qualities.
A king should not kill a messenger on any occasion; however, the slayer of a messenger goes to hell along with his ministers.
For one who has no admixture with another [being] regarding the womb, the karma,
or the seed, his mind does not delight in evil even when he has fallen into hardship.
O King, the members of the assembly should be those who desire the Dharma, are skilled in its purpose, of noble birth, speakers of truth,
and impartial toward both enemy and friend.
Whichever object the king elevates to a position of primary importance in his affairs,
the king’s favorites strive to bring about its destruction.
One should not enter an assembly, or one should speak what is appropriate; for by either remaining silent or speaking falsely, a person becomes a partaker of sin.
Therefore, having entered the assembly, a member of that assembly, free from passion and hatred,
should speak such words as will ensure that he does not fall into hell.
He shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of it in accordance with their offenses;
he shall deprive the wealthy of their riches and subject the poor to execution and imprisonment.
Neither father, nor mother, nor brother, nor wife, nor son,
nor domestic priest is exempt from punishment by the king if he persists in unrighteousness.
Ghouls, those with evil desires, thieves who seize the property of others, and deceitful ones—these are the Rākṣasas acting as officials; one should protect these subjects from them.
O King, what sin could be greater than this: that the treasuries of one who is free from fault are plundered for the sake of wealth by greedy officials?
Even a king who has passed the test should not take what is not to be taken;
nor should he, even if prosperous, abandon what is rightfully his, however small the matter may be.
When the excellent cow has already been milked by many and the milk drunk by her calf,
can even a well-trained cowherd, despite his effort, still milk her?
Just as fire, whether kindled or unkindled, is a great deity,
so too the knower or the ignorant one is a great Brahman-deity.
The twice-born would turn what is not divine into a deity, and even a deity into something non-divine;
they would treat the guardians of the world as mere mortals, and likewise create other worlds.
But due to the excellence of its arrangement, even that which is ill-spoken shines forth,
like smudged collyrium applied to the eyes of a beloved.
Whether it be pleasant or unpleasant, one should speak words that are consistent with the Dharma and the truth to anyone who does not wish for one's downfall— even if unasked.
O King, men who always speak pleasant words are easy to find;
however, one who speaks what is unpleasant yet beneficial, and one who listens to it, are rare indeed.
That king whose physicians, astrologers, ministers,
and courtiers speak only pleasant words quickly falls away from his storehouses of health and merit.
He who, disregarding his master’s likes and dislikes, speaks what is unpleasant yet beneficial by relying on the truth and the Dharma— by him the king has a true companion.
"O Śrī Vyāsa Muni,
that king who does not delight his subjects through qualities such as protection and the like has a name as meaningless as the teat of a goat's horn."
Having said, "I am your protector," the king who does not protect [his subjects] should be approached and slain,
like one who is insane or afflicted by disease.
"This fool here is devoted to pride in his own intelligence and is possessed of both [qualities]," thinking thus,
a king who understands the nature of servants is filled with servants.
Servants and ornaments should each be assigned to their proper places;
for a crest-jewel is not bound upon the foot on the grounds that it is incapable [of such a task].
In the *Pañcatantra*, it is said:
"Whatever the knower of the mind intends, that very quality is accomplished;
a servant who does not understand the master's mind does not partake of the fruit at all."
Vallabhadeva states that the definition of an *ari* (enemy) is one who is intent upon the same objective; however,
a *sattru* (foe) is traditionally defined as one who possesses the qualities of a conqueror and is cruel.

One who has not committed sin abandons fear; friends abandon one who is deceitful or negligent; knowledge abandons one who lacks shame; prosperity abandons the lustful and the lazy; and the world abandons a woman who is cruel and a person who is wicked.
Fortune does not wish to conceal herself behind one who is lacking in resolve, indolent, dependent on fate, and devoid of human effort—
just as a maiden does not wish to hide behind an aged husband.
The Righteous One says: "One who eats wholesome food attains prosperity; one who is healthy attains well-being and freedom from disease;
one who practices attains the end of knowledge; and one who is disciplined attains success in both Dharma and wealth."
An unmanageable servant, deceitful friends,
a stingy master, and a wife devoid of discipline— these are the four thorns in one's head.
Because the variety of effects is observed, even that which is eternal is not always sufficient;
for a mirror is made of bronze alone, and never of gold, even for kings.
Even when won over by virtues, subjects do not submit without punishment;
even when placed upon its neck, the lute does not sound unless struck with the plectrum.
Straightness alone is not necessarily a virtue, nor is crookedness necessarily a fault for a living being;
for even a straight arrow kills, while a bowstring, though curved, protects the body.
"Even those who have never seen the sun become knowledgeable of refined conduct through association with the noble;
indeed, it is the intoxication of youth itself that instructs amorous women in their graceful charms."
"It is not an absolute certainty that fear does not arise from one whose body is peaceful;
do not lamps with white wicks produce black soot?"
This wood in the form of a skeleton, and this uncertainty that "there is danger from this"— even these,
though most terrifying, become auspicious for the sake of Śiva alone.
Ascend to the high station! For the world is generally deluded regarding the true principles;
even one who has climbed to the peak of a mountain summit perceives the uneven as level.
"In this very world, misfortune generally corrupts even a person of excellent character;
firewood alone spreads the power of burning in the consumer of oblations."
One should not place trust in the nature of a wicked person simply because he is of noble birth and virtuous;
surely even fire arising from Malaya sandalwood burns.
Only the wicked are capable of pacifying the wicked; a virtuous person never is.
Those afflicted by the disease of leprosy seek a medicine suited to their condition, even if it is more harmful than the tree [from which it was taken].
One who is fully satisfied weighs actions and their results, never being afflicted by thirst;
what desert traveler would ever deliberate over whether water is sweet or pure?

The heavy burden of old age strikes first those who are virtuous, neither too tall nor too short; for it is upon the breasts of women that beauty first falls, and there indeed that old age descends at the outset.
In some particular instance, even a fault may attain equality with a virtue;
for indeed, upon the lower lip of beautiful women, even a scar becomes an ornament.
These belong to Ravigupta,
for whom supplicants are never turned away; he is indeed that king whose fame removes all suffering, and who [bestowed] a royal consecration,
a turban, and a fly-whisk even upon a mere wound.
"I am not this body, nor does it belong to me"—
through such detachment from what is unsubstantial, why does even a great thunderbolt not shatter the head of Mount Meru?
Even from the worthless, those possessed of virtue arise; even from the virtuous, those of wicked conduct emerge. From mud the lotus rises, yet from the lotus also worms are born.
That man who, having become subject to others, endures even a single instance of humiliation,
is filled with humiliations as the ocean is filled by the paths of rain.
A king who is devoted to giving, yet possesses excessively haughty pride, brings about division among his mountain-like ministers;
enslaved by addiction to women, he becomes like a lordly elephant under the control of another.
Even a king of great splendor does not achieve his purpose if he is addicted to drink;
even the forest fire, though capable of burning grass, cannot do so if it drinks incessantly.
Servants who have finished their tasks become empty-handed and indolent;
therefore, one should ensure that those who are full [of wealth] become empty, just like leeches.
One should not treat a bad son as if he were a good son by assigning him to his father's duties, thinking, "This was done by my father.
In the ritual of offering oblations to the fire-eaters, sesame seeds are praised, but not the oil.
In whatever action a person possesses superior skill, they should be employed therein;
the fragrance of the *sahakāra* tree serves for great excellence in honey, but not in milk.
One who is full of the splendor of marks says, "I have no fear," due to the sleep of delusion;
yet even for the moon that is fully complete, there is fear from the son of Siṃhikā.
Where success is achieved through conciliation alone, a wise person should not employ punishment there.
If bile is pacified by sugar, what is the use of *pāṭola*?
These are the verses of Aṅgāraka.
That which is capable of being split is soft; it is not such that it is hard. Even water, if excessively soft, does not pierce a mountain or a rock, even with effort.

One who knows the task at hand is to be consulted, and not merely someone who is respected or dear to me; even a teacher must be served while seated, but when will the minister’s beloved hips ever be so honored?
"What foreign land could ever equal my virtues? Such a thought is but a fragment of base pride;
collyrium shines when applied to the eyes, but not upon the lips."
In this world, one who is stiff by nature receives great honor, not one who is excessively humble;
in this matter, the breasts of lotus-eyed women are a clear illustration.
The anger of men who lack self-control leads to their own ruin;
a cauldron boiling excessively burns its own sides most severely.
These are the misfortunes of the decline of the enemy faction during the reign of Prakāśavarṣa— though he was beloved by kings and born of a noble lineage—
yet as long as a man does not bow down, he remains like a bow made of bamboo that possesses no string.
One who desires a superior basis should serve a lofty person, even one difficult to approach;
for even if such a person should fall from that height, he remains above those who are base.
One who puts you to shame with pleasant words, displays respect while acting with negligence, and diminishes your excellence through praise— such a fool’s friend is to be avoided in every way.
Smitten by calamities themselves, they listen to the words of evil friends; for to those overcome by misfortune, even that which is most unwholesome tastes sweet.
Among these, the wise man who is upright and easy to approach should be served with diligence by those who are learned and honest; however,
the upright fool should be pitied, while the dishonest fool should be avoided under all circumstances.
Toward one with whom one has shared both joy and sorrow, and spoken secrets with confidence—
how could even the hearts of the wicked not turn toward him until death?
A king who, like the sun, causes suffering to some but attains imperishability through his virtue and dispassion;
yet, though bringing happiness to others, he quickly goes to ruin if he hates them, like the moon.
The qualities of things are generally the causes of their effects, just as flowers are the causes of fruits;
for this very reason, qualities are not seen in those who possess wealth, as if they had already achieved their purpose.

To one who has not awakened, the state of being a speaker is useless for men, just as the graceful charms of beauty are useless for lustful women when there is no one to lead them away. —Kapilāsvāmin. Subhāṣitāvalī 2888–2.
Bribery, flattery, threats, intimidation, the theft of wealth, and deceit—these six must be employed at that very moment;
they cannot be obtained at any other time.
Rivers end at the waters of the ocean; the hearts of kinsmen end with the estrangement of women; friendship ends with wicked people; and families end with bad sons.
What is the use of that person being learned if, like a child, he does not perceive reality?
Both of these are blind: the one who lacks supervision and the one whose eyes are not clear.
That quality by which one conceives an activity in the world and through which one attains renown must be increased and manifested by the possessor of that quality.
One should not treat a friend or a relative with excessive affection that causes pain;
even a cow strikes her own calf with the tip of her horn while it is drinking.
Generally, contempt arises even toward an exalted object due to excessive familiarity;
people living near the Ganges usually perform their ablutions in a mere well.
A certain noble birth excels by its own conduct;
the jar drinks only a limited amount of water, yet the one born from the jar drank the ocean.
Through association with someone who possesses virtuous qualities, the entire world becomes devoted;
being thus devoted, he is approached by allies and joined with prosperity.
How indeed can constant discord not arise among brothers who are always taught the science of hatred by their husbands night after night?
By performing favors for friends and by inflicting harm even upon enemies, patronage of a king is esteemed by the wise;
who does not merely support his belly?
In those with well-rounded and elevated shoulders, duality does not arise as long as the sword,
like the edge of an axe, has not entered between them.
He who commits adultery with another's wife, he who covets the wealth of others,
and he who is always disrespectful toward his teachers and elders— neither in this world nor in the next does he find happiness.
O Rāhulaka,
for that person whom people do not speak of as great, nor of his death or victory in battle, nor of his learning,
generosity, or great wealth— his existence is equal to that of worms and insects.
O Varāhamihira,
he who possesses the power to go everywhere— why would he meet his destruction through attachment to his own country?
Calling this well "the well of my father," base men drink its salty water.
Whatever is improper is indeed improper; a wise person should not direct their mind toward it.
For even by people tormented by extreme thirst, water found on a public road is not drunk.
One should not perform an action impulsively, for lack of discernment is the path to the ultimate downfall.
For prosperity, which yearns for virtue, chooses of its own accord those who act with deliberation.
What will a person who prattles much accomplish by practicing what is beneficial for himself in every way? For there exists no such means that can bring satisfaction to the entire world.
O Bhārata,
a son who is obedient, wealth that is well-managed, knowledge, freedom from disease,
association with the virtuous, a beloved wife who is submissive, and these five are the uprooters of suffering.
An assembly of the learned, reflection on the *Bhārata*, the playing of stringed instruments, well-executed song,
a beloved wife, and a friend who is like oneself— these seven immediately dispel sorrow in this world.
Generosity for the poor, self-control for the powerful, austerity for the youth, silence for the wise,
the cessation of desire for those accustomed to pleasure, and compassion toward all beings— these lead one to heaven.
Even Brahmins who strike, revile, or speak harshly to us are to be honored with affection;
for in our lineage, even defeat is equal to victory, lest we become conquerors of Brahmins.
Water is led by a downward slope, cattle by green pasture, children by kind words, and the virtuous by discipline;
women are won by wealth and the gods by austerity—for indeed, the entire world is captivated by that which is dear to it.
Whosoever would search for even a single coin that has strayed onto a wrong path, as if it were worth a thousand niṣkas— even if he must search through millions of places—
Lakṣmī, whose hand holds the lotus, does not abandon him; she remains with her hand freely bestowed upon him.
Fortune herself desires to dwell with one who is endowed with courage, not prolix in his actions, knowledgeable in the methods of undertaking tasks, unattached to vices, brave,
grateful, and firm in resolve.
He who undertakes his own task after carefully considering the place, the strength, the action, the means,
and the time— prosperities attend that man, just as rivers flow into the overflowing great ocean.

A man should exert effort to eliminate his lack of virility even when fate is adverse; for a steadfast person, fearing no further drowning, will surely cast their hands and feet out even while sinking in the ocean.

The conceit of one who thinks, "I am a sinless sage; whence can there be fear for me? does not lead to well-being. For what indeed is unassailable by those of evil soul who harbor envy toward the prosperity of others?
Those of deluded intellect go to ruin, for they do not act with guile toward those who are deceptive.
Indeed, like sharp arrows, such rogues enter and destroy those whose limbs are unguarded and unsuspecting.
Mastery over the senses is the cause of discipline; excellence in virtue is attained through discipline.
People feel affection for a man who abounds in virtue, for prosperity indeed originates from the affection of the people.

Those who desire a friend through sycophancy, righteousness through deceit, prosperity through the oppression of others, knowledge through ease, or a woman through harshness, are surely unwise— these are the words of Bhāravi.

Dharma, artha, and kāma should be pursued equally; for that man who is attached to only one of them is base. They declare that he who is devoted to two of them is mediocre, but he who is intent upon the threefold set (trivarga) is supreme.
O King, he who possesses dull and feeble intelligence is to be avoided from afar;
for the rays of the sun become even more piercing when it is freed from the clouds.
"A head well-washed, feet made stainless, attendance upon excellent women, moderate eating,
not sleeping naked, and avoiding sexual intercourse on forbidden days— these six bring back prosperity that has long been lost."
Disparagement, recounting one's own difficult deeds, lack of wonder at words during the course of conversation,
not giving a seat, and eating what was prepared beforehand— these are the characteristics of a man whose mind is dispassionate.

One should quickly avoid such a woman as this: one who disregards her husband’s household duties, who always speaks in opposition to her husband, who delights in the house of another, and who is devoid of shame.
Even a wise man endowed with power should not himself provoke enmity against another;
for what discerning person would consume deadly poison, thinking, "I am capable of enduring it"?— Vyāsa.

The wise do not consider the expenditure of wealth as a loss in these eight instances: in performing meritorious deeds, in gathering friends, in pleasing beloved women, in supporting kinsmen, in sacrificial rites, in marriage, in times of calamity, and in the destruction of enemies.

A king, even when propitiated, must be regarded with suspicion by one whose intellect has thoroughly mastered the treatises; likewise, a young woman, even when made one's own, must be guarded. For where is there stability in a treatise, a king, or a young woman?
Out of delusion, the ocean carries precious gems of noble birth to the depths, yet it always bears aloft common pebbles;
it pollutes its waters and supports the world of serpents—for one whose mind is clouded regarding what must be done generally becomes great.
For one eye is the stainless, innate [wisdom], and the second is dwelling together with the wise in solitude.
He who possesses not these two is clearly blind; tell me, what other fault could there be in his straying onto the wrong path?
That friend is one whose conduct toward both adversity and prosperity is equal; he is a son who pleases his father through his virtuous deeds;
she is a wife who desires only the welfare of her husband. These three are obtained in this world by those who have performed meritorious deeds.

The fame of the arrogant perishes; the friendship of the treacherous is lost; the family of one intent on wealth perishes through lack of ritual action; the servants of one devoted solely to riches desert him; the power of knowledge belongs to the indolent; happiness to the wretched; and sovereignty to a king whose ministers are negligent.
Where an elephant and a young calf are equal in their intoxication, and where there is no distinction between a horse and a donkey;
where the learned and the ignorant are not differentiated—how indeed could virtuous men feel any attachment to such a place?
Fire arises from wood through friction; the earth gives water when it is dug.
A traveler reaches the end of the road even by walking slowly. What, then, can a man not accomplish here if he has begun his task?
Do not despise those scholars who have realized the ultimate truth, for fortune does not cling to them as it does to the light and fleeting [surface of] the earth.
A lotus fiber cannot serve as a barrier against elephants whose temples are dark with the lines of flowing temporal ichor.
A wise person should diligently ascertain the transformation of the multitude of effects produced by one who performs both virtuous and non-virtuous deeds.
For actions performed with excessive haste, when they lead to misfortune, their ripening results in a heart-burning like a piercing thorn.

Even for those [who are powerful], that which retreats from them is the cause for striking back; yet the lion, out of extreme rage, crouches and leaps up. For what indeed do the wise not forgive, when they harbor enmity in their hearts but employ secret stratagems?
One who possesses intelligence and desires to attain a desired result— whether small or great— from the cultivation of merit should not remain inactive for even a moment.
If a potter does not rotate the wheel with his staff, no bowl or jar will come into being, even though the clay is present.
One who grasps the entire meaning from merely hearing it is worthy of being heard; one who understands the speaker’s words even when they have been uttered twice has achieved the fruit thereof;
but he who does not comprehend the meaning of what is written, even though it has been clearly stated many times, is no better than a beast.
For a wise person whose efforts therein are fruitless, the vow of silence is fitting.
Out of intoxication,
he regards his wife as his mother and his mother as his wife;
he treats his own house as a well and his well as his house, for his character has grown lax.
Through delusion, one regards a mere trifle as a vast ocean; one mistakes water for dry land and even treats a friend as an enemy. What else might a drunkard not do? Nothing.
Having consumed [this], one becomes angry even with one's teacher without cause, weeps likewise,
falls into delusion, commits acts of rashness,
becomes a locus for disease, exposes one's private parts before the public, and behaves like a madman.
The wise should not drink intoxicants, which obstruct great shame and produce delusion.
In some places he sleeps on the bare ground, and in others he lies upon a couch;
in some places he eats only vegetables, and in others he relishes meat and rice;
in some places he wears a mere rag around his neck, and in others he wears garments of diverse colors.
The wise person, intent on their task, takes account of neither suffering nor pleasure.
In one place there is dancing and singing; in another, the wailing of "Ha! Ha! and lamentation.
In one place there is an assembly of the learned; in another, the brawling of those intoxicated by wine.
In one place there is a beautiful woman; in another, a body worn out by old age.
I do not know whether this saṃsāra consists of nectar or whether it consists of poison.
For those who dwell in the vicinity of Malaya, even sandalwood serves as mere fuel;
for those residing on the shores of the ocean, the jewels of the sea are like stones;
and even among the people dwelling in Kaśmīra, there is no regard for saffron.
The high value of one who stays at a distance turns into contempt when living together.
Fire can be warded off by water, the heat of the sun by a parasol,
a rutting lord of elephants by a sharp goad, and oxen or donkeys by a staff; likewise,
disease by the collection of various medicines, and poison by the application of mantras.
Everyone possesses the medicine prescribed by the scriptures; for the fool, however, there is no medicine.
A desire for association with the virtuous, affection for the good qualities of others, humility toward one’s teacher, devotion to learning, delight in one’s own wife, fear of public scandal,
devotion to the Wielder of the Trident (Śiva), dedication to self-restraint, and freedom from contact with the wicked.
Homage to those men in whom these stainless qualities dwell.
A king perishes through bad counsel; an ascetic through attachment; a son through over-indulgence;
a Brahmin through neglecting his studies; a family through a bad son; character through associating with the wicked;
a wife through drinking liquor and lack of supervision; agriculture through neglect; and affection through residing abroad.
Loving-kindness arises from non-hostility, prosperity from right conduct, renunciation from lack of attachment, and wealth from vigilance.
Compassion for one's own kin, guile toward one's servants, likewise deceit toward the wicked,
affection for the virtuous, pride toward the base, and straightforwardness even toward the learned;
valor toward enemies, forbearance toward elders, and craftiness toward women.
And those men who are skilled in the arts—in them alone lies the stability of the world.
Transplanting those that had been uprooted, gathering those that were flowering, quickly increasing those that were small,
bending down those that were too tall, pruning those that were broad, separating those that were entangled,
cutting off those that were sharp and thorny, and protecting those he had planted himself— thus he tended the forest.
Like a skilled garland-maker, he remains long in power through his proficiency in application.
Bathing is indeed that which produces clarity of mind, destroys evil dreams,
is the locus of purity, removes impurities, increases vitality,
illuminates the complexion, subdues enemies, and kindles the digestive fire of the body.
And for women, it is heart-stealing; these are the ten benefits of bathing that remove fatigue.
Birth as a human, in a noble family, wealth, long life, health,
good friends, virtuous sons, a beloved and faithful wife, devotion to Nārāyaṇa,
wisdom, goodness of character, mastery over the senses, and delight in giving to worthy recipients.
Without merit, these thirteen qualities are difficult for worldly beings to obtain.
Now begins the Path of Dispassion (*vairāgyapaddhati*).
First of all, the discourse on Dharma:
"Listen to the essence of all Dharma; having heard it, one should indeed comprehend it."
One should not do toward others that which is disagreeable to oneself.
But one who desires both sensual pleasure and wealth should practice the Dharma from the very beginning;
for it is my conviction that nothing whatsoever harmful can arise from the Dharma.
A person should always seek knowledge and its objects like one seeking food; seized by death as if by the hair, one should practice the Dharma.
Relatives together with their kinsmen turn back like the crest of smoke;
therefore, perform those meritorious deeds by which you must follow after death.
Having cast off this mortal body, which is like a log of wood upon the earth, the relatives depart with averted faces; but Dharma alone follows after one.
Like chaff among grains of rice, or like gnats among birds,
such are those among men for whom the Dharma is no cause.
He whose days come and go devoid of the Dharma,
though still breathing, does not truly live, like a blacksmith’s bellows.
Acquire that wealth which brings no fear from kings or even from thieves,
and which does not abandon you when you have died.
Even when occupied with other duties, you must certainly attend to the Dharma within yourself;
