for even a cow, though tied to a tethering post, devours the grass as it wanders about.
Honesty, freedom from guile, self-restraint, and control of the senses—
Manu declared these to be the common duties for all four castes.
The very faculties are all that constitutes both heaven and hell;
when restrained or unleashed, they lead either to heaven or to hell.
One should always abandon the ten paths of unwholesome action: those threefold by way of the body, those fourfold by way of speech, and those threefold by way of the mind.
One should always avoid these three misdeeds of the body: taking life, theft, and the taking of another's wife.
O King of kings, one should neither speak nor even think of these four verbal transgressions: idle chatter, harsh speech, slander, and likewise falsehood.

One should practice threefold mental conduct: regarding the possessions of others as worthless, maintaining friendliness toward all sentient beings, and reflecting that there is a fruit for one's actions.
"Due to bodily faults and the corruption of karma, a human being goes to the state of an immobile being;
through verbal [faults], to the state of birds or wild animals; and through mental [faults], to the condition of the lowest castes."
The purity of intention (bhāva) among human beings should be understood as essential in all actions;
otherwise, a beloved wife may be kissed with one intention, while she is regarded as a daughter with another.
One should not abandon the Dharma out of desire, nor out of passion, nor out of hatred;
for the Dharma alone is the refuge for the virtuous, both in this world and in the next.
When one who has seen or experienced an object does not conceal it when questioned,
this speaking of things exactly as they are is the characteristic of truth.
That which is a statement of reality is not necessarily true, nor is that which is not a statement of reality necessarily false;
that which is ultimately for the welfare of beings as it truly is—that is called the truth.
Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping,
whatever is not for the sake of the welfare of beings is like the activity of a sovereign.
If it were established that "one who stumbles is one who has stumbled and is thus to be killed," then perhaps two or three might survive; for human beings are full of many faults.
One must never approach another's wife, regardless of her caste;
for there exists nothing in the three worlds that shortens the life-span of a recluse as much as this.
There are these two persons in the world who stand above heaven:
the giver of food during a famine, and the giver of gold during times of plenty.
A righteous person does not give a gift out of hope for reward, nor out of fear, nor to one who has done him a favor,
nor to those whose character is dancing, singing, or laughing.
There is a distinction between worthy and unworthy recipients, just as there is between a cow and a serpent:
from grass milk is produced, and from milk poison is produced.
Even a single coin acquired and given according to the law yields great fruit; but thousands acquired and given through unjust means do not serve the purpose of others.
The ignorant person does not give away wealth for fear of becoming poor again;
yet the wise person also gives away wealth for fear of becoming poor again.
He who, having taken away the wealth of others, bestows it upon others—that giver goes to hell; for the fruit belongs to the one whose wealth it was.
The distinction between the donor and the recipient has been demonstrated by the hands themselves:
one hand moves below while the other moves above.
The place, time, arrival, substance,
field, donor, recipient, and mental disposition— these are the causes for the excellence of the fruit of even a small gift.
By the destruction of the property of the gods, by the seizing of the property of Brahmins,
and by the transgression against Brahmins, families fall from their noble status to lowliness.
Even those who undergo a certain transformation when touched by a mere thorn eat the flesh of an animal that has been cut up by a weapon.
Is this not sufficient reason to completely renounce meat,
such that even when it has fallen upon one's own body, it causes pain as if from a blade of grass?
For one who sees the difference between the eater and that whose meat he eats:
for one there is momentary satisfaction, while the other is deprived of life.
What deluded man would eat the flesh of that person whose weapon becomes a leaf and whose executioner becomes a father?
Even if one has committed a sinful deed, he who gives food to a petitioner—
especially to Brahmins— is freed from that evil.
O lord of men, O best of the Bharatas, by disregarding his father, his mother,
and his teacher, a man falls into hell.
O King, an atonement has been prescribed for the killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, and likewise for one who has broken his vows;
but for the killer of a fetus, there is no atonement.
O King,
even the ocean of the Vedas does not reach its end when describing the ungrateful and the grateful, the wicked and the virtuous.
We have never heard of any atonement for these four: the betrayer of a friend, the ungrateful person, the killer of a woman, and the slanderer.

Know that there are four types of executioners— those who are ungrateful, those who do not recognize what ought to be done, those who are long-lived, and those who lack uprightness— and the fifth is one by birth alone.
A son does not hate his father because of the nature of his own seed;
one should know that a son who hates his father has another's seed.

On the new moon, the fourteenth day, the full moon, and the eighth day, a twice-born man who has taken the bath of initiation (snātaka) should always remain celibate, even outside the period of his wife's season.
One should greatly comfort a person who is distressed by the loss of wealth, afflicted by fear,
tormented by disease, deprived of property, or overcome by calamity.
Absence of anger, patience, truthfulness, non-violence, and compassion;
affection, serenity, gentleness, and straightforwardness—these are the ten restraints (yamas).
Charity, sacrifice, austerity, meditation, Vedic study, restraint of the generative organ,
vows, fasting, silence, and bathing— these are the ten observances (niyamas).
Sacrifice, study, giving, austerity, truth, patience, compassion,
and non-greed— this is remembered as the eightfold path of Dharma.
Among these, the first group of four may be practiced even for the sake of hypocrisy; however, the latter group of four does not abide in those who are not noble-souled.
He who is tranquil in his youth is called "tranquil";
when the elements are wasting away, who would not become equanimous?
One who desires prosperity should practice the Dharma with one shoulder;
with one shoulder he may also pursue sensual pleasures, while increasing the other shoulder.
For one who has abandoned the pursuit of the meaning of the Dharma in this world, non-pursuit is superior;
for it is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off.
Even with thousands of earthen vessels and hundreds of water-pots,
those whose minds are afflicted by impure dispositions are never purified.
O King, unrighteousness does not bear fruit immediately like a cow;
however, returning slowly, it cuts away the very roots of the doer.
Just as a base man might cut down a tree in the forest with an axe,
the sin belongs only to the cutter and never to the axe.
Dharma, artha, and kāma—these three are the fruits of life;
these three should be attained by the complete avoidance of adharma.
Just as one might be hoisted with great difficulty to the peak of a mountain,
so too is the self cast down in an instant from its virtues and faults.
That which has been heard, which leads neither to dispassion, nor to the Dharma, nor to peace—
even if it is well-bound by sound, that is merely the cawing of a crow.
It does not cover the private parts, nor does it ward off gadflies and mosquitoes;
like the tail of a dog, wisdom devoid of Dharma is useless.
He whose strength has the welfare of others as its purpose, whose wealth consists of the pursuit of Dharma,
and whose speech has truth as its meaning— he alone, as a father, possesses true sons.
Truthful speech, compassion for all living beings,
and giving equally according to one's ability— this is said to be the dharma of the householder.
When a guest has been honored and departs from the home of a householder,
the wise have said that there is no other dharma superior to that.
Having first honored the gods, the ancestors, humans, servants, guests, and the deities of the household,
the householder may then eat.
Know those gods who do not honor their elders, guests,
and children to be like Rākṣasas, devoid of the auspiciousness of respectful conduct.
Having remembered that most terrible suffering which is experienced in the world of hungry ghosts (preta),
what person with a sensitive heart would not even renounce their own flesh?
There is no true merchant-dharma that does not involve returning a favor;
even in that regard, those who do not act accordingly are beasts, not humans.
One should give sight, one should give mind, and one should give speech that is well-composed;
furthermore, having risen, one should offer a seat—this is the eternal Dharma.
O Vyāsa Muni,
even in their own homes, liberation is attained by those best of men who have earned their livelihood through their own righteous deeds, who are ever devoted to their respective wives,
who have conquered their senses, and who are fond of guests.
One who desires to enter the heavenly realm like a householder should not desire what is not given, nor drink intoxicants, nor harm living beings, nor speak falsehoods,
nor even mentally covet the wife of another.
The compound name of the venerable sage Vālmīki, *Śrībhagavad-vālmīki-muneḥ*, is appropriately formed and well-constructed;
it destroys the sins of those who utter it a thousand times. Since this name belongs to Viṣṇu, the case endings attached to it may be elided.
One whose inner self is corrupted by a desire for the fruits of giving examines the excellence of the recipient as if it were a vessel; however,
one who is compassionate acts out of mere solicitude to give to the wretched person.

For one who does not worship the gods, there is nothing else in this world that serves as a cause for the suffering of people. Therefore, it should be nurtured with constant effort like a helpful friend.
How can one who lacks mindfulness—wondering, "By what karma have I been born here? or "Where must I go from here?"—be intent upon the Dharma?

One who observes the restraints (yamas) but is not devoted to the observances (niyamas) falls, whereas one who observes the restraints but is lazy regarding the observances never does. Thus, having reflected upon the restraints and the observances with the intellect, one should fix the mind upon the path where the restraints predominate.
May your mind be fixed upon the Dharma, remaining ever alert; for that alone is the kinsman who follows one to the next world.
Wealth and women, even when pursued by the skillful, never attain the status of one's own self, nor do they possess stability.
"I am Śrī Vyāsamuni, mounted upon an excellent chariot with a troop of elephants and horses resplendent with gold; my radiance is shielded by a white parasol.
As I depart from my noble palace, the wicked are subdued by the sounds of musical instruments, conchs, and the cries of 'Victory!', accompanied by throngs of foot-soldiers."
With hair grey with dust, throat choked with tears, his body bent low under the heavy burden resting on his shoulders,
and his feet wounded by stumbling against rocks and stones, he goes along gasping and helpless because of his refusal to give that which is being begged.
Venerable Prajñāśānti,

that gift which is not given to those who have first rendered assistance is effectively abandoned; yet why is it not given to a beloved person who is destitute and whose only wealth is their begging, since that [gift] is based on passion?

Is that gift not truly fruitful which, out of a fondness for the abundance of its results, is bestowed upon a destitute person who has approached you with longing? But what is that gift which is given to one who is indifferent and impoverished?
For someone,

the act of watering has been performed with the water of mental clarity through blamelessness, where the seeds were sown in a field of merit and the rows of sprouts were bound together by affectionate words.

O King, this donor—a tree of generosity—triumphs even over the wish-fulfilling tree and others; for at the time of fruition, it surely yields whatever each person desires, even if that person is but a child.
Birth among the gods is censurable for those whose delusion is fixed in the thickest darkness, since it is devoid of the human state.
For a man who is devoid of intelligence is like a beast, lacking the fruits of auspicious action and possessing conduct identical to that of cattle.
Intelligence devoid of wisdom wanders in the investigation of the principles of existence and non-existence;
wisdom devoid of Dharma is merely a fruitless affliction, even when expressed in words resembling those of the blissful ones.
Dharma is a refuge for people both in this world and in the next; in the darkness, Dharma is the sun.
Dharma is the equalizer that pacifies all calamities, a treasure-trove called Dharma for those of noble mind. Dharma is a kinsman to the friendless on the vast path; Dharma is a steadfast friend.
In the desert expanse of saṃsāra, there is no celestial tree superior to the Dharma.

He alone is blind who is devoid of sacred learning; he alone is a eunuch who seeks worldly gain but finds no purpose in it; he alone is dead who possesses no fame; and he alone is to be pitied who has neither the Dharma nor wisdom.
Truth resides in her speech; she is devoted to clarity through her entire being; she dwells within all the senses.
Generosity and liberation are in her hands; the thought of ending the suffering of giving birth to a son is in her mind.
Compassion alone is her beloved, firmly established in her heart; and the exertion for the sake of others is in her body.
He alone is a true person who lives; others merely wander through existence as living beings.
All actions are constantly performed for the protection of living beings;
indeed, there is nothing in the entire world dearer to living beings than their own life. It is impossible to calculate the merit of one who possesses perfect compassion.
The virtuous one who observes the vow of non-violence grants fearlessness to living beings.
Beauty is the fruit of generosity; learning is the fruit of equanimity; hands are the fruit of worshipping the gods;
movement is the fruit of dharma; life is the fruit of the practice of relieving the suffering of others;
speech is the fruit of truth; and the expansion of one's influence is the fruit of the happiness of the world.
The intellect of the fortunate, which bears as its fruit the contemplation of both worldly existence and peace, indeed leads to prosperity.

For those who practice ethical discipline, who maintain their lineage, who cultivate sincerity, who avoid hypocrisy, who enumerate virtues, who fix their minds upon the Dharma, who contemplate patience, who subdue their darkness, and who listen to the hearing of reality— Subhūti.
In this cycle of existence, I do not see any merit for the virtuous that is even equal to the act of benefiting others.
He who, having attained the abundance of human virtues after many eons, does not, out of delusion, accumulate even the slightest wealth of merit in this world; Kṣemendra [describes him as follows].
Having departed from this world for the next, he encounters intense sorrow,
like one who has gone empty-handed from his own house after traveling to an island of jewels.
Indeed, for whatever wealth has been acquired by anyone, renunciation alone is its true preservation,
just as a drainage channel is for the waters collected within the belly of a field.
Wealth that does not satisfy those who have not requested it, a mind devoid of pride toward those in the midst of its thoughts,
and a body that has wandered beyond the sacred fords— these at the end shall lead to lamentation.
In this world, which is most deluded, the wealth of King Śrī Jona-raja— consisting of heaps of pearls from oyster shells and golden ornaments— is universally renowned as the very essence of wealth.
Whatever treasury is established, I do not see any pleasing fruit therein,
except for the giving of wealth to those who are destitute, to kinsmen and servants who have no other refuge, and to supplicants.

Alas, this earth is not made too heavy by trees, nor by mountains, nor by oceans; rather, it is burdened by that birth which did not exist for the sake of fulfilling the mental inclinations of those who entreated Vyāsadāsa.
"This person, having departed from this world for the next, departs at death leaving behind wealth all alone"—
thinking thus, his kinsman, with a heart stirred by rising compassion, surely carries away that wealth of his.
When one is human, it is difficult to attain the status of a man; when a man, the status of a Brahmin;
when a Brahmin, great learning; when learned, proficiency; when proficient, knowledge of the meaning for one who possesses learning.
For one who knows the meaning, eloquence in diverse speech is also worldly knowledge;
for one who possesses worldly knowledge and is learned in all the treatises, an understanding of the Dharma is difficult to find.
For whom, indeed,
are these bonds of kinsmen— the multitude of virtues acquired through the constraints of life— worth anything,
when at the final day they become objects of reproach for the shedding of tears?

The realization of the True Dharma, the cessation of worldly activity, association with the virtuous, and self-restraint— these are the kinsmen of the good whose minds are detached and who remain unshakable even at the end.

The five Pāṇḍavas were indeed the sons of the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa— the grandson of Śuktimatī, who destroyed the widowhood of his own kinsmen' wives— and they were born from the wives of the cowherd Golaka. They were, as it were, "vessels" (kuṇḍas) [born of adultery].
Those five, being of equal birth, [attain] this destruction of suffering;
the sages declare that their recitation is the subtle course of the Dharma.
In a vessel made of lapis lazuli, he cooks a mash of sesame seeds with heaps of sandalwood for fuel;
having cut pieces of camphor, he scatters them here all around as fodder for the *kodrava* grass.
For the sake of the root of the sun, he plows the earth with golden-tipped plowshares.
Having reached this land of action, that unfortunate person who does not practice austerity is a mere human being.

Upon the head of both the donor and the rain-cloud, there is the praise of swarms of intoxicated bees in the springtime, which bestows fruits and flowers upon trees and is adorned by the peaks of the mountains of that region.
On this mountain, which is a protector of beings and a giver of livelihood, there is worship with waterfalls as chowries;
yet such hospitality is shown even to these insentient things—how much more so, then, to those who are givers and knowers?
Now, the virtue of Rājashekhara is non-malice toward all living beings through action, mind, and speech.
The wise know that favor and generosity constitute this very morality.
One should protect one's conduct with effort, for wealth comes and goes;
wealth is lost through lack of conduct, but one who lacks conduct is utterly ruined.
Just as one sits anywhere at all with soiled garments,
even so one whose conduct has lapsed does not preserve the remainder of his virtuous behavior.
It is my conviction that family is not an authority for those devoid of conduct;
for even among those born of the lowest castes, it is conduct alone that distinguishes them.
Whether of low birth or of noble birth, he who does not transgress the bounds of propriety,
who regards the Dharma, and who is gentle and self-controlled— he is superior to hundreds of those of noble birth.
The sage Vyāsa said:
"Let the wise man, desiring to attain the three kinds of happiness— praise,
the acquisition of wealth, and rejoicing in heaven after death— protect his virtue."
For some, wealth is found in foreign lands; in times of calamity, wisdom is wealth;
in the next world, merit is wealth; indeed, virtuous conduct is wealth everywhere.

Sweetness is the ornament of Kṣemendra’s learning; restraint of speech is that of valor; tranquility is that of knowledge; humility is that of sacred revelation; and expenditure upon worthy recipients is that of wealth.
Freedom from anger is the austerity of the patient; sincerity is the power of dharma;
and likewise, for this entire world, virtuous conduct is the supreme ornament.
Better than being tormented by the pain of a seatless bed is death;
better than falling into a well covered with grass where serpents swarm is [death]; better than perishing in the midst of deep water within a whirlpool is [death].
May there be no falling away from morality for one born of noble family who is possessed of learning.
Then, at the end of the Kali age, there will arise Rākṣasas in human form;
they will devour men for their wealth, not for their bodies.
The *Śruti* of Vyāsa has been lost, the *Smṛti* has vanished, and for the most part the twice-born have fallen; the learned have been defiled by impurity— alas, the Kali age prevails!
O Mādhava,
people have been brought to such a state by the wicked Kali that devotion to harming one's master and friends is now considered a virtue.
"May there be a righteous king who is exceedingly virtuous, staying far away;
I choose this so that unrighteous people may not exist at present."
"There was once a person who repaid kindness with ingratitude, and now there has arisen one who destroys even as he performs a service.
Such is the reflection in my mind: "How will the world come to be?"—Vallabhadeva.
O Blessed Earth, how can you support that man who acts wickedly toward one who has been helpful, trusting, and pure-minded— a man who is blinded by falsehood?
In the Kṛtayuga, there existed among people who had conquered themselves that which was called self-restraint (dama);
in the Kaliyuga, that very same thing exists among men as intoxication (mada), due to its transformation.
When the Kali age has arrived and the king is greedy for wealth, what is the use of riches? One must protect life itself.
Is it not a gain if a sheep, though stripped of all its wool, is released by the butcher?
Now this world of living beings is afflicted by various terrible diseases, oppressed by thieves of evil conduct,
distressed by famine, ruined by royal punishments, and trampled underfoot by the wheels [of power].
Abandon useless affliction regarding the acquisition of virtues; take refuge in that confidence by which one lives.
That time has passed when one flourished through genuine virtues accompanied by the conduct of the virtuous.
The word "heart" is merely a harsh term for a wicked person; the thought "I have done much for him" has vanished.
This ancient word "good person" is nowadays used by people only as a pretext for a small amount of wealth.
Virtuous conduct has been conquered by the wicked, and noble conversations have been obstructed by the darkness of the talk of the base.
Even those of low station have attained the status of eminent men; O Dharma, beloved of the virtuous, what will you do?
Go away, O shame! Cease, O patience! O intellect, why do you falsely torment yourself here with pride in being a man?
When wretchedness—whose virtues have long been cast aside and whose army of faults is honored—commands us, then we shall act accordingly.
[Thus spoke] Dharmadatta.
O you whose hearts are unassailed, I speak the truth to you who are self-restrained:
having now gone to the forest, let your dwelling be made with the deer;
for in this world, which abounds in the rise of the wicked, the conduct of the virtuous is being destroyed.
O Lord, this time does not prevail in the houses of those such as you during the Kali age.
Malice toward those who are humble, contempt for the virtuous, a mind set on misconduct, and falsehood even toward friends and children;
speech that is artificially sweet yet destructive when heard by others— such is the nature of the wicked.
These are the sovereign powers of the great king of the Kali age.
O King, for both [the virtuous and the wicked], your rule causes sorrow; time is most equal, yet it is clouded by its own stain.
The virtuous possess happiness along with their wives, while the wicked are deprived of livelihoods despite having servants.
Wealth is difficult to acquire, friends are unstable, and the body is a vessel of disease;
it is nearly decayed and powerless—what news can there be regarding the alleviation of its suffering?
O brother, where have you wandered at the shore of the ocean? I am going to the royal camp; what is the use of service there?
Who is the king to be served, and how so? By what virtues of one's own? What are those virtues that [are prized by] the virtuous?
What have they done today? Go to another forest; or have you not heard this:
that those such as rogues and the miserly are honored, while those who whisper into the ear are the true servants?

May my lineage, which is noble by virtue of its mountain-like steadfastness and moral conduct, not be consumed by fire; may even the name of one who exerts himself in vain for worldly fame never exist;
and may the thunderbolt of valor fall swiftly upon my enemies, so that my purpose may always be fulfilled.
Without which single one, all these virtues are as worthless as the chaff of straw.
She who treats the virtuous as scoundrels, the wise as fools, and the beneficial as harmful;
she who makes the manifest seem hidden and the untrue appear real—
worship that Goddess Cakrikā, if you desire to enjoy your wished-for fruit.
O virtuous one, do not harbor vain anxiety for those who are afflicted by calamities when their efforts have proved fruitless.
Although Śrīvardhana’s body was as beautiful as the abode of the earth with its lofty peaks,
it attained an exceedingly lovely luster by nature and removed the suffering of the virtuous.
Even there, alas, this misshapen form does not obtain its own appropriate splendor without a retinue of followers; behold, it is like a parasol that cannot be held aloft without a handle.
The Dharma of Rāṇāditya has departed; asceticism and austerity have wavered; truth has gone far away;
the earth yields little fruit; people are deceitful; and the Brahmins abide in ignorance.

In the Kali age, kings are intent on punishment and devoid of discernment; sons treat their fathers as enemies; wives are antagonistic toward their husbands; and those people who have died are truly fortunate.
For someone else,
the nights— filled with the fragrance of the wine from the mouths of courtesans in their pleasure-houses,
and rendered bright by the full moon— were passed in the intense savor of amorous festivals.
"An omniscient one," "an ascetic," "one who has long maintained the *agnihotra* fire," "a knower of Brahman," "one who is consecrated"— thus is the world deceived by rogues during the day.

Alas, these hypocrites steal the wealth of the rich: they stand upon cool stone slabs placed on the banks of the Ganges; they are surrounded by radiant ascetics; they carry staffs topped with clusters of *kuśa* grass and shine with rosaries; their fingers are busy grasping individual seeds from rings of thread strung in alternating patterns.
Now we pay homage to the deeds of Kṛṣṇa’s son,
who, though he has struck down the gods and the laws of fate, remains under their very control.
Even that Creator is to be worshipped because he bestows fruits obtained from specific actions.
If the fruit depends upon action, then what is the use of the gods and what is the use of a Creator?
Homage to those actions, before which even the Creator has no power!
Just as shadow and form are always closely and inseparably connected for anyone,
so too are action and the agent connected in all living beings.
Just as a calf finds its mother among a thousand cows,
so does previously committed karma follow after its doer.
Just as flowers and fruits, though not urged by anyone,
do not pass beyond their own proper time, so too are the actions of embodied beings.
For diseases, both physical and mental, arise from karma within bodies;
like arrows released by firm archers, they fall here upon the world.
This very thing is a great marvel resulting from past karma:
that the lifespan of those who lack self-mastery, and the prosperity of those who lack wisdom.
Whatever one might desire, however one wishes for it, that very thing one would obtain in that manner,
provided that the fruit of a person's action were not dependent upon another.
For a man is not born after having accumulated [merit] for the end of a hundred years;
rather, men with a lifespan of a hundred years live by means of skillful methods (upāya).

What is the use of despondency in times of adversity, and what is the use of astonishment in times of prosperity? That which is destined to happen will surely come to pass; such is the certainty of karma.
Otherwise, the wise man, with an intellect imbued with the essence of the scriptures, exerts himself;
like a master, he ordains his former karma in a different manner.
Who shows the path for those going from here to yonder world—
the path of the waters that flow according to their own will and of past karmas?
Intelligent, highly energetic, wise, heroic, and of noble birth,
they were endowed with hands and feet, yet they fell into the state of servitude to others.
Wisdom is not for the acquisition of wealth, nor is birth for the attainment of prosperity;
the wise man understands the nature of the world's transitions, and no one else.
And a great equality of results is observed in the conjunctions of karma:
some carry the palanquin, while others ride upon it.
The intellects of even the great, when bound by the noose of destiny and their minds struck down by fate, become crooked in their course.
The gods do not protect one by taking up weapons like a cattle-herder;
however, him whom they wish to protect, they endow with intelligence.
To that person whom the gods intend for defeat, they withdraw his intelligence; he then perceives things perversely.
When the intellect has become clouded and destruction is at hand,
this confusion regarding what is right and wrong does not depart from the heart.
Time does not raise a staff to cut off the heads of embodied beings;
such is the power of Time: it is the perception of things in their reverse.
Whatever skillful action one has performed oneself, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
that alone shall be one's dowry when departing for the next world.
The heirs divide among themselves the wealth acquired by one who is dead through life-threatening labors;
yet that very evil deed which was committed out of a desire for gain becomes the dowry for one struck down by fate.
Neither physical appearance, nor lineage, nor character, nor even a thousandfold learning, nor purity of speech bears fruit for one who lacks [inner virtue].
Just as trees bear fruit in their own time, so too do the deeds accumulated through a previous store of merit come to fruition for a person.
The long vine of Aśvaghoṣa’s poetic work is ever filled with ancient fruits;
it is wondrous and accompanies embodied beings there as well, remaining perfectly steady.
Even when cut, wrapped, split apart, torn out, released,
rubbed away, or even ground into powder by skilled craftsmen, it never undergoes destruction.
By him Brahmā was fashioned like a potter within the cosmic egg; by him Viṣṇu was cast into the dense thicket of his ten incarnations during the great deluge;
and by him Rudra was made a mendicant wandering for alms forever with a skull in hand.
Homage to that Karmic Agent, by whose power the sun wanders through the sky.
Whoever sowed the seed of karma in the past, by whom it was determined, he alone experiences its fruit;
for that which was performed previously cannot be made otherwise even by fate.
The sky is vast for Somadeva, and the horses of the wind are swift;
yet even so, the sun goes to the face of its enemy— for there is no such thing as an unrequited deed.
Having obtained birth together with Fortune herself, he became the very foundation of the three worlds;
for the sake of stability, he approached even the Blue-Throated One (Śiva) and was borne by him upon his head;
yet even so, the Moon did not attain growth, but instead reached its ultimate waning.
Generally, which previous karma would be powerful enough to assist whom?
Then, for someone, fate was the giver and Bali the beggar; the enemy of Mura gave a gift of the earth in the midst of the horse-sacrifice.
Let the fruit be born as bondage itself; homage be to Fate, the doer of what is desired.
Alas, when the ocean of the heart of the wise man is tossed by the wind of adverse fate and abandons its boundary, there arises a succession of waves!
Where there are virtues in Govindarāja, there is no wealth; where there is wealth, there are no virtues.
Oh, what supreme skill the Creator possesses in the art of distribution!
After examining noble lineage, learning, age, valor,
and excellent character, Fate, though skillful, bestows poverty just as it bestows a daughter upon a man.
Even that which has not been touched by the mind, or that which has been abandoned from afar,
Fate bestows it through various means whenever it so desires.
For both [beings],
not only among humans but even among the gods, fate is the sovereign;
when the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) was his friend, Hara wore a garment of skin.
No one is able to overstep destiny through human effort; no one can overstep the path ordained by the Creator.
O Śrī Vālmīki,
whatever action a person afflicted by fate performs at any time,
that very act, once performed, is thwarted by fate.
Discipline belongs to that method which one follows;
even a correctly applied method becomes a bad method for one who lacks fortune.
That which lies beyond the range of the mind’s desires, which even the words of a poet cannot touch,
and wherein even the occurrence of a dream is difficult to find— that very thing the Creator brings about with effortless ease.
Whose is this unrighteous, miserly, virtue-shunning man, harsh in speech and of many crooked thoughts,
who enjoys such prosperity? Tell me, is this the work of men or of fate?
Rāhu,
though armless, destroys even the thousand-rayed sun in the expanse of the sky;
for when the moon is crooked and situated within, where can the heroes prevail?
Indeed, even the rare attainment of Carpaṭi’s state serves only as a calamity for someone else, who,
having obtained his own body free from disease, [is ruined] by Rāhu.
Indeed, in this world, some attain renown through even a small quality;
an elephant is called "elephant" by a single tusk, but the sun is not so called even by a thousand.
This is the nature of one who showers forth light.
Even a fish can distinguish milk from water;
however, the renowned glory of the royal swan is attained through merits alone.
For when fate has turned adverse, even great effort becomes fruitless;
even a thousand rays were unable to support the sun as it was about to fall.
O virtuous ones, abandon pride in your virtues; in assemblies you are merely servants of those who possess virtue.
Even the root of a lotus, though filled with excellence, sinks into the mud.
O Rudra,
if Fate were self-composed and acted according to its own rules, it would grant wisdom to one born of a noble family, wealth to the learned, and both charity and enjoyment to the wealthy.
Ugliness for women, the leadership of the wicked, poverty for the virtuous, and a short lifespan for the learned—
by whom was this created, whether knowingly or unknowingly?
All that lack of self was drunk up by him with that vessel.
For some,
there is the affliction of the planets by the sun and the moon;
for others, even the binding of elephants and serpents.
And observing the poverty of those possessed of intelligence,
it is my conviction that, alas, destiny is powerful.
First, he creates the jewel among men, a mine of all virtues and an ornament for the earth;
yet if, immediately thereafter, he causes it to perish in that very instant—alas, what a tragedy, what a lack of wisdom on the part of Fate!
O Phalguhaṣṭinī,
for those who possess incomparable courage and excellent resolve, and who cause wonder to the entire world—
if their desired goals are not accomplished, it is due to the cruelty of fate; it is not the fault of the spirited ones.
In this world of living beings, a wise man should certainly not engage in the torment of a miser for the sake of his livelihood, even for a single moment.
Even while lying down motionless,
he hears that goal which is to be attained by one who relies on the certainty of its fruit.
Whether in battle where weapons are brandished,
or in a house, or in a blazing fire, or in a mountain cleft, or in the great ocean;
or whether one dwells together with all beings whose minds are agitated.
That which is not destined to exist does not come into being, and that which is destined to exist does not perish.
From birth, he had been devoted to the Venerable Vāsudeva, having no other protector,
and was appointed to the office of charioteer by virtue of his fitness.
Even though he has not yet descended from the sun’s path,
his desired goals will not fail to be realized without merit.
To Vāsudeva,
even the moon becomes the sun, sandalwood paste becomes fire, and friends become enemies;
when fate is adverse and the mind is distressed, all things are turned upside down.
The Lord of Sindhu, who had acquired another head for the sake of drinking Soma,
experienced the falling of his own head as a boon from Vṛddhaśaktidhara Āḍhya.

O Goddess, that very mace of yours, which slew Śrutāyudha in battle in the form of a thunderbolt—by the power of fate, it was not recognized by him as he fled; had it been recognized, he would have perished by its very blow.
Whatever means a person employs for the purpose of harming another,
by that very means his own destruction shall surely come to pass;
just as fire emits smoke that causes blindness of the eyes.
Having become a cloud, he shall satisfy that very [earth] with waters.
O Creator, you who are the dark age (Kali) that shatters the multitude of lotuses that are various learned men—
what would happen if such partiality of yours toward the wicked were to exist even in a dream among the virtuous? What could possibly come of it?
Bhaṭṭa Vāsudeva [composed this] on Mount Sumeru, where the people have their desires fulfilled by wish-fulfilling trees,
and in the deep waters of the lord of rivers, which are filled with jewels.
The Creator, who constantly places prosperity among the wicked,
has indeed placed a lamp that is exceedingly brilliant inside a jar.
In this world, the Creator— who is deluded by the emptiness of causes— is fickle regarding the path strewn with dust and thorns, as he is indifferent to both merits and faults.
Like a child playing with impetuosity,
he draws something or other with handfuls of dust, and then wipes it away again.
The wicked Creator, having placed the mind of some person upon the ever-shifting wheel of anxiety— which is set in motion by a succession of falls from the edge of the staff of misfortune—
forces it, like a lump of clay, into a ball and whirls it about like a skilled potter; we do not know what he will fashion here.

O dull-witted Fate, whose own course has been disrupted by the dissolution of the aeon, if you wish to behold the collapse of the great ones' fortitude in the face of calamity— [do so] from this [world], which is difficult to master due to the fruitlessness of valor and exertion.
O mountain peaks, these are not Śūdras, nor are they serpents dwelling in the water.
The wise have indeed said that food obtained without effort from the earth is like a gift from the gods; beasts,
on the other hand, were created by the Creator to feed on grass-blades and shoots, sleeping upon the bare ground.
This commentary on the *Samādhirāja-sūtra*, which crushes the ocean of saṃsāra, has been composed for the sake of men;
by its mere hearing, all virtues suddenly reach their full completion.
For a man who is preoccupied with his wife and troubled by thoughts of his family, all his learning, character,
and virtues perish along with his body, like water poured into an unbaked clay jar.
One day, scorched on the head by the rays of the sun, a certain man,
longing for the shade of a lordly tree, went by the power of fate to the root of a *bilva* tree.
Even there, as he fell with great force, his head was shattered and burst with a loud noise;
for misfortunes generally go to that very place where one is already struck down by fate.
Even one who exerts himself for the sake of Divīrādeśāditya may fail to obtain the fruit sought; conversely,
someone else, though making no effort toward any undertaking, obtains the desired result.
In this world, the wealth of one person perishes, while another is joined with it;
for the workings of this destiny are manifold, like the behavior of children, madmen, and the insane.
O Venerable One,
for Āryaśūra, whose body was crushed by a stone pillar, whose limbs were withered, and whose senses were failing,
hunger at night caused a mouse to fall of its own accord into the mouth of a serpent.
Immediately upon being requested by him, he departed along that very same path;
therefore, remain at ease, for destiny alone is intent upon the increase and decline of human beings.
O protectors of the earth, those who hate virtue, though possessed of intellect, are submerged in the mire of envy;
the virtuous are always in a state of misfortune, while the wealthy long for the practice of sin.
Those with innocent eyes are the abode of passion, yet those who are well-restrained turn away from attachment through love.
In this cycle of existence, what indeed is more intoxicating than the wicked? It is that which is not even lamented by Fate.

If I could ever behold him—him who always takes delight in the creation of the world, which is insipid for those who have seen its transience; he who is firm in uplifting the lowly and helping the virtuous when they are in distress;
and who speaks with words that are compassionate, reproachful, and full of sorrow—then I would see him somewhere.
Shame! I would make even the Creator himself utter words of failure through my lack of accomplishment.
I am that very Pārtha; this too is that bow obtained as a boon;
these are those very arrows which have crushed the armies of the enemies of the gods;
and these are the young women of the Vṛṣṇis, headed by the strength of Hari.
Men are carried away by cowherds because the power of destiny is exceedingly strong.
Even for those who are destined for liberation, there is no grasping of the ultimate limit; rather,
their longing runs toward that direction in which the Creator’s desire flows.
Just as grass is carried away by the wind,
so too is a person led along by the mind, which is under the sway of intense obsession.
Through the physician’s skill, the patient who eats wholesome food recovers;
yet the poor man remains destitute, guarding his wealth from thieves, sleeplessness, and ruin as if protecting a wound.
He is the one who brings about the accumulation of these [virtues], possessing unwavering sovereignty and fortitude; by his very command, he is the subduer whose power is sharpened by self-mastery.
It is said that there is a stain upon the moon,
thorns upon the lotus,
poverty upon the virtuous, and black serpents upon the sandalwood tree.
He by whom the water of the ocean was made undrinkable through his creation in this world—
that Creator is indeed seen to be devoid of discrimination in the world.

O Fate, you who are ever intent upon the task of fashioning the universe, we entreat you with our heads bowed like kinsmen: let there be no further birth for us. Moreover, if we should wander once more in this world, may it be [only] then.
Brahminhood, generosity, wealth, fame, and knowledge—these are our [possessions].
Where Bṛhaspati is not the leader, where the thunderbolt is not the weapon, where the gods are not the soldiers,
where heaven is not the fortress, where grace does not belong to Hari,
and where Airāvata is not the vehicle— even though he was endowed with such wondrous powers, the Conqueror of Bala was defeated by the Asuras in battle.
Therefore, it is surely destiny alone that is the refuge; fie, fie upon futile human effort!
For some, the ocean becomes dry land; dry land becomes the ocean; a speck of dust attains the state of a mountain;
Mount Meru becomes a mound of clay; grass becomes a thunderbolt; and a diamond becomes as fragile as a blade of grass.
Salutation to that Fate, who by his own will causes fire to become cool like frost and coldness to turn into heat— a Fate addicted to the wondrous vice of capricious self-indulgence.
Why do you wander about in vain? Let the mind find rest somewhere.
Whatever comes to pass happens by itself; it is exactly as it is and not otherwise.
Without recollecting the past nor forming intentions for the future, [let the mind remain at peace].
I experience enjoyments that arrive unexpectedly and beyond my reach.
Whatever is destined to be will happen, even without effort; and whatever is not destined to be will not happen, even with great exertion. (Kṣemendra’s *Subhāṣitaratnakośa* 3154–3155)
In this world of living beings, which is thus fashioned by the Ordainer and subject to his will, what suffering can there be for a discerning man?
Through the rise of fortune, a powerful man may even find a servant superior to his own son;
yet later, when fate turns adverse, that very servant reviles him as if he were an enemy. What is the use of this arduous devotion and intense service performed day and night?
The fruit of a living being, whether auspicious or inauspicious, remains entirely governed by destiny.
Fie on the pure eye of Kṣemendra, which is a vessel for the ash of collyrium;
while the ear, though full of holes, stained, and crooked, is the receptacle for gold!
Now, for someone,
the path to misfortune is folly; for what misfortune is there that does not culminate in ignorance?
He who is not attached even to that—where else could he be attached?
If one is born into a noble family, for what purpose is there poverty?
Even in the midst of poverty, there is the folly of ignorance—alas, what a succession of sufferings!
Who could understand the profound nature of these external objects if they were not revealed by that which is like a young child or a servant?
It is said: In this world, even a stranger becomes a kinsman to those who possess wealth;
yet to the poor, even their own kin vanish while they are still alive.
For even when present, other virtues do not shine for one whose purpose is base;
like the sun among living beings, prosperity is the illuminator of virtues.
The executioner and the pauper—these two persons are equal:
people do not accept gifts from the executioner, and the pauper has nothing to give.
Indeed, dwelling in hell is better than living in a house of evil conduct;
for in hell one’s sin is exhausted, whereas in a wretched home it increases.
Śambara said that there is no state more wretched than that in which,
my dear, there is no food to be found either today or tomorrow morning.
O King, a person who is poor by nature is not so greatly afflicted as one who,
having attained prosperity, is later deprived of those very blessings to which he was accustomed.
Better is the birth of even a tree that is humpbacked, with its roots dug out, its wood consumed by fire, and its bark withered,
yet stands in a pool of water, than that of one who is a suppliant.
For a poor man who lacks virtue, wealth, and pleasure, and who eats the food of others,
a long life is merely a mockery, like that of a crow.
"Come here! Go away! Fall down! Stand up! Speak! Observe silence!"—in this manner do the wealthy play with supplicants who are seized by the grip of such expectations.
Cold weather,
a long journey, poor food, the passing of women, and opposition from the mind— these are the five causes of old age.
For those who have given their desired affection to friends by relinquishing their wealth,
it is better to live or die than to be unable to repay that kindness.
O Vyāsa Muni,
for this modest and well-born man who desires to ask for wealth,
her speech causes him to go back and forth like a pigeon at a pillar.
Stammering, perspiration on the face, pallor,
and trembling— these very signs that belong to one who is dying are present in the beggar.
Blessed are those who do not witness the ruin of their country, the destruction of their family,
nor the misfortune and suffering of their wives, children, and others who have entered the hearts of enemies.
For those afflicted by hunger and thirst,
even palaces, sandalwood, moonlight,
beds, and carriages with young women in their prime are not delightful; for all such undertakings are rooted in a mere *prastha* of rice.
Poetry is destroyed by prose, poetry by song;
song is destroyed by the dalliance of women, and the dalliance of women by hunger.
No gift was given, no austerity was practiced, and neither Śaṃkara nor Vāsudeva was propitiated; nor was the body offered as an oblation in fire or in battle. O body, why do you pray for pleasures?
Those who subsist on fruits, roots, grass, and water; who are naked and sleep on the bare ground;
though bewildered by their homes, they wander like sages—yet their austerity is equal [to others'] only in being devoid of fruit.
I have not practiced patience; I have not renounced the pleasures appropriate for householders out of contentment;
I have not performed ascetic penance through the eightfold hardships of unbearable cold winds and heat;
nor have I meditated day and night on the state of Śambhu with restrained breath.
Whatever karma was performed by those various sages has been abandoned along with its respective fruits.
Their limbs shattered by those with fierce weapons who treat them with contempt, utterly consumed by the cruel fire of poverty,
they have here experienced even that which was intended as a benefit from their kinsmen.
While we are still alive, can the son of the Sun (Yama) have any sleep?
There are no objects [to give], yet my wicked hope does not let me go;
my mind is ill-behaved and does not shrink from giving. Begging brings me low, and there is sin in killing myself.
O vital breaths, depart of your own accord; for what is the use of lingering?
For some of them,
as they sink into the ocean of thought— like a piece of meat pulled from a spit while still warm—
their throats are parched as they blow upon their extinguished fires, their lips trembling.
Sleep has gone far away, as if insulted by her beloved;
the night does not diminish, like the earth bestowed upon a worthy recipient.

For those who protect their integrity, life is lowly when wealth is lost, yet it is sustained through begging, hardships, and deceptions; for the virtuous who are mute with pride for their lineage, there is no such thing as a life devoid of these.
O Kṣemendra,
there are companions for a living being only so long as it does not encounter hardship;
when death has descended upon the head, who is capable of protecting whom?
For Ravigupta,
who is sick, long away from home, eating the food of others, and sleeping in the dwellings of others,
what he lives is his death, and what he dies is his rest.
O King, tell me, whose fault is it?
It is not my mother’s, nor my daughter-in-law’s; it is not my mother-in-law’s, nor my daughter’s;
it is not mine, nor hers. Whose fault is it?
O venerable Kapardin,
when the sun has risen I expand, and as it sets I undergo contraction;
submerged in the lake of poverty, I experience the lotus-like state.
The moon by night, the sun by day, and the fire at both twilights—
thus have I brought coolness through the moon, the sun, and the fire.
For a person of even vast intelligence, the intellect perishes day after day through anxiety over ghee, salt, oil, rice, vegetables, and fuel,
due to the meagerness of their resources.
Generally, the intellects of those whose defeat is imminent become most severely perverted;
even so, Rāma lusted after a deer that could not possibly be made of gold.
People do not feel joy at that [state] because of their lack of sovereignty, for they have not seen its majesty;
rather, due to the loss of their accustomed pleasure, those who have fallen from their prosperity experience suffering,
just as those whose eyes have been plucked out suffer when repeatedly remembering the objects of their vision.
O friend Bhaṭṭānandaka, do not yield to grief; indeed, cultivate those innate arts of yours.
Prosper through your own fame; for where, indeed, has this resolve of yours not already been accomplished?
If it is argued that this [effort] is not in vain because its manifestation is here, we say this is not appropriate:
for those of manifold resolve, is this entire triple world merely this much?
Of the illustrious Vāsudeva,
the kitchen was empty of cooking pots, the servants were eating parched grain, and at night,
without lamps, the darkness was completely dispelled by the dense smoke.
A house whose doors are not guarded by those who are affectionate, and where the festival of joy is never fulfilled,
truly becomes like a prison and leads to suffering for the householder.
The conduct of the wicked has been witnessed; contempt has been received from one's own peers.
For the sake of alms, I have performed humble service for the wealthy; I have eaten even from begging bowls.
I have repeatedly traveled on foot along the road and slept upon beds of straw.
And whatever else is not yet done, O Kṛtānta, perform it; we are ready for that as well.
O noble lady, first utter these pure words of Vikramāditya in their proper sequence; let your face attain clarity,
let your mind find composure, proceed with gravity, and cultivate steadfastness in wisdom.
O Shame, turn away for a moment; O Thirst, stay before me for a while, so that I, a wretch, may utter the piteous words "Give" to the wealthy man.
“Arise for a single moment, my friend, and carry this heavy burden of poverty! I am weary; let me first experience the long-lasting bliss of death.
Having been addressed thus by the wise man who was destitute of wealth, the corpse went to the cremation ground.
Having realized that death is better than poverty, he remained silent.

What person of noble mind would say "Give! with words whose syllables are faltering, broken, and dissolved due to a throat choked with the fear of a refusal to beg, for the sake of his own wretched belly?
In my house, O Lord of Fortune, the dog barks like a jackal, the female mouse acts like a cat, the cat behaves like a dog, and the wife speaks like a beggar; what more can be said of other people?

Having thus fallen into this state, she abandons her children; and with cries of "Jhili! and "Samprekṣa!", the woman, her face covered by a web of spider-silk, weeps for a long time in the corner of the hearth.
If I am unable to support my family while living at home, and if I resort to the forest of sages— the means for attaining happiness— thieves will plunder me.
"If I cast my body into the abyss, I shall fall from the heights of self-respect into hell;
O Fate, I do not know what I should do—whether to die or to live."
Let there not be birth in a great family; and even if that occurs, let there not be misfortune. Even if there be many wives, let there not be a heart tender with compassion.
If such a heart exists, let there be death; and if there is no moment for even that [death], then let it be.
Let its persistence exist in another location that is indistinguishable from that previous birth.
Those whose own self-interest was not reckoned as significant compared to the welfare of others because they were embraced by compassion;
those who, being possessed of ultimate pity, did not leave the requests of supplicants unfulfilled;
and those whose minds were pained by the suffering of others—those virtuous ones have passed away.
Restrain the surge of tears from your eyes; for whom are you weeping now?
She spreads out the parched grain, prepares the offerings, and soothes the crying children;
she pours water from a jar and guards the beds.
Holding a fragment of an old winnowing basket upon her head, she wanders distractedly through the empty house.
What is that which she does not do? When the rain falls heavily from the sky, the wife of a poor man [does not weep].
With unseasonable praises, he causes a piercing pain in the ears;
he speaks of his own poverty while displaying his tattered garment.
Moving like a shadow, he neither stays before, nor at the sides, nor behind; this wretched man sheds sweat for the wealthy, a malady as difficult to cure as a disease.
