In an assembly devoid of great people, for those who are proud, death itself is better than seeking refuge in another protector for the sake of one's welfare;
by the grace of that [refuge], my own husband became a lord who dispels poverty.
I beg for my life and clothing, and for the ten directions as a dwelling in the abode of the gods.
Since you have taken refuge in my enemy, thinking "my foe has found a patron," you have assigned my livelihood to him; what indeed is my own livelihood?
"Lighter than even a blade of grass, and lighter than even cotton—why has this beggar not been carried away by the wind? He might even ask me for something."

My body, which was once made of copper, has now become the color of gold; the streams of drops from my pearl necklace have formed a garland for me as I sigh. My youth, so very brief, has now been made to seem like a vast eon.
O Moon-faced One, through the hundredfold grace of Your Majesty, what is there that I have not obtained?
Now, the method of service:
Servants indeed endure cold, wind, heat, and hunger;
therefore, by performing austerity even with a hundred [verses] of truth, one shall become happy.
When kings' minds are corrupted and base people are easily found, oh, how strange it is that those who do not live [by such means] survive even for a moment!
Of all modes of livelihood, that which depends upon the royal court is the most base;
for it is full of unrighteousness and is constantly attended by fear, O Bhārata.
The fear that remains in the heart of one being pursued by an enemy does not remain at all in the hearts of those who dwell in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits.
The servant abandons both happiness and even his very name;
that very purpose for which he strives here is lost to him.
For one who has sold himself, who is impotent, whose mind is always suspicious,
and who is perpetually tormented by the loss of what he desires— what happiness can there be for such a wretched servant?
Like courtesans out of greed for wealth,
fools themselves repeatedly refine their own selves and make them a means for serving others.
Even among those of equal human birth, servitude is indeed contemptible;
yet even he who is not subject to it there is counted among the living.
This alone is the fruitfulness of birth: that one's livelihood is not dependent on others.
For those whose births are subject to the will of another—if they live, who are they? They are as good as dead.
Birth itself is suffering, and from that follows a miserable rebirth; in such a miserable state, one must subsist by servitude—alas, what a succession of sufferings!
Even though his throat is constricted by the guards at the gate who strike him, he nevertheless performs service; oh, how great is thirst!
If a servant survives even when being struck by sticks, he returns again at that very moment; fie on such shameless wretchedness!
With your neck bent down, having gone to the earth with face cast downward—O shameless one, do you feel no shame? How has your pride not dissolved away?
There is no fool in all the three worlds more wretched than a servant who,
out of delusion, desires advancement day after day by bowing down.
O Sage Vyāsa,
these [people] are exceedingly harsh, stubborn, and filled with violent creatures;
they are difficult to approach and as treacherous as mountains ruled by capricious lords.
Somadeva’s *Sevā*:
"Those by whom 'one's own livelihood' has been described have not spoken correctly.
Where is the one who acts according to his own will, and where is the servant who is subject to the whims of others?"
What benefit does one derive from respect toward someone who is devoid of gain?
What quality does the moon receive from being borne upon the head of the Lord (Śiva)?
Even that gaze which is fickle by its very nature and falls even upon the impure—
servants hold such a glance from their masters in high esteem.
For men, serving a king involves embracing the five fires, kissing the face of a serpent,
and treading upon the edge of a sword.
For some,
there is hatred toward food, a fondness for meat, and a constant distaste for heavy meals;
and in their mouths there is perpetual bitterness, like that of wealthy men who are suffering from fever.
He who stands at the gate of kings upon seeing an abundance of wealth is bound like a dog by a butcher; he withers away and does not flourish.
A master who is patient,
a giver, and one who appreciates merit is difficult to find; O King, even a loyal servant who is well-behaved and long-standing is hard to obtain.
O Śrī Hara, for those whose six duties— service to the gods,
fame, protection of the Brahmins, charity, enjoyment, and the safeguarding of friends— are not being fulfilled,
what purpose is there in their seeking refuge with a king?
Servants whose minds are puffed up by being the king’s favorites abandon their noble pride;
with whom can there be friendship toward kings who are like serpents, watching for one's weak points and whose counsel is unrestrained?

It is not at all surprising that someone who is being propitiated in many ways might not be won over; but this is an unprecedented distinction of a portrait, in that when it is served, it attains the status of an enemy.
When his master laughs, he laughs; when his master weeps loudly, he too weeps.
Having prepared himself, he runs about, panting with sweat.
He censures and reviles one who is endowed with virtues and free from faults.
A servant who has been purchased for a mere trifle of wealth bows down and dances.

For Dharmakīrti, there was perspiration; his hair stood on end and became coarse; he trembled from agitation; he felt an internal burning; his fortitude failed him; his face grew pale; and he was overcome with distress.
Alas, that teacher who, though heavy with authority, has become light through various such means— he, indeed,
touches the path of the word "begging," which is like a fever born of a malarial relapse.
“O King, my ears have been filled by me with words whose meaning is emptiness;
you too have made many ‘ear-fills’ for me from those very [words] that are most empty.
As we thus deceive one another, this time passes away for us.”
The Kṣatriyas say: "I am conquered, you are unconquered, O King; you are praised as the victor."
Out of a desire for wealth,
she bows to her husband for the sake of her youth, stands outside to honor the lord of the household,
and squanders her own property with the reckless expenditure of a foolish and passionate woman.
In battle, he releases his very life-breaths; through desire for enjoyments, he suffers;
his servant, whose vision is blinded by craving, performs everything quite the opposite.

In the forest there are excellent trees with sweet fruit; there is pure water from mountain torrents; bark provides clothing, and mountain caves serve as dwellings; the bed is made of creepers and young shoots;
at night, the moonbeams provide light, and one has deer for companions.
Alas, even when their own wealth is at their disposal, foolish men beg from the king!
Even among them,

those whose minds are suspicious and terrified, who are intent on deception and fraud, who are as fruitlessly stubborn as massive rocks, and who are prone to excessive anger over even a slight fault— [such people are not fit vessels].
Arrogant, agitated, speaking malicious words, wicked in their mockery of the Dharma, hostile toward the virtuous, and utterly base— such, in every respect, are the rulers of the earth.
He stands idly at the gate and somehow fails to see what has arrived before him;
he employs deceptive maneuvers and verbal sophistry in his perception;
and for even a minor offense, Yama counts up a multitude of faults against one who has gone forth.
If that Lord is served by you, O Maruts, what have the Piśācas not done?
Even a lion may kill while bowing; even a serpent may strike while coiling;
even a Vetāla may laugh; and even a king may praise.
Purity in a crow, truthfulness in gamblers, fortitude in a eunuch, contemplation of reality in a drunkard,
clarity of knowledge in women, and the pacification of desire— by whom has a king been seen or heard of as a friend?
Now, the Section on Craving (tṛṣṇāpaddhati):
Mounted upon the chariot of desire, yoked with the horses of the sense-faculties,
and impelled by craving as its charioteer, the entire world indeed wanders about.
The face is overcome by wrinkles, the hair is turned white with gray;
the limbs grow slack, yet craving alone remains youthful.
Youth is seized by old age; health is struck down by diseases;
life is overtaken by death; yet craving alone remains unassailed.
Just as the horn of a cow grows as the cow grows over time,
so too does craving increase as wealth increases.
Just as an unchaste wife incites her husband toward what ought not to be done, craving drives a person toward evil;
yet shame protects that very person from all sins, like a mother.
Hope is powerful and painful; freedom from hope is the supreme happiness. Having cast away all hopes, Piṅgalā sleeps in peace.
By whom can this thirst be filled, which is unfathomably deep like a pit and impossible to satiate?
For even when great quantities are poured into it, it is merely dug deeper by those very fillings.
O Thirst, you too, tormented by thirst, are attached to three things:
to those who are diseased, to those who are childless, and to those who are decayed with old age.
Having displayed existence after existence before me, one after another,
thirst has led me far away, like a goat toward a handful of green grass.
If a person cannot proceed without something, let him indeed desire it;
but when asked for an answer that provides a meaning superior to that, what could he possibly give?
Even for those who are wealthy, prosperity is not respected by beggars here; yet some do not honor the destitute.
He who is clothed in yellow garments obtained the Goddess of Fortune from the ocean, while the one clad in the directions received the crescent moon as a gift.
These are the qualities of Vyāsa Muni so long as he does not seek anything from another;
when he abides in a state of neediness, there are neither qualities nor dignity.
A single woman of wicked character ruins a family’s wisdom, its solar brilliance, its benevolence,
and its noble lineage through her constant begging.
The teeth have fallen out, the hair has turned white, and there is a stumbling at every step;
yet this wretched body, ready to fall, is not abandoned by the virtuous Thirst.
One who possesses a thousand desires to possess ten thousand; one who possesses ten million desires kingship; and even a king, alas, desires the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Even a wheel-turning monarch desires the state of a god, and even a god seeks the sovereignty of the gods;
yet even the king of the gods seeks a higher rebirth—nevertheless, craving does not cease.
For some, she who was the cause and the instrumental factor for the world’s contempt,
and the very reason for even the Lord of the Gods’ own humiliation—
O Lord, that craving always deceives me; O Blessed One, cut it off by force so that there may be no further rebirth.
"Having propitiated the king and obtained wealth from him,
we shall indeed enjoy constant pleasures as ascetics."
Thus, for those whose minds are deluded by existence through such inclinations,
time passes until death becomes the limit for men.
First there is the milk, and then that which is boiled; from that,
its sweetness is forcibly taken away and churned out,
until it is born again in the form of butter and fresh cream.
Attachment is the bond for the succession of misfortunes.
Out of delusion, I took a wife, thinking "I shall live happily as a householder";
from that attachment arose the birth of sons, slaves, kinsmen, wealth, and relatives.
Afflicted by the thought that it is improper to cause distress or humiliation to those who support him, he reflected:
"What happiness is there? What kind of household life is this? Why have I accepted such a calamity?"
For someone,
while intent on propitiating him, even the laughter suppressed within their heart was somehow restrained by the elders with empty minds.
O you who possess a false luster, I have already offered salutations with my mind fixed upon the pillar of wealth; what more than this can you do to make me dance?
In a land filled with many difficult and uneven terrains, my husband has wandered and achieved no fruit; my youth has been spent in vain by a mind exhausted with longing.
Having abandoned service performed in a manner befitting your noble lineage, you have rendered it fruitless; O Tṛṣṇā, tell me what else you desire, for we remain attached even to that.
Ah, the clever craving of someone, which deludes all people,
robs the innocent of their composure while they are rendered powerless!
The rogue of passion, with eyes like those of a deer in distress, tremulous with fear, and with deceptive glances from his brow, casts sidelong looks at his beloved.
In Janasthāna, my mind blinded by the pursuit of the Golden Deer, I wandered;
at every step, I uttered the words "O Vaidehī" in delirious lamentation.
I have fashioned the face of the Lord of Laṅkā into a stage for my performance;
I have attained the state of being Rāma, yet I have not achieved the status of being Kuśa and Lava.
Now, the Exposition on Impermanence:
O impermanence, though you are censured by the world, you are now worthy of praise,
for you bring about, as a consequence, the impermanence of even sufferings.
Truly, sensual pleasures are enchanting; truly, sovereign powers are delightful. But life, alas, is as fickle as the flickering side-long glances of an intoxicated woman.
If this person perceives death standing upon their very head, they would even renounce food;
how much more so the performance of unwholesome deeds?
Having fallen from sight and having returned to sight again, they are not yours, nor are you theirs; what cause for lamentation is there in that?
For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain. Therefore, you ought not to grieve over that which is inevitable.
O Bhārata, all beings are unmanifest in their origin, manifest in their middle state, and indeed unmanifest again in their end;
what cause for lamentation is there in this?
The one who should not grieve grieves; why does he grieve for that which is worthy of grief, or why is that which is not worthy of grief not grieved for?
And who here is to be grieved for by whom, in this body that is like a bubble?
Even those who think "there is no [retribution]" are tormented by their own powerlessness;
in just a few days, the Ender brings them to equality with all.
For those who are awakened by sweet-sounding drums, songs, and instrumental music,
and for those who are destitute and dependent on the food of others, time acts with equal impartiality toward them all.
That which has passed is gone; that which is yet to come is far off.
The distinction between the pleasure of the present and the delusion of the two—the wealthy and the poor—is but a fleeting error.
What logic is there in maintaining this body— which ends in worms, ashes, or excrement— by inflicting suffering upon others?
Even that body, at the end of which one sleeps with feet raised to the head in apprehension,
is indeed maintained by men only after they have slain their enemies.
How can those of manifestly evil conduct sleep peacefully at night,
when their rebirth in the hells is separated from them only by death?
By good fortune, I have reached this land of old age, far removed from the states of woe;
with skill, I have traversed the great wilderness of youth.
That man is not truly a man who, pained and wailing piteously, broken by old age,
dies in the midst of weeping kinsmen.
For the sake of this body— a mere repository of all impurities, ungrateful,
and perishable— fools commit sinful deeds.
"One should perform one's own duty this very day, as well as that which belongs to the forenoon and the afternoon;
for death does not wait to see whether one's work is finished or not."
When the sun has already set and wealth was not given to those who sought it,
I truly do not know whose property that wealth will belong to tomorrow morning.
Whatever one gives and whatever one eats, that alone is the wealth of the wealthy;
others merely play with the wife and the riches of the deceased.
Death is certain for embodied beings, and life is indeed impermanent;
for who knows whether death will come today or tomorrow?
In thousands of ages, there might be a single day without birth;
yet even that has now come to pass—what then can be said of the end of death?
Know that destruction, which is inevitable, is present because it is destined to occur;
for this very time was previously your future.
Just as two pieces of wood, having come together in the great ocean, might meet and then drift apart,
so too is the coming together of living beings.
Thousands of mothers and fathers, and hundreds of sons and wives, have passed away in age after age; to whom do they belong, or to whom do we belong?
Nine years have passed that were equal [to my time], yet they are no longer equal for me;
I grieve for myself like a traveler who has lost his caravan.
Rising up again and again, one must remain vigilant: a great terror has arrived;
which of these—death, disease, or sorrow—will fall upon me today?
In this cycle of existence, there is no pleasure whatsoever that is not a meeting with the virtuous;
for one whose mind is consumed by the fire of separation from them, there is no remedy.
What will men, who rely on what is fragile, do with wealth? For whose sake they desire wealth—that body, for whom is it permanent?
"White fragments of bone fall before you;
do you not see them as your life is being severed by death?"
Death draws closer day by day,
like a condemned man being led step by step to the place of execution.
O mortal, why do you fear death? For one who is already afraid is not released from it; nor does one who is unborn undergo it.
Therefore, exert yourself for the sake of being unborn.
"Whether standing or lying down, death indeed approaches;
why then, my son, do you sleep so happily like a fish in a small pond?"
Through the thought "I shall do it, I shall do it,
I shall do it," I have forgotten that "I shall die, I shall die, I shall die."
You behold those of equal birth, age, and appearance being struck down by death;
how is it that you feel no world-weariness? Indeed, your heart is made of iron.
The body is accompanied by its own destruction; prosperity is the ground of calamities;
meetings end in partings; everything is fragile and subject to decay in the end.
Some,
even at the departure of their own life-breaths, do not remember the Enemy of Smara (Śiva);
they are submerged in the mire of their household, deluded by ignorance like children.
Oh,
this memory of Śrī Hara is intent on inflaming passion and the like;
having produced aesthetic flavor (rasa) for everyone, it subsequently brings about a sense of distaste.
Enveloped by ignorance in childhood, intoxicated by pride in youth,
and with limbs failing in old age— when shall I become a partaker of the wholesome?
Stricken by ignorance in childhood, struck by passion in youth,
and afflicted by anxiety for his wife in old age— what can a person do, and when? (By the scholar Śrī Bakasimha)
Today there is childhood, and in just a few days the splendor of youth follows; then comes old age.
Even within the body there is no single form; how much less so in external objects?
Through these words of the sage Vālmīki,
uttered with a faltering voice as the roots of his thighs trembled,
I have experienced a union with old age as if with a new bride.
O King, men— never satisfied with dharma, wealth, pleasure, fame, and life—
both go toward and have gone toward servitude.
Not even a single moment of life can be obtained even for ten million gold coins;
homage to that king who spends it in vain!
Where the earth is consumed by fire and even Mount Meru is shattered to pieces, what need is there to mention the waters of the ocean? They too will perish within that body.
Thousands of Purandaras and hundreds of Cakravartins have been extinguished by time, like lamps by the wind.
By this [staff], which has become like a youth with a strong grip though my body has grown old,
I have taken two or three steps with difficulty, just as Hari did.
It is straight, firm, well-rounded, radiant from the grasping of the hand, and fashioned from fine bamboo.
She supports me as I fall, just as a housewife supports her staff.
Childish play is desired, then the pride of youth, and then the renunciation of old age;
that too has passed, that too has passed, and that too has passed—this is like a dream or an illusion.
This attainment of the favorable moment, so difficult to find and capable of accomplishing the goals of human existence, has been obtained by some;
if one does not reflect upon what is beneficial here, how will such a convergence occur again?
O Bodhisattva, if there were no birth, old age, and death; if there were no fear of separation from what is dear;
and if all this were not impermanent—then who here in this world would not find delight?
Prosperity is fickle, youth perishes in an instant, and life dwells between the teeth of Death;
yet, even so, men show contempt for the means of achieving the next world—oh, what a marvelous and astonishing course of action!
Prosperities are as flickering as waves upon the water; youth lasts but three or four days; life is as unstable as an autumn cloud. What is the use of wealth? Perform deeds for the benefit of others!
The feet of the one whose nature is Dharma were here saluted by me, and here I held conversations with him along with Bhīma;
and here Arjuna and the twin-born sons followed him—these are indeed sacred places, for they are no mere mortals.
These heart-stealing young women of Vyāsa are his friends, ever-favorable; his servants have speech filled with affection;
there are elephants and horses as various implements; yet, when the eyes are closed, none of that exists at all.
For King Śrī Vikramāditya,
one moment he was a child, another moment a youth indulging in the pleasures of love;
one moment he was destitute of wealth, and another moment possessed of abundant riches.
O Bhartṛhari! A man whose body is adorned with wrinkles, as if marked by the lines of old age,
enters the marketplace of Yama’s realm within the theater of *saṃsāra*.

From the abode of hell he goes to the residence of pretas, and from there to the abode of the thirty-three gods; from the celestial realm of the thirty-three he goes to the animal womb, and from a state of auspicious existence he returns again to the animal womb or even to the human state.
The world, pierced by karma, wanders helplessly like the wheel of a chariot.

I was born from the ocean of milk; this is my father and she is my mother. My wife, my field, my family, my sons, friends, enemies, wealth, home, brother, sister, and kinsmen—[all these are but transitory].
O mind, alas! Just as one might sleep for a very long time on a bed in this saṃsāra—a sleep consisting of ignorance—you are shaken about and see these various kinds of dreams.

O wise ones, serve the enemy of Andhaka, the son of Kṛṣṇā; do not distress yourselves with hardships. For he alone is Śiva, the protector in this world, in the next, and throughout the three worlds, as heard in the scriptures.
When the terrifying Kālarātri has arrived due to the power of destiny,
where is there room for formal exposition, where for the quarrels of logic, and where even for the labor of poetry?
In the home of the illustrious Rājanaka Kaulaka,

there is a heap of saffron and sandalwood paste, fine silken garments, moonlight, and the embrace of breasts marked with the saffron-stain of the lover’s nails upon the cool tree-like surface of their bosom.
At night, there is the sound of lutes and the most excellent, delightful songs; by day, there is the assembly of the virtuous.
For whom is such a body desirable, which is ungrateful yet seemingly stable?
O Death, release this man; do not, do not seize him by the hair with the hand of old age!
For passion and the other afflictions remain as the guarantors of his failure to flee from cyclic existence.
Do you not know that this world has its crest of the mind bound by the fetters of craving? Come; shall I not destroy for you these words of yours spoken with such earnestness?
When pride has withered away, when youth— so turbulent with enjoyments—

has dissolved, when kinsmen have been gradually worn away by time, and when the dawning of discernment is slowly attained; then, for those who have abandoned desire and are freed from the triviality of pleasures whose opportunities have been severed, there is the supreme [state].
Truth, truth—indeed, the very absence of wealth is what I know to be happiness.
Is the delightful terrace of the palace not sufficient for dwelling? Is there no music, song, and the like that is pleasant to hear?
Or is there no joy greater than the happiness of union with those dear as one's own life?
Yet, perceiving that everything is as flickering as the shadow of a lamp-flame trembling in the wind caused by a moth falling in its confusion, the wise have gone to the edge of the forest.
Day by day, with the rising and setting of the sun, life is diminished;
yet, due to activities heavy with the burden of many duties, time is not recognized.
Having witnessed birth, old age, separation, and death, fear does not arise.
Having drunk the intoxicating liquor of delusion, the world has become like one who is insane.
Alas, for them too, that brother has gone; woe is me! That king, that circle of vassals, and that assembly of wise courtiers with faces like the orb of the moon have all departed from his side.
Salutations to that Time, by whose power all this— the multitude of princes who have been cast up, those bards, and those stories— has come within the path of memory.
Having enjoyed happiness for a very long time in this cycle of existence along with his friends and kinsmen, a person who has attained the protection of the auspicious Kamalāyudha shall,
at the end, be spared from the agony of being crushed by the teeth of the cruel God of Death.
Therefore, having carefully investigated what is to be done, the wise find that liberation is attained through this very assembly;
yet such an assembly is not possible even in countless eons [if one relies on other means].
Life is momentary; youth too is generally beset by old age.
Unions end in separation, and enjoyments perish in an instant.
Even though they know that this entire world is established in such a manner, people [act otherwise].
It is strange that those whose minds are conditioned by heavy pride become angry and intoxicated.
O dull-witted one, rising again and again toward evil, your mind turns toward sin; for you who commit such a wicked deed, there is neither fear, nor shame, nor even compassion.
Surely you have not heard that terrifying roar of the Raurava hell, with its blazing peaks of fire?
The royal city of Yama is called Tīkṣṇāyaskīlacakrakra-kaca-pāturavā.
Now, for some there is derision regarding sense objects;
the minds of men have been practiced upon sense objects for hundreds of previous births.
Like an old ox from the crops, for she is driven away with great difficulty.
Moreover, it is possible to restrain the surging flow of the great ocean stirred up by a fierce wind, but not the mind that is full of attachment.
O venerable Sage Vyāsa,
if indeed that which is inside this body were to become outside,
then people would raise their staffs to ward off dogs and crows.
The world is agitated by instability and craves fermented liquor;
yet one deceives oneself with the names and concepts created by one's own mind.
Living beings are oppressed by urine and excrement in the morning, by hunger and thirst at midday,
by sensual desire, and at night by sleep.
O King, these which you behold as the snares of the hunter Madana are,
by their very power, the fires of hell that blaze forth.
Those who are passionate carry away one's entire wealth, while those who are dispassionate take even one's life;
alas, women are indeed most difficult to deal with through both passion and dispassion!
These female demons constantly deceive even a minister who is wise, disciplined, of good conduct, and learned.
Nakedness, contact with impurity, foolishness, and unintelligible speech— all these are characteristic of a lustful person and of a madman alike.
Who, being free from worms, could ever feel attachment for this putrid wound of a woman, which resembles a bloated, swollen, and festering belly?
By this distorted wound, smeared with the impurities of sweat and carrying urine and feces,
this entire world is blinded;
by this downward-facing single tooth that discharges semen and mucus.
By this incurable one, who is devoid of fortune, the world has been devoured.
In one who meditates, an attachment to sense objects arises;
from that, desire is born, and from desire, anger is also born.
From anger arises delusion; from delusion, the confusion of memory; from the loss of memory, the destruction of the intellect;
and from the destruction of the intellect, one perishes.

For those who find pleasure in the sovereignty and happiness of peace, the grounds of miserable rebirths are far away; yet for those bound by the noose of desire for enjoyments, there is humiliation at every step.
For one whose mind is contented, there is prosperity everywhere;
for one whose feet are covered by shoes, is not the entire earth indeed covered with leather?
In the mouth of that great one, who is truthful, satisfied, and of perfected mind—
pure like the ocean of milk— the Goddess of Fortune shines resplendent.
Oh, how wondrous! Though the mountains are bound by threads produced from lotuses, all beings have been brought under control by that ignorance which does not even exist.
O Sage Vālmīki,
in this birth so full of afflictions, what indeed could be more painful than this:
that there is no fulfillment of desire, and yet the desire does not cease?
Even after hundreds of years, one who possesses faults will eventually come to an end;
what need is there to mention the cessation of faults for one who takes pride in grasping those virtues?
Desire is never appeased by the enjoyment of desires;
rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with sacrificial oblations.
There is suffering in the acquisition of wealth, and suffering in the protection of what has been acquired;
there is suffering in its loss and suffering in its expenditure—fie on wealth, which brings suffering upon those who possess it!
They delude one in times of prosperity and cause distress in times of adversity;
when will enjoyments, which weary one at the time of their acquisition, ever bring happiness?
Desire for wealth is the abode of unrighteousness and the source of suffering;
the abandonment of attachment is the state of liberation, while the habitual pursuit of enjoyments is the state of misery.
For just as these birds devour one another in the sky,
as wild beasts do on the earth, and as fish do in the water, so too does everyone prey upon the wealthy man.
For those who possess wealth, there is constant fear from kings, water, fire, thieves, and even from their own kinsmen,
just as there is for living beings the constant fear of death.
O high-minded one, do not harbor ill-will toward those who have wronged you;
for they will perish of their own accord, like trees of poor lineage.
Those who are free from malice do not incur enmity even if they were to kill [someone] for as long as they live;
however, he who destroys anger itself has thereby destroyed all his enemies.
By those who lack far-reaching vision, who are cruel and deluded, and whose senses act like arrows,
karma is performed while laughing, but it is experienced while weeping.
If the self itself does not restrain itself from what is harmful,
who else is more capable than it of restraining it?
He who does not seek a cure for the disease of hell while still here,
what will he do when he has gone to that place where no medicine exists?
Even one's own sense faculties, for the sake of achieving their own ends,
act contrary to one's welfare toward friends, acquaintances, and kinsmen, as if they were mere pieces of wood.
This very Lakṣmī,
the beloved of the kings of the earth and fondly cherished on the lap of the elephant,
having aroused desire in the minds of men, brings reproach upon those of exalted soul.
"May you have well-being; may this pleasant experience be remembered now as it was in the past"— thinking thus, she,
like a dream, attained the state of being his beloved.
O Bhārata, in childhood one is absorbed in mother and father; in youth, in the beloved wife;
and thereafter, in their offspring. Thus, the fool is never absorbed in the Self at any time.
Being born, he takes away his wife; growing up, he takes away one's wealth;
dying, he takes away one's life—there is no enemy equal to a son.
"O Śrī Vyāsa Muni, there is an exceedingly great difference between these two:
poison and sense objects.
Poison kills when it is consumed, whereas sense objects kill even by mere remembrance."
In the *Mṛgajātakam*, Candragomin says: "The deer is led by the hunter to the range of his arrows;
for those who are greedy for the horses of sense objects, calamities arise in this world."
Who would consider her who, out of a love for wealth, gives herself to one she dislikes,
to be truly attached, when she has no affection even for herself?
Who indeed could escape from that merchant community by means of merit,
where even the prosperity of the lords of the Guhyakas is frustrated?
These two belong to Kṣemendra.
From whatever [object] one turns away, from that one is liberated;
for by turning away from everything, one does not experience even the slightest suffering.
What fruit has not been obtained by that person in this birth, which is a proximity of faults, wherein youth— with its exceedingly dense and unreflective mind— is spent without reproach?
Even a woman born into a great family, who for the most part is like a garland of honey-flowers,
if her heart is devoid of generosity, will kiss even the face of an elephant.
For victory arises from violence for both [parties], and its fruit is fleeting happiness born of that [victory]. Who would abandon pure Dharma and fame in order to attain such [a result]?
For men, the practice of the Venerable Bhāskara arises from the cause of pleasure, not from the excellence of the object's qualities;
for even when there is an accumulation of flesh, the breasts and buttocks do not lead to passion [in the same way].
Wives cause humiliation, kinsmen are a bondage, and sense-objects are poison.
What is this delusion of people that they regard those who are enemies as friends?
Even the mere sitting together of two people whose minds are bound by equal pleasure causes distress; how much more so, then, sexual desire?
Even dry land quickly burns the feet; how much more so, then, a body that is like glowing embers?
Just as someone severely afflicted by thirst, whose own body is crushed by the clashing of its own dry bones,
finds its own blood produced from that [crushing], so too does one blinded by the senses find pleasure in women.
In the speech of some there is honey, yet in their hearts there is only the *hālāhala* poison; for this very reason, their lower lip is drunk from and their heart is crushed with fists.

That very fact that Kālidāsa and Māgha are the cause of their insignificance because they are supplicants, that the dust of contempt falls upon their heads, and that the arrows of insults graze their minds— that, O dear one,
is what makes mortals truly noble.
Whether standing, sitting, lying down, turned away, well-adorned,
or even unadorned— a woman being gazed upon draws in even a very weak man, even when she is merely depicted in a painting.
Through smiles, glances, modesty, and fear; through sidelong looks with faces turned away;
through words, jealous quarrels, and playful gestures—with all these emotional states, women are indeed a bond.
When poison and sensual objects are compared, poison is better than sensual objects when they are indulged in;
for poison destroys one in a single lifetime when drunk, whereas sensual objects cause torment throughout many future births.
—Candragomin.
O wise ones, desist from the pleasure of union with women, which is fragile as a moment; practice compassion, loving-kindness, wisdom, and association with virtuous people.
Indeed, the circle of a woman’s breasts adorned with necklaces does not exist in hell.
Or else, [one should visualize] the reflection of the river, with its waves as a jeweled girdle.
For anyone,
objects of the senses must inevitably depart after having been enjoyed for a long time;
what difference is there in their departure between those who abandon them themselves and those who do not?
Those who, out of their own free will, depart from the world with minds free from incomparable torment—
having renounced it themselves— indeed bestow infinite, equal happiness.
By Jayāditya:
"When he is thirsty, he drinks cool and fragrant water;
being oppressed by hunger, he devours mouthfuls of meat along with the accompanying greens."
When the fire of passion is ablaze, one embraces a woman with dense attachment;
people perceive the remedy for this affliction as happiness, thus falling into error.
He embraces a dense mass of flesh with the thought that it is a breast;
he drinks from a mouth full of saliva, thinking it to be a cup of wine; and on a path wet with the moisture of filth, he delights in touch as one who relishes its flavor.
For those blinded by great delusion, what in the three worlds could possibly be desirable?
Even well-washed silk, fragrant flowers, and saffron paste—
whatever falls upon it instantly descends into impurity;
it exudes foul-smelling fluids from its nine wound-like openings.
O fortunate one, why do you have such great pride in that body? What is it to those venerable ones?
The wise Nāga is emaciated, blind, lame, deficient in hearing, devoid of a tail, with eyes like those of a crow, aged, and with his hands placed upon a skull-bowl.
Even when it enters a woman whose vulva is moist with secretions, filled with swarms of worms, and overflowing with discharges,
wine surely intoxicates her as well.
In the body of a single woman, there are three deceptive perceptions: for a wandering mendicant it is a corpse; for a lustful man it is a beloved; for a dog it is meat.
Slowly, very slowly, through childhood and through youth consumed by voracious desire,
the life-span of men clearly perishes due to the decline of their vigor.
Now, O lamentation,
whose essence is nothing but a mere wish, our life has passed away in this very manner;
yet even today, the virtuous have not performed even that which is worthy of remembrance.
Our youth has now departed for the forest;
alas, the time of those beautiful women, adorned with shimmering necklaces of large gems, has passed away.
Hail to all forms of happiness! For now, even the very mention of love is like a handful of water poured out.
Alas, those tremulous-eyed women look upon me with pity as if I were far older than my years, seeing how I stumble.

Wealth was not enjoyed by time; we ourselves have enjoyed it. Austerity was not practiced by time; we ourselves have practiced it. Time did not pass away; we ourselves have passed away. Thirst was not worn out by time; we ourselves have been worn out.
For whomsoever the time for the purchase and sale of beauty and amorous play has passed, and whose youthful charms of the first bloom of youth have faded—
for such a person, my heart, casting aside shame, belongs only to a young man, even though my body is variegated with a thousand waves of wrinkles.
The desire for enjoyments has ceased, pride toward men has dissolved,
and friends who were once equal and as dear as life have suddenly departed to heaven;
slowly one rises from one's seat, while the eyes are obstructed by thick darkness.
Oh, how bold is this body, even though it is terrified of death and its perils!
The body is a vessel for suffering; the happiness of friends and children is devoid of stability.

Wealth is a great disease; the taste of the blue lotus (the world) is like the sting of a thorn. Attachment to the home is affliction; even prosperity, though flickering in its activity, is indeed treacherous.
Though Yama was his own master and an enemy, even that was not made into a benefit for him.
The science that subdues the elephants of disputants has not been mastered on this earth;
nor has fame been brought to heaven by those with sharp tusks who split the temples of elephant herds; nor has the nectar of the beloved’s tender bud-like lips been drunk at the rising of the moon.
Compassion has indeed departed due to its fruitlessness, like a lamp in an empty house.
Then Manoratha said:
"When will [he] release me, who am bound within the snare of saṃsāra by the cords of the three guṇas?"
I shall liberate myself by means of the probe of devotion to Śiva.
O Lord, having dedicated my actions of speech, mind, and body to you,
and becoming one with you, may I at some time become free from the pairs of opposites.
O Lord, when indeed shall I be approached by you with the lamp of wisdom, which burns away the coils of latent tendencies toward cyclic existence that are smeared with the oil of impurity?
Alone, free from attachment, peaceful, using my hands as a bowl and the directions as my garment— O Blessed One, when shall I become one who is capable of uprooting the cycle of existence?

With the fickleness of investigating the meaning of well-composed treatises stilled, with curiosity for various worldly arts and poetry ceased, and with the disturbances of conceptual construction and the influx of latent impressions cast away—
The mind of the Wheel-turning King desires to attain [this].
O Kṛṣṇa, when shall I— my body dusted by the pollen from the multitude of bees that are the lotuses of your two feet—
become a bee capable of dispelling the thick darkness of the Lord of the Dead (Yama) by the fanning of my own wings?
Just as I remained with a mind attached to existence while the dense darkness was spreading,
so too may I remain with a mind attached to existence even when that [darkness] has passed and awakening has arisen.

Residing in a cave, delighting in the Dharma, and possessing the renown of a mountain king, may I—through your grace—become like you, O Lord of Existence: one who finds joy in the truth and is undiminished in devotion.
May I always be devoted to giving on auspicious days, skilled in the service of others, intent on the contemplation of the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña), and absorbed in meditative concentration;
may I be dedicated to the praise of the Lord at all times, bowing before my gurus, with a mind detached from all worldly enjoyments.
O heart, why do you enter that which is turbid with afflictions, when you might instead win over the minds of others day by day through manifold acts of kindness?

When you yourself have become serene, having attained the state of one who has mastered the contemplation of what is appropriate, what desired object would that solitary intention not bring to fruition for you?
In your hand, a rosary of rudrākṣa beads strung with a sacred thread is fitting;
on your neck, auspicious ashes;
upon your head, matted locks as tawny as lightning-tips; and on the surface of the tree, your dwelling is the worn bark-garment of your two arms—thus you appear, O tranquil one.
For those who dwell in the higher stages of life, what other discourse could possibly befit their ears?
To him who dwelt on the banks of the Gaṅgā, whose senses were restrained,
whose soul was tranquil, who had abandoned worldly activity, who wore the pure bark of the Tāra tree,
who slept upon a bed of *darbha* grass, and who daily cried out, "Śiva! Śiva!"— to him [I bow].
O Subhūti, when will my mind, purified by the bath of ashes, attain nirvāṇa?
Whether upon a mountain peak or in a grove, on a bed of flowers or before my eyes,
in a jewel or in iron, toward a powerful enemy or a friend,
toward a blade of grass or a woman— my days pass with equal regard for all.
When, in the forest, will I be crying out, "Śiva! Śiva! Śiva! while my merits are exhausted?
As one who has emerged from the desert path into the cool shade of a dense grove,

as one who has reached a well of pure water after a parching drought, as one who has obtained nectar after the ripening of poison, or as one who has regained their natural state after the madness of intense separation.
O Śaṅkara, when shall I obtain devotion to you, whose flavor is incomparable?
O son of Śrī Hārādeva, O lord of speech! He who is motionless with intense bliss, a partaker of merit and skill,
scorched by his stay on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī, is hidden somewhere deep within its roots.
Having taken refuge in the one who is beloved by the daughter of the Lord of Mountains and who possesses every form,
the fortunate one, delighting in his own self, attains the tasting of the nectar of equal bliss.
In the water, fragrant with the mass of foam from the river Surasrotasvatī,
whose currents were made resonant by the stumbling against the masses of mountain rocks—
[therein] those whose misfortunes of worldly existence had been removed by their limbs being joined together [in meditation].
When shall I attain satisfaction through the essence of the bliss derived from serving the feet of Hara?

When, having worshipped with love the Lord Candraśikhara— whose peak is fashioned of magnificent mandāra flowers— my body adorned with profuse horripilation, shall I honor that Sovereign with words of praise whose interior is resonant with the humming of unrestrained bees, exulting in the intoxication of the dense fragrance?
May the two lotus-feet of the one whose head bears the moon— feet that bestow incomparable bliss and dissolve the calamities of heavy suffering— be placed upon our heads.
When will the mass of fuel that is the bondage of worldly existence become like a forest fire through the waves of the celestial river, variegated by the waters of the Yamunā?

These [actors] of Pañjagaddhara are marked by streaks of vermilion, their arms adorned with bracelets of carved conch-shell, their limbs made bulky by knots of pride, and their necks encircled by theatrical ornaments.
What kind of nature do these lords have? What is the use of discussing wicked rulers?
May that very Lord, who is distinct from the three worlds, grant us the fruit of truth.
May these days pass for me— days that are well-established in the removal of obstacles,
days for one who has reached the ninefold jewel-city, and days for one who has been purified by the bath.
Having departed from the dwelling of one's own kin, whether by means of wealth or by force,
one should quickly construct a home upon the earth using clay or leaves,
providing incomparable sustenance for life with fruit or water.
When will this forest region become empty for me, [cleansed] of either dust or wicked people?
On the banks of the Svāh-sindhu,
where the wind blows gently, where the waters are easily accessible,
and where the banks are adorned with Vasāṅku trees— having donned coarse garments there, I have no desire for a body that is difficult to sustain.

O Hara, O Hara, take away from me the disease of the body, separation from loved ones, the onset of a flood of sins, the command of a wicked master, the practice of begging for alms, association with the wicked, and the consumption of wretched food.

Out of a desire for the enjoyments of Raurava, out of a lack of detachment, out of a wish to seize false impurities, out of a longing for the excellence of the Brahmāṇḍa, and with the intent to cross the great ocean of worldly existence— [this is the prayer].

May my alms-bowl be a water-pot, my home the foot of a mountain, my enclosure the bark of trees, and my garment the skin; may I always be a performer of the drama of sovereignty at the banks of the Gaṅgā, and may I be one who is worthy of service.
Now,
let the dwelling place for various mixed objects be made in the waters of the Gaṅgā, which purify sin;
or rather, in the pair of breasts of the deer-eyed woman, which are captivating and enchanting.
Scholarship and kingship are never equal;
a king is honored in his own country, but a scholar is honored everywhere.
"Obstacles arise even for the great when they pursue what is excellent;
but when one encounters what is not excellent, the impediments vanish somewhere or other."

For some, the Vedas have the *agnihotra* sacrifice as their fruit; sacred learning has the fruit of virtuous conduct and livelihood; wives have the fruits of pleasure and progeny; and wealth has the fruits of giving and enjoyment.
Whose body, even though it is afflicted by manifold faults and diseases, is not dear?
He who remains dear even while committing deceptions is indeed truly dear.
The house of a poor man is poison; a young wife for an old man is poison.
Unlearned knowledge is indeed poison, and undigested food is poison.
Speech has poetry as its ornament; the night has the moon as its ornament;
a woman has virtuous conduct as her ornament; and Fortune has discipline as her ornament.
The man who eats what is produced by the power of knowledge eats well here;
indeed, even while sleeping, he enjoys the fruit from the mere movement of his own fingers.
As it grows, it brings unhappiness to the three vehicles of man—
his friends acquired in the past, his wife, and his home.
All the virtues of those with little merit dissolve away within their bodies,
like the breasts of noble women consumed by the grief of youthful widowhood.
Having arisen, they dissolve into the heart like the desires of the poor,
or like the breasts of noble women consumed by the early loss of their husbands.

Those who do not study the sciences in their childhood, and who remain poor and wifeless when they reach youth—they are to be pitied in this world of living beings; they wander in human form as mere beasts.
The reasoning of some is unstable: "The scriptural traditions are diverse; there is no sage whose word is not authoritative.
The root of Dharma is hidden in a cave; that is the path by which the great multitude has gone."
It has been stated by Diṅnāga that "a single fault indeed sinks away when submerged in a collection of virtues"— this is an improper statement.
Does not a single instance of folly destroy all virtues, such as beauty and the like, in those who possess a body?
It has been said that "a single fault sinks [the whole] when it falls amidst a multitude of virtues," but this is an improper statement;
for surely even that poet did not perceive that poverty alone is the destroyer of a multitude of virtues.
Better is a poor man who recites the Vedas and the scriptures, even if he lacks wealth and is devoid of learning and good character;
for one with beautiful eyes, though his garments be worn out, shines, whereas one deprived of eyes does not shine, even if adorned with gold and other ornaments.
For those afflicted by the loss of wealth, there is neither friend nor kinsman; for those afflicted by lust, there is neither fear nor shame;
for those afflicted by ignorance, there is neither happiness nor sleep; and for those afflicted by hunger, there is neither body nor luster.
There is no bodily sensation equal to hunger; there is no bodily suffering equal to anxiety.
There is no bodily ornament equal to knowledge; there is no bodily nourishment equal to livelihood.
The beloved form, when analyzed by a mind agitated by the fierce force of passion, appears as something entirely distinct;
likewise, when analyzed part by part by one possessed of dispassion, that same beloved form appears as something else entirely.
For one whose intellect is empty of discerning between the harmful and the beneficial, who is excluded from the many scriptures and traditional precepts,
and who desires nothing more than the mere filling of his belly— what difference is there between such a man and a beast?
Like a mother she protects; like a father she enjoins one to one's welfare; and like a beloved wife she brings delight by removing suffering.
She spreads one's fame in all directions and extends one's fortune; what is there that knowledge does not accomplish, like a wish-fulfilling creeper?
The supramundane conduct bestows a firm foundation upon men; for birth in a noble family is not the cause of magnanimity.
The drinking of the ocean by the Sage who was wind, fire, and heat was merely a plaything, whereas the drinking of the unsealed ocean is his true sport.
You descend into the netherworld, you traverse the sky,
and you wander through the circle of the quarters with the fickleness of your mind;
yet even after wandering to other lands, you remain centered within yourself.
You do not touch upon Brahmā, nor do you reach Nirvāṇa, by means of which [you would attain them].
When women compare the lotus, the moon, and the blue water-lily to his limbs— which are yet more fragrant and beautiful than those [celestial objects]—
then the poets incur this terrible and inexorable fruit: that they enter into the womb within those very [limbs].
Some indeed serve a person of disciplined character out of fear; others, people who exert themselves out of greed for wealth, do so as well.
Some, moreover, do so out of a desire for fame in the assembly of virtuous men. Yet, in this world, there is no one at all who is truly virtuous.
Candragomin says:
"Almost all these people are disciplined by hypocrisy, greed, fear, or shame;
O best of men, I consider a heart disciplined through dispassion to be truly rare."
Fortune has been attained by the venerable Śrīdatta; what more than that? He is a vessel for all desires. What more than that?
His foot has been placed upon the heads of his enemies. What more than that?
What is the use of satisfying those who are dear with worldly riches?
What is the use of bodies for embodied beings if they remain for only a single eon?
Therefore, if you possess discernment and always desire that supreme, infinite, undecaying, and ever-expanding Brahman,
to which these things— lordship over the worlds, enjoyments, and the like— are but miserable attachments in the eyes of the wise.
O Lord of the Earth, what is the use here of these many arguments and empty prattlings? She alone is to be served by men at all times.
Is it the youth of beautiful women, languid with fresh decorative lines and weighed down by the burden of their breasts, or is it the forest?
In this world, what is it that people practice day after day which brings ever-new delight to their hearts? [The answer is: the study of the *Subhāṣita*. 3454–1, 3454–2. Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa.
But it is known to me that this is the delight of the company of the virtuous,
or perhaps the delight of young women, or even the *Bhārata*—
to whom does it belong?
I do not perceive any wholesome conduct arising within saṃsāra; as I reflect upon it,
the ripening of merits produces fear in me,
for sense objects have long been seized by great floods of merit.
Great men are born to bestow, as it were, calamity upon those addicted to sensual pleasures.
When I was a man of little knowledge, like an elephant blinded by rut,
my mind became arrogant, thinking, "I am omniscient.
But when I understood even a little, little from the presence of the wise...
Then, like a fever, my intoxication vanished with the thought, "I am a fool."
The husband’s crest-jewel,
the victorious elephant in rut slain by a weapon,
and the autumnal riverbank with its sandy shores— these are the objects of her gaze.
A crescent moon on a darkened vessel, a young woman exhausted by lovemaking, and men whose wealth has vanished yet who remain generous toward supplicants— all these shine with beauty.
A day is a desert; a passionate woman whose youth has faded is like a lake devoid of lotuses; a beautiful form is without eyes;
a lord is devoted to wealth; and a virtuous person is perpetually destitute.
O venerable elder, this wicked man who has gone beyond the range of my sight carries away the seven arrows from my mind;
he does not come within the scope of my vision, yet he nourishes something [within me] with his entire being.
For those who bestow upon seekers the supreme, stainless prosperity that they receive,
their wealth known as knowledge does not perish even at the end of an aeon; O kings, abandon pride toward them— for who can rival them?
The fruit of learning is tranquility; therefore, for those who desire wealth,
the effort of the wise in this regard is in vain— what is there to wonder at?
Those who seek a result cannot otherwise initiate an undertaking that has a fixed fruit;
for indeed, a seed of rice never becomes a sprout of barley.

Those wicked men who are proud of their wealth, while the virtuous are devoid of it— in this matter, Fortune (Śrī) should certainly not be censured by those eloquent in speech; for who in this world would count the foolish as even worth a blade of grass once they have fallen from wealth?
But who would not honor those who are wise and naturally beautiful?
Standing in their midst, the hero—equal even to the Teacher of the Gods—is noble toward the ignorant;
though he has attained liberation, he falls into the throng of wretched people. Having gained no victory, this hero dwells together with those whose minds are distressed by fear.
Alas, how miserable he lives, his mind alienated from knowing their conduct!
Whatever purpose there may be for a person here through some pretext, that is indeed a sin;
and those scriptures which have been handed down that do not lead to the destruction of passion— that is mere labor.
That which is done together with a wicked person out of a hatred in the heart is bondage; that prosperity which does not bring joy to one's affectionate kinsmen and friends is calamity.
Whatever wealth there is, and whatever virtues there are—these two are difficult to encounter;
yet, O mind, since you desire union with that One alone, I am your companion in this.
Therefore, why do you indulge in this cruel lamentation, which is like the pain of sleeplessness?
Or what else could it be but a lack of respect? ...

[It consists of] the analysis of the meaning of excellent poetry, pleasant conversation, staying in private, and the expression of the emergence of grief for a dear friend through a soft song within one's throat.
Lamentation arose from their awakening, and sleep came to those whose souls were moist with passion;
these are the grounds for consolation for one whose heart and mind have been stolen away.
If there is a delightful mansion for a noble wife, wealth for renunciation and enjoyment,
speech in the mouth that is sweet with nectar, and the movement of the mind toward Keśava—
if all this exists, O mind, enjoy the happiness of worldly existence; do not think of anything else.
Fie, fie upon this state of existence, which is characterized by grasping and attachment, and where heaven itself is nothing but absolute suffering!

If there truly exists the song, so full of essence and sweetness, at the front; the sounds of singing from the sides; and behind, the tinkling of playful bracelets from those who hold the fly-whisks—then indulge in the taste of worldly existence with abandon.
If you do not wish this, enter suddenly into the non-conceptual samādhi.
Generally in this world, those of noble lineage find themselves without kin; the unfortunate find themselves beloved by women; the generous find themselves objects of pity;

the upright find themselves surrounded by the crooked; the spirited find themselves cowards; those marred by deformity find themselves with beautiful bodies; and those established in virtuous conduct find themselves poorly situated.
And fools always revile the person who investigates various philosophical systems.
By whom can destiny be transgressed? Where do calamities not cast their foot?
Who has not become a target for desire? Whose prosperity is stable?
Yet, there is one virtuous person capable of winning over all people.
Where is the woman who seeks her own goal and is highly esteemed by men; and where is charity given in vain?
What man on earth has not become arrogant after attaining wealth? Whose misfortunes have not come to an end?
Alas, whose mind has not been shattered by women? Who indeed is dear to kings?
Who is not within the reach of Time (Death)? And what petitioner has ever attained dignity through wealth?
Or who, having fallen into the snare of wicked people, has gone home with his body unharmed?
Those men who are not even capable of properly enduring the threat of a single raised finger from their teacher—
those whose minds are puffed up with pride— behold the entire world as something beneath them.
Afflicted by passion, which destroys their fortitude,
those wretched men carry out the commands of women upon their heads like a garland of withered flowers.
For some,
there are no vegetables in the mountain caves and river thickets, nor roots;
indeed, this very life is ordained for them, and nothing else exists anywhere.
Then, standing before the kings whose minds were deluded by the intoxication of pride, he spoke these words: "Give! with his eyes distressed by the gasping for breath.
"You are a king; we too are puffed up with pride in our wisdom, having served our gurus. You are renowned for your riches; poets spread our blessings in all directions.
Thus, O giver of honor, there is not much difference between us two."
If you are turned away from us, we too are absolutely devoid of any attachment.
You are the Lord of meanings, and we too are masters of speech for as long as we desire. You are a hero in the task of subduing the pride of disputants;
those blinded by wealth serve you, while those desiring to hear me seek me out to destroy the impurities of their intellect.
If you have no faith even in me, then it is all the more so for me that I have entered into this king.
We here are content with bark garments, while you are possessed of splendor;
yet in this world, our contentment is equal, being indistinguishable from your excellence.
But he alone is truly poor whose thirst is vast.
But when the mind is fully satisfied, what need is there for wealth? Who would be poor?
Out of servitude and wretchedness, he never bows his head in supplication;
he does not speak the humble words before those intoxicated by wealth, saying, "O Master, give the command";
nor does he pass through the midst of wicked men, who are like venomous serpents emitting the fire of malice.
One who perceives all things leads others to a fruitful cycle of births with ease.

For those kings, there was unimpeded command; for the sages, whose mental fluctuations were governed by restraints and observances, there was devotion to their master; and for those endowed with excellent wealth, there was attachment to renunciation and enjoyment.

The purity of conduct of women, the sweetness of speech in the compositions of great poets, and the unwavering adherence to the path of righteousness and justice like a sage— these are the ornaments of the learned.
Sukhavarmā:

"Terrified by widowhood, she would abandon even a hero, and likewise a wise man produced through her learning; and as a virtuous wife, she would cast away her open-handedness, saying, 'May no other person ever touch me.'"
If Fortune resorts to a man who is impotent, foolish, or miserly...
[she quickly abandons him].

The unwavering bliss of liberation from hope and fear, the stability of the mind under its own control, the cessation of affection, hatred, malice, and greed, and a mind that is perfectly tranquil and contented; constant reflection on impermanence, and detachment even amidst attachments— this is the state of the wise.
For those whose minds are purified by the sprinkling of self-awareness and discernment, this is the sequence of liberation.
Logic, bound by its harshness, causes extreme shame; for it is indeed the throat of literary composition.
Furthermore, the path of the Smṛtis is endless and exceedingly difficult to traverse. Even the river of the Mīmāṃsakas is terrifying. Why do you wander and suffer in vain?
O mind, if you possess consciousness, you should take refuge in this vessel that produces the nectar of immortality.
The multitude of names belonging to someone has been offered there along with all one's own power;
the time for recollection is fixed.
O Blessed One, such is your compassion; nevertheless, such ill fortune has arisen here that there is no attachment [to it].

O Lord, when you are the object of one's devotion, there is no obstruction, nor is there an inopportune moment; there is no lack of access in the heart, nor any contempt, nor fear of base people in the act of supplication; there is neither wretchedness nor failure.
Nevertheless, we shall employ many further means and even extend our service to others.
When her two friends had gone somewhere, the lotus grove remained with its mouths closed;
seeing the female crane standing before her beloved, who was close at hand, while the bees were crying out, [the lotus grove] stood there.
The lotus stalk was neither tasted nor discarded by the lover named Cakrāhva;
it was merely placed upon his throat like a bolt against his departing life.
With his own hand, having kindled a fire of wood-faggots for the burning of his grief,
he cast the Brahmin couple [into it]; he who daily attended upon Varuṇī,
and who brought from the lotus-pond the teacher’s heavy golden necklace that had been taken away.
O friend, is not association with a Kāpālika a fault that produces only defects?
Abstention from food, total withdrawal from the entire range of sense objects,
the eyes not directed toward the tip of the nose— this is one thing; and the mind being single-pointed, this silence, and that the entire universe appears empty to you— this is another.
Therefore, O friend, tell me: are you a yoginī, or are you a woman separated from her beloved?
Now begins the *Śrībhagavatsvarūpavarṇanapaddhati*:
What is the use of gifts for him, what is the use of sacred pilgrimage sites, what is the use of austerities, or what is the use of sacrifices,
for him in whose heart dwells the Blessed Lord Hari, the abode of auspiciousness?
This mantra is for Śiva; this speech is the sovereign Vaśavartinī. Oh, the greatness of delusion, by which one perceives hell!
For anyone, that alone is meditation wherein Govinda is present; that alone is discourse wherein Keśava is present; that alone is action which is for His sake—what is the use of much other talk?
That is the true tongue which praises Hari; that is the true mind which is free from pride. Only those two hands are truly praiseworthy which perform His worship.
A day spent bathing in the waters of the Gaṅgā, listening to the noble discourse of the Mahābhārata,
and worshipping the lotus feet of Acyuta, is superior to a hundred eons.
If a compassionate person, seeking the welfare of others,
endures those very sufferings for the sake of that welfare, he shall not undergo birth again, provided he seeks the Dharma.
Whether bathed or unbathed,
whether pure or impure, whoever remembers the lotus-eyed one is pure both externally and internally.
Hari alone is the Great Physician; his majesty is increased by the supreme medicine. By the application of the great medicinal herb of dispassion (*vairāgya*), he pacifies the disease of birth.
To the Vidyādhara,
the Protector is indeed the supreme physician in times of illness, the lamp of light in the midst of darkness, the bridge across difficult terrains,
the protection in times of fear, the kinsman in times of calamity, and the raft in the bottomless waters of misfortune.
In this world, where the power of the virtuous has remained but briefly and is no longer appropriate, there arose a brilliant splendor at the end of the Kali age for the illustrious Vikramāditya.
If this assembly for drinking the nectar of the discourse on the recollection of Nārāyaṇa—
which provides such delight to the mind— were not to exist, [what else could there be]?
If the mind of men delights in young women,
and if it likewise should delight in the bearer of the excellent wheel (the Buddha),
then who would [not cross] the force of the great waves of suffering in the ocean of existence?
Having transcended that supreme abode, the Puruṣa does not go further.
If the world were like the passion men feel for another's wife, or like their passion for seizing another's wealth—
O Lord of the World— if it were so, why would the state of liberation remain far away?
For those who have entered the ocean of existence, struck by the winds of dualities, burdened by the weight of sons, daughters, wives,
and kin, and sinking without a raft into the turbulent waters of sense objects;
It is said: "The boat of the Viṣṇu [teaching] is the sole refuge for men."
I constantly remember the young Mukunda, reclining within the fold of an *aśvattha* leaf, as he places his lotus-hand upon his lotus-foot at his lotus-mouth.
The two feet of someone— tender as lotus filaments, thrilled by the succession of offerings, supremely delicate, meritorious,
and a staff for the destruction of the sins of the fallen— have attained renown upon the earth.
Before long, my feet shall be worn away by the trampling of the multitude of mountain-dwellers;
may the wise worshiper of the Lord of Beasts behold them here before him with affection.
O Lord, let these piteous words of Pañcaka, who has not yet attained entry within [the city] and is crying out for deliverance from without,
be heard with compassion.
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, you who have been worshipped by the gods, be merciful; be the refuge for those who have no refuge.
O Supreme Person, be gracious to us who are submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra.
I am afflicted, O Lord; there is no one like me, and no one other than you is more devoted to compassion.
Our spiritual connection is indeed equal; why then, O Protector, do you not look upon me?
Death runs toward me with a raised mallet;
O compassionate one with lotus-like eyes, protect me who has come for refuge! If I am not a great sinner, Gaṅgādatta, and if I am not overwhelmed by fear—
If there is no attachment to the sense faculties, then what is the purpose of my wandering?
O Bhadra Sunandana, wherever I may be born— even in a family distressed by suffering— may my wealth there always be the propitiation of Mādhava.
O Hari,
whether I am walking or standing, waking or even sleeping,
may my mind never at any time be separated from you.
O Lord of the Heart, in whatever womb I may enter as directed by my own past actions,
may my devotion to You remain firm in each and every one of them.
If you say, "I have not served you for long," that is not the case, for you do not protect me; that cannot be so.
Does ambrosia, once drunk, fail to make one ageless and immortal immediately?
O Lord of Malaya, protect, protect me, O Blessed One, who am terrified by worldly existence and oppressed by unbearable sense objects!
O Protector, O Protector, Supreme Lord Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa— you are indeed my supreme refuge.

O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Supreme Lord Viṣṇu, protect me, protect me! Protect me, a miserable and deluded being, who am being tormented in the midst of the mire of worldly existence by desire, greed, pride, envy, and anger.
O Supreme Lord,
as long as this body of mine,
afflicted by disease, does not perish, show me the auspicious path toward the highest good, by which there shall be no further birth upon this earth.
O Janārdana, if my devotion to you, the Sun, should be unwavering and not fruitless,
may I turn away from liberation— which is directed toward the cessation of desire— and once again take up a physical body in this world.
O Enemy of Mura, you have not been meditated upon by me; you have not been celebrated, nor have you been praised, nor has any account of you ever been composed.
Furthermore, you have not been worshipped by me even with blades of grass out of devotion. Even so, show compassion to me, who has come to you for refuge.
Bhāṣya: "O Lord, as long as this body of mine— which is the abode of all calamities, unstable, lacking independence,
prone to imminent fall, devoid of discernment, and a mere semblance of essence— does not perish, employ me in virtuous deeds."
O Lord, I am one who has fallen away from asceticism, blinded and robbed of the great wealth of discernment by the powerful thieves known as the senses;
having been cast into the deep pit of the well of delusion, O Lord of Gods, grant the support of Your hand to this wretched man.
O Rājanaka Kamalākara,
in every birth, on every path, and in every temple,
may I be your praiser— intent upon you, devoted primarily to you, and seeking only you.
O Lord of the Earth, let there not be even a moment of delay, like a season whose fruit has vanished,
in which the daughter of Bharata, though slow by nature, might become attached to another with your approval.

For one whose seed is the conceit of "I," whose root is the grasping of "mine," whose constant memory is the sprout, whose leaves are children, friends, and kinsmen, whose trunk is the acquisition of a wife, whose flower is humiliation, and whose fruit is an evil rebirth—
By that [mind] of mine, which is intent upon the service of mindfulness of you, may the creeper of craving be severed.
Victory to both of you, O Kṛṣṇa and Mahābāhu, who are the time for the destruction of the heat of the misery of saṃsāra,
and who are like a rain-cloud with the stream of the Nandaka sword, quenching the forest fire of the pride of the asuras.
O Lord,
even though our difference has vanished, I am not yours, nor are you mine;
for a wave is indeed part of the ocean, yet the ocean is not the wave.
I, Śaṅkarācārya, pray to this crest-jewel of the Śaśikīśa lineage, an ocean of the nectar of compassion:
may my body, in birth after birth, become a means for the worship of you.
Blinded by ignorance, without a kinsman, devoured by demons called the senses,
and cast into the deep pit of the great darkness of delusion by wicked inner enemies—
he who cries out, having come for refuge, deprived of fortitude, and the abode of all calamities.
O Maheśa, do not, do not abandon me; with your compassionate glance, grant us relief from our terror.
I am indeed ignorant and dull-witted, and thus I am unable to compose charming four-line verses by which I might become a worthy object of your compassion.
However,
let this cry of a miserable and helpless person in distress reach your ears.
Having done so, come quickly and place your foot upon my head, for I am most fortunate.
Thinking "this is the destruction of my evil," you ought not to abandon me; for what need is there for protection for one of settled mind who is free from fear on all sides?
Since I am wicked, base, and a doer of unmeritorious deeds, I am therefore all the more worthy of your compassion.
For Jagaddhara, chanting is all speech; every craft is the fashioning of mudrās;
movement is the practice of circumambulation; and the offering of oblations is the act of subduing the senses.
May all this activity of mine— my prostrations, my taking refuge,
and my offering of myself— be an act of worship unto you.

The venerable Śaṅkarācārya performed neither acts of charity nor ascetic penance, nor did he practice meditative absorption (samādhi), which is difficult to achieve even by traveling to sacred pilgrimage sites in every direction.
Therefore, for me who has not yet attained merit and knowledge, what other course is there in the hereafter except for your remembrance?
"I have fallen into a certain state; I am one who seeks refuge, I am in every condition, and I am so at all times.
O Blessed One, I have come to you for refuge; protect me, who have sought your protection."
